en: Preface to *The Direct Pointing at the Source*:

The World-Honored One appeared in this world for the sake of the one great causal matter, to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that they might awaken to and enter the Great Way of true permanence.
That people of the world fail to comprehend this principle and instead reject what they deem heterodox is just like...
That an unfilial son turns his resentment toward his parents is truly a matter of deep pity!

I have long resided beneath the forest trees, yet because my "Dharma-eye" (do-kan) is not clear, it is as the saying goes: "There are none who do not eat and drink, but few are able to know their flavor.
Alas! A Confucian who can embody the Buddha may be called a true Confucian. Have you not seen what the State Chancellor Zhang Shangying said? He declared: "I study the Buddha."
"That one can later understand Confucianism is precisely what this refers to. Master Yuanben of Yanqing Monastery studied Confucianism in his youth and later followed the Buddhist path;
having attained profound realization of the nature of the Dharma, he specialized in the Pure Land practice. He was truly a man of wisdom among the common crowd.
Driven by a sincere desire to benefit others, he compiled this book and came one day to my mountain retreat specifically requesting a preface. I encouraged him [to write it].
Those who study the Way, having already gained faith and entry, must practice with vigor; they must not be hindered by the teachings or allow their minds to become deluded.

To take the finger for the moon is entirely a matter of shattering the subtle dust to let forth the great thousand-fold sutra-scrolls, universally saving all sentient beings so that we may together achieve perfect enlightenment—how could this depend on merely one or two scrolls?
*Ei!* If you truly reach such a state, even my words shall become superfluous.
A Dreaming Speech to You.
Preface by the Layman of Deer Park, Wan Biao, on the Buddha’s Birthday in the second month of the fourth year of the Longqing era.

*The Jewel Mirror of the Lotus School* states: "The Land of Bliss of the Mind alone pervades the ten directions; the Amitābha of one's own nature is perfectly interfused."
A single wisdom wondrously responds to the realms of form and sound, its radiance flowing between the mind and the eyes;

therein, one turns back from delusion to return to the truth, immediately turning away from the dust of the world to unite with awakening. Formerly, my Dharma-treasury (Dharmakara) gave rise to great vows, opening the profound path to Ultimate Bliss;
thus the World-Honored Buddha pointed toward the West to reveal the wondrous domain for Vaidehi. This is the broad and long tongue that covers [all worlds].

While all other sutras have been praised and subsequently exhausted, this one alone remains, for it increases the joyful mind of benefiting sentient beings and expands the capacity of compassionate transformation.
The Great Teaching is divided into nine grades, thereby separately opening the gate of expedient means;

it clarifies the true path of the One Mind as the direct route for returning to the source. The meeting of the holy and the ordinary is like a long-traveling guest returning to their hometown—a feeling of profound resonance.

The Way should be understood as being like a young child casting itself into the arms of a compassionate mother; though one may be dimly aware of this ultimate principle, by touching upon its various manifestations, all become objects of faith.

When encountering such perfect discourse, there is nothing to which one does not penetrate. How much more so when the light of compassion embraces one through vows and the power of the Buddha is inconceivable?

It is like riding a boat downstream—no personal effort is required—or pushing a door that falls into a mortar: how could it be otherwise? Where there is a vow, there is surely a welcome; where there is no capacity, none shall be reached.
The boat-stone can ferry one across and the fires of hell are instantly extinguished. For those Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas born there, they are immeasurable and innumerable;

the sages of past and present who have attained the Way may be examined and sought out. Even the śārikā and kalaviṅka birds still sing forth the sounds of the Dharma, and all that crawls and wriggles receives the grace of transformation.
How could this sacred realm be false? How could the Buddha’s words be deceptive? Why is it that...?
They drown in the waves of the river of craving without anxiety, and they burn within the flames of the house on fire without fear.
They weave a dense web of delusion that the blade of shallow wisdom cannot cut; they plant deep roots of doubt that the power of superficial faith can never uproot.
Thus, they willingly submit their hearts, seeking fortune through calamity and delighting in disaster. They revile the land of purity while remaining greedily attached to afflictions.
In this world, moths burn their wings and silkworms scorch their cocoons, remaining under the lingering calamity of their own deeds; caged birds and fish in boiling cauldrons yet claim to find joy.

All this arises because the power of wholesome roots is slight while the force of karma is overwhelming, and the faculty of faith is meager while the roots of transgression are many. Thus, the three realms are vast and desolate, and the four modes of birth are in turmoil;
all greedily cling to life in a state of frantic delusion—who understands the path home? All are pursued by their karma, drifting aimlessly on.

Seeking no means of escape, the kalpas of past birth-and-death are as inexhaustible as the rubbing of the劫石 (kalpa-stone), and the cycles of future transmigration are as endless as the mustard-seed city.
Were it not for the good fortune of past lives, how could one encounter such a cause? Now that the drum has been struck to open the gates of the prison, you should emerge with haste;
having met this boat to rescue those drowning in the abyss, how can you hesitate? Respectfully obey the golden script and follow it well.
Those who have not heard or understood the Buddha’s teachings are truly pitiable and lamentable;

how much more so in this world of five turbidities, where the fires burn from all four directions, and only the Buddha alone possesses the power to provide rescue and aid. Having now heard the wondrous Dharma, one should plant pure conditions:

with a single thought of sincere faith, sow the seeds of myriad virtues. Strive to emulate the ancient sages, aspire to awaken to the True and Constant, and may all universally practice in accordance with what has been taught.
Prostrating with all one's heart and receiving it with faith, he asked: "Since you have spoken of 'faith,' I do not yet know what dharma-gate this faith pertains to. He replied:
"Faith is to believe that, as taught by the Buddha in the sutras, mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) will certainly lead to rebirth in the Pure Land;

that mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly extinguish all transgressions; that mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly secure the protection of the Buddhas; that mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly secure the certification of the Buddhas; and that at the time of death, mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly be attained."
The Buddha comes to welcome those who believe in reciting the Buddha’s name; they will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Those who believe in being born in the Pure Land through recitation will certainly not fall into the three evil realms. Therefore, it is urged that one believe in reciting the Buddha’s name.

If one receives this Dharma and maintains this mindfulness, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. For this reason, the Buddhas of the three periods, the great Bodhisattvas, and the patriarchs of successive generations have practiced [this].

For those who possess all meritorious practices and the power of great vows, entering the realm of the Buddhas and accomplishing Bodhi has never occurred without entering through this very word, "faith.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit;
faith can nurture all roots of goodness; faith can transcend the paths of all Māras; faith can enable entry into samādhi; faith can..."
To cross the sea of birth and death, one must rely on faith to achieve the Bodhi of the Buddhas. Alas!

In these times, those who observe the precepts during the fast believe in the observance of the rules but not in the recitation of the Buddha’s name; those who revere the Buddha believe in him but not in rebirth in the Pure Land.
All such people lose their own great benefit. Thus, Vimalakīrti said: "Deep and firm faith is like a diamond; if one wishes to reach the Western Land..."
One must rely on profound faith; behold how the Buddhas of the *saṃsāra* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were all people of right faith in their own time.

**Chapter Two: Honoring the Three Jewels and Their Teachings** Above the heavens and below the heavens, the Three Jewels are most honored; throughout the mundane and supramundane worlds, the Three Jewels are supreme. What are the Three Jewels called?

The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—the Three Jewels—comprise three types: first, the Three Jewels of Identical Essence (*sābhinnasvabhāva*), which means that the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is, by its own nature, awakened, and is thus named the Buddha Jewel;
its virtuous functions and norms are, by their own nature, authentic and true, and are thus named the Dharma Jewel;
and its movement is without conflict or contention, being pure by its own nature, and is thus named the Sangha Jewel. Second, the Transcendent Three Jewels (*lokottara-triratna*), which means...

The manifestation of the Dharma, Reward, and Transformation bodies according to the capacities of beings constitutes the Buddha Jewel. The exposition of the meaning of the Six Perfections and the principles of the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination constitute the Dharma Jewel.
The Ten Sages, the Three Grades of Worthies, the Five Fruits, and the Four Stages of Approaching Realization constitute the Sangha Jewel. Thirdly, there are the Worldly Sustaining Three Jewels:
clay stupas, niches, and modeled images are called the Buddha Jewel; the yellow scrolls and red axes [of scripture] are called the Dharma Jewel.

Those who shave their heads and dye their robes are called the Sangha Jewel; those who take refuge in them have their sins extinguished as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and those who look up to them with reverence increase their merit immeasurably.

Now, there are the perverse and ignorant who, failing to understand this, falsely compose the *Zhenzong Miaoyi Jing* (Sutra on the Sublime Meaning of the True Source), falsely claiming that the essence is the Buddha Jewel, the breath is the Dharma Jewel, and the spirit is the Sangha Jewel. This causes those entering the gate of goodness to believe in such heterodox teachings.
To lack reverence for the Triple Gem is truly pitiable. If one does not revere the worldly Triple Gem, how can one obtain the supramundane Triple Gem that is of the same essence?

To deceive oneself is still forgivable, but to deceive others as well may be called blocking the true path between humans and devas, blinding the eyes of humans and devas, destroying the authentic teaching of cause and effect, and diluting the purity of meditative concentration and wisdom.

There is no wind more violent than this. The Buddha said that if all sentient beings do not take refuge in the Triple Gem, they will fall into the three evil realms for eternal kalpas and fail to encounter the ancient teachings.
As the scriptures of the Buddhas of the ten directions state in the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*:
"The merit of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Saṃgha is inconceivable. Those who take refuge in the Buddha shall not fall into hell; those who take refuge in the Dharma [shall likewise not fall]."
Those who do not fall into the realm of hungry ghosts take refuge in the Saṃgha; those who do not fall into the realm of animals likewise take refuge in the Saṃgha. Why is this?

The Buddha is the unsurpassed King of Physicians, the Dharma is the excellent medicine that removes illness, and the Saṃgha is the guide and spiritual friend for humanity; together they constitute the field of merit that is truly pure.

To turn one's back on them is to follow the path of evil; to turn toward them is to follow the path of correctness. Upon seeing any image of the Buddha, one should conceive the thought that it is the Tathāgata. Upon seeing even a single...

One should conceive the thought that all the holy teachings are difficult to encounter; regarding all bhikṣus, one should give rise to the thought that they are patriarchal masters, paying them homage and making offerings, never treating them with contempt or deceit.
Adorned by the adornments of the Buddha, one thus possesses the Three Jewels as a single essence within one's own mind.
O virtuous ones, if you wish to attain the Way, you must rely on the words of the Buddha; if you were to attain it by contravening them, [it would not be so].

"It is impossible," some might say. "When Bodhidharma came from the West, he did not establish reliance on words and letters; he pointed directly at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Why then is it necessary to study the scriptures and teachings to awaken to the Way? The answer is:

"The teaching of the Great Patriarch Bodhidharma was truly an excellent medicine for a specific ailment. People today do not understand the fundamental intent of the Patriarchs; instead, they take the medicine itself as their illness."
The Patriarch intended for people to awaken to the mind in accordance with the teachings;

thus he spoke these words out of fear that students would become mired in the literal text without investigating the fundamental Buddha, or that they would be hindered by the finger and lose sight of the moon. The Sixth Patriarch said:
"Dharma’s statement that 'it is directly pointed out' is already a detour. Why? To know that even the two characters 'non-establishment' (of words) are themselves words."
How can it be said that there are no words? If one truly does not establish words, then a person likewise ought not to speak;

yet this very speaking is itself the characteristic of words—how then can it be said that they are not established? When fools hear it said that words are not established, they immediately cling to emptiness in a one-sided manner.
By merely saying "words are not established," they instead slander the Buddhist scriptures, thereby creating karmic obstacles.

How grave and profound this is—how can one not be cautious? Have you not seen the verse from the *Dharmatrāṇa-dharmaparamparā* that says: "I have come to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings;
when the single flower opens into five petals, the fruit will naturally be formed"? The Patriarch further said:
"I have the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which I also entrust to you. This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended for all sentient beings."

If [the Buddha] reveals, shows, awakens, and causes others to enter in this manner, how could Dharma have been without words and letters for people? A former master said: "One who reads the sutras clarifies the principle of the Buddha.
This means that one relies on the teachings to clarify the fundamental essence (*zong*); when the mind and the teaching merge, one seals mind with mind, without duality or distinction.
Thus, one should know that to reach the True Vehicle, one must personally consult the scriptural texts; only by receiving the teachings can one achieve clarity.
Only after clarifying the principle can one practice; when practice and vows are without deficiency, the fruits of the Way may be realized.

Since studying the teachings offers such benefits, how can one treat the Dharma-teachings with contempt? As the *Cautionary Verses of Mount Wei* states: "If one does not apply oneself to the teachings and principles, there will be no cause for realizing the profound Way.
By the time one has reached an advanced age and long standing in the community, one may find oneself empty-minded and arrogant, refusing to associate closely with those who are truly virtuous."

I have reflected that my arrogance has led to a state of rustic indifference; when confronted by matters, I am like one facing a wall. When junior students come to inquire, I offer no words of guidance.
Even when I do speak, it does not touch upon the classical teachings. If they speak lightly, I instead rebuke them for their lack of propriety.
As soon as I am noticed, I declare, "I am a mountain monk," and with such pride and conceit, I oppress the younger generation. Thus, I have caused...
Once born, if one regrets it too late, there is no way to turn back; transmigrating through the cycle of rebirth, when will there be rest? Alas!

If there are those of middling capacity who cannot yet transcend suddenly, they must apply their minds to the teachings, diligently study the palm-leaf manuscripts, thoroughly investigate the principles, and propagate them by chanting and expounding so as to guide future generations and repay the Buddha’s kindness;
in this way, time will not be spent in vain, and one must certainly [strive].
To support and maintain one's dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) in this way is to be a vessel of the Dharma within the Sangha.
Have you not seen how the climbing vine that relies upon a pine tree soars to a height of a thousand fathoms? Only by attaching itself to such a superior cause can it bring about vast benefit.

How could one who acts thus possibly disparage the teachings or disparage their spiritual mentor (*kalyāṇamitra*)? To disparage one’s spiritual mentor is to disparage the teachings; to disparage the teachings...
To disparage the teachings is to slight the Buddhas and Patriarchs; to slight the Buddhas and Patriarchs is to deceive one’s own mind;

and to deceive one’s own mind is to sink back into the sea of suffering. Alas! Even Śākyamuni Buddha abandoned his entire body to seek a half-verse, and used his own body as a seat to seek the wondrous Dharma.
As it says in the *Pratibhāna-pāramitā* chapter: "He peeled his skin to make paper and split his bones [to make pens]..."
For the sake of the Dharma, one pricks one's finger with a pen and uses the blood as ink to transcribe the scriptures until they accumulate like Mount Sumeru;
because of the gravity of the Dharma, one does not begrudge even body or life, let alone kingship, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, or the seven treasures.
Since the World-Honored One honors the Dharma in such a manner, how could ordinary people disparage its teachings? Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja offered his own body as a lamp to repay the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita deeply repaid his debt of gratitude by selling his heart and liver to study the Prajñāpāramitā; Shen Guang severed his arm to seek instruction;

and Sudhana wept blood as he traveled southward—these were all instances of sacrificing one's body for the sake of the Dharma. As soon as one attains clear realization, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If sentient beings who have not yet emerged wish to practice, they should seek out those with right knowledge and vision, and they will immediately achieve success."
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* on the Perfection of Wisdom states: "One should conceive of all teachers as World-Honored Ones.
If there is anyone who can expound profound meanings and unravel the knots of doubt, thereby benefiting me, one should honor them with all one's heart and mind, disregarding any other faults.
This is like a worn-out bag containing jewels; one does not fail to take the jewels because of the bag’s poor condition. It is also like traveling at night through a dangerous place."
The Way is in decline, yet people hold up torches; they do not take advantage of their illumination because of the wickedness of others. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"One should conceive the thought that those who can expound the Buddha-dharma are difficult to encounter; one should conceive the thought of illness and suffering regarding oneself; one should conceive the thought of a king of physicians regarding the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);
one should conceive the thought of excellent medicine regarding the Dharma being taught; and one should conceive the thought of healing regarding the practice being cultivated."

Regarding the perception of illness: if one hears even a single phrase or a single verse of this unprecedented Dharma, it is superior to obtaining the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system filled with the seven treasures, as well as the rank of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin King. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"One who is able to preach this sūtra should be honored with the same offerings as the Tathāgata; one should scatter celestial jewels over them. Heaven.

This supreme heap of jewels should be offered as an oblation. Why is this? Because this person joyfully expounds the Dharma, and upon hearing it for even a moment, one immediately attains ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says:
"Just as the nature of fire within wood is the primary cause of fire; if no one knows it and it does not rely on expedient means, it cannot spontaneously burn the wood."

It is impossible for sentient beings to be otherwise; even though they possess the power of the permeation of the true cause, if they do not encounter the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas or the guidance of all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), it is impossible for them to achieve Buddhahood on their own.
Is it not as the former masters have said: "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who perfect me are my teachers and friends"? How could this not be so?
Indeed, one must understand that the Mahāyāna sūtras are what all Buddhas take as their teacher, and that the Buddha-fruit of Bodhi emerges entirely from within them.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that those who practice the three types of pure karma and attain birth in the highest of the high grades are all those who read and recite the Mahāyāna and understand the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Those who can act in this way will certainly attain rebirth there. What are these Mahāyāna sūtras? They are the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

If those who cultivate pure karma take up, read, recite, and practice according to the instructions of the *Nirvāṇa*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Awakening of Faith*, the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, and all other sūtras exclusively discussing the Pure Land, one might ask: "Can those who cannot read perform this?
What is to be done for those who are illiterate? The answer is: although they may not know how to read, [they may still practice].
One may also read, recite, print, and circulate these words; furthermore, by daily performing prostrations and taking refuge, one will naturally come to understand them in time.
Consider that Sudhana attained fruition in a single lifetime and the Dragon Girl became a Buddha at the age of eight—this was because they had exerted themselves over many lifetimes;
how could such things be accomplished in a single day? As the *Chapter on King Subhavyūha* states: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family..."
Because this woman has planted roots of goodness, she has obtained spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in life after life.
These spiritual friends are able to perform the work of a Buddha, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening others, leading them to enter into Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Venerable sirs, you should know that a spiritual friend is a great causal condition; for they provide guidance and transformation so that one may behold the Buddha—how could their contribution be anything but profound?
Those who do not understand the principles of the Buddha in this life are all due to having treated the Buddha-dharma with contempt in previous lives;
if they do not revere it again in this life, they will become even more ignorant and distressed in future lives. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

"For thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, such persons shall neither hear the name of the Buddha nor hear the True Dharma. Such people are difficult to deliver—how bitter, how bitter! If it is thus...
To disparage the sutras and revile Dharma masters is a sin greater than slandering the Buddha; how can one not be cautious?
If you do not believe this, it may be seen in the "Fire House" and "Second Chapter" [of the Lotus Sutra]. I exhort future students who wish to cultivate unexcelled bodhi:
they must attend upon and pay homage to enlightened masters and listen to their teachings. If you encounter a blind master and seek to point the way toward transcendence, [you will fail].
Otherwise, one will sink and fall; it can be said that "to cross a river one must use a raft, but once on the shore, the boat is no longer needed.
*Essay on Filial Piety and Nurturing Parents to Repay Kindness*:
The *Three Treasuries of the Lotus School* (*Sanlian zong baojian*) states: "Buddha-recitation is the essential among all dharmas; filial nurturing is the foremost among all deeds. Filial piety..."

The mind is itself the Buddha-mind; filial conduct is nothing other than the practice of the Buddha. If you wish to attain the Way that is identical to that of all Buddhas, you must first practice filial piety and support your two parents.
Therefore, Chan Master Ji said: "The single word 'filial' is the gateway to all wonders. The Buddha’s words take filial piety as their core; the Buddha’s sutras take filial piety as their precept.
When one speaks without delusion, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth; it is clear and distinct right here and now.
Suddenly opening the ground of the mind: Now, filial piety consists of both the filial piety of the householder and the filial piety of the renunciant.

As for the filial piety of the householder, when one’s parents love them, they rejoice and never forget it; when their parents dislike them, they labor without resentment. They follow and comply with the expression of their countenances to fulfill the requirements of nourishment and care.
As for the filial piety of the renunciant, they sever their attachments and bid farewell to kin; consuming the subtle, they accord with the fundamental source and enter deeply into the Unborn.
To provide this principle is to repay the boundless kindness of one's parents, to enter the essential path toward liberation, and to find the swift shortcut for honoring one’s compassionate kin.
This not only yields benefit in future lives but also achieves success in the present world. Thus, the Tathāgata’s son [Mahāmati] scaled the city walls at midnight;

Dàoyuán [Huineng] traversed the Snowy Peaks; Lúnéng [Huineng] presented gold to his mother; and the Dharma was transmitted from Huangméi. Nevertheless, it is through the Dharma that these matters are resolved.
One ought to contemplate repaying the kindness of one's parents; thus, Kāśyapa visited his father in Kapilavastu and Śakra comforted his kin in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

When one is destitute and without support, it is only right to personally attend to them; for this reason, Piliṅga gave rise to the precept of exhausting one’s heart, the Great Master had a hall for raising his foster mother, Muzhou wove sandals to provide for his kin, and Dharma Master Lang carried his parents on his shoulders while traveling to study. Thus it is said: [text continues].
Thus, those who have left the household life take the flavor of the Dharma as their sweet sustenance, never forgetting the heart of returning nourishment;

they regard Buddhist service as their diligent toil, never neglecting the rites of worldly truth. It is not only the parents of this single lifetime whom they repay, for they repay the parents of many lifetimes;

it is not only the parents of this single body whom they deliver, for they deliver the parents of the entire *dharmadhātu*, ascending together to the shore of enlightenment. How could it stop at this?
The Duke of Zhou’s emulation of Heaven universally demonstrates the ford for those lost; thus, his pure filiality surpasses that of Cao Koushu.

The benefit of the filiality of one who leaves the household is vast indeed! If, however, due to unripened conditions your parents do not grant permission, you should exhaust yourself in the filiality of the householder and encourage them to cultivate the causes for transcending the world.
If you can realize the truth while remaining within the secular, there is likewise a path to Buddhahood—may you look forward to returning [to this state].

The conduct of an infant does not fail to honor the gravity of the space beneath the parents' knees; by repaying the labor of the parents’ nurturing care, one attains the stage of the perfection of the One Vehicle.
Thus, it enables the lay bodhisattva to practice and understand without doubt, while those who have left the secular world may thereby reflect upon this.
There are those who, being restricted to serving the Buddha, are unable to fully serve their parents; seeing this, they are moved within their hearts.
Thus one may fully realize filial piety. Alas! Time passes swiftly, yet parents are difficult to forget. When one’s parents dwell in the hall, it is as if the Buddhas dwell in the world.
To repay the virtue of one’s parents in this way is to perfect the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
Know that when parents rejoice, all Buddhas rejoice; when this mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. This may truly be called the "wild color" [of the natural landscape].
No mountains further obstruct the light of heaven; it flows directly and connects with the waters.
A Preface for Seeking Teachers on Foot to Request Instruction, composed by the fourth disciple Zongben, born of the Chen clan of Siming, Chenguang.
My parents raised me and requested that a teacher instruct me so that I might enter school and study the books. My father was a strict teacher, and I became quite proficient in the Odes and Rites.
When I was fifteen years old, my elder cousin, the Recluse Xiumu, passed away due to illness; his corpse lay in an empty hall.

As I was passing by the door of the hall, I saw my deceased cousin’s four elements (the physical body) and was struck with great terror and apprehension, sighing to myself: "Such is the nature of the world."
My life is not firm; like a candle in the wind, impermanence will suddenly arrive, difficult to avoid and impossible to escape.
I thus desired to leave the household life to study the Way and transcend the cycle of saṃsāra, yet I did not know the path of cultivation and remained hesitant in my heart.

Upon arriving at a tea pavilion in my own district, I paid homage to the Buddha and happened to see a monk sitting there with a solemn and upright demeanor. I then questioned him, asking, "What great virtuous one are you? The monk replied:
"I am a wandering Chan practitioner. Upon hearing these words, I was overcome with joy and immediately invited him back to my home, where I prepared incense and vegetarian offerings.
Once the meal was finished, I bowed and asked the Master, "I, your disciple, wish to escape birth and death;
I do not know upon what Dharma I should rely to practice Chan. The Master asked me, "What is your name? How old are you?"
Zongben replied, "I am a disciple named Chen Jingxiu, fifteen years of age. The Zen Master praised him, saying, "Though you are young in years, your resolve is loftily sublime;
this is rare among those of the world. Good son, with a single-minded stillness, listen to what I say:
there is only the path of direct cultivation—merely recite the name of Amitābha Buddha."
The Head of the Sect asked, "If one merely recites the name of Amitābha Buddha, how can one transcend birth and death?

The Chan Master replied, "To rely on the Buddha’s teaching, there is no better remedy for liberation from suffering than the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name). If one does not practice nianfo, it will be difficult to escape birth and death."
Question: From what source does the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha arise? Answer: The Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is not recorded in only one sutra or one teaching;

rather, within the vast collection of sutras as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the great trichiliocosm, there is not a single one that does not contain this Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
If one practices according to this method, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Question: How much merit does the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) possess that enables one to be reborn in the Pure Land? Answer:
If a person were to offer the seven treasures of the four continents as an offering to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, the resulting merit would be immense;
yet it would not equal the merit of exhorting another person to recite the Buddha’s name even once, for the latter’s merit surpasses the former.
Question: How can the recitation of a single name of the Buddha be superior [to other merits]? Answer: The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* states:

"For example, suppose there were a person who, immediately upon being born and falling to the ground, could travel a thousand li in a single day; and suppose this were done for a full one thousand years, during which time they offered the seven treasures filling the world as a gift to the Buddha.
This would not equal the merit of another person who, in a later evil age, is able to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha even once."
If even those whose merit exceeds that [of others] reflect thus upon themselves, how much more so for one who encourages others?

Question: Although the virtues of the Buddha are indeed such as described, the karmic offenses of ordinary beings are many; how can one attain rebirth in the Pure Land by recollecting the Buddha for only a single lifetime?
Answer: The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra in Sixteen Contemplations* states: "With a sincere heart, recite: 'Namo Amitābha Buddha.'"
A single utterance extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

If there are those who, throughout their lives, have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, yet at the moment of death recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times and still attain rebirth in the Pure Land, how much more so for one who observes the precepts and recites the Buddha’s name throughout an entire lifetime?
Question: For what reason does Amitābha Buddha possess such vast merit, vast practices, and vast vows? Answer: Great.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: One day, the countenance of Śākyamuni Buddha was exceptionally radiant. His attendant Ānanda, finding this strange, questioned him.

The Buddha said, "Excellent! That which you ask about surpasses the merit of making offerings to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas throughout a single world-system, as well as bestowing gifts upon all devas, humans, and even down to the smallest crawling insects—even if such acts were performed for many kalpas."
Even a hundred thousand million times [the merit of other deeds] does not equal the merit of that which you have asked. Why is this?
Because all the heavenly kings, emperors, and people, down to the smallest crawling and wriggling creatures, shall all attain liberation by means of what you have asked.
Viewed in this light, when Śākyamuni Buddha first intended to speak of Amitābha Buddha, he preserved [this teaching].

If the expression of one’s mind in outward appearance already differs from that of ordinary days, then it goes without saying that the manner in which Amitābha Buddha moved all the Buddhas was extraordinary;
how much more so his movement of all sentient beings? Why is this? Observe that when Amitābha Buddha first made his vow, he said:
"When I attain Buddhahood, my name shall transcend the ten directions, and humans and devas shall joyfully obtain [it]."
It is heard that those who come to be born in my land include those from the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animal realm;
thus, it can be known that there is no one within the three realms and six paths of saṃsāra who is not saved.
Amitābha Buddha currently dwells in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and furthermore, he teaches and transforms countless devas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

From humans down to the classes of creatures that fly or wriggle—where "flying" refers to minute insects and "wriggling" refers to minute maggots—even such beings as these the Buddha still seeks to transform and deliver; how much more so, then, for human beings?
Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha has made this vow: "If anyone invokes my name, they shall certainly be born in my land; if it were otherwise, may I never attain enlightenment."
Because he has become a Buddha, he extensively delivers sentient beings without end; yet when a person takes refuge with even a single thought, they are reborn in his land.
From this we can infer that the merit of reciting the Buddha's name is truly inconceivable. Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha said:
"If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land in the highest grade, they must employ a heart of compassion, refrain from killing, and cherish [all life]."
Protecting all sentient beings, observing the various precepts, reciting the Mahāyāna, understanding the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
deeply clarifying its meaning, making offerings to the Triple Gem, showing filial piety to one's parents, feeling compassion for the poor and suffering,

teaching and transforming sentient beings, and sustaining spirits and deities with consecrated food (*dharmabhakta*)— if one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this way, one will certainly [attain liberation].
Those of the highest grade attain rebirth in the highest level and proceed directly to Buddhahood;

however, if one’s strength is not yet sufficient, provided they personally maintain the precepts and fasts with single-minded recitation of the Buddha’s name, and if they can do so continuously from thought to thought, they will certainly not be born in the lowest grade.

Furthermore, this Dharma gate makes no distinction between the worthy and the ignorant, does not select between the noble and the lowly, is indifferent to wealth or poverty, does not differentiate between male and female, and takes no account of old age.
From childhood onwards, regardless of whether one is a monastic or a layperson, and irrespective of how long or short one has been practicing, all may recite the Buddha’s name.
As for the methods of recitation, there are likewise no restrictions: one may recite aloud or in a low voice;

recite in a continuous flow, prostrate while reciting, concentrate the mind while reciting, investigate through inquiry while reciting, visualize while reciting, rotate the prayer beads while reciting, recite while walking, standing, sitting quietly, or lying on one's side; or recite in silence.
Clarify your mindfulness: a thousand thoughts, ten thousand thoughts, are all but a single thought; it requires only the resolute mind of faith to seek birth in the Pure Land.
If one can practice and maintain this, what need is there to seek out other teachers? It may be said that the entire journey of a boat rests with the helmsman;
those who attain this will together ascend to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). (Qiān [yuan] ruan [ruǎn] qū [qī yú qiè]).

Zongben asked: "Many people in the world say that they are entangled by family affairs and bound by worldly duties, and will therefore wait until old age before reciting the Buddha's name. I pray that you will explain such words."
The Chan Master said, "Alas, alas! What kind of foolish and deluded words are these? Have you not seen what Master Sīxīn said:
'People of the world have wealth and treasures as high as mountains and wives and concubines filling their rooms; they enjoy themselves day and night. Do they not desire to live long in this world?
Yet how can they resist that their future is limited and that they are driven on in secret? When the summons arrives, they must go.'"
There is no room for delay; the Old Man Yama does not follow human sentiment. What face will the King of Impermanence have?

Furthermore, based on what you have personally seen with your own eyes and heard with your own ears in the streets and alleys before and behind you—how many relatives, kinsmen, friends, brothers, and strong youths have died? Have you not heard the ancients say: "Do not wait"?
Only in old age does one begin to study the Way; the solitary grave is filled with those of my youth. It is further said:

"Since my early years, I have sought a wife, raised children, and managed the household affairs, enduring tens of thousands of hardships. Suddenly, when the three-inch breath is severed, all must inevitably cease at once.
If there are filial descendants who can provide vegetarian offerings for several monks, have them read a section of the scriptures and burn incense."
On three days of spring and nine days of autumn, one makes a bowl of soup and rice; for how many times can one weep before even the memory of one’s parents fades?

If an unworthy son, while his parents are still dying and their bones are not yet cold, squanders their property and sells their fields and gardens to indulge in pleasure, how can this compare to the urgency of the matter? Grandchildren have their own children.
"Sun Fu, do not let this be a distant worry for your descendants. He further cited an ancient master who said: "The wealthy old man smiles coldly;
his livelihood is as frantic as a speeding arrow. Rice in his granaries breeds worms; coins in his treasuries rot in bundles. By day he weighs them on scales; by night he counts them by lamplight.
His physical form is like a puppet—do not let the strings snap. Such was the bitter admonition regarding the dead heart.
Do you encourage others by saying, "First attend to your worldly affairs as promised; wait until old age before you recite the Buddha’s name"?
You should reflect that how much time does a human life have in this world? It passes in the blink of an eye, like a spark of stone-fire or a flash of lightning.
While you are still young and free from illness, shake off your body and mind and cast aside mundane matters. Use each day’s light to recite the Buddha’s name for that very day.

If you devote yourself to the practice of pure karma for a single period of time, then at the moment of death, whether it be a "good death" or a "bad death," it will depend solely on whether you have prepared your provisions in advance.
If my future journey is thus made secure and steady, there will be no room for regret later;
reflect on this, reflect on this! Furthermore, rejoice that Amitābha is so easy to invoke and that the Pure Land is so accessible.

The soil is very fertile and easily productive; although people of this world find it difficult to avoid managing household affairs, they must nevertheless burn incense and recite the Buddha’s name morning and evening.
Moreover, this Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha can be practiced by all people alike. It is like a dark room of a thousand years:
a single lamp illuminating it brings forth light. Therefore, even those who slaughter oxen or butcher horses may set down their butcher knives.
Furthermore, that which is cultivated through this practice is not difficult and does not obstruct any worldly affairs: for those in office, it does not interfere with their duties;
for scholars, it does not hinder their study; for merchants, it does not impede their trade; for farmers, it does not prevent their cultivation;
for women, it does not obstruct their domestic labors; and for those in public service, it does not conflict with serving their superiors.
It does not hinder monastics from practicing *chán* (meditation); indeed, all activities whatsoever do not obstruct it.

Whether one is performing prostrations and recitations at dawn or dusk, or finding leisure amidst busyness, one may recite the name a thousand or a hundred times daily, or three, five, or even ten times.
The only requirement is that one must dedicate the merit and make a vow to go to the Western Land. If one can truly act in this way, [rebirth there] is certain.

"You shall certainly attain rebirth there," Chen said. "Good man, if you maintain the precepts with strict purity and single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name yet fail to be born in the Pure Land, I [Chen] shall fall into the Hell of the Severed Tongue.
Seeing that the Chan Master’s vow was so profound and grave, I was struck with awe;
I knelt and prostrated myself, and was moved by his compassionate instruction on the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation.
The Chan Master said: "If one were to speak of the teachings of the Pure Land school, they could not be fully expounded even in the course of a hundred million kalpas;
therefore, I have merely cited a few words. As the ancient masters said: 'The superior person, with a single resolution, understands everything;
the middling and inferior persons, despite much hearing, lack much faith. Truly, these words are so! Indeed, a practitioner who possesses true faith must seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land."
Having said this, one must simply let it rest; it must be treated as if it were a momentous matter.

If you can truly believe it, then from this very day forth, arouse great courage and great diligence. Do not concern yourself with whether you understand it or not, nor whether you have seen your nature or not;
simply hold fast to the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha," as if leaning against a solid wall.
Seated upon Mount Sumeru, unshakable; this single thought is your original teacher.
This single thought is the transformation Buddha. This single thought is the fierce general who shatters hell.
This single thought is the precious sword that slays all evils. This single thought is the bright lamp that opens the darkness. This single thought—
This single thought is the great vessel for crossing the sea of suffering; this single thought is the excellent remedy for escaping birth and death;
this single thought is the path for exiting the triple world; this single thought is the Amitābha of one's own nature;
this single thought is the Pure Land of the Mind-only. It is simply enough to remember these words: "Amitābha Buddha."
In mindfulness, do not allow it to be lost; let mindfulness be ever-present before you. At every moment, do not depart from the mind. Whether there is nothing to attend to, contemplate thus;
whether there is something to attend to, contemplate thus. Whether it be peace and happiness, contemplate thus; whether it be the suffering of illness, contemplate thus.
Whether it be birth, contemplate thus; whether it be death, contemplate thus. When this single thought is clear and distinct in this way, what further need is there to ask?
If one seeks the path home, it can be said that with the single phrase "Namu Amitābha" and no other thought, one reaches the Western Land without even the effort of a finger-snap.
The Zen Master earnestly repeated his instruction, saying: "Good man Chen, I now entrust to you the Dharma of the ten realms of existence."
"You must also reveal this Dharma to future generations and practice it with diligence so that they may likewise attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Zongben replied, "I shall extensively expound it for later ages, hoping it will be of benefit to those who come after.
The Zen Master said, "Excellent, excellent! As for the ten dharma realms: the Buddha-dharma realm, the Bodhisattva-dharma realm, and the Pratyekabuddha-dharma realm..."

The dharma-realm of śrāvakas, the dharma-realm of devas, the dharma-realm of humans, the dharma-realm of asuras, the dharma-realm of hungry ghosts, the dharma-realm of animals, and the dharma-realm of hell-beings—these ten dharma-realms are fully present within a single mind. One receives according to what one creates;
based on the causes you have made, you receive the fruits of those very actions. Thus, virtuous conduct and evil conduct are the causes of the mundane world.
The three realms and six paths of existence are the fruits of the mundane world. Upholding the precepts and reciting the Buddha’s name are the causes for transcending the mundane world.

Attaining Buddhahood in the Pure Land is the fruit of transcending the mundane world. On the path of humans and devas, cultivating merit is the prerequisite; within the sea of birth and death, reciting the Buddha’s name is supreme.
Now, there are those who desire the happiness of the human and heavenly realms yet do not cultivate merit, and those who wish to transcend birth and death yet do not recite the Buddha’s name.
To die without recollecting the Buddha is like a bird wishing to fly without wings or a tree wishing to flourish without roots; how could such things be possible?

One must take the recollection of the Buddha as the primary cause (*nidāna*) and the cultivation of merit as the auxiliary path. By practicing both merit and wisdom together, one achieves Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Thus, the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause; there is no discrepancy between cause and fruit, and from beginning to end they are inseparable.
Why is this so? Because when the form is straight, the shadow is upright; when the sound is harmonious, the echo follows suit. One should know that because the cause is real, the fruit is not empty.
The present life is the cause, and the moment of death is the fruit. If one commits evil, an evil realm will manifest before one;

if one recollects the Buddha, the Buddha-realm will naturally arrive. Does one not see what the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should..."
"To contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm as being entirely fashioned by the mind alone" refers to this.

Zongben asked, "By relying on what dharma does one practice until reaching the Buddha-dharma-realm? The Chan Master replied, "You should know that all sentient beings of the six realms possess Buddha-nature;
they are equal in true suchness and of one substance. Contemplate them as being identical to the Buddhas, regarding them as you would your own father."

If one regards all beings— whether immediate enemies or kin— with the thought that they are one's mother, and strives to deliver them all until the end of the future while practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra,
then by cultivating according to this Dharma, one will become equal to all Buddhas.

Question: By relying on what dharmas does one cultivate and attain the Dharma-realm of a bodhisattva? Answer: One attains it by relying on the perfection of generosity to transcend stinginess and greed;

the perfection of ethical discipline to transcend transgressions; the perfection of patience to transcend anger; the perfection of diligence to transcend laziness; the perfection of meditative concentration to transcend dullness and agitation; and the perfection of wisdom to transcend ignorance.
If one can practice in reliance upon these dharmas, one is equal to a bodhisattva.
Question: Based on what dharma does one practice until reaching the dharma-realm of a pratyekabuddha? Answer: A person of the Middle Vehicle delights in solitary tranquility;
although they understand all dharmas, because their conditions do not lead them to universal salvation, they reach only the dharma-realm of a pratyekabuddha.
Question: Based on what dharma does one practice until reaching only the realm of the śrāvakas? Answer:

Those of the Hīnayāna are terrified of birth and death, leaping forward like a wild deer without looking back at its herd; desiring to quickly exit the triple world and seek their own nirvāṇa, they therefore reach only the realm of the śrāvakas.

Question: By relying on what dharma does one cultivate *śamatha* to be born in the realm of the devas? Answer: By cultivating the ten wholesome karmic paths, one attains birth in the dharma-realm of the devas.
Question: By relying on what dharma does one again attain birth among the human lineage? Answer: By firmly upholding the five precepts, one attains birth in the dharma-realm of humans.

Question: What kind of karmic offenses must one commit to fall into the realm of the asuras? Answer: If a person, despite cultivating wholesome deeds, constantly harbors a mind of competitiveness, anger, and pride, they will fall into the dharma-realm of the asuras.

Question: What evil karma must one create to fall into the realm of hungry ghosts? Answer: One falls into the dharma-realm of hungry ghosts by being stingy and greedy, refusing to renounce, and eating alone while deceiving the multitude.
Question: What evil karma must one create to fall into the realm of animals? Answer: By creating the karma of ignorance and perverse evil, one will certainly fall [into that state].
The realm of animals.
Question: What evil karma must one commit to fall into the realm of hell? Answer: One who slanders the Triple Gem and commits various evils will certainly fall into the realm of hell.
These ten realms above are generally according to what people have done and cultivated.
Zongben prostrated himself and thanked the Master, saying, "Were it not for the auspicious fortune of my past lives, how could I have encountered an enlightened teacher to reveal these teachings?
The Chan Master took his leave and further said, "If you have any doubts that remain unresolved, you may consult the *Lianzong baojian* (Precious Mirror of the Lotus School),

the *Jingtu zhigui* (Guide to the Pure Land), the *Longshu jingtu wen* (Treatise on the Pure Land by Longshu), the *Wanshan tonggui ji* (Collection on the Convergence of All Good Deeds), and the works of the Great Master Zhiyi."
*Deciding on Doubts Regarding the Pure Land: A Rhapsody on the Spirit Dwelling in An-yang*, by the Dharma Master Tianru of the Yi Lun school.

All those who praise the scriptures and teachings concerning the Pure Land should read this work. The Preface states: "I respectfully receive my teacher’s command and shall faithfully uphold and practice it.
The details regarding his renunciation, travels for study, and the principles of phenomena and noumenon are too extensive to be recorded here.
An Exhortation as a Mirror for Zen Practice The gateway to the fivefold path of cultivation possesses nothing extraordinary;
it consists solely in cleansing the sense-bases and their objects, taking awakening as the standard.

O worthy ones, if you wish to cultivate unsurpassed Bodhi, you must resolutely maintain the observance of the precepts. If the practice of the precepts is not strictly maintained, Bodhi will ultimately remain unattained.
Why is it that precepts are not accomplished? It is because precepts are the vanguard of the myriad practices and the foundation of the six perfections.
Just as one building a house first secures its foundation, if there is no foundation, one merely constructs in the void. Now, these precepts are the Mahāyāna Threefold Pure Precepts:
the precept of restraining from misconduct, which means severing every evil—that is, "do no evil"—and the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas...
The precept of accumulating all that is good is the practice of "following all wholesome deeds";
the precept of benefiting sentient beings is the universal salvation of all living beings. These three clusters of precepts are the precepts by which a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood.
Only if one possesses these three precepts may one cultivate dhyāna; if one does not give rise to this mind, what benefit is there in practicing Chan? Have you not seen [the story of] Fan...?
The *Jingang jing* (Diamond Sūtra) states: "If sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.

Is this not so? The Buddhas and Patriarchs have said: "Precepts can give rise to concentration; concentration can give rise to wisdom; wisdom then clarifies the mind; clarifying the mind leads to seeing one's nature; seeing one's nature leads to becoming a Buddha;
and becoming a Buddha leads to becoming a Patriarch. None of these paths fail to depend upon these precepts. Now, the matter of Zen meditation (*chán*) is truly the most direct approach.
The supreme profound mechanism is not something ordinary or trivial; one must give rise to great courage and great diligence.
Furthermore, one must still the thoughts and forget external conditions, withdrawing the gaze and turning back the hearing.

One must sweep away all habitual likes and dislikes, views and attachments, hatred and love, and right and wrong, completely clearing them away as if using a sharp blade to cut a handful of silk—once it is cut, everything is severed—or like cutting a mooring rope.
Setting sail and heading straight ahead is like a single person fighting ten thousand men; there is no room for even a blink of an eye, so how could one afford to hesitate?
If you can truly give rise to such a resolute will, only then do you possess the true air of one who studies Zen.
Once you have this air of Zen study, holding fast to the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" is like leaning against Mount Sumeru.

Swaying and shaking as if in a trance, yet remaining unmoved, concentrate your mind and unify your intent. Recite the name three or five times, then turn the light back upon yourself to look within, asking:
"Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? In your practice, you must see from where this single thought arises.
After a long while, having scrutinized it until you see through it, add further doubt upon this doubt. Ask again: "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"
Who is it that ultimately arrives here? You must hold fast to the end of the rope and not let go of it. It is like encountering a mortal enemy of birth and death;
you must seize them and settle the matter immediately, without allowing for hesitation or deliberation. Practice Zen in this manner, resolving to achieve the goal within a fixed period.

If you cannot yet do so, listen further to these redundant words regarding the actual application of the practice of investigation. As for the work of investigating: [The text continues with instructions on the method of inquiry.]
The method of this Dharma is like a person who has fallen into a well over a thousand feet deep;
from morning until night they contemplate and reflect, employing nothing but the mind intent on seeking escape, with no other thoughts. It is also like having lost a vital object;

one searches for it in the morning and searches at night, searching horizontally and searching vertically. Though one searches and cannot find it, one continues to ponder and reflect deeply, just as before.
A cat catching a mouse is the same whether inside or out; it is like crossing a narrow wooden bridge, where one must be even more careful.

If you apply your mind in this way, dullness and distraction will naturally recede. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you should be as protective of an infant and avoid any sudden violence.
Therefore, to seek the pearl, the waves should be calm; if the water is stirred, it is difficult to obtain. When the water is clear and still, the pearl of the mind will manifest of itself.
An ancient said, "When digging a pond, one does not wait for the moon; once the pond is finished, the moon comes of its own accord.

Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states, "Unobstructed, pure wisdom all arises based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). If you can practice and maintain this method, you will certainly gain entry into the Way.

Even if meditative concentration manifests before you, you must not dwell in a stagnant, barren state of concentration; you must investigate the Great Matter and clearly realize the Perfect [Enlightenment].
Regarding the attainment of the All-Knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), former masters have said: "Do not merely forget the body and lose the mind;
this is a disease difficult to cure and the most profound. One must sit in contemplation to explore its source and origin before one can realize one's nature and recognize the true Heavens.

This is truly what is meant by "taking another step beyond the hundred-foot pole," waiting until one lets go at the precipice, passes away, and is revived again—only then can it be called [true realization].
For one who has settled this matter, although this one principle is resolved, there remains another:
perhaps there is doubt regarding whether a *huatou* can be raised or not, whether it is clear or obscure, whether one gains strength or not, or whether there is light ease or not.
One must not cling at all to such gains or losses, existences or non-existences; simply maintaining the intent of investigation is itself the practice that brings resolution.
Regarding this one point, there is another point of doubt: when a favorable state appears before you, do not rejoice, for fear that the demon of joy may enter your mind;
when an unfavorable state appears, do not become distressed, for fear that the demon of affliction may enter your mind.
You must know that these states do not come from without, but are all produced by dullness (*styāna*) or by the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
All that is perceived—whether seen by the eyes or heard by the ears—is entirely illusory; do not cling to any of it, but apply yourself with diligence. An ancient worthy said:
"Your skillful means are finite, while my non-grasping is infinite. This is truly like having an illness within one's physical body;
this cannot be forcibly overcome. You must urgently pay homage to the Buddha, repent, and recite the Buddha’s name to dispel it.
After the illness has passed and its source has been completely shed, one must then investigate further. If there is a person of wisdom, they may likewise investigate this:
they must know that the four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates are not-self; from where does the illness arise, and who is it that suffers the illness?
If one can awaken and reflect in this manner, there will surely come a time of realization. Even though this matter is thus resolved, there remains another point of doubt.
If any clever insights should manifest before you, do not cling to them; you must immediately sweep them away.
If you dwell within the realm of such knowledge and views, you will bury your original face. As the former masters said: "The Buddha-dharma is not fresh fish;
one need not fear it rotting. It is like peeling a plantain tree: peel one layer, then another; peel one layer, then another.
One must strip away layer by layer until reaching a point where there is no longer a place to grasp, only then can everything be forged into a single whole.
Thereafter, whether dressing or eating, defecating or urinating, moving or still, speaking or silent, there is nothing that is not the one Amitābha Buddha.
From this point on, the flower of the mind blooms brilliantly, illuminating the ten directions like the brilliant sun shining in the sky or a clear mirror facing the light.
The platform does not transcend a single thought-moment; to achieve perfect enlightenment instantaneously is not merely to clarify this one great matter.

From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past onwards, all diverse causes and conditions have been thoroughly penetrated to their very core. There is nothing—whether the Buddha-dharma or worldly dharmas—that is not clearly understood.
Even when one reaches such a state, one must not yet remain attached or settled; one must further seek realization and entrust oneself to a master of true attainment.
Once the seal of approval has been received through the karmic capacity, the distinction between sage and ordinary person no longer stands, and both grasping and rejecting are forgotten.
What need is there to speak of heaven and hell? What need is there to differentiate north, south, east, and west? The entire Dharma-realm is one's own self;
Amitābha, throughout all of space, is the Pure Land of the Mind-Only. Thus, one can manifest the jeweled king’s realm upon the tip of a single hair and sit within a mote of dust.

To turn the Great Dharma Wheel amidst the dust, to guide and lead those of the future, and to support the final age—only such a Chan practitioner is a transcendent man of extraordinary caliber and a hero who surpasses his peers.
If this is not yet the case, then rely upon the power of that Buddha’s vows to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Why?
For fear that when the dark realms of the moment of death appear before you, your hands and feet will be in disarray; at such a time, one must act.
One cannot take control of one's destiny and avoid being driven away by the conditions of one’s karma;

rather, one must resolutely practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, cultivating both merit and wisdom, directing the mind toward the Land of Bliss, and await the end of life with single-minded devotion. This may be called: "Though it be an old hall and a vacant field, only when it has been reclaimed once does one finally rest.
Alas! Since the time of the Sage has long passed, the various streams have become increasingly divergent. Recently, there has been one...
These people are like the common, drifting masses; their wisdom-eye is neither clear nor pure, they lack faith in the Pure Land, and they misinterpret the pivotal words of the Patriarchs.
They speak erroneously of the Sage’s intent and conduct, failing to investigate through practice. With single-minded devotion, they are instead preoccupied with the four elements.
Today for two days, tomorrow for three, they teach others how to manipulate and fabricate, stumbling and rushing about so that concentration and wisdom cannot manifest.

In the end, this leads instead to recklessness and delusion; one squanders the offerings of the faithful and betrays one's own spiritual nature, transmigrating through the three miserable realms and undergoing all manner of suffering.
This is simply because, from the very beginning, one did not encounter a true master, and thus until old age one has become nothing but a useless relic.
Such blind practitioners and those who engage in reckless cultivation—even if they were to continue their antics until the descent of Maitreya—will have no day of liberation. This is precisely so.
What is called "no dhyāna and no pure land" refers to iron beds and copper pillars; for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is no one to rely upon.
Alas, how bitter! I urge later students and eminent worthies to take this most carefully. I now clearly explain it for you;
yet even this explanation may provoke the resentment of others. To the wise, this is like clarified butter (amṛta); to the deluded, it becomes a poisonous drug.
If one errs by a hair’s breadth, one misses the mark by a thousand li. Alas!
When the sky clears and the sun comes out, or when rain falls and the ground becomes damp, I have explained everything with full sincerity; yet I fear you may not believe it. Take care.
A Discourse on the Ease and Difficulty of Chan and Pure Land Sixth:

Someone asked, "In this world, there are those who separately cling to *gong'an*, causing others to apply themselves to spiritual practice solely with the aim of investigating Chan and attaining enlightenment, while having no wish to be reborn in the Pure Land.
What is one to say of such a method? The answer was: "This concerns those of keen faculties and superior wisdom."
For a person to engage in genuine investigation and attain true awakening, even a slight error leads to a great mistake.

One might ask: How do we know it is a mistake? It is because the point of error lies in not having attained awakening; one will consequently continue to transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death.

It would be better to focus on recitation and cultivation, for these will surely lead to direct rebirth in the Pure Land. It is not that spiritual friends do not teach you to practice Chan meditation; rather, they fear that you may not [attain realization].
Why is it that attaining enlightenment through Chan meditation is difficult while rebirth in the Pure Land through mindfulness of the Buddha is easy?
Have you not heard the ancient masters say: "Among those who practice Chan to resolve the matter of birth and death, only one or two out of a hundred succeed;

among those who mindfully seek rebirth in the Pure Land, not one in ten thousand fails"? This is truly what is meant by the saying: "Those with Chan but no Pure Land—nine out of ten go astray. Is this not so?
How much more so when practicing Chan does not hinder reciting the Buddha’s name, and reciting the Buddha’s name does not hinder practicing Chan;

when the Chan school and the Pure Land school are thus mutually compatible, the ease or difficulty of their respective paths becomes clearly apparent today. This Dharma gate of direct pointing is such that even the eighty-four thousand teachings are not equal to a single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha.
Though there are seventeen hundred koans, they are still not equal to a single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha."
Why is this? The teaching gate of Amitābha Buddha possesses both the sudden and the gradual, as well as the principle and the trace.

Those of superior faculties and wisdom directly accept [the truth] and realize Buddhahood by seeing their nature; those of middling or inferior capacities who cannot yet transcend suddenly rely upon the power of that Buddha and likewise attain rebirth there.
For this reason, the teaching gate of mindfulness of the Buddha surpasses all other teaching gates. As for the rest...
The merit of these *gong'an* is such that the merit of the *nianfo gong'an* does not equal even one hundredth part of it;
even ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a billion, or ten billion parts do not reach it. Why is this?
If these merits were equal, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time would not praise Amitābha Buddha, nor would they point toward the West within the sands of scriptures.
Regarding the Pure Land, have you not heard that every ancestral master of successive generations recited the Buddha’s name? Every renowned sage of past and present recited the Buddha’s name;
monks and laypeople, men and women alike—all recited the Buddha’s name. If this Dharma-gate is so impartial, why do you single it out as distinct from other teachings?
Observe the people of the world: whenever they open their mouths and utter a sound, they first recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
In short, one must know that Amitābha Buddha’s power of vows is boundless; for this reason, he alone is specifically extolled and singled out.
As the Verse in Praise of the Buddha says: "Among the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost;
with forty-eight vows, he delivers sentient beings, causing all nine grades to ascend to the other shore. Inferring from this, the kōan of mindfulness of the Buddha is truly transcendent.
This transcends all public cases (koans). I shall now speak again: the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) all practice for the sake of birth and death;
they simply fail to attain liberation. Why is this? It is entirely because they encounter blind teachers who take the True Dharma to be false dharma, and feign the Buddha-dharma as demonic teachings.
Because of this, many have been deceived and led astray. While it may be forgivable to deceive oneself, [to deceive others is not].
Furthermore, to deceive others is precisely what is meant by "one blind man leading many blind men, pulling one another into a fiery pit.

Long ago, the Tathāgata told Maudgalyāyana: "For example, when the long-flowing currents of ten thousand rivers carry floating plants and wood, the front does not look back and the back does not look forward;
they all converge at the great ocean. The world is likewise: though there be those of noble rank, wealth, and pleasure,"

In this world, none can escape birth, old age, sickness, and death; it is solely because they do not believe in the Buddhist scriptures that they cannot attain rebirth in the lands of the thousand Buddhas.

For this reason, I say that the land of Amitābha Buddha is easy to reach and easy to attain, yet people fail to practice for rebirth there and instead serve the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths. I declare that such people are called "those without eyes."

Regarding the person named "The Earless One": For instance, within the *Wangsheng lu* (Records of Rebirth) and the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), both the worthy and the foolish are born together;

this has been so throughout past and present. Casting off the defiled land, all proceed toward the Pure Land. Conceived in the pool of the seven jewels, they abandon the suffering of the womb and transition from the mundane to the sagely.
Attaining the Way and realizing the Truth, they achieve Buddhahood without passing through the three great kalpas—is this not the power of the Buddha?
This is inconceivable. If one wishes to transcend the cycle of birth and death forever and attain the bliss of nirvana, there is no method superior to the Dharma-gate of Rebirth.
Why is this? In the turbid realm of Sahā, where all manner of suffering gathers, it is difficult to accomplish the Way;

whereas in the joyful land of the Pure Land, where all virtues are accumulated, one attains the stage of non-retrogression. Those who recite the Name are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, and thus they go [to that land].

Those who give rise to the Bodhicitta are illuminated by Amitābha’s light, whereby they progress; bodhisattvas and arhats, along with their peers, as well as the water birds and forest trees, all constantly recite the Buddha’s name.
By their ears, they perpetually hear the wondrous Dharma, and within their hearts, greed and anger are instantly severed.

Their joy is inexhaustible, and the limit of their lifespan is beyond measure. Having been born in that land in a single lifetime, they immediately attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression); how could this be compared to the realms of humans and devas?
On the path, everything one encounters is largely either adverse or favorable; on the road of the provisional vehicles, roots of goodness are rare.

Even those at the stage of the three worthies prior to the ten stages, who have not yet seen the Way, lose mindfulness; even those at the sixth stage encounter adverse conditions and retreat from their resolve.
Thus, in the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, five thousand withdrew from their seats, and in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, those who lost the Way were still numerous.
If one observes that even in the Buddha’s own era it was thus, how could it not be so now?

This shows that while practitioners of the Three Vehicles may pass through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges without completing their meritorious practices, the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha allows one to reach the stage of non-retrogression in the mere blink of an eye.
Therefore, those born in the Pure Land advance without ever retreating and are certain to attain Buddhahood; hence, the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* speaks of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
All those born among the beings of this land are *avaivartika*; "avaivartika" refers to the stage of non-retrogression. Alas!
For those with a beginner’s mind and shallow faith, it is difficult to advance in practice without the power of others (*tara*). Our Buddha’s vow is profound;

all who have a karmic affinity are gathered and sustained by it. O virtuous ones, the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past established the teachings and revealed the method of the Buddha-remembrance practice (*nien-fo*).
How much more so for the practitioners of Chan today who do not believe in rebirth in the Pure Land! For those who cultivate the Pure Land are by no means hindered from practicing Chan;
why then do those who practice Chan disparage the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it?
*Discerning the Heretical and the Orthodox to Resolve Doubts*.
Master Jueyi of Mingjiao said: "The teachings bestowed by the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) necessarily take Chan as their essence and the Buddha as their patriarch.
The patriarch is the great model of his teaching, while the essence is the great system of his teaching. If the great system is not clarified,"
Consequently, the world cannot find a single point of convergence; if the great paradigm is not upright, the world cannot find a standard by which to verify its realization.

Indeed, that those who study Buddhism throughout the ages compete to establish their own sectarian gateways and vie with one another over right and wrong stems from the affliction of an unclarified lineage and an unrighteous patriarchal tradition.
Alas! In recent times, there have been certain heterodox teachers who have created...

The demon-possessed outsider composed the *Yan hao bao lin fa lun* (commonly known as the *Yuan huo lun*) and falsely authored the *Zhen zong miao yi jing*, arrogantly claiming it to be the Unsurpassed Dharma-Jewel.
He deluded later generations so that nine out of ten were in error and ten out of seven were perverse;
thus, people failed to recognize their own inherently pure *dharmakāya* and became entirely absorbed in this sack of pus and blood.

Using dream experiences to validate their practice, they instead slander both *chan* meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name, claiming these are all merely "Hīnayāna" acts of giving for the sake of making connections, which yield only turbid merit.
They teach that one need not bow to the Buddha, burn incense, uphold the precepts, or chant the sutras;
from this point on, they harbor such perverse understandings and speak recklessly of the Sage’s intent, asserting that sexual desire does not obstruct bodhi.

Killing, stealing, and other such acts are practiced without hindering the Prajñāpāramitā; these have been transmitted among us within our school, where we fail to observe pure regulations and bring disorder to the True Dharma.
These are demons and ghouls who gather by night and disperse at dawn, falsely claiming to follow official law while concealing the majestic Buddha-Dharma.
You should blow out the lamps and candles and transmit the wondrous Dharma in secret. You must all practice and uphold this according to my instructions. Seven.

"Daily seeing one's nature and awakening to the Way, furthermore teaching the disciples of the society to take a vow of penance, write out the petitions, and seal them in accordance with the celestial statutes to burn and send them up to the celestial court—only then can one attain Buddhahood. This is an exquisite and marvelous matter; it must not be known by outsiders.
