If you leak this divine mechanism, you shall surely fall [into hell]. May you all again pledge to patrol behind several houses and before their gates."
Fearing that the wind might carry the sound so that those in neighboring rooms might hear it, one ought to exercise such extreme caution! Alas, why such toil?

If this were truly the Dharma of the Buddha, when the bell and drum summon the great assembly to ascend the hall, arrange their seats, and proclaim the teaching with clarity and open exposition, how could there be any reason for concealment?
One fears only that the transmission will not be widespread; how could one fear people obtaining it?
I have come to know that because these are followers of Māra, they deceive both others and themselves. Year after year, many of this sort stir up trouble among the laymen and laywomen of pure faith;
unaware and unknowing, they are driven into the path of Māra. Alas!
To mislead them regarding their spiritual direction is still somewhat forgivable, yet they further falsely claim that the Sixth Patriarch said, "It would be better to deliver ten million laypeople."
Those who do not cross the threshold of the Gate of Emptiness as even half a monk—such individuals not only delude future generations, but they also slander the former sages.
Have you not heard what Yongjia said? "The first was Kāśyapa, who first transmitted the Lamp; twenty-eight generations later, it was recorded in the West.
Upon entering this land, Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch; the transmission of the robe for six generations was known throughout the world."
Since those who attain the Way in later generations are infinite in number, how could it be that one is granted deliverance while another is excluded from the Gate of Emptiness?

These words are truly a slander upon the Triple Gem and a destruction of the monastic tradition. To propagate such evil and violate its prohibitions, when the truth is revealed one day, Heaven’s principles will find no room for leniency:
alive, one shall face the king's law; dead, one shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Even if a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, there shall be no opportunity for repentance. How [could this be]?
For this reason, when the retribution for the sins of the Avīci Hell has been exhausted, one falls again into various hells;
once the karma of those hells has been consumed, one enters among animals and hungry ghosts, undergoing suffering in succession without rest. This is precisely what is meant by the saying:
"If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. Do you not see that the Path of the Ancient Sages reveals even a single Māra?

The situation is like ten thousand arrows piercing the heart; hearing even a single demonic sound is like a thousand awls stabbing the ears. You must distance yourselves from it immediately and avoid seeing or hearing such things.

Each of you must investigate your own minds with care and do not treat this lightly, O worthy ones! These kinds of demons and obstructors arise solely because of karmic seeds cultivated in past lives.
When encountering a false teacher, the power of goodness is easily diminished while the roots of evil are difficult to uproot—how much more so for those who belong to such a faction!
Such things are extremely prevalent in the world today; I shall briefly cite several examples here to dispel your doubts.

Furthermore, there are false teachers who falsely claim to represent the authentic teaching of Bodhidharma, instructing people to contemplate the two characters "Buddha" and "No," or to practice the application of breath.

They also teach them to exert effort in forcefully lifting [the mind] and pressing the vital energy upward until it strikes the crown of the head, speaking of such absurd methods as the "broom-handle" technique and urging them to apply themselves with fierce diligence. These kinds of...
All such people harbor heterodox views and follow deviant paths; even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they shall not emerge from saṃsāra.

Furthermore, there are false teachers who claim that the *dantian* (elixir field) is the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the dwelling place of all Buddhas, instructing people to practice visualization, contortion, and artificial effort, manipulating the essence and vital energy to pass through the Three Barriers.
They speak of "returning to the root and restoring the source," claiming that one thereby realizes the nature and achieves Buddhahood.
The Buddha heard a sound from within his belly and spoke of the six kinds of earth tremors and the lion’s roar;

such people, having grown old into demons, shall sink forever into the cave of ghosts. Furthermore, there are heterodox teachers who do not recognize the great name of the Sage and fail to understand the merit of reciting the Buddha's name;
they erroneously speak of the "male of the Kan" and "female of the Li," and the "water and fire already in harmony," falsely applying the term *Namo* [to these].

To divide the six characters of "Amitābha Buddha" into six separate types of perverted interpretations to deceive and delude people, and to treat the Great Sage with contempt, is a sin equal to cutting off one's limbs or shedding the blood of a Buddha. Such individuals—both teacher and disciples—shall enter hell together.
Furthermore, there are false teachers who claim that the Dharma-gate of sudden enlightenment renders it unnecessary for people to recite the Buddha’s name.
Discerning the principles of yin and yang, he strips off his clothes and lies on his back to gaze at the void;

again, he speaks of the "double-barrier" behind the spine and names the Caoxi lineage, teaching people to curl their feet and circulate the vital breath (*qi*), falsely claiming to emit the great light of wisdom (*mahāprajñā*).
Such fabrications and practices are entirely the livelihood of ghosts; they do not realize that all Buddhas are accomplished through the accumulation of merit and virtue—how could it be otherwise?
If one clings to emptiness, one merely attains the Buddha-way of the Buddha-dharma, yet this remains a dust-like obstruction; how could such a person possibly preserve the yin and yang?
Such individuals become companions to Māra and sink into the abyss for eternal kalpas.

Furthermore, there are heterodox teachers who falsely transmit one hundred and eight characters, calling them the "One Hundred and Eight Maṇi," placing names upon the various limbs and joints of the body—above, below, left, and right—to symbolize the Dharma.

To cause people to turn [the prayer beads] once and consider it a full session of practice—such that they do not even adjust their robes with solemnity when bowing to the sun, moon, or the Northern Dipper;
or that they expose their bodies, wear light garments, or act with such rashness as to show disrespect toward their ancestors and parents;

or that they obstruct others from making offerings to the Buddhas and providing for the Sangha, while conversely claiming that "clay Buddhas cannot cross water" and "wooden Buddhas cannot cross fire"—[is a grave error].
Golden, silver, and bronze images likewise cannot save one; the "passing through the furnace" is but a tangle that cannot be resolved by mere recitation.
From this point on, those who slight the Buddha and treat the Dharma with contempt will act recklessly.

It must be that every person becomes like Danxia before he is permitted to burn the Buddha, and every individual becomes like Baizhang before they may say "there is nothing. If it is not yet so, you will enter hell as swiftly as an arrow. Furthermore, there are false teachers and impostors...

They devise various and manifold doctrines, falsely claiming the simultaneous cultivation of both nature and life, and further labeling this "the Great Way" or "the Golden Elixir," thereby deceiving the men and women of the world.
These people do not recognize true investigation or genuine realization;
they consistently practice demonic arts, calculating the twelve months of the year as twelve stages of cultivation and equating the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind with the various Buddhas.

When the Bodhisattva pressed his skin, flesh, blood, veins, bones, and joints, he suddenly heard voices at the ears of the eight classes of devas and nāgas, signifying the attainment of the stages of Śrāvaka and Arhat;
before his eyes, he suddenly beheld the dark Māra, signifying that the meditative state could not yet be fully delineated;
or he saw golden sand spread upon the ground, or saw thousand-petaled precious lotuses, or saw towers, pavilions, and palaces.
The practitioner may see a lion or an elephant king; or hear the roar of a dragon or a tiger; or see the sun and moon shining together;
or see the Buddhas of the ten directions; or see billions of transformation bodies who claim for themselves the titles of Śākyamuni, Maitreya, or the Supreme Dharma King.
Such persons shall fall forever into hell, with no time of release. Furthermore, there are heterodox teachers.
Some, having practiced illusory arts or engaged in silent meditation and dark contemplation for many years, naturally attract various spirits and demons into their hearts and viscera.
These individuals become skilled in discourse and claim, "I have attained the five eyes and six supernatural powers;
I know the past and future. They falsely proclaim the good and bad fortune, calamities and blessings among humanity, saying, "Today, such-and-such a person has come to see me."
On such-and-such a day, when certain matters arise and one perceives impending calamities, some people falsely claim that by severing greed and desire, one will obtain profit;
they further say, "I am an incarnation of a certain Buddha who has come specifically to save you. You need not strictly observe the precepts of fasting, nor need you worship other teachers;
simply by making offerings to me, I shall teach you how to naturally attain Buddhahood. There are those of this sort.
Foolish men and women believe this to the very marrow of their bones and submit to it upon hearing the wind of its fame;
from then on, they form gangs and groups to secretly practice perverse deeds. Such people shall forever be kinsmen of Māra and shall long remain seeds for the hells.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If a practitioner of the Way does not sever lust, killing, stealing, and falsehood, yet wishes to seek the Way..."
It is just as if one were to steam sand to make rice; though it continues for immeasurable kalpas, it can never be accomplished. O virtuous ones!

If you study the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* thoroughly, you will recognize all demons, heretics, and heterodox teachers. Furthermore, there are blind masters who, despite teaching people to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, do not understand the great principle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
they speak recklessly and confusedly from beginning to end, failing to recognize the ultimate destination of purity.
Some do not form the right vow for rebirth in the Pure Land, but merely crave wealth and status in future lives. How could they know that such wealth and status are temporary?
When their merit is exhausted, they will inevitably return to the cycle of birth and death, drifting through many kalpas in the evil realms. Such people are pitiable and tragic; alas, what suffering!

Furthermore, there are blind masters who do not entrust their disciples with the koan of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), but instead assemble the masses to practice seated meditation upon ascending the hall.
Failing to recognize the starting point of one’s investigation, they claim to have attained the stage of "several levels" of practice;

today they speak of Chan and the Way, and tomorrow they speak of Chan and the Way. Today their bodies feel heavy, while yesterday they felt light; or, when pressed by the breath, they claim it is due to diligent effort;
or, when spitting up phlegm and blood, they take it as the removal of defilements; or they sit in a state of dull stupor and death-like stillness.

Regarding those who speak of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), some stumble and leap about while attempting to manifest [realization], or see Buddhas surrounding them preaching the Dharma within their own eyes, or hear music with their ears and wander at will;
such people merely waste their years in vain, betraying their own spirits, and shall suffer through the cycle of rebirth forever without any means of liberation.
Alas! To practice Chan and study the Way is itself the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*). Yet, when encountered—

For such people, this instead becomes poisonous pleasure. Have you not heard that the ancestral masters of successive generations have directly pointed to the heart-source, teaching that seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha?
It is truly lamentable that deluded people do not know their own minds are the Buddha!

The Buddhas and ancestral masters merely employ various skillful means, parables, and teachings because the faculties of sentient beings vary—some being sharp and others dull, some awakening quickly and others slowly.
When people of the world do not awaken, what can be done? They are instead bound by worldly toil and fettered into the cycle of saṃsāra;
at that time, regret will be of no avail, for it will be too late. I exhort those who study the Way:
if you cannot achieve sudden awakening, then constantly recollect, constantly remember, constantly awaken to, and constantly illuminate a single phrase—namely, "Namo Amitābha Buddha. Why is this so?
At this time, even if one has not yet attained awakening, once one passes away and achieves birth in the highest grade of the Pure Land, what need is there to worry about not attaining awakening?
Good friends, you must know that the single gate of Buddha-recitation truly transcends all other gates.
As it is said in the *Lianzong baojian*: "To study the Way through other gates is like an ant attempting to climb a high mountain; [only] in the Pure Land can one attain rebirth."
Like a wind-blown sail sailing upon favorable currents, one is received by Amitābha and proceeds directly toward Bodhi. Supported by the assembly of sages, one transcends the three realms;

those of the highest grade ascend immediately to the fruit of Buddhahood, while even those of the lowest grade are superior to dwelling in the celestial palaces. I entreat you all to refrain from doubt and practice together without regressing.
If a person wishes to be born in the Pure Land, they must prepare the provisions for the Pure Land. What are these provisions for the Pure Land?
The three characters "Provisions" (糧), "Faith" (信), and "Aspiration" (願) are complete; with these three fully present, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land. It is further said:
"From here to the west, passing ten thousand myriad leagues of distance—if the provisions are complete, why worry that one cannot go? Regarding the *Avalokiteśvara* Samādhi, it says:
"Recalling the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, in the present and in the future, one will certainly see the Buddha. To "recall and mind" means that the mind is uninterrupted.
"Cutting off" refers to seeing the Buddha in the present life; "coming" refers to seeing the Buddha in future lives.
Whether one is diligent or indolent depends entirely upon the person themselves; provided you simply possess a resolute mind, you will certainly not be deceived.
An Exposition on Encouraging the Development of True and Great Vows for Certain Rebirth in the Pure Land:
The Eighth Patriarch, Cizhao, said: "If there is practice without vows, that practice will surely be solitary; if there are vows without practice, those vows will surely be empty.

To have neither practice nor vows is to dwell in vain within Jambudvīpa; to have both practice and vows is to enter directly into the non-outflow state (anāsrava). This is the teaching of the Buddha."
The Patriarch’s cultivation of pure karma is the very foundation. Why is this so? Practice is guided by wisdom, and practice is initiated by vows.

When vows and wisdom are balanced and both are fully present, one is complete. Now, "vows" refers to joy and desire. To desire birth in the Pure Land of the West and to wish to behold Amitābha Buddha, one must necessarily make a vow;
only then can one attain rebirth there. Without the mind of aspiration, even roots of goodness will not suffice.
The *Submerged Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Those who do not give rise to great vows are possessed by Māras; all Buddha-activities arise from great vows.
Because one desires to accomplish the unsurpassed path, it is necessary to attain the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

Thus, Samantabhadra has an ocean of vast and boundless vows, and Amitābha has the six or eight gates of vows. From this we know that this is the way of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the ancient sages of antiquity.
All are accomplished through the power of vows and bring about the realization of Bodhi. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle 8) Question:
Since the practices and deeds of all Bodhisattvas are pure, they naturally obtain superior rewards; why is it necessary to establish vows before attaining them?
For example, when farmers obtain grain, do they wait for a vow? Answer: Performing prostrations without a vow leaves nothing established. It is by means of a vow that one establishes a goal.
To govern oneself for the sake of the Way so as to achieve accomplishment is as the Buddha has taught:

if a person cultivates little merit and little precept-keeping, yet does not know the true cause of liberation, and upon hearing of the joys of humans and devas, their mind constantly aspires to them, then after their life ends, they will each be reborn therein;
all of this is brought about by the power of aspiration. For a Bodhisattva to seek birth in a Pure Land depends upon the strength of their vow.

Thereafter, one attains it; furthermore, it is said that although one may cultivate only a small amount of merit, because of the power of one's vows (*praṇidhāna*), one attains great retribution and great adornment.
The *Mahāvyūha-sūtra* states: "The great matter of the Buddha-land cannot be accomplished by practicing meritorious deeds alone;

it must be assisted by the power of vows to attain rebirth there and see the Buddha according to one's wish. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra) says: "If there are those who have faith, they should..."
Regarding the aspiration to be born in that land, the "Chapter on the Vows of Conduct" (*Caryāpraṇidhāna*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"When such a person approaches the end of life, at the final moment, all their faculties shall completely dissolve and perish; all kinsmen and relatives shall completely abandon them;
all power and influence shall completely fade away; and even such things as elephants, horses, carriages, precious treasures, and hidden hoards—all these shall likewise [vanish]."
No longer following one another, may we only never be separated from this very vow, and at all times lead it before us;
within a single kṣaṇa, we shall attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.

Inferring from this, one should appropriately make vows at every moment, longing for and yearning toward rebirth there, praying daily so as not to let [the aspiration] decline or be lost; therefore, it is said that "this dharma-gate is vast and great."
Since there is no wish that is not fulfilled, the Buddha accords with the minds of people to satisfy their aspirations. Alas!
Observing those of the present age who place their faith and take refuge in the Buddhist assembly, some resolve their hearts because of the suffering of illness;
some raise their intent to repay their parents; some seek to protect and support their homes; and some observe the fasts out of fear of transgression. Although they possess this faith, yet...
Regarding those who lack practice and vows, although they are said to "recite the Buddha's name," they do not reach the fundamental root;

all the wholesome conditions they cultivate are merely for the sake of fulfilling their worldly desires, and it is rare to find anyone who makes a vow for their own birth-and-death to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Often, the words of aspiration and dedication used at incense altars and ritual sites are merely expressions for offering to the spirits and deities to eliminate calamities and prolong life.
The aforementioned [practices] contradict the original intent of the sutras and repentance rituals and do not accord with the fundamental vows of the Buddhas.

Even if one spends a lifetime reciting them without clarifying their underlying principles and applies effort in error, this is called "counting another's treasures all day long while having not even half a coin for oneself.
The reason one cannot attain rebirth in the Pure Land at the time of death is precisely because of a lack of practice and vows.
Furthermore, there is a class of deluded people who, having taken refuge with the Buddha and received the precepts, burn incense before the Triple Gem and make a vow, saying:
"If I break the precepts, may I willingly endure evil diseases afflicting my body and fall forever into hell"; or they say:
"May my left eye bleed and my right eye ooze pus. They thus voluntarily accept such retribution. I have often seen those who, though possessing the words, lack the heart, and thus violate the fast.

Violating the precepts brings calamity and misfortune, leading to various evil retributions in this very body; one may encounter kings, judges, and officials in the present life, or after death fall into the three miserable realms and the hells.
Alas! One does not realize that the Buddhas and Patriarchs give rise to compassion and exercise pity;
they have never taught people in such a manner. All of this is the fault of false teachers who mistakenly take punitive incantations (*dhāraṇīs*) for the arousal of vows. How deluded!
"How profound this is! I have often felt compassion for you and urged you to together make the right vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land and aspire to become Buddhas.
Yet you replied, 'I am but an ordinary person; how would I dare hope to be born in the Pure Land or to become a Buddha?
To harbor such a thought would only result in delusive fantasy. I responded to him, saying: 'Not so, O Good Friend. A Buddha is awakening (buddha), and purity..."
Earth is the mind; who does not possess this mind? To awaken is to be a Buddha; to be deluded is to be a sentient being.
Worldly people turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses, transmigrating through the three realms, the four modes of birth, and the six paths.

Whether they receive retribution for good or evil karma—whether it be pleasant or ugly—it is all because they falsely identify the four elements as their own body and regard the six sense-objects as truly existent, following after illusory appearances day after day.

Wandering through the night without ever briefly reflecting upon returning the light [of the mind], one observes the precepts and recites the Buddha’s name; yet from birth until old age, one worries only that domestic affairs are not settled and wealth does not satisfy the heart.
The more one possesses, the more one seeks; the more greedy one becomes, the less one feels sufficient.

Though one may claim to accumulate merit by serving the Buddha, prostrating, performing acts of virtue, and burning incense, it is only for the sake of wishing for wealth, nobility, splendor, longevity, and immortality—doing only this much.

Upon encountering even minor good fortune, one immediately harbors numerous hidden aspirations: wishing to ensure that grain fills the granaries, that silkworms yield ten-thousandfold silk, that descendants become illustrious, and that cattle and horses multiply.
Yet, as soon as even a single thing does not go according to plan, one complains that the Buddha fails to provide full protection.
Only when wealth and joy increase day by day does one claim it is a response from devas and nāgas. Such greedy scheming is precisely deluded thought.
To claim that those who contemplate and seek birth in the Pure Land are creating delusive thoughts is surely a great perversion.

All so-called cultivation of merit belongs entirely to the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); it is a worldly cause with outflows (*sāsrava*), not the supramundane path of unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta*).
Practitioners of the Buddha-way should reflect well upon this: having encountered the Buddha-dharma today through favorable conditions, you must investigate its true meaning.
Do not compete over the branches; rather, turn the light of a single thought back toward the source to cultivate the supramundane Dharma.
Wish to abandon *saṃsāra* and wish to be born in the Pure Land, just as a long-term traveler in a foreign land longs to return to his native village.

This aspiration to be born in the Pure Land and the mind that desires to become a Buddha—how could these be compared to the deluded thoughts of ordinary people? Have you not seen what is said in the *Sūtra of Repentance*: [text follows]?
"May I, when the time comes for my life to end, be completely freed from all obstacles, behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face,
and immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. This may be called "one morning treading the path by which one came,
only then realizing that all along one's mind was applied in error."
Preface and Verses on the Vow of Those Who Practice Nianfo, by the Patriarch Cizhao The *Nine Essentials of Amitābha* states:
"For those who practice nianfo, the most urgent matter is that their practice not correspond with unwholesome states. Why is this?
Although one may be said to uphold the precepts and practice nianfo, if one has never resolved the mind to be reborn in the Pure Land, it is all merely burying one's head while passing the days."
Having lost the great benefit for oneself, one who practices the recollection of the Buddha must first resolve to transcend birth and death and be reborn in the Pure Land.

One should take the Great Vow as one’s primary intention and constantly recite the Buddha’s name. Morning and evening, one must single-mindedly prostrate to Amitābha, never missing these two times, just as one would attend upon an emperor.
As the days pass, one draws closer to the Buddha; when mind and mouth are in accord with the Buddha, one approaches him.

Without being far from the Buddha, one recites His name with the mouth, contemplates Him with the mind, and desires to see Him with the heart, making deep and solemn vows with resolute faith and no doubt.
As days and years pass and one’s practice becomes mature, the samādhi of spontaneity is naturally accomplished.

At the time of death, Amitābha will welcome and guide one, and the Pure Land will appear before one. Furthermore, may one, within this present life, constantly encounter virtuous spiritual friends and never meet teachers of false views.

Without delusion, my mind shall not give rise to indolence. If one practices *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) in this manner with deep faith and makes a vow, then these three—faith, practice, and the vow—will not be deficient.
At the time of death, seeing the Buddha is not something that comes from without; it is entirely a manifestation of one's own mind.
It is just like seeds sown in the earth that sprout when spring arrives: how could they come from outside? They all emerge from the earth itself. Now...

The practice of this is likewise so: by maintaining the mindfulness, faith, and aspiration for Amitābha within the ground of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñānas*), they will manifest at the moment of death as the Pure Land and Amitābha;
these do not come from outside, but emerge entirely from one's own mind. As the verse says:
All phenomena arise from the mind; all phenomena cease within the mind. Thus has the Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly taught.
If one upholds the precepts but lacks faith and aspiration, they shall not be born in the Pure Land, but shall instead receive only the blessings of humans and devas.
When these blessings are exhausted, they undergo saṃsāra, revolving through it and finding it difficult to escape.
Reading the sutras without the eye of wisdom, one does not recognize the Buddha’s profound intent;
though one may attain intelligence in future lives, a distracted mind makes liberation difficult. It is better to recite the Buddha’s name;
in this life, free from fame and profit, whether walking or sitting, with no more distraction than a few moments, through the power of making vows and upholding the precepts, one is indeed Amitābha.
Dedicating merit to be born in the Land of Bliss is precisely what one should practice. "Among a thousand, not even one shall be lost"—this was spoken from the golden mouth of Śākyamuni;
Amitābha himself will embrace them, and all Buddhas will protect and mind them.

When the various devas see these practitioners of mindfulness of the Buddha, they will provide excellent protection and support. Such people who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are not far removed from the Buddha.
One should sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the great wheel of Dharma, universally delivering boundless multitudes.
Just as the daughter of a poor family conceives a Wheel-Turning King in her womb, whom the various devas constantly protect,
yet the poor woman herself does not know that there is a noble son within her womb— so it is with these people who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Their intention is likewise thus: they recollect the Buddha and constantly think of him, yet they do not know for themselves that before long they shall attain Buddhahood, being well protected by all Buddhas.
They desire instead to be born in a pure land only in a future life, so as to be reborn among humans once again—just like a poor person’s house.
Within the earth there are hidden treasures, Guarded constantly by treasure deities, Yet they cause no loss;
the poor simply do not know of them. Within one’s own home there is a precious store, Yet day after day one seeks work as a laborer to provide for oneself with food and clothing.
Now, this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha— Their situation is just like this.
Those who do not know that the person who recites the Buddha’s name is fully endowed with the *tathāgatagarbha* say of themselves,
"I have no share [in it]," yet they instead seek rebirth among humans. It is like a sick person’s house where there is naturally a truly wondrous medicine,
but because they do not know the nature of this wondrous medicine, they cannot cure their own illness, even as they lie day after day by their bedside.
Suffering is immeasurable, yet for this person who now recollects the Buddha, their mind is likewise such that they do not know [the existence of] a mind that does not recollect the Buddha.
This is able to extinguish the diseases of greed and hatred;
it is able to act as a Great King of Physicians and a Great Treasury of Jewels, benefiting and delivering all people, and acting as a Great Dharma King.
Protecting all sentient beings, [he] considers them as mere ordinary persons;

unable to be born in the Pure Land, they must first maintain the fasts and precepts themselves. Wishing to become human in future lives, they practice the path further and further until they may finally be born in that land.
Seeing many practitioners, he constantly speaks in this way.
Not praising the vows of Amitābha, And not conforming to the Pure Land sutras— When the mind is shrouded by such false views, it will ultimately be difficult to escape them.
This is not the obstruction of others; It is entirely the obstruction of one's own mind.
If you do not attain birth in this very life, One missed opportunity is a hundred missed opportunities. I exhort you, O practitioner!
Believe me when I say that the Tathāgata speaks no words that are not true; how could these be empty or deceptive?
You should simply exert yourself with diligence and seek the Pure Land with a single mind.

Just as fire fanned by the wind requires little effort to spread, if you possess the heart of mindfulness of the Buddha and turn your vows toward transcending the three realms, you will surely succeed.
Meeting with jewels, one does not take them; Encountering food, one suffers from hunger and cold.
Alas! Great man, you do not perceive the true meaning. I now briefly offer this exhortation and praise:
Pass it on from person to person, and for my sake let it be widely circulated. Act as the messenger of the Tathāgata; You shall truly be a child of the Buddhas.
Truly repay the Buddha’s kindness; May all universally practice as taught. [Together] be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Tiantai Master Zhizhe encourages people to single-mindedly cultivate the Pure Land. Tenth, he poses a question:
"If the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their primary vocation, and if they wish to rescue and deliver sentient beings, they ought only to..."

If one vows to be born within the three realms and amidst the five turbidities and the three miserable destinies to save suffering sentient beings, why would one instead seek birth in a pure land to secure one’s own person, abandoning sentient beings?
To do so would mean lacking great compassion, acting solely for one's own benefit, and obstructing the path to Bodhi.
Answer: There are two kinds of bodhisattvas. The first are those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path and attained [non-arising wisdom]...

Those who have produced the patience of realization (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) truly deserve this responsibility; however, those who have not yet attained it—beginning from the stage of initial resolve down to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)—are called "ordinary bodhisattvas.
Such ordinary beings must always remain inseparable from the power of the Buddha’s patience;

only when they have perfected that power are they capable of dwelling within the triple world (*tridhātu*) to rescue suffering sentient beings amidst evil ages. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ordinary beings bound by all fetters may possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)."
It is impossible for one who wishes to be born in an evil world to save suffering sentient beings. Why? Because in an evil world, afflictions are powerful;

lacking the power of patience, the mind turns according to external conditions and is bound by sounds and forms. One will fall into the three miserable realms oneself—how then could one save sentient beings?
Even if one were to be born among humans, the Path of the Sages is difficult to attain, perhaps only through the observance of precepts and the cultivation of merit.

Even if one is born among humans and attains the status of a king, a high minister, or enjoys wealth, nobility, and sovereignty, should they encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) yet refuse to trust or follow them, becoming greedily deluded and negligent while extensively committing various transgressions;
by virtue of this evil karma, they shall enter the three miserable realms (trāya) and pass through immeasurable kalpas.
Upon emerging from hell, they will receive the body of a poor and lowly person; if they do not meet a virtuous friend again, they will fall back into hell.
The prison of saṃsāra is like this, and from beginningless time until today, every person has been thus;
this is what is called the "difficult path. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "It is impossible for one who cannot save oneself from illness to be able to save those who are ill.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "For example, there were two men, each with relatives who had been drowned by water. One man..."
If one rushes directly into the water to rescue others, because they lack the power of skillful means, both parties will drown.
However, if one possesses skillful means and goes to fetch a boat or raft, they can board it and rescue them all, so that everyone escapes the peril of drowning.

A bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind is also like this: having not yet attained the power of patience (*kṣānti*), they cannot rescue sentient beings; for this reason, they must always remain close to the Buddha.
Only after attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) can one save sentient beings, just as one who has obtained a boat [can cross the sea]. Furthermore, the treatise says:
"For example, an infant cannot be separated from its mother; otherwise, it might fall into a pit or well and die of thirst for milk.

Or, like a fledgling whose wings and feathers are not yet formed, it can only rely on the tree and cling to the branches, unable to travel far; only when its wings and pinions are fully developed can it fly through the air of its own accord."
For ordinary beings who lack the power for unimpeded liberation, there is only the practice of single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha to achieve samādhi.

Because this is accomplished through the power of karma, at the time of death, by concentrating the mind, they will certainly attain rebirth without doubt; they shall behold Amitābha Buddha and realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having done so, they return to the triple world, riding the boat of the patience of non-arising to rescue suffering sentient beings and perform extensive Buddha-works as they see fit.

Because of mastery over the mind, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that practitioners who sport in the hells, having been born in that land, attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and then re-enter the realms of birth and death to teach and transform those in the hells, rescuing sentient beings from their suffering.
For this reason, you virtuous ones should single-mindedly cultivate the Pure Land and seek rebirth there; may you recognize this teaching. Thus says the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*.
The title of this treatise is *The Path of Easy Practice*.
Chan Master Yongming Zhoushou stated that those who have not attained realization should not disparage the Pure Land, for eleven reasons.
Someone asked: "If one merely sees one's nature and awakens to the Way, one transcends birth and death; why then is it necessary to fix the mind on that Buddha and seek rebirth there?"
Another [person] replied: "A true practitioner of cultivation should examine themselves with scrutiny; as the saying goes, 'When a person drinks water, they know its temperature for themselves.
I now present this mirror of truth to shatter many delusions.

You virtuous ones should observe whether your own practice and understanding truly constitute seeing one's nature and awakening to the Way, receiving the prediction of the Tathāgata and succeeding to the rank of the Patriarchs—can you be like Aśvaghoṣa or Nāgārjuna?"
Can one match the Venerable Tiantai Zhizhe, who attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* with unimpeded eloquence, such that both his doctrine and practice were universally esteemed?
Can one match National Teacher Huizhong, who was proficient in both exegesis and cultivation? These great beings all clearly bestowed instructions and earnestly encouraged rebirth;
since this is for the benefit of both self and others, how could they have feared it themselves, especially when the Great Hero [the Buddha] praised it?
The Buddha’s own words were earnest and sincere; following the examples of the sages of old, we respectfully receive his instructions, certain that they contain no error.

Furthermore, the deeds of the eminent worthies of past and present recorded in the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Those Who Attain Rebirth) are numerous and manifest; one should diligently study them to reflect upon oneself.
Moreover, one must personally examine whether, at the moment of death, one will certainly attain mastery over life and death and over going or staying. If not, [one must prepare].
Since the beginning, have your heavy karmic obstacles from past evil deeds definitely ceased to manifest? Is this retribution-body definitely liberated from saṃsāra?
Do you move freely through the various classes of beings in the three miserable realms and evil paths, appearing and disappearing at will without any suffering or affliction?
Can you dwell wherever you please throughout the heavens, the human realm, and the worlds of the ten directions without any hindrance? If this is not yet so, do not [be complacent].
Because of a momentary arrogance, one may instead cause oneself to sink into eternal samsara and lose the benefit of the good; whom else can one blame? Alas, how lamentable!
What sighing can avail now? The "Fourfold Selection" says: First, there are those who have Chan but no Pure Land—nine out of ten go astray.
If the realm of the shadows manifests, they will suddenly follow it away. This refers to those who clarify only the principle-nature alone.
I vow that those who would otherwise fall back into the cycle of transmigration within this Sahā world shall instead be delivered.

Regarding the "five aggregates" (skandhas), these refer to the manifestation of the *māras* within the state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), as clearly explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. When fifty kinds of demonic activities arise within the realm of the five aggregates, the person initially fails to perceive them;
thus, the demons take possession of them, and they falsely claim to have personally attained supreme *nirvāṇa*, remaining utterly deluded.
Those who fall into the Avīci Hell are such as these. Second: "No dhyāna, yet there is the Pure Land; ten out of ten who practice will go.

This means that although one has not yet clarified the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), by simply aspiring for rebirth and relying on the power of the Buddha, one will certainly attain it without doubt.
Third: "Both dhyāna and the Pure Land exist; it is like a tiger with horns appearing."

Having served as a teacher to humanity in this world and being reborn as a Buddha or Patriarch in the next, one who has deeply penetrated the Buddha-dharma is fit to be a teacher for humans and devas;

furthermore, by making the vow to be reborn there, one may swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression. This can truly be called "wrapping ten thousand taels of gold around one's waist and riding a crane up to Yangzhou.
Fourth: "Neither Chan nor Pure Land—iron beds and copper pillars; through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is nowhere to go."
Since people lack a clear understanding of the Buddha’s principles and have no desire for rebirth in the Pure Land, they will sink into eternal delusion; by what means can they escape?
O virtuous ones, if you wish to transcend birth and death and swiftly realize Bodhi, you must select and practice these four kinds of wholesome deeds.
Chan Master Changlu Ze’s Exhortation for Those Who Practice Chan to Also Cultivate the Pure Land, Part Twelve:
To take mindfulness as having something to mind and to take birth as having something to be born is the error of common views.
To take non-mindfulness as being without mindfulness and to take non-birth as being without birth is the delusion of false views. [Yet] to be mindful while being without mindfulness and to be born...
That which is non-arising is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, on the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust is received;

consequently, above there are no Buddhas to be contemplated, and below there is no pure land to be born into. Yet, within the gateway of Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*), not a single dharma is abandoned;

thus, all faculties are universally encompassed. This reveals the essential art for returning to the source through the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), opening the way for those who have departed.

The reason for being born through the single gate is that one recites the Buddha’s name all day long without deviating from non-recollection, and burns with fervor toward rebirth without deviating from non-birth.
Thus, while ordinary beings and sages each abide in their own positions, the path of resonance and response intersects;
though there is no coming or going between east and west, the spirit migrates to the Pure Land. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If a person hears it said that Amitābha Buddha..."
Those who uphold the Name—even such a person, at the time of death, will have a mind free from delusion and shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Alas! Those of shallow faith who give rise to groundless doubts and slanders do not believe the sincere words of the Buddhas;
they do not believe in rebirth in the Pure Land—is this not a profound delusion? If one believes the words of the Buddha and gives rise to [faith]...
As for the Pure Land, the karma of accumulated fetters cannot bind it, and the fires of the kalpa-ending conflagration cannot burn it.
It transcends the eight sufferings of the human realm and lacks the five signs of decline found in the heavens; even the name of the evil realms does not exist there, let alone their reality.
As the Sūtra says: "The beings of that land have no manifold sufferings, but experience only various joys; therefore, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī). Now, by means of this...
When comparing this Sahā world with that [pure land]: here, all who possess a physical body of flesh and blood suffer the suffering of birth;

there, one is born by transformation from a lotus flower and thus lacks the suffering of birth. Here, the seasons change and pass, and aging gradually encroaches; there, cold and heat do not shift, and thus there is no suffering of aging.
Here, the four great elements are difficult to harmonize, resulting in many illnesses and ailments; there, the body is a transformed manifestation.
[In this world] one is fragrant and pure, yet suffers from illness; here, those who reach seventy are rare, for impermanence is swift.
[In that world] one’s lifespan is immeasurable, and there is no suffering of death. Here, one has affection for kin, and where there is love, there must be separation.

There, one has no parents, wives, or children, and thus no suffering of being separated from what one loves. Here, one has enemies and foes, and where there is enmity, there must be a meeting. There, however...
Those of the highest goodness gather together, free from the suffering of meeting with those one hates;

whereas these [others] suffer from hardship, hunger, and cold, never having enough despite their greed, those [beings] possess clothing, food, and precious jewels for their enjoyment, all spontaneously present.

These have ugly and impure bodies with many defective sense organs, while those are of upright and majestic appearance, their bodies possessing radiance. These revolve through birth and death, while those have forever realized [liberation].
In this [world], there are mounds, hills, ravines, pits, thornbushes, forests, mountains of earth and stone, and it is filled with foul impurities;
in that [world], the ground is of pure gold, jewel-trees reach toward the heavens, towers soar high, the seven treasures abound, and flowers of four colors bloom.
In this [world], the Twin Trees have already perished and the Dragon Flower has not yet appeared; in that [world], Amitābha Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma. In this [world]...

While Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are merely admired from afar for their illustrious names, here [in this realm], those two superior beings personally serve as one’s most excellent spiritual friends;
while there, the various māras and externalists disturb and disrupt correct cultivation, here, the Buddha’s transformation is unified and the traces of māras and externalists have vanished;
while there, seductive forms and licentious charms delude practitioners, here, the primary retribution is pure and truly no women exist. Furthermore, here...
While malevolent beasts and *chi-mei* demons there spread perverse sounds, the waterfowl and forest trees in that land all proclaim the sublime Dharma.
When comparing these two lands, their environments and conditions are vastly different; yet the excellences of the Land of Bliss are infinite, and it is impossible to enumerate them all here.

Therefore, in the definitive Mahāyāna teachings, there is nothing that does not point toward the Pure Land; sages of both past and present, as well as those seeking their own and others' benefit, all aspire to it.

In the aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land, if one wishes to deliver others, one must first practice mindfulness of the Buddha oneself. Alas! If a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will surely encounter immediate distress.
Once this human body is lost, it is difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas;

therefore, lead the great assembly of the ocean-like multitude to each recite the name of Amitābha Buddha—whether a hundred times, a thousand times, or even ten thousand times—and dedicate these merits toward the common vow to be born in that land, earnestly aspiring for rebirth among the lotus flowers.
When the excellence of the assembly at the pond and the brilliance of the Dharma at the Golden Ground mutually support one another, this vow will surely be fulfilled;
it is like rowing a boat downstream with the current—by adding the effort of oars and paddles, even a journey of a hundred thousand li will be reached without toil.

In the winter of the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, (Zongze) dreamed at night of a man wearing a black cap and white robes, approximately thirty years of age, with a refined and handsome appearance and graceful demeanor.
The man bowed and said to Zongyi, "I wish to enter your Amitābha assembly;
please record my name as Zongze. Thereupon, [Zongyi] took up the *Record of the Supreme Assembly of the Lotus* and, holding his pen, asked: "Sir—"

"What is your name? he asked. "I am named Puhui (Universal Wisdom)," he replied. After the monk had finished writing, the layman spoke again, saying, "My elder brother also told me to address you by the name Zongze.
He then asked, "What is your elder brother's name? The man replied, "Puxian (Samantabhadra). Having said this, he suddenly vanished.

When Zongze awoke and inquired of the senior monks, they all said that in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are two great bodhisattvas by those names.
Zongze believed that when a son of the Buddha performs Buddhist deeds and assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation, there must be worthy sages who provide subtle support.
Thus, those who participate in this assembly must surely possess no small karmic affinity. Now, two great Bodhisattvas shall serve as the leaders of this assembly.
Alas! The Dharma of the Pure Land is revered by the Great Sage; how could ordinary practitioners of Chan meditation afford to treat it with negligence?
The Layman Wang of Longshu exhorted people to practice the Pure Land method directly.

Throughout thirteen generations, there have been those who specialized exclusively in Chan meditation, claiming that "the pure land is solely within the mind" and asserting that there is no other pure land apart from the self-nature Amitābha, such that one need not seek to see Amitābha externally.
All of these views are mistaken. Why? Because these words are exceedingly lofty and profound.
I fear it will not be easy to reach that Western Pure Land where there is no greed, no attachment, no anger, and no delusion;
can my own mind be free from greed, attachment, anger, and delusion? In that Western Pure Land, if one thinks of clothing, one obtains clothing; if one thinks of food, one obtains food;
if one desires stillness, one is at peace; if one desires to go, one may go. But if I think of clothing and have no clothing, I am distressed by the cold.
If the mind craves food but there is no food, hunger distresses the mind; if it desires stillness but cannot attain it, the multitude of disturbances distresses the mind;
if it wishes to depart but cannot do so, its fetters distress the mind. This is what is called the "Pure Land of Mind-Only," which is truly not easy to reach.
That Amitābha Buddha is fully endowed with merit and wisdom, and his spiritual powers are vast.
To transform the great Avīci Hell into lotus flowers as easily as turning over one's palm, and to behold infinite worlds all present before one’s eyes—my karmic obstructions are heavy;
I fear falling into hell, so how could I transform it into lotus flowers?
If one cannot even see what is happening in the next room, how much less can one see infinite worlds? This is what is called "Amida of one's own nature" (jishō Amida).
Truly, it is not easy to reach that state. How can those who practice Chan meditation today neglect the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it, or abandon Amitābha and refuse to desire to see him?
The Great Amitābha Sūtra states: "In the ten directions, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
If even those bodhisattvas desire to be reborn there, what person am I that I would not desire to do so?
Is being born there not a fruit superior to that of all other bodhisattvas?

From this it may be said that the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the Amitābha of Self-Nature are vast yet not unnecessary, and sublime yet not irrelevant; those who have not reached this level of practice have misled many people.
I shall briefly cite several instances as evidence: Qingcaotang was the reincarnation of the late Prime Minister Lu Gong, and Zhe Lao was the reincarnation of [the monk] Duohua.

The nun of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* who was reborn as a courtesan in a later life—all such cases involve a lack of faith in the Western Pure Land, leading to successive cycles of saṃsāra and the suffering thereof.
If these individuals had practiced the Western Pure Land, they would certainly have attained birth in the highest grade of the highest class;
it is solely because of their lack of faith that they instead met with such ruin. It would be better to "plant one's feet on solid ground" by upholding the recitations and practicing the path.
To attain direct rebirth in the Pure Land and straightway escape the cycle of saṃsāra is worlds apart from those whose words are empty and devoid of substance.
Someone said: "While it is indeed difficult to see one's nature through Zen meditation, how does the study of the Immortals (*xiān*) compare? I replied:

"To seek to study the arts of the Immortals without first cultivating the Pure Land is like casting aside a beautiful jade gem found before one's eyes to search for a *wǔfū* stone that may not even exist. How could this be right?"
How unconfused they are! Why is this? According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are ten kinds of immortals who all live for a thousand million years;
yet when their lifespan is exhausted, they re-enter the cycle of saṃsāra because they have never realized the true nature.

Thus, they share the same name as the sentient beings of the six realms—these are all people within the seven destinies of saṃsāra. Among the world’s seekers of immortality, not one in ten thousand succeeds; even if they...
Even if one attains it, one cannot escape the cycle of *saṃsāra*, for one remains attached to form and spirit (*rūpa* and *citta*) and is unable to relinquish them.
Furthermore, form and spirit are but delusive thoughts manifested within true nature; they are not reality. Thus, Hanshan’s poem says:
"Even if you were to become an immortal, you would be no different from a ghost guarding a corpse. This is unlike the Buddhist state, where one is at ease amidst birth and death.
There is nothing that can restrain it. In recent centuries, those who attained immortality were limited to none other than Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin;

yet among those who studied under Zhongli and Lü, surely there have been thousands and tens of thousands. Among my own personal acquaintances, such individuals were not few, yet in the end they all died and were buried beneath the earth.
Thus, their lifelong expenditure of mental and physical effort ultimately yielded no benefit whatsoever. Is this not so?
I heard that Lü Dongbin flew his sword to slay the Yellow Dragon, yet he was instead subdued by the Yellow Dragon;

only upon meeting Master Huanglong did he realize his true nature and perfect the Way, whereupon he spoke this verse: "Having cast away my gourd-bag and smashed my lute, I no longer cling to the eternal gold within.
Since the moment I first beheld the Yellow Dragon, I have finally realized that all my previous efforts were a waste of mind."

Furthermore, one has not heard that when Dharma Master Tanluan of the Later Wei first obtained ten fascicles of the *Sūtra of the Immortals* from Tao Hongjing, he was filled with joy, believing that the state of a transcendent immortal could certainly be attained. Later, he encountered the monk Bodhiruci, who asked him:
"In the Way of the Buddha, is there eternal life? Can one ward off old age and become immortal? Bodhiruci replied: "There is no such thing as eternal life."

"Death is the very path of my Buddhahood. He then gave him the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* and said, "If you can recite this, then you shall not be born again within the three realms, nor shall you wander further through the six destinies.
Neither abundance nor depletion, neither fortune nor misfortune, neither success nor failure shall reach you.
As for the measure of such a lifespan, there are kalpa-stones and there are river sands; yet the number of these sands and stones is finite, whereas the span of such a life is not."
"The number of such measures is infinite; this is the longevity of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha).

Luán believed this deeply and subsequently burned the *xianjing* (immortal scriptures) to devote herself exclusively to the practice of the *guan jing* (Contemplation Sutra). Despite the changes of cold and heat and the onset of illness, she never slackened.
King Wei, moved by her aspirations and admiring her practice of transforming both self and others, saw that her teachings spread very widely; he bestowed upon her the title "Divine."
One day, Tanyuan Luan told his disciples, "The various sufferings of the hells must not fail to inspire fear;
the pure karma of the nine grades must not fail to be cultivated. He then instructed his disciples to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha aloud.
Facing west and closing his eyes, Luan prostrated himself and passed away. At that moment, both monastics and laypeople alike heard the sounds of pipes, strings, and flutes coming from the west.
After a long silence, he finally ceased speaking. From this we can observe that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is the most direct and swift path.

Furthermore, as for the practitioners of the Way of the Immortals (xian-shen), once they have attained something, they keep it extremely secret and do not transmit it, fearing that by leaking the celestial mechanism (tian-ji) they will incur sin.

In contrast, the Buddha’s Dharma-gate fears only that its transmission may not be widespread; it desires nothing less than to deliver every single sentient being before it considers its task complete—this is its compassion.
Vast and immeasurable, it is beyond comparison with the attainments of immortals or seers.
In the *Essay on Encouraging the Cultivation of Pure Land* by Chancellor Zheng Qingzhi:

"Fourteen people all claimed that the cultivation of the Pure Land was inferior to Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya; I alone maintained that among the Dharma-gates of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, none [surpass it]."
It is like the cultivation of the Pure Land: the true, pure, luminous, wondrous, and profoundly penetrating nature is inherently present in all beings, whether wise or foolish.
Yet, as the sensory faculties, their objects, and illusory appearances mutually involve one another, they sink into the cycle of birth and death, continuing without end throughout kalpas.
Therefore, the Śākya-muni established the expedient means of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya to lead people through these gates so that they may all attain transcendental awakening—only "A" and "Ho."
Amitābha Buddha alone has opened a single gate, saying: "Cultivating the Pure Land is like treating a disease with a singular remedy;
it is simple, direct, and straightforward. With single-minded concentration, one immediately reaches the other shore. Whether monastic or lay, all may practice this.
To think it is merely a shallow teaching for transforming the ignorant and the vulgar is a mistake; in reality, it is the swift path to attaining Buddhahood. This is the study of the present day.
As for the Buddha’s teachings, none surpass those of Chan, which are ultimate, perfect, and sudden;

yet unless one possesses keen faculties and a superior vessel capable of spiritual reception and mental comprehension, one cannot avoid the error of falling into a dull emptiness. As for the study of the Three Vehicles, none surpasses that of the Teachings (Jiao);

yet unless one can forget the trap upon catching the fish or see the moon through the pointing finger, one cannot avoid the ailment of poring over old paper. To protect the good and shield [the ignorant]...

Nothing is more evil than violating the Vinaya. Unless one’s body and mind are pure and there is a perfect correspondence between inner intent and outward expression, one cannot avoid the suffering of self-entanglement.

Viewed as a whole, if we consider the gateways through which one enters, they are Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya; yet if we consider where they ultimately converge, they are Precepts, Samādhi, and Prajñā.
Is there any gateway other than that of Pure Land through which one may attain these precepts, samādhi, and prajñā? It is none other than this.
When recollecting the Buddha, chanting with the mouth and contemplating with the mind, "Commit no evil"—is this not the binding of precepts?
When the pure object of mindfulness and illusory dust both cease—does this not constitute concentration (*samādhi*)? When the mind of non-thought blossoms in stillness—is this not wisdom (*prajñā*)?

If one can cast aside myriad concerns and direct the single intention toward the Western Land, then without the application of staffs or shouts, one will awaken to the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden teaching, even without reading the Great [Vehicle].
To store the scriptures and thereby attain the Eye of the True Dharma; to attain great mastery without being constrained by the four modes of deportment;
to be neither defiled nor pure, neither bound nor liberated—at such a time, what are precept, concentration, and wisdom? What are meditation, teaching, and discipline?
My own mind and the Buddha-mind are entirely without distinction. This is the ultimate attainment of the Pure Land path: the water of eight virtues.
Why need one doubt the golden lotus pedestal? The composition of this *Essential Pivot of the Pure Land* has been undertaken with diligence.
It clarifies the Western Pure Land of the Great Master the Sixth Patriarch.
A Zen practitioner asked: "The Master says that by reciting the Buddha’s name one will certainly go to the West, yet the Sixth Patriarch said that the West is one's own nature."
"Why need one further seek the words of both houses? Why are they not of a single school?

It is said that the words of the Sixth Patriarch use principle to subsume phenomena, such that there is ultimately no principle outside of phenomena; my own words use phenomena to manifest principle, such that there is ultimately no phenomenon outside of principle.
One must know that there are no objects apart from the mind, for objects are entirely the mind; mental dharmas are all-pervasive, encompassing both phenomena and principle."

Equality exists only because people possess varying degrees of sharpness or dullness in their faculties, which results in differences in their views. If one were able to reach the level of the Sixth Patriarch, there would not even be a Buddha to be mindful of;
how then could there be a Pure Land to be reborn in? If you have not yet attained this, listen to my ultimate teaching. [The interlocutor] said, "I wish to hear it.
[The Master] replied, "The Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch, was an ancient Buddha who returned to this world; he was not an ordinary person of the present age."

Furthermore, the Sixth Patriarch’s teaching of the Dharma focused exclusively on the essential principles of nature (xingli), urging people to let go of all external conditions to achieve Buddhahood in this very moment.
People today do not understand his meaning and merely imitate his words; they are no different from a parrot.
A parrot can only learn human speech but cannot perform human deeds—this is what is meant by "no difference. They have not yet reached the level of the Patriarchs.
Regarding the matter of the ancestral masters' words discussed previously, one might laugh at how they failed to examine themselves.
When asked, "The Sixth Patriarch further stated that if people of the East commit sins, they should recite the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the West;

if people of the West commit sins, they should recite the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in which land? the Sixth Patriarch merely used the metaphors of 'East' and 'West' for monastics and laypeople; he never [meant it literally].

It is said that there is no Buddha-land; the *Platform Sutra* states that practicing while remaining at home is like the people of the East who are without fault, whereas not cultivating while having left the home life is like the people of the West who have transgressions.
Nowadays, people do not investigate the ancient teachings but instead insist on the "fox-speech" and "bird-language" [of eccentric masters].
Furthermore, they take the instructions of the Sixth Patriarch to teach others how to sever delusive thoughts—the mind of greed, the mind of anger, and the mind of jealousy.

The deluded mind, the afflicted mind, the deceitful and hypocritical mind, the false and counterfeit mind, the mind of hatred and attachment, the distracted mind, the mind of right and wrong, the conceited mind, the mind of subject and object, the mind of defiled attachment, the mind of self and others, the mind of grasping and rejecting, the mind of existence and non-existence, and the mind of cultivation and realization—only after one has cast aside these various minds may one be permitted to see one's nature and attain Buddhahood. I ask you: which of these have you been able to eliminate?
I ask you again with all my heart: Are your supernatural powers, wondrous functions, distinct insights, wisdom, and moral virtue equal to those of the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch?
If you have not attained even a fraction of this, you are not permitted to speak such words.
To speak such words is the teaching of a demon, for it severs the seeds of the Buddha; later, in the Avīci Hell, I shall certainly not let you go.

What is the transgression? If there are beginners among practitioners who believe what you have consistently taught—that by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha one will attain birth in the Pure Land of the West, escape the cycle of birth and death, and avoid the sufferings of hell—yet they still fall into hell themselves, they can even bring others along with them into hell; their sin is grave indeed.
It is superior [to other paths] because one's offenses, compared to those of ordinary people, increase by one degree; this is why one has a share in the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, have you not heard the ancient masters say: "If a person slanders and destroys the Pure Land, or does not believe in rebirth there, they shall suffer the torment of having their tongue pulled out"?
Why is this? One must know that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is proclaimed with one voice by all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Chan school proclaims a single sound to expound the Dharma, yet how is it that later students barely heed it? They destroy their own true cause and instead practice demonic teachings;
being unable to cultivate themselves, they further obstruct others from cultivating. To enter hell under such conditions is like an arrow shot;
truly, this is to be pitied. You should quickly and urgently repent, single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, and in a future life you shall be born by transformation within a lotus flower.
Only then did he realize that my words today were not empty; thereupon, the Chan practitioner was struck with awe and trepidation, received the instruction, and withdrew.

These preceding questions and answers, along with their context, all originate from the language of the ancient *Platform Sutra*; they have been deleted and removed by later generations. It may be [restored].
How painful and regrettable!
Regarding the "Text on the Ancestral Masters’ Pointing to the Pure Land":
the number of ancestral masters who pointed to the Pure Land is like motes of dust; now, I shall briefly cite several of them to serve as proof.
Master Tianru said: "I have often observed that many who practice Chan today do not investigate the definitive meaning of the Tathāgata, nor do they understand the profound mechanism of Bodhidharma.
With empty bellies and haughty minds, they habitually act with arrogance;
when they see those who cultivate the Pure Land, they mock them, saying, 'They are merely practicing what fools and commoners do—how vulgar! I have once remarked:"
It is not that these are base, ignorant men or women; rather, it is that they disparage Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and others like them.

Such individuals are not only deluded regarding the Right Path themselves and sever the seeds of Buddhahood within themselves, but they further create the karma of slandering the Dharma and incur the calamity of reviling the sages.
How can one not be cautious? As for all other teachings, it is difficult to escape the cycle of birth and death; therefore, one should practice the recitation of the Buddha's name.
While upholding the cycle of saṃsāra as something easily escaped, one should merely preserve the name of Amitābha Buddha to deliver sentient beings;
those who do not believe and instead slander him shall fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering.

Master Lingzhi said: "Ordinary beings of this vast world are bound by karma and delusions, transmigrating through the five realms for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas while undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Yet, if they suddenly hear of the Pure Land and resolve to seek rebirth there, calling the Buddha’s name but once, they will immediately transcend to that land.
This may truly be called a rare encounter once in ten thousand kalpas, met but once in a thousand lifetimes. If a person is willing to contemplate Amitābha Buddha, they shall transcend [samsara]."
Transcending all roots of goodness, even if one can practice giving, precepts, meditation, and recitation, these do not equal the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha. Why is this?
Although one may cultivate all manner of meritorious deeds, if there is no correct faith in seeking birth in the Pure Land, they are all merely minor roots of goodness.
However, if one mindfully recites the name of Amitābha Buddha and makes a vow to seek birth in the Pure Land, this is called a great root of goodness.
Master Gushan said: "Those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land rely upon three factors:

the power of the other, the compassionate vow of Amitābha, and the encouragement of Śākyamuni along with the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. When these three are complete, if one possesses faith, rebirth is as easy as crossing the great ocean;
having obtained a massive vessel and a skilled guide, and being aided by a favorable wind, one will surely arrive there swiftly."
If one reaches the shore yet refuses to board the boat, lingering instead on the perilous path, whose fault is it?
Prosecutor Yang said: "There is the Buddha Śākyamuni, the Great Teacher, who points toward the Pure Land as the Land of Peace and Bliss;
Amitābha Buddha is the Master of that Pure Land. If you, all sentient beings, are born in that land, then there will be no sufferings whatsoever."

Those who do not hear or know this are truly pitiable; yet there are also virtuous gentlemen who give rise to three kinds of thoughts, and those who do not seek rebirth therein are all the more to be lamented.
The first says: "I shall transcend both Buddhas and Patriarchs; the Pure Land is no place for me to be born. The second says: "Everywhere is a pure land;
the Western Quarter need not be sought for rebirth. The third says: "The Land of Ultimate Bliss is the realm of the sages; we are but ordinary beings [how could we go there?]"

Indeed, one cannot claim an inability to be reborn there. One travels the immeasurable oceans [of worlds] with the vows of Samantabhadra, beholds Amitābha Buddha’s land, and though it may seem empty, Vimalakīrti constantly cultivates the Pure Land.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions offer praise with their broad tongues, and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions share the resolve to go together.
Try to reflect for yourself: who among us can compare with these sages? To say that one is not fit to be reborn—how self-centered is such a thought!
How deceptive it is! Even regarding the patriarch Nāgārjuna, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* contains a prophetic passage concerning him;

and as for Vasubandhu, the founder of the Yogācāra school, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* contains verses on seeking rebirth there. In the *Comprehensive Praise*, the founder of the Ci'en school refers to him first among the "Ten Superior Wise Ones.

When he analyzed the principles and clarified the ten doubts, these were all men of supreme wisdom who, through diligent practice, attained rebirth there. How can one say that rebirth is not necessary?
How self-deluded they are! The fire chariots may be extinguished, and the boat-stones may not sink;

none suffer more severe karmic retribution in the present than Zhang Kui, yet he transcended to the supreme realm through ten recitations. None descend to hell more swiftly than Xiong Jun, yet he was restored to life and realized the wondrous cause.
If the transgressions of worldly people are not necessarily like this, why do you say that rebirth is impossible? How can you be so self-abandoning?
The Patriarch Zhongfeng said: "Saha, Saha! Who can enumerate the sufferings of this Sahā world?

Yet worldly people instead take suffering for pleasure and dwell therein with relish, thereby losing their true selves. From within this stinking skin bag they emerge, nurturing the disease of ignorance until it becomes a malignant parasite.
Suddenly, when the three-inch breath ceases, one is transformed into cold ashes buried beneath the earth."

The five realms of existence flow on without a moment’s rest; for hundreds and thousands of kalpas and lifetimes, one endures bitter suffering. O virtuous ones, why do you not sooner bring to mind Amitābha?
Abandon this suffering of Saha and seek the bliss of the West! The bliss of the Western Land—who can awaken to it?
Both its people and its lands are utterly sublime, free from cold and heat, as well as the three evil paths; there, all dwell within the womb of lotus flowers.
When you emerge [from this world], you shall hear the sounds of the Dharma and celestial music; the lapis lazuli ground is so brilliant it is utterly free of even the finest dust;
pavilions are formed of gold, silver, and precious jewels; transformed robes and transformed food provide natural splendor; and one’s lifespan is immeasurable, beyond calculation.
O virtuous ones, why not contemplate Amitābha early on and attain the bliss of that Western Land?
Master Bianxiu said: "I am devoted exclusively to the Vinaya and mindful of the Buddha, taking the Pure Land as my destination for peaceful nourishment.

There are those who have not mastered the Chan school who claim that *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha's name) is a provisional teaching of the Lesser Vehicle, or that it is merely the Mahāyāna with characteristics (*sanimitta*).
These are the words of those whose minds are as crooked as brambles; they are not the insights of those who have attained profound penetration."

"Whatever words Ya'ou utters, they immediately manifest his true nature; whatever thoughts he conceives, they are all suchness and one. There is not a single color or a single fragrance that is not the Middle Way—how much more so my own right mindfulness!
Master Jishi showed the true vision of the Pure Land, saying: "Those who do not cultivate pure karma falsely claim that their minds roam [in liberation]."
Those of meditative concentration and true insight, upon hearing the teachings on the Pure Land, would invariably say: "The Pure Land is but the mind;
if my own mind is pure, then the land is pure. What need is there to seek another place of rebirth? Jishi said:
"Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states that when the Tathāgata pressed the earth with his toe, the Sahā world was seen to be entirely magnificent and pure, yet the assembly did not perceive it."
Only the Brahma King Śaṅkhakuṇḍala can perceive what I have now described; can those who have awakened their natures truly see the Pure Land as the Brahma King perceives it?
Furthermore, you who dwell in humble rooms and dilapidated houses must surely envy the grand mansions and lofty halls;
those who eat coarse rice and millet soup must surely envy exquisite delicacies and superior flavors; and those who wear tattered robes and short homespun garments must surely envy—
To speak of fine silks and gauzes as if one’s mind were pure and the land were pure is unnecessary conceptualization;
how much more so when, amidst this world of suffering from old age, sickness, and death, and contrary to one's own feelings, one’s appearance is identical to that of the unawakened?
To chant with the mouth the words "the mind is pure and the land is pure," while the body remains bound by the afflictions of this defiled land, is the height of self-deception.
Otherwise, one must have faith in the teachings and look up to the principles, following them to practice in the Pure Land.
Zen Master Zhenxie Liao said: "The shortcut dharma-gate is none other than the merit of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha's name), which is sublime and easy to advance in;
thus, *nianfo* comes first. If one seeks liberation without reciting the Buddha's name, one will ultimately gain nothing. I universally exhort all those of pure faith.
If you recite the Buddha’s name with a focused mind and seek rebirth [in the Pure Land], you will certainly not be mistaken.
Master Guyin said: "The single phrase 'Amitābha Buddha' is a public case (*gong'an*) at the head of the Chan school;
it is like riding a horse while holding a staff—this secure way of life is not restricted by the four classes of practitioners, and whoever maintains it will surely receive its response."
