It is verified that those who currently cultivate merit will have their calamities extinguished, and when their retribution is fulfilled, their karmic obstacles shall be forever removed.

If one stands firm upon this earth and upholds [this teaching], there are none whose wishes are not fulfilled according to their hearts' desire. It is fortunate to be born in the Central Land as a human being;

having once reached such a precious mountain, do not let it pass empty-handed or return in vain. What you must attend to should be prepared with urgency; for King Yama does not value gold or pearls, but prizes only the single name of Amitābha.
Volume One: Riches and nobility arise like clouds; a hundred years of life pass as swiftly as lightning. O you who understand this, do not delay; quickly effect a transformation.
The Buddha is the vessel for crossing the sea of suffering; I urge you to cross to the other shore early. First, take the observance of *śīla* (precepts) as primary;
second, reform evil and turn toward the good; third, rely on a wise teacher and virtuous friends; fourth, apply yourself to liberation and the Right [Dharma].
First, vow to know the cause through the use of wisdom; second, apply various skillful means through the use of practice; third, accumulate merit and virtue through the use of effort;

fourth, bestow blessings and conditions upon one another through the use of compassion. Amidst walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, do not let even a single recitation of Amitābha’s name be interrupted.
You must believe that if the cause is profound, the fruit will be profound. By ensuring that every thought-moment is not empty, you will surely achieve the state of single-minded recitation.

If, at the moment of death, one recognizes the person of Amitābha appearing before oneself as being identical to oneself, one immediately enters the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and personally realizes the inner court of the Pure Land.
Those who have achieved this supreme merit shall see Amitābha face-to-face and receive his prediction of enlightenment;
they will then become companions to the Bodhisattvas and proceed directly to unsurpassed Bodhi, remaining with them for eternal kalpas according to their own wishes.
Having truly relied upon this path, I have returned with the certainty that my attainment of Buddhahood lacks nothing.
Bai Juyi’s verse says:
At seventy-one years of age, I shall no longer devote myself to chanting and recitation; I shall instead observe the scriptures, sparing my eyesight.
I perform meritorious deeds yet fear the toil and bustle; how can I cross over with the eye of the mind?
One invocation of Amitābha—walking, it is Amitābha; sitting, it is Amitābha. Even if one is as busy as a speeding arrow, one does not depart from Amitābha.
The man of realization should laugh at me for having "too much Amitābha."
If you have attained it, how so? And if you have not attained it, what then? I universally exhort the multitudes of the Dharma-realm to together recite the name of Amitābha.
If you wish to escape the suffering of saṃsāra, you must recite the name of Amitābha. Master Wujin said:

"I lament that while my body occupies the rank of a high minister, my heart’s inclination delights in the Gate of Emptiness. Contemplating this world... (The text continues with the five [corruptions]).

With a mind turbid and chaotic, my nature is defiled by manifold evils; lacking the power of right contemplation and the power of the cause for realization, I am unable to awaken to and penetrate the Pure Land of Mind-Only that is the original nature of Amitābha.

Therefore, strictly adhering to the oral teachings of Śākyamuni Buddha, I single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, seeking the empowerment of that World-Honored One’s great vows and mighty power.

Those who are embraced [by the Buddha] will be reborn in Sukhāvatī when their karmic retribution is fulfilled, just as one riding a boat downstream reaches the destination without exerting personal effort.

The Venerable Master Huiyuan said that those in the Chan school who see practitioners of nianfo (buddha-recitation) cultivating the Western Paradise all claim they are practicing with attachment to forms.
This is not yet marvelous; it is better to practice Chan and see one's nature to achieve sudden enlightenment into the true and eternal.

Those of shallow roots believe in that [Chan] alone, neither reciting the sutras nor studying them, and while amidst worldly affairs they speak of practicing Chan with their mouths but do not walk the Path with their minds.
They disparage the Pure Land and do not believe in rebirth there; their error is great indeed, for they do not know Amitābha Buddha.
This is the unsurpassed, most profound dhyāna. People today do not fathom the great principle and recklessly give rise to conceptual discrimination;

yet, if they wish to practice Zen and see their nature, they need not separately raise a *huatou*. Simply hold the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" and investigate it yourself, recite it yourself, examine it yourself, and doubt it yourself.
After a long time, you will naturally attain something. At that time, even if you do not awaken before death, when your life ends, you will—
If one attains birth in the highest grade, what concern could there be that one has not attained great enlightenment?
Take, for example, Chan Master Baizhang Dazhihai, who was the dharma-heir of Mazu of Jiangxi;
the monastic communities throughout the world were established based upon him, and from ancient times until the present, not a single person has dared to dispute his errors.
The Pure Rules (qinggui) are implemented by others from beginning to end, such that not a single matter may dare to violate their regulations.

Observe the rules for reciting for a sick monk: the assembled community raises their voices in unison to chant a verse in praise of Amitābha Buddha, followed by chanting "Namo Amitābha Buddha" together, whether a hundred or a thousand times, before dedicating the merit.
I humbly pray that while various conditions have not yet ended, you may swiftly attain peace; that as the great life-force cannot be avoided, you may ascend directly to An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
Is this not the ultimate destination of the Pure Land? Furthermore, observe how they escort deceased monks, reciting mantras during the Great Night and dedicating the merit, with the prayer:
"May the spirit transcend to the pure realm, and karma cease its toil in the dusty world; may the lotus bloom as a flower of the highest grade, and the Buddha grant [the disciple] a single..."
Does this record of birth not point toward the ultimate goal of the Pure Land? As for the occasion of cremation, there is nothing else to be done;

one simply has the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) lead the chanting of "Namo Amitābha Buddha of the Great Compassionate One in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss" ten times, with the assembly responding ten times in unison—this is collectively termed the "Ten Recitations."
Having finished the chanting, he further directed the merit, saying: "The ten recitations of praise just performed to assist in rebirth—could this not be the ultimate aim of the Pure Land teachings?
Since the time of Baizhang, all methods for escorting deceased monks have been based on this practice.
Thus, it can be said that among all the Chan monks throughout the world, encompassing the lineages of the five houses, there is not one who does not [rely on this]."
Regarding those who do not return to the Pure Land, as I observe the words of the venerable masters, they all have their basis and point toward the Pure Land as the ultimate goal.
Those who practice Chan today neither understand the intent of the Patriarchs nor give rise to a mind of self-reflection and awakening;
they recklessly claim that those who have attained enlightenment have no desire for rebirth there, yet later find themselves with no way to escape their regret.
*The Text on the Ultimate Aim of All Sutras: Pure Land* Section Seventeen: The Teachings on the Pure Land Gateways.
As numerous as the sands of the Ganges River are the teachings regarding the Pure Land; here, I shall briefly cite several instances to dispel doubts.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* states: The Buddha addressed Maitreya: "In this world, there are seven hundred and twenty billion..."
Bodhisattvas who do not regress are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; the number of bodhisattvas of minor practice who attain rebirth is beyond calculation.

Not only in my own land, but throughout the worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable multitudes of great bodhisattvas all contemplate Amitābha Buddha and vow to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If there are good men or good women who hear the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and hold fast to his name, by virtue of reciting that name, all their transgressions will be extinguished.
When such persons approach the end of their lives, they shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Śākyamuni Buddha said: "You all should believe and accept my words."
Furthermore, as the Buddhas have taught, if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make a vow to be born in that land.
The *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* states: "If good men or good women merely hear the names of the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas..."
It is said that this eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas;
how much more so for those who, with every thought, recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha"—a single utterance extinguishes the grave sins of birth and death from eighty billion kalpas.

Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha should know that such a person is a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among men, and that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva will serve as their supreme spiritual friends.

The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta* states: "If one hears this sutra and practices according to its teachings, at the end of life here, one will immediately go to the world of Sukhāvatī, to the dwelling place of Amitābha Buddha surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas, and be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne;
there, one will no longer be afflicted by greed, nor will one be troubled by anger or delusion."

They are neither afflicted by ignorance nor troubled by the defilements of pride, envy, and jealousy; they attain the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma King, and the great bodhisattvas serve as his ministers of the Dharma."
That which I, your servant, hold in the highest esteem is only the Buddha, the King of the Dharma.

There were certain bodhisattvas who, reflecting upon their past, realized that they had slandered the Prajñāpāramitā and consequently fallen into the evil realms, undergoing immeasurable suffering. Although they spent immeasurable kalpas thereafter practicing other dharmas, they could not escape the sea of suffering.
Later, they encountered virtuous friends who instructed them to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; immediately, they attained the eradication [of their karmic obstacles].
With my karmic obstacles transcended, I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. I now ought to pay homage and offer thanks to Amitābha Buddha. Why is this?
Neither parents, nor relatives, nor friends, nor kings, nor gods can deliver me from the ocean of suffering;

it is only through the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows that I am gathered in and thus able to escape the ocean of suffering. As the verse says: "If a person aspires to become a Buddha, they should bring Amitābha to mind..."

Because Amitābha immediately manifests his body [to him], I take refuge in and pay homage to him. Furthermore, it is said that during the Buddha’s lifetime, an old man sought to leave the household life, but Śāriputra did not permit it.
The Buddha observed that in a past kalpa, this man had been forced by a tiger while gathering firewood;

as he climbed a tree, he lost his voice and cried out, "Namo Buddhāya. By virtue of this slight merit, he encountered the Buddha and attained liberation, obtaining the fruit of Arhatship. How remarkable!
If even a single recitation of his name can bring about liberation, how much more so for one who practices mindfulness of the Buddha throughout their entire life?

The *Shinjitsu Kan* (True Mirror of the Lotus School) states: "Among the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Amitābha is foremost; among the Buddha-lands as numerous as the motes of dust in the ten directions, Sukhāvatī is the ultimate refuge.
One should have deep faith that Sukhāvatī is the wondrous gate of true liberation and contemplate Amitābha with earnest attention."
The Buddha is truly the compassionate father of all sentient beings; thus, when a single thought arises, the myriad spirits take notice, and as faith is born, the Buddhas appear.
As soon as one invokes the Precious Name, the seed is cast into the lotus womb; once bodhicitta is awakened, one’s name is inscribed upon the Golden Land.

Those with the karmic affinity encounter this spontaneously, awakening and practicing through self-effort. Yet those of shallow faith who do not uphold it commit great folly and grave error—how lamentable!

Alas, in these final ages, many encounter false views and are deluded by the current; they disparage pure practice as a provisional vehicle and mock the recitation and upholding [of the scriptures] as coarse behavior.

Is this not to wallow in the burning house, willingly enduring eternal sinking and ruin? It is a betrayal of one’s compassionate parents and a profound tragedy that a single lifetime is spent in vain.
One must believe that without relying on the power of another, there is no way to sever karmic afflictions.
To encounter this gateway yet have no path to escape birth and death is for the light-minded to utterly disparage themselves and for the slanderers to bring about their own ruin;
as false attachments are easily cultivated while the True Dharma is difficult to hear, they will transmigrate through the three evil realms for long kalpas without finding liberation.
The Essential Gate to the Contemplation of the Pure Land Realm states:

"Now, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is the essential path for sentient beings of the final age to transcend birth and death, and the vessel for crossing the sea of suffering. Once born there, one shall never again regress;
with a golden body, one travels with sovereign ease, food and clothing appear spontaneously, and by beholding the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one swiftly enters the ranks of the sages."
It is free from the afflictions caused by tigers, wolves, lions, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice; it is not scorched by thunder, lightning, wind, rain, cold, heat, hunger, or thirst.

There, one is born through transformation upon lotus flowers with immeasurable lifespan. Since there are no sufferings such as birth, old age, sickness, and death, this is called the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
Therefore, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni desires to cause the beings in this land who are lost in delusion—
It gives rise to renunciation from all sufferings and opens the gate of subduing [afflictions]; Amitābha, the Compassionate Father, reveals the path of acceptance.
This is precisely why he speaks with such earnest and repeated exhortation, singularly praising the Pure Land and universally encouraging rebirth therein.

For this reason, the number of sages and worthies, as well as monastics and laypeople, who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and attain rebirth is beyond counting; yet it is only because inferior ordinary beings are greedily attached to the mundane world...
To toil without seeking liberation and to willingly wander through birth and death is deeply pitiable. The *Anle ji* states:
"If one can mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, all karmic obstacles will be severed and one shall attain birth in the Pure Land.
Why is this? It is like a person who uses a lion’s sinew as a lute string; once its sound is struck, all other [strings]..."
If the strings of a lute are all snapped, it is like a person who, within the mind of bodhicitta, is able to recollect Amitābha Buddha;
all afflictions and heavy obstructions will be completely severed and extinguished. It is also like a person who takes the milk of cattle, sheep, donkeys, and horses and places it in a single vessel;
if they were to cast a single drop of lion’s milk into it, all the other milks would be transformed entirely into water. If a person...
If one can maintain mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha within the bodhicitta, all evil Māras and obstacles will naturally vanish, and one shall attain birth in the Pure Land.
The *Jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) states: "Human birth is difficult to obtain, yet birth in the Pure Land is easy. Why is this? Because those who do not observe the five precepts..."

The celestial path is cut off; only by maintaining the purity of the five precepts can one obtain human form. How much more so when the five precepts are difficult to uphold and one lacks the power of aspiration to sustain them—this is what is meant by the difficulty of obtaining a human body.
For those who practice the Pure Land, it does not necessarily depend on whether they maintain the precepts fully or incompletely;
provided they simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, even if they have sinful karma, it is permitted for them to repent at the moment of death.

At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Ocean, each with their respective powers of aspiration, will together come to welcome and receive them;
this is what is meant by the ease of rebirth in the Pure Land.
The *Pure Conduct Dharma Gate* states: Repentance is like diligently polishing an ancient mirror, gradually eradicating the dim dust accumulated over kalpas;
reciting the Buddha’s name is like privately meeting an enlightened sovereign, suddenly obtaining deliverance for future times.

Within the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, and amidst the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one should diligently contemplate the adornments of the Pure Land and constantly remember Amitābha Buddha. Thus should one practice mindfulness.
One need have no doubt that through the Buddha’s presence in samādhi, one will be born in the Pure Land.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Candragarbha Sūtra* states: "During the age of the Final Dharma, although billions upon billions of sentient beings may initiate practice and cultivate the Way, not a single one attains it;
this is because in the evil world of the five turbidities, various studies are difficult to complete. Only the single gate of the Pure Land is [accessible]."
One should know that entering the path through universal penetration is difficult when relying on one's own practice, yet easy when relying on the power of others.

It is like a man of inferior status who soars through the four heavens by attaching himself to the might of a Wheel-Turning King, or like an ordinary person who ascends to the Three Isles by borrowing the efficacy of elixirs from an immortal;
these are truly paths of easy practice for swiftly attaining realization. The compassionate intent [of the Buddha] is earnest and repeated; it must be engraved upon one’s very flesh and bones.
The *Ratnarāja-śāstra* states: "One who bathes in the great ocean has already utilized the waters of the hundred rivers; one who recites the Buddha’s name will necessarily achieve samādhi.
It is just as when a clear pearl is cast into turbid water—the turbid water cannot fail to become clear;
when mindfulness of the Buddha is directed toward a distracted mind—the distracted mind cannot fail to become the Buddha."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If a person recollects the Buddha with a distracted mind, they shall still attain liberation from suffering, and their merit will be inexhaustible;
how much more so for one who recollects the Buddha with a concentrated mind! From the highest level of 'one-pointedness without distraction' down to the successful completion of ten recitations."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "If a person, even with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and once utters 'Namo Buddha,' they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
It further states: "When the name of the Buddha is heard throughout the ten directions, it extensively benefits sentient beings;
all shall possess roots of goodness, thereby assisting their aspiration for the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In all modes of conduct, one should constantly recollect the merits of the Buddhas, day and night without even a moment’s interruption;

such is the practice one should perform. It further says: "One would rather undergo the sufferings of hell to hear the names of the Buddhas than receive immeasurable bliss while failing to hear the names of the Buddhas."
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If sentient beings from other realms hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitābha and are able to give rise to even a single thought of pure faith,
with joy and delight dedicating all their roots of goodness toward the vow to be born in that land, they shall be reborn there according to their wish,
attain non-retrogression, and proceed directly to the attainment of Buddhahood."
The "Chapter on the Difficulty of Hearing the True Dharma" states:

The Buddha said that if people of the world hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, with a heart of compassion and joy, their will becomes pure, their hair stands on end, and tears immediately flow from their eyes, these are all those who have constantly practiced the Buddha-way over successive lifetimes, or who have practiced the bodhisattva path under other Buddhas in other directions; they are certainly not ordinary people. If...
Those who do not believe the Buddha’s words, those who do not believe in the practice of *nien-fo*, and those who do not believe in rebirth in the Pure Land have all come from the evil realms;
their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, and being ignorant and deluded, they do not understand and are not yet fit for liberation.

There are many bodhisattvas who wish to open this sutra but are unable to hear it; however, if they should hear it, they will never again regress from the Unsurpassed Way. Therefore, one should believe.
Uphold, recite, and practice according to these teachings; I now proclaim this Great Dharma for you all so that you may behold Amitābha Buddha and his land.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, I have specifically preserved this Dharma verse, which says:
"If one has not cultivated merit and wisdom in the past, one cannot hear this True Dharma; because I have already revered and served the Tathāgatas, it exists."
Having heard this meaning through causes and conditions, one realizes that the bliss of those Buddha-fields is boundless; it can be known only by Buddhas and Buddhas.
Even if śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were to fill the world and exhaust their spiritual wisdom, they could not fathom it.

When the Great Sage, the Dharma King, proclaims the wondrous Dharma to rescue and deliver all beings from sinking into the depths of saṃsāra, anyone who receives, upholds, and expounds it truly possesses the most excellent and sublime bodhi.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and the eight classes of beings— devas, nāgas, and so forth—
all rejoiced, accepted it with faith, and practiced accordingly.
This concludes the eighteenth discourse on the causes and conditions of Amitābha Buddha’s stage of practice.
Someone asked: "The Master constantly exhorts us to recollect Amitābha Buddha; I do not yet know whether Amitābha Buddha has a causal ground (in-dì).
Zongben replied: "The causal grounds of Amitābha Buddha are recorded extensively throughout the Tripiṭaka teachings.
I shall now briefly cite one or two instances to answer your question. The *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* states that in the distant past, many kalpas ago..."
The country was named Abhirati; the king was named Kauśika.
His grandfather was King Viśuddhadeva, his father was the Cakravartin King Candrasūryavimalaprabha, and his mother was Queen Viśiṣṭamukhā. He begot three sons:
the eldest was named Candraprabha, the second was named Kauśika, and the third was named Indrasena. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata. Kauśika—
Renouncing his royal throne, he left the household life to become a monk under the Buddha, known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
Facing the Tathāgata with reverence, he made forty-eight kinds of vast and great vows to universally deliver all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

He vowed that if even a single vow were not fulfilled, he would never attain Buddhahood. At that time, the devas scattered flowers, the earth shook, and from the sky there came praise, saying: "It is certain!"

He will certainly attain Buddhahood. Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In a past kalpa, there was a universal monarch named Araṇemin, whose minister Ratnasāgara served as his spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Together, they resolved their minds on Bodhicitta in the presence of the Buddha Ratnagarbha.
The universal monarch made this vow: 'When I become a Buddha, I shall dwell in a world of pure peace and happiness, gathering and sustaining all beings.'"
The minister *Sattva* made a vow, saying: "When I become a Buddha, I shall deliver all sentient beings within this world of the five turbidities and suffering.
This King *Araṇemin* is none other than Amitābha Buddha; the minister *Ratnasāgara* is Śākyamuni Buddha.
When such a ruler and his minister act in harmony, it is called the two gates of "subduing and gathering" (*nigrahānugraha*).
Therefore, Amitābha Buddha welcomes and guides sentient beings in that Pure Land,
while Śākyamuni Buddha teaches and transforms sentient beings here in this Sahā world. Furthermore, prior to kalpas as numerous as motes of dust,

during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, Amitābha and Śākyamuni were once sixteen princes who, by lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others and vowing to deliver sentient beings, brought forth their original resolve.
O virtuous ones, you must know that throughout immeasurable kalpas, [the Buddhas] have never departed from their original vows;
the kindness of the two masters, Amitābha and Śākyamuni, cannot be repaid even by grinding one's bones to powder.
Again, it was asked: "The Buddhas of the ten directions are exceedingly numerous; why is it that people in the world think only of Amitābha Buddha? He replied:
"Amitābha Buddha shares the same principle (*li*) as all others, yet his manifestation (*shi*) is distinct; for this reason, he is specifically remembered.

If one investigates the principle behind this thought, mindfulness of one Buddha is itself mindfulness of many Buddhas, and mindfulness of many Buddhas is itself mindfulness of one Buddha. Why is this? Because the essence (*tǐ*) of all Buddhas is identical."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All Buddhas possess a single Dharma-body; True Suchness is equal and without discrimination—is this not so?
I shall now once more employ a metaphor to resolve your doubt.

For example, if a hundred thousand mirrors are suspended within a single room and a single lamp is placed inside to illuminate them, the light of the lamp will enter and pervade all the mirrors. It is like a person calling out.
All Buddhas, including Amitābha Buddha, are fully mindful of one another;

the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states that when the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla asked Śākyamuni Buddha how future sentient beings might see the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Buddha instructed them to be mindful of Amitābha Buddha, whereby they immediately see the Buddhas of the ten directions. For this reason:
Because the essence of all Buddhas is identical, they are said to share the same names and titles;
however, one must understand that this principle applies not only to the Buddhas, but to all four classes of sages and six realms of beings alike. Why is this?

Because all Buddhas realize this nature and thereby become sages, while sentient beings are deluded regarding this nature and thus remain ordinary beings; for this reason, they too share this same principle. To cite an example: Amitābha Buddha.
Because his compassionate and vast practices and vows are profound and far-reaching, he holds this in special remembrance. The *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"When I become a Buddha, if the adornments of my land are not more sublime and surpassing than those of the lands of the ten directions, may I never attain Buddhahood.
It further states: "When I become a Buddha, my preaching of the sūtras and my practice of the Way shall be ten times greater than those of all other Buddhas."
"If I do not attain this vow—that I shall never become a Buddha unless those who invoke my name are certain to be born in my land—then may I never become a Buddha.
Because this vow is so vast and its conditions so powerful, it moves the hearts of worldly people until they all bring me to mind.
Furthermore, have you not seen the verse of praise by the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrī, which says: "Among the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, Amitābha is the foremost"?
Is this not so? Not only do Bodhisattvas praise the Buddhas of the ten directions, but they also praise him;
how much more so should we, inferior ordinary beings? Inferring from this, what doubt can there be regarding single-minded mindfulness of that Buddha?
Again, it was asked: "When those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha (nianfo) approach the end of their lives, the Buddha comes to welcome and guide them.

Since there are immeasurable people in the worlds of the ten directions practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, how can [the Buddha] know the time for each of them all, and be able to welcome and guide them all? The answer was:

"Furthermore, the sun and moon are but a single small world-system, yet their radiance is still able to universally illuminate all myriad things; how much more so the radiance of the Buddha? Have you not seen Maitreya?"
The Sūtra says: "For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha? Śāriputra, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable;
it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without obstruction. For this reason, he is named Amitābha. You should know that the light of the Buddha is vast and beyond compare.
If even Arhats of the Hīnayāna possess the three clarities and six supernatural powers to manifest transformations according to the types of beings, how much more so the Buddha?"

Is this not the wondrous power of his supernormal faculties? Why is this so? Because his body constantly pays homage to the Buddha, the Buddha sees him through the supernormal faculty of the divine eye;

because his mouth constantly recites the Buddha’s name, the Buddha hears him through the supernormal faculty of the divine ear; and because his mind constantly remembers the Buddha, the Buddha knows him through the supernormal faculty of knowing others' minds.
O virtuous ones, you need only practice with sincere devotion yourselves; there is no need to doubt the Buddha.

[The Buddha] is able to lead [beings] forth. Again, [a disciple] asked: "The Buddha possesses immeasurable radiance; why do I not see it? He replied: "When the bright sun adorns the sky, the blind man does not behold it.
It is not that the sun lacks light; it is the fault of the blind man. Sentient beings, with their heavy obstructions of dark karma, do not see the light of the Buddha."
It is as clear as being beneath a red raspberry; it is not that the sunlight does not shine there.

If a person maintains strict purity through fasting and vigilance, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name, they will see Amitābha face-to-face at the moment of death and immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
He asked again: "Since there are such merits [in reciting the name], why must one raise it in thought with continuous sound?
For example, when calling out one's own name, it does not exceed one, two, or three calls; if one calls out incessantly, my mind would instead become resentful and annoyed.
What do you say to this? He replied: "Your heterodox explanation deludes and confuses people. Furthermore, the great names of the Buddhas and Great Sages are not for the ignorant and foolish."
Has it not been stated in the *Commonly Seen [Sutra]* that calling my name ensures rebirth in my land?

The *Contemplation Sutra* says that a single recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas; how much more so when the voice is continuous and uninterrupted?
The *Amitābha Sūtra* says that by virtue of calling the name, all transgressions are extinguished. And the *Śrī-Ānanda-bodhisattva’s Perfect Penetration* says: "Recall..."
The Buddha contemplates the Buddha; one will certainly see the Buddha.

From those who reach the stage of single-mindedness without distraction while exclusively upholding the Name, down to those who achieve rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations—how could you allow yourself such idle chatter and nonsensical talk? I now exhort people to constantly invoke the Buddha’s name.
Why is this necessary? It is because one must first cleanse the karma of the mouth, and only then can the body and mind be purified. Alas!
When ordinary people recite the Buddha’s name, delusive thoughts still arise; how much more so when they do not recite it?
Now, as I observe this, the very act of reciting that Buddha is nothing other than awakening the master [of one's own mind] so that one does not lose sight of one's original nature.
Once this single nature is no longer lost, the three karmas naturally become pure. At this point, Amitābha and I are of one essence.

There is no distinction between me and Amitābha; we are fundamentally non-dual. This is precisely the matter of the mutual resonance of the Way, where mother and child meet, such that principle and phenomenon are clearly distinguished and both nature and appearance are fully present.
**Exhortation on Oral Karma from Longshu** The Layman No. 19 said:
To recite the names of the Buddhas with one’s mouth is like spitting out pearls and jade; it brings the retribution of the heavenly realms and the Buddha-lands.

To speak of virtuous deeds with one’s mouth is like spraying forth fragrant incense. To praise the virtues of others is like proclaiming the teachings through one’s own mouth; it is like emitting radiance that shatters the delusions of others.
To speak with sincerity is like spreading fine silk; it truly benefits others. Speech that is useless is like chewing wood shavings;
it is better to remain silent to nourish one's vital energy. Deceptive speech is like falling into a concealed pitfall;
it causes people to stumble. A fondness for jesting is like brandishing a sword; it sometimes inflicts injury. To speak of evil matters is like emitting a foul odor.
If a person’s speech is as foul as flowing maggots, they will receive the retribution of the hells or the animal realm. A human life does not exceed the karma of body, speech, and mind:
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three karmas of the body; false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words constitute the four karmas of speech;
and greed, anger, and delusion constitute the three karmas of the mind. These are collectively termed the ten non-virtues (*daśākuśala*). If one maintains [the precepts against] them...
Not committing [evil] is what is called the ten wholesome actions. According to the Buddha’s words, the retribution for vocal karma is greater than that of the two karmas of body and mind.
Why is this? When an intention arises, it has not yet manifested externally; once words are spoken, they are immediately seen.

Even when one commits evil with the whole body, there are still times of difficulty and obstruction, whereas the mouth is easier to employ for such purposes. Therefore, let us first set aside matters concerning future lives.
Speaking of the present world, there is a single word by which one may praise another, and that person shall receive blessings for life, extending even to their descendants;
yet there is a single word by which one may ruin another, and that person shall suffer harm for life, bringing calamity upon their descendants as well.

Is the karma of speech not, therefore, grave? What goes out from you shall return to you; though it is indeed fearsome when directed toward others, it is likewise so when directed back at oneself. However, in this regard...
Those who resent Heaven are impoverished; those who resent others lack wisdom. One should simply exercise caution and vigilance.
Therefore, I have set forth the intent of the sages and worthies to offer this specific exhortation and warning.
*Discourse on Distinguishing the Great Principles of the Three Teachings and Assisting the Transformation of Governance*, Part Twenty.
Now, within the Three Realms, the three teachings circulate; these three teachings are Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism.
The laws established by these three teachings all aim to lead people to reform their evils and turn toward the good, to turn away from depravity and return to the upright.

Yet worldly people do not comprehend the fundamental root and recklessly differentiate the branches and leaves, claiming that for exhausting principle and governing the world, nothing is greater than Confucianism, and that for exhausting one's nature and transcending birth and death, nothing is greater [than Buddhism].

Regarding the teachings of Śākyamuni, you further command that the governance of the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) has nothing greater than the Dao, yet you also call this the "Nirvana" of Śākyamuni, which is not close to human sentiment;
that the "emptiness and non-being" of the Dao is insufficient to govern the world, and that the "names and meanings" of Confucianism cannot transcend birth and death.
Is it not the case that each school clings to one-sidedness and thus slanders the others? It would be better to don the robes of the Confucians and recite [their texts].
To speak as a Confucian and act as a Confucian is simply to be a Confucian; to wear the robes of a Śākya, recite the words of a Śākya, and act as a Śākya is simply to be a Śākya.
Someone said, "The teaching of the Buddha is fundamentally a heterodox path and is not to be trusted.
Wuyuan said, "Do you know the teachings of this heterodox school? Can you describe them? He replied, "I have no leisure to read them."
His book says: "Since you have never read his book, how can you know that there are heterodox teachings?

Now you merely read the books of Confucius and immediately suspect that he is wrong; you are like a dog of Shun, who hears someone say something is wrong and immediately condemns it as such, or like a concubine or wife.
He spoke with an angry countenance and a harsh voice, saying: 'The Buddhists'..."
"Teaching that there is neither father nor sovereign—is this not heterodoxy? I replied:
"The blind man who feels the elephant and calls it heterodoxy does so simply because he has not seen the true body of the elephant; there is nothing strange about that.

When the Buddha established his teaching, when speaking with ministers he necessarily relied on loyalty (*zhōng*), and when speaking with sons he necessarily relied on filial piety (*xiào*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: 'We and...'"
"All sentient beings together shall attain the Way of the Buddha; how much more so, then, for sovereigns and ministers, fathers and sons!
The other said, "There are three forms of unfiliality, and failing to have posterity is the greatest—is this not a heterodox view? I replied, "Your words go too far.

Confucius and Mencius adopted [the principle] based on its righteousness, not merely based on outward appearances. In the past, Bo Yi and Shu Qi left no heirs, and Chao Fu and Xu You had no descendants, yet they were still honored."
Confucius praised him as "sage and pure," yet we have never heard him criticize him for lack of filial piety;

how much less so in our own tradition, where propagating the Way and benefiting living beings—providing salvation for both oneself and others—is the ultimate expression of supramundane filial piety, a merit that is unsurpassed. Now, you know only of the ordinary world of womb-birth;

how can you know that in the Buddha-land there is also transformation-birth? Furthermore, the Buddha’s establishment of the teachings employs both provisional and ultimate methods, as well as sudden and gradual approaches.
Those who leave the household life according to the Dharma subdue their body and mind and diligently cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

Those who remain in the secular world maintain the distinction between husband and wife and do not commit illicit or deviant acts; they simply require a pure mind and few desires. How could this prohibit people from procreating and continuing their lineage?
The opponent says: "Every hair and every skin are born from one's parents. The parents give birth to the child in its entirety, and the child returns to them in its entirety."
This may be called filial piety; yet now we see these monks who have destroyed and removed their hair and beards—how can this be filial piety? I replied:
"What you say truly shows that you know the near but not the distant, and see the small but not the great.
In the past, Taibo tattooed his body, Jing Ke sacrificed his life, Bi Gan cut open his own belly, and Jieyu burned his body to ashes—all of these were acts of destruction."
How profound! Yet the sages and worthies all extol them as possessing ultimate loyalty and ultimate virtue; how can they be held accountable for not preserving their physical forms?
Moreover, we śramaṇas uphold the precepts, practice cultivation, follow the Buddha-way, deliver deluded beings, and transcend the sea of suffering;

compared to such acts as self-immolation, [the preservation of the body] is already far removed—how much less need one concern oneself with the minor matter of hair and beard? The opponent said: "The followers of the Buddha..."

"Why do these followers eat without plowing and wear clothes without sericulture? I replied, "Those who have not yet attained the level of the Buddha eating like silkworms from among people is still somewhat excusable.
But now there are those who have not yet reached the level of Confucius and Mencius, yet they too eat like silkworms from among people—why is this?
He said, "The Confucianists' eating like silkworms from among people has merit for the world. I replied, "The transformation of the Buddha likewise has benefit for..."
What is the reason for this? Is it not because that which the Śākya school diligently teaches to the world is nothing other than the prohibition of evil and the exhortation toward goodness?
Who does not know that the Confucian teaching is likewise so? To speak of the present day:

the Buddha regards killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the three karmas of the body, whereas Confucius spoke of surpassing the remnants of disorder by eliminating killing, and Shun was fond of life.
The *Shi* (Book of Poetry) speaks of the evils of killing, saying that King Wen’s virtue reached even to birds, beasts, and insects; does this not show he was cautious about taking life?

Yet the matter of theft is certainly not what is being discussed here. In the time of our Master, people did not pick up lost items on the road; if one had not given a single blade of grass or a single leaf, one would not take it—how much less would they commit robbery?
Confucius said, "I have never seen anyone who loves virtue as much as they love beauty. This is from the *Shi*.

That people despise virtuous character while delighting in beautiful appearances—is this not a warning against sexual misconduct? The Buddha took false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words as the four karmas of the mouth;
Confucius said, "If a person lacks trustworthiness, I do not know how they can be effective"—is this not a warning against false speech?
He said, "Those who are artful in speech and have a pleasing countenance have little of benevolence"—is this not a warning against frivolous talk?
The Book of History states: "Do you not face one way when in his presence and speak otherwise behind his back? Is this not a warning against double-tongued speech?
To speak ill is called the sound of malice; it has not yet reached the level of foul language. Xunzi said that words that wound others are more piercing than spears and halberds.
Is this not a warning against the mouth of malice? Furthermore, the Buddha identified greed, anger, and delusion as the three poisons of the mind.
When Confucius said, "To see gain and think of righteousness," this was a warning against greed.

When he said of Boyi and Shuqi that they did not dwell on past grievances, this was a warning against anger. When he said, "One who is in distress yet does not study—such a person is among the lowest of the people," this was a warning against delusion.
Judging from these points, it is clear that Confucianism and Buddhism have never been different. The only point where they differ is that Confucianism stops here.
Regarding worldly dharmas, the Śākya [Buddhist] tradition further possesses supramundane dharmas;

whereas the Confucian school speaks only of a single lifetime and returns all to Heaven, the Śākya tradition understands the beginning and end of karmic conditions across successive lifetimes—this is precisely where they differ.

If one wishes to know the strengths of the Śākya tradition, one must examine the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and gain an understanding of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
If principle can be such as this, one may transcend the cycle of birth and death;
yet if one fails to realize it and instead rejects it, then should one not be cautious of what Confucius called "acting without knowledge"?
If this is indeed the case, then the teachings of the Śākya clan are trustworthy. How could one fail to believe his words regarding the Pure Land? This is what is meant by "transcending."
Among the worldly dharmas, the purification of the Pure Land is especially vital; one must not fail to exert oneself in this.

It is further said that the Five Precepts of the Buddha—namely, abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants—are identical to the Five Constant Virtues of the Confucian tradition: not killing is the greatness of benevolence (*ren*); not stealing is the integrity of righteousness (*yi*);
not engaging in sexual misconduct is the rectitude of propriety (*li*); not drinking intoxicants is the clarity of wisdom (*zhi*); and not lying is the ultimate of faithfulness (*xin*). This is so.
The virtuous Master Ye said: "In a village of a hundred households, if ten people observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and prudent;
in a town of a thousand houses, if a hundred people practice the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will be harmonious. Indeed, if one can practice a single good deed, one eliminates a single evil;
if one evil is eliminated, one instance of punishment ceases. When punishment ceases within the family, it ceases throughout the nation. Therefore, I..."
The teachings established by the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) provide great benefit to governance and transformation. Alas!
If every person were to uphold the five precepts and cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, the state's punishments could be dispensed with, and peace could be achieved effortlessly.

If this were truly possible, how much more so when one further moves the eight classes of celestial beings to descend upon Jambudvīpa to protect the mundane world, resulting in harmonious winds and timely rains?
The five grains will grow in abundance, fires and bandits will subside in secret, and calamities and misfortunes will be utterly extinguished.
Such benefits not only supplement the administration of governance, but also benefit both the living and the deceased. The *Lianzong baojian* states:
"If one person can practice this Way to instruct their household, to guide their village, and from the village reach the state, until it reaches the realm of no [bounds]."

When one reaches the ultimate limit, the people of the world are immersed in the Way and swim in its virtue; their spirits merge with the true aspect (*dharmatā*), and they stride high into the *anabhilāpya* (ineffable) realm, reaching the very pinnacle of the Buddha’s domain.
How could this be merely for the sake of being a "good person" or a "gentleman"?

If this is so, then why worry that loyalty and filial piety will not be cultivated, or that ritual propriety and yielding will not be manifest? Viewed in this light, is this not indeed the Way of the Benevolent One (*Śākyamuni*)?
Is it not to serve as a complementary counterpart to the Way of Zhongni (Confucius) for the instruction of the people? Yet many people today fail to examine the origins of this;
seeing that some of his disciples are unworthy, they transfer their anger toward the teachings of the virtuous.
How can one disparage Laozi because some Daoist practitioners are unworthy, or disparage Confucius because some scholars are unworthy? This is surely not the way of the wise.
One does not reject words because of the person who spoke them; how much less can one disparage a teaching because of its followers?
Is this not as different from blaming Yao for Danzhu, or faulting Shun for Shangjun?

Or like attributing the failure of a medicine to Shen Nong when one has taken it in excess, or resenting Cui Ren for a fire that results from one’s own negligence? This humble and unworthy person has thus studied the Way of the Buddha.
It has been some years since I have roughly grasped its essential meaning and developed a sincere intention to support what is tottering;
I do not dare act out of private interest, but rather desire to act for the public good in order to remedy these defects. My only wish is that—
There is one person above who is lofty yet not precarious; the Three Teachings circulate everywhere without obstruction.
Because there is one person, the Three Teachings are promoted; because there are the Three Teachings, they assist the principle of that one person.

This is like the three luminaries of heaven, the three cardinal relations of the world, or the three legs of a tripod—none can be lacking. Furthermore, for those who have become monks, none is comparable to Dao’an.
Huiyuan befriended Xi Zuochi because he revered Confucianism; no monk has equaled Huiyuan in seeing off Lu Xiujing beyond Tiger Creek because he esteemed the Way.
I admire these two eminent monks for their love of Confucianism and their respect for the Way; yet even fellow disciples of the Buddha may still find fault with them.
Since I value others, how could they hold me in low regard? I ask that you believe in the deeds of Hui’an and Huiyuan, for they are worthy of emulation.
The poem says: "In hewing the handle for the axe, the model is not far off. Mencius said: "Heavenly timing is not as good as the advantage of terrain;
the advantage of terrain is not as good as human harmony. Is this not what that means?
Discourse on the Single Principle of the Three Teachings by Chan Master Dufeng Shan 2.
First: Before the empty kalpa, there was no form yet there was awareness; luminous and quiescent, it is the root of heaven and earth.

Descending from its source and flowing to its branches, it is the ancestor of the myriad paths. Returning to the source and reverting to the root, it is the patriarch of the single Dharma. If one pursues it, it cannot be seen.
Its head lies in wait, yet one hears nothing of its rear; it cannot be known through intellect, nor can it be seen through physical signs.
Only a true sage knows it through personal realization within. Long ago, a monk asked Xiangyan, "What is the Way?
Xiangyan said, "A dragon’s roar from within a withered tree. The monk asked, "What is one who walks the Way? Xiangyan said, "Eyes within a skull."
Only those with eyes like this and hands like these can discourse upon the Three Teachings; thus, the Layman Ruru’s "Treatise on the Unity of the Three Teachings" says:
"Hard as a tuft of cotton, soft as iron—a single snowflake in the midsummer heat. The incense pillar and the lantern smile and nod their heads;
the mute man has had a dream, but to whom shall he tell it? Since antiquity, the Three Teachings have been forcibly assigned names; Śākyamuni [remains] concealed."
Master Śāriputra said, "One should silently recognize it"; Laozi said, "Great eloquence is like being dull.
Even if one were to analyze this to the point of establishing a distinct school, one would still inevitably fall into the "second moon. This brings to mind the words of the Layman Dongpo:
"He has completely revealed all three teachings: the mountain scenery is nothing other than the pure body, and the sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue."

To go about in such a manner is not merely a matter of the grass growing ten feet deep before the Dharma Hall; it extends to the entire Dharma-realm where not a single person is fit to serve as a blade of grass for planting.
Since time immemorial, the Sages have given rise to compassion and extended their pity for those wandering in the world;

unable to remain aloof, they lowered their clouds from on high and, at a shallow and accessible point—the second gate—enticed their children to move toward the past, which has gradually become remote.

If, at this time, a single path were not opened for universal passage, the people would become increasingly deceitful and cunning; they would eventually become *chī* and *mèi* spirits, never returning [to humanity].

Therefore, the Three Sages were born together in the Zhou dynasty to preside over and lead the orthodox teachings: Confucianism teaches one to exhaust principle and perfect nature (*qióng lǐ jìn xìng*);
Buddhism teaches one to illuminate the mind and realize its nature (*míng xīn jiàn xìng*); and Daoism teaches one to... [preserve breath/attain immortality].
In the cultivation of the spirit and the refinement of nature, this alone is the one true reality; the other two are not truly so.
Each person naturally possesses within their own breast the three teachings in perfect harmony; one must by no means look outward to "ride the ox in search of the ox. Thus, a predecessor said:
"One Buddhist, one Daoist, and one Confucian—these three sages have conversed for many years. One knows not what they have been discussing for so long."
The matter remains such that even now one cannot stop smiling; this poem is entirely devoid of even a trace of the "smoke and fire" flavor of worldly concerns.

To say that it begins with the Three Teachings and leaves nothing to be desired is true; yet, as for claims of regulating the family, governing the self, serving the sovereign, and benefiting the people—these are merely the secondary matters of Confucianism.
As for claims of conserving the essence, nourishing the spirit, and ascending as an immortal—these are merely the crude traces of Daoism. If...
It is said that "passing from death to transcend life" and "benefiting oneself and others" are merely the *quan* (traps) and *lü* (nets) of the Śākya clan. Alas!

When a single character is transcribed three times, how can it fail to become a horse? In later generations, errors have been transmitted such that people claim the Three Teachings consist only of their superficial traces.
Often, they rely on empty echoes and forget the root to pursue the branches, contending over right and wrong based solely on what can be perceived by the ears and eyes.
It is even said that their halberds clash and the points of their verbal arrows compete; have you not seen what was said in the Gate of the Sages:

"My great worthiness—what is there among men that I do not tolerate? Furthermore, while the sages of the Three Teachings each have their own gateways, when one reaches their ultimate point, they have never been anything other than one.
These [disputes] are all due to a lack of capacity to tolerate others, consisting of asserting oneself right and others wrong, and speaking thus...
Regarding one's own life, you treat it all as empty, non-existent, and preposterous talk; all day long you call the false true and mistake a thief for your son.
As for the daily grace and power you receive from others, when questioned about even a single point, you possess no correct view or correct realization whatsoever.
Since you lack such realization, if you were to turn back and depart this very moment, toward what path would you head?
Remaining in this state, one increasingly appears as if deluded or intoxicated, unable to discern where one has fallen. Such a perspective might otherwise be called nihilistic or preposterous;
yet, if one were to skillfully discourse upon the Three Teachings, one should discard their chaff and husks and seek instead the single turning-point.
Alas! I understand it now: one who carries a water-jar must necessarily be outside the jar; if one sits within the jar, how can they carry it?
Being unable to carry a water jar within, one is already buried and submerged in the realm of right and wrong; thus, one will never be considered a person of sound discourse on the Three Teachings.
One who would discuss the Three Teachings must possess the skill to seize a great whale alive and the sharp wit to capture a fierce tiger alive.
Only when one has transcended the Three Teachings with total detachment can they emerge from the narrow well to speak of the Eastern Sea. If [one lacks this],...

To meagerly gather the spittle of former sages and pilfer their stale words from paper, only to claim that this is right and that is wrong—it is rare indeed that such a person does not incur the laughter of the great masters.
Furthermore, there is another saying: "It is not difficult to know; it is only the practice that is difficult.
When one has not yet reached old age and infirmity, who cannot engage in lofty discourse and expansive talk about the mind?

To speak of "nature" while disparaging the ancients for their profound and subtle discourse that transcends the mundane is to look at one's own conduct and practice throughout the twelve periods of the day and wonder:
can there not be a single thought of craving, attachment, joy, anger, or resentment lodged within the breast?
Can there not be a single thought of wine, women, wealth, or status that blinds one’s right view? Looking up, one beholds the Master’s silent realization of the "One Thread" (Yan Hui).

The "mental fasting" (*xinzhai*) and "sitting in oblivion" (*zuowang*) of Confucius, the "embracing the One" (*baoyi*) and "guarding simplicity" (*shoupu*) of Laozi, the "tortoise and the cicada" and the "carefree wandering" (*xiaoyao*) of Zhuangzi,
the "plucking the flower and smiling" of the World-Honored One, and the "attaining the skin and attaining the marrow" of Bodhidharma—
fearing that the ancient sages did not necessarily practice in such ways, the Master [Confucius] said: "First practice, and then follow with words," implying that he had not yet heard of such things.
The Dharma Master Suffering from Leg Disease could preach but could not practice. Thus Xuefeng said: "Having awakened, one must practice;
if one does not practice, it is called 'dry wisdom. When faced with the critical junctures of life and death or gain and loss, such a person will ultimately find no power.
One knows, therefore, that it does not lie in many words, but rather depends on how one practices. Since antiquity, the three teachings have been divided like the tripod of a cauldron.
These resources serve as tools, just as a state employs weapons; how could one help it?

If in future generations every person were to forget their neighbors and dwell in a realm where they do not even visit one another’s walls, and a pure breeze should sweep in, there would be no day that was not spent like a man of the era of the Sage Kings Xi and Huang.
I know that these three sages would certainly not stir up wind and waves upon level ground; yet alas, what can be done about people of today?
The ancient ground of realization is not antiquated, nor is the ancient practice;

what is called "a thousand kinds of wondrous eloquence spoken with the mouth" cannot erase even a speck of dust when one sets foot [in the world]. Thus, the Sage could not help but compassionately extend a hand.
I have observed that since the time he first passed the imperial examination, the Song dynasty layman and metropolitan graduate Zhang Wugou never failed to roam freely within the Zen groves.

One morning, Master Sanmei suddenly went to pay his respects to Chan Master Miaoxi to discuss the principle of "investigating things" (*gewu*). Miaoxi said, "Master Gong, you only know how to investigate things;
you do not know that there is the 'investigated' (*wugé*). Gong asked, "Does the Master have no skillful means (*fangbian*)?

Miaoxi cited the story of Emperor Minghuang’s visit to Shu and his striking the statue of the Governor of Lang with his sword. Upon hearing this, Gong suddenly awakened to the profound principle and composed a verse, which he titled "Zishao."
The subtlety of investigating things (*gewu*) lies in the essential realization that things are investigated; one must recognize the single thread running through two sets of five hundred.
If you are truly one who possesses the eye and knows the sound, simply look at such a public case (*gongan*): how could the Three Teachings possibly obstruct or hinder a person?
Otherwise, listen further to this verse of reckless talk: "The Three Teachings have existed since ancient times; do not take yellow leaves to stop a child's crying."
"Pushing through the azure void, pines rise a thousand feet; cutting off the red dust of the world, a stream flows through a single ravine. I have once said to the assembly:
"Confucianism is my footwear, Daoism is my cap, and Buddhism is my garment.

If one of these three is lacking, it is like trying to travel a thousand li while barefoot, wishing to receive a great guest with one's head bared, or attempting to appear before others in total nudity."
I have composed this "Chao Tianzi" (Song of the Emperor) to honor the True Man. How could I, in my present state, possibly exhaust the Way of these three sages?

Yet, even as a mosquito drinking from the ocean, I am able to partake of its flavor. Thus, I have reverently painted these images to carry with me for veneration, expressing my sincerity that the Perfect and Ultimate is all-encompassing and without limit.
Furthermore, I have written this preface so that each person may restore their own original nature and realize the reality inherent within it.
Therefore, I have merely recorded it here.
The Discourse on the Indestructibility of the Buddha-Dharma by Yao Shaoshi.
Someone asked Master Shaoshi: "The Buddha was a man of the Hu [Central Asians]; his Dharma has long been a source of harm and affliction to this Middle Kingdom."
"Can the Buddha-dharma not be extinguished? The Junior Master replied, "The Buddha-dharma cannot be extinguished. Someone asked, "Why is it that it cannot be extinguished?
He said, "It is not merely that it cannot be extinguished; no one is able to extinguish it.

Another asked, "The Buddha-dharma is a calamity to this Middle Kingdom even more severe than floods, droughts, or heatwaves. Why should it not be extinguished, allowing it instead to flourish and spread?"
"It is like this: when a great flood occurs, if there is a way to manage it, one can drain and channel it;
when there is a drought, if there is spiritual efficacy in prayer, one can eliminate it. The Buddha is a person who possesses power; he will surely be able to extinguish [this calamity].
The Junior Master laughed and said to him, "As for those with power, have you not heard of the three Wu emperors and Emperor Huizong of the Song? They were extinguished as soon as they arose."
This is not merely a matter of following what perishes and what arises, much less a case where what arises becomes increasingly flourishing.
Even if one possesses the power to extinguish [something], one can only extinguish that which it governs; how could one extinguish that which pervades all under heaven and encompasses all the land?
Someone asks: "If those who possess human power cannot extinguish it, can Heaven extinguish it? He replies: "Heaven can extinguish it."
Yet they do not dare to extinguish it. Someone asked: "How can your words be so preposterous? Why would Heaven not dare to extinguish it? I replied:

"The teachings of Confucius and Laozi take Heaven as their model; therefore, they do not dare to contravene Heaven. As for the teaching of the Buddha, all the devas receive and uphold it—how then could they dare speak of its extinction?
For what reason? Because when the Buddha was in the world, the Brahma Kings, Śakra Devendra, and the various devas, nāgas, and spirits [were his followers]."
In the presence of the Buddha, I once made a great vow: "Wherever there are teachings of the Dharma, I shall protect them; how could I ever dare speak of their extinction?
However, were it not for the power of the various devas, they might indeed cause the extinction [of the Dharma].

They could, in a single moment, mobilize thunderous fires and pestilence so that all the teachings, the monastic community, and their dwellings—both within and without the world—would be utterly consumed and destroyed.
"How difficult it would be! Yet the various devas uphold the Buddha’s teachings, fearing only that they might fail to keep pace; how much less would they dare speak of their extinction?
Someone said, "According to your words, the Buddha-dharma can certainly not be extinguished.
Please explain this further for me in detail. The Junior Master said, "Indeed, I shall tell you. Listen attentively: the Buddha appeared in the world in the West."

The Sage was born into the royal house of Śuddhodana in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. At the age of nineteen, he renounced his royal throne and left the household life to dwell in the Snowy Mountains to cultivate the Way.
He sustained himself on horse- oats for six years of ascetic practice until he attained Perfect Enlightenment.
The mountains, rivers, and the great earth all shook; he constantly took compassion as his heart and regarded all sentient beings in the world with equanimity.

Just as one teaches an only son to reform his evil ways and follow the good so that he may leave suffering and attain happiness and achieve all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), how much more so is the Buddha’s guidance of humanity free from any personal seeking?
Having renounced the royal throne and left the household life, it was not for the sake of seeking wealth or status.
Eating horse-grams daily and practicing austerities to realize the truth, it was not for the sake of seeking gain or offerings. Since there is nothing sought—
Regarding humanity, his method was solely to transform people through goodness; how could he have been concerned with the calamities of the Central Kingdom?
How extreme is your ignorant speech! If the sages of the world, such as Confucius, were to see the Buddha, they would surely revere and take him as their teacher.
Have you not heard that Confucius took Lao Dan as his teacher, and that [the Duke of] Yan, Chang Hong, and Yao Shixiang were his teachers?
If one considers whether these sages and worthies can equal the Buddha, how much less so the Buddha’s Great Way? It cannot be washed away by water, nor burned by fire;
it cannot be bound by shackles, nor cut by swords and blades; it cannot be harmed by poisons. It arises yet does not arise, does not arise yet arises;
it ceases yet does not cease, does not cease yet ceases. It remains undiminished among the ordinary, and remains undiminished among the sages.
Yet, it does not increase, being like the vast void; how could it possibly be extinguished?

Figures such as Han Yu of the Tang and Ouyang Xiu of the Song sought to extinguish it with mere empty words, just as the Jingwei bird wishes to fill the Eastern Sea or ants wish to burrow into Mount Tai—how laughable, that they do not measure their own capacity!
Perhaps upon hearing my words, someone might bow with a sense of shame.
Having thanked [the Emperor] and retired, he composed the *Treatise on the Indestructibility of the Buddha-Dharma*.
Regarding Liu Xueshi’s *Treatise on the Balanced Mind of the Three Teachings*:

In the second and third [sections], I have observed that China has possessed the Three Teachings since the time of Fuxi, who first drew the eight trigrams (*bagua*), thereby initiating the Confucian Teaching.

In this regard, Daoism began with Laozi’s composition of the *Daode jing*, while Buddhism began with Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty’s dream of the golden man; such is the sequence of the Three Teachings in China.

Generally speaking, Confucianism establishes its teaching through rectitude, Daoism establishes its teaching through veneration, and Buddhism establishes its teaching through greatness. Observe these...
To love life and loathe killing is the same as practicing benevolence; to regard others as oneself is the same as practicing impartiality;

to punish anger, stifle desire, and restrain transgressions and prevent wrongdoing is the same as practicing self-cultivation; to cause thunder to deafen the multitude and the sun and moon to blind the masses is the same as practicing transformative influence.
Judging from these coarse manifestations, the principles of the world do not exceed good and evil.
Although there are two paths, the intent of the Three Teachings is none other than to desire that people return to goodness.
Therefore, Emperor Xiaozong composed the "Discrimination on the Origin of the Way," stating: "Use Buddhism to govern the mind, Daoism to govern the body, and Confucianism to govern the world.
He truly understood that the mind, the body, and the world cannot tolerate even one remaining ungoverned; thus, how could the Three Teachings—[be anything other than a unified whole]?
There may be one among these that is not established; thus, the Layman Wujin composed the *Treatise on Protecting the Dharma*, saying:
"Confucianism treats the skin, Daoism treats the blood vessels, and Buddhism treats the marrow. One truly knows that there are the skin, the blood vessels, and the marrow;
it cannot be that one of them is not treated. If this is so, how could it be that one of the Three Teachings does not have its own practice?"
In China, Confucianism rectified the fundamental principles of social order and clarified human relations;

it ensured that ritual, music, law, and governance spread everywhere without contradiction, so that heaven and earth and all things were properly situated and nurtured. Its contribution to the world was truly great;
thus, when the First Emperor of Qin sought to eliminate the Confucians, they ultimately could not be eliminated.
In China, Daoism causes people to maintain themselves through purity and emptiness and to sustain themselves through humility and weakness;
it thoroughly washes away the habits of worldly confusion and entanglement, leading one back to the realm of stillness and non-action. Its contribution to the teachings of the world is thus supreme.
This is why Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty sought to eliminate Daoism, yet Daoism ultimately could not be eliminated.
In China, Buddhism causes people to abandon the ornate for the substantial and turn their backs on the false to return to the true;
it leads from the practice of effort to the attainment of effortless spontaneity, and from self-benefit to the benefit of others.

As the refuge and reliance of the common people, there is nothing that surpasses it. Therefore, although the emperors of the Three Wu eras sought to extinguish Buddhism, Buddhism ultimately could not be extinguished.
Li Shiqian of the Sui dynasty, in his discourse on the Three Teachings, stated that Buddhism is the sun, Daoism is the moon, and Confucianism is the five stars.
Is this not because the three luminaries in the heavens cannot be missing one, and likewise the three teachings in the world cannot lack any one?
Although their relative merits differ, they must certainly not be neglected in favor of one another. Nevertheless, people have differing minds.

There are those with divergent views who admire the Way yet claim that the Buddha is not as venerable as the Way; those who turn toward the Buddha yet claim that the Way is not as great as the Buddha;
and Confucianists who maintain their own orthodoxy while simultaneously denouncing both the Way and the Buddha as heterodox.
Thus, right and wrong have been muddled and confused for a thousand years. I shall clarify and distinguish them with urgency.
One must not judge with a private mind, nor judge with a heart of love or hatred;

only by leveling one's mind and contemplating the ultimate fruition can all doubts be dissolved like ice melting away. For "ultimate fruition" refers to the point where causes are gathered and results are realized.
Among all things in the world, every activity has its ultimate fruition: for the farmer, it is the work of soaking his body and smearing mud upon his feet.
When granaries and storehouses are filled to capacity, this is the ultimate achievement of the farmer;

to travel through grass and sleep under the open sky is the business of the merchant, and when gold fills his basket, this is the ultimate achievement of the merchant. It is the same with the Three Teachings:
Confucianism has its own ultimate achievement, Daoism has its own ultimate achievement, and Buddhism has its own ultimate achievement, each arising from its own path.
If one examines their relative merits through the ultimate achievement of their teachings, there are aspects that are clear even without further analysis;

judging from the present day, the teaching of the Confucian school proceeds from the individual to the family, from the family to the state, and from the state to be extended throughout the four seas, filling the six realms of space—it may truly be called "adhering to the concise while applying it extensively. As for the four seas...
As for what lies beyond the six directions, their doctrine states: "It flows eastward and spreads westward, reaching as far as the four seas.
This means that the furthest extent does not exceed the four seas; once it reaches this limit, it stops here and there is no further place to go.

Such is the teaching of the Confucianists. Therefore, those who study Confucianism preserve their minds, nourish their natures, tread upon benevolence, and walk in righteousness, becoming purely refined.

A person who is fully equipped with the Way and perfect in all virtues—one whose principles are manifested in their practical applications and deployed in their undertakings, such that they can assist their sovereign, benefit the people, stabilize the state, and profit the altars of the land and grain;

one who can transform the teachings of the world and bring about Great Peace—when their work is accomplished and they grow old in body, their name remains in the annals of history. Such is the ultimate achievement of the Confucian. Zengzi said:
"To cease only after death—is that not far-reaching? Indeed, it reaches its ultimate limit at death.
The teaching of the Daoists extends from one's own person to the mysterious and obscure realms; it transcends from the human world to the heavens above;
and it proceeds from mountain forests and rocky caves to the vast Great Luo and the towering Golden Gate—this may truly be called "transcending the mundane."
As for those who have entered the state of the sages, what can be said of that which lies beyond the creative transformations of Heaven and Earth? Their doctrine states:
"The great encompasses the celestial realm, and the minute extends into a single mote of dust. Thus, the greatest possible extent does not exceed the celestial realm;

since the realm is limited to this, that which lies beyond it is not something within the scope of knowledge. This is the teaching of the Daoist school; therefore, those who study the Way [should understand this].
With the spirit concentrated and movements in harmony with the formless, one stands aloft in a state of purity, serenity, and few desires;

by exhaling the old and inhaling the new, accumulating merit and refining conduct, one may achieve *shijie* (corporeal liberation), ascend to the heavens, command ghosts and spirits, summon wind and rain, assist in the transformative processes of nature, and establish profound achievements.
One’s lifespan becomes infinite, and one dwells in joy and autonomy.
The ultimate achievement of the Way is simply this. As the *Huangting Jing* says: "With longevity and far-reaching vision, one then flies away.
This implies that once one reaches longevity, the goal is consummated.
In the teaching of the Buddha, when a single Buddha appears, he takes a trichiliocosm as his field of retribution (*vipākakṣetra*). For the time being...
Speaking of a single world-system: within this one world-system there is Mount Sumeru, which rises from the great ocean up to the heights of the nine heavens.
The sun and moon revolve around the waist of the mountain, dividing day and night. On the four sides of Mount Sumeru are the four continents:
to the east is Pūrvavideha, to the west is Aparagoyānī, to the south is Jambudvīpa, and to the north...
It is said that among the four great continents, each has three thousand islands; this present world is Jambudvīpa.
This present China is one of the three thousand islands within the southern continent.
Śākyamuni descended to be born in India, which is the very center of the southern continent. To the four sides of Mount Sumeru, it borders above—
The abode of the sun and moon is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; above that is the Heaven of Śakra;
and further up, dwelling radiantly within the midst of space, the four layers of cloud-banks are collectively named the Realm of Desire (Kāmadhātu).

Above that, the eighteen layers of cloud-banks are collectively named the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu); and further up, the four layers of empty strata are collectively named the Formless Realm (Arūpyadhātu).
Regarding the realms: within these three realms, all classes of sentient beings undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death;
this constitutes one world-system. One thousand such world-systems are called a small chiliocosm.
One thousand such small chiliocosms are called a medium chiliocosm, which is one million worlds. One thousand such medium chiliocosms are called a great trichiliocosm, which is...
