Because the term "thousand" is stated three times, it is called a "trichiliocosm" (three-thousandfold great thousand-world system), though in reality it is but one great thousand-world system.
Within one great thousand-world system, there are ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, and ten billion sets of four continents.
This is like placing one coin for each world-system across one million strings of small coins; when all one million [strings] are exhausted, this constitutes the full extent.
Guān fāng [states]: "This Great Trichiliocosm is the single Buddha-field of retribution for one Buddha.
When one Buddha appears, his hundred billion bodies appear simultaneously within the hundred billion worlds. Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "One flower contains ten billion lands;
in each land is a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, attaining the Way of Buddhahood at once. Such instances occur in the hundreds and thousands.
The *vairocana* bodies of the hundred billion worlds each receive a multitude of beings as numerous as motes of dust; this is what is called the hundred billion transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
By means of these hundred billion transformation bodies, they bring to spiritual maturity the inhabitants of the hundred billion worlds—those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation;
those without feet, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; and those with form or without form, with perception or without perception.
To cause all beings from the realm of perception up to that of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to attain liberation is indeed the teaching of the Buddha’s household;

therefore, those who study the Buddha should recognize that the five aggregates are entirely empty, clarify the six sense faculties in purity, distance themselves from the ten unwholesome actions and practice the ten wholesome ones,
contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness and apply the four right efforts, and eliminate the sixty-two views so that no more falsehoods or deceptions remain.

He was able to sever the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) so that no afflictions could disturb him; he scrupulously observed all three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices.
He constantly cultivated the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). In his quest for the Dharma, he forgot his own body:

he would write out scriptures by flaying his skin and drawing blood from his veins, and he severed his arms and cast himself away as offerings in his petitions for instruction, never shrinking from such acts.
Without doubting that one might forget oneself for the sake of others, one is like one who endures suffering to cut flesh to feed a hawk or sacrifices life to nourish a tiger with one’s own body;
one does not fear or dread wealth, treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, or children, casting them aside like worn-out sandals;
one discards limbs, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain as if discarding a sloughed-off skin, passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of births from life to life.
From birth, this mind does not regress; from kalpa to kalpa, passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, this mind becomes ever more diligent.

Thus, the fruit of the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas is fulfilled, the merit of the ten thousand virtues is perfected, one is free from the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations, attains mastery over immeasurable and boundless dharma-gates, skillfully enters immeasurable and boundless samādhis, and accomplishes the five [supernormal powers].

Fully endowed with the faculties and powers, perfecting the three insights and the three knowledges, manifesting the four wisdoms and transcendingly realizing the three bodies, attaining the six supernormal powers and the five eyes,
and obtaining the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence to preach exhaustively; entering the four bases of power so that supernatural penetrations are sovereign,
the eight stages of mastery and the eight liberations are constantly present before them, and the four fearlessnesses and the four means of integration are enjoyed without end.
Exhausting the eight branches of the noble path and the eighteen unique qualities, which are not equal to those of the three vehicles;

adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, this subtle and wondrous Dharma-body perceives all things without exception throughout past kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and future kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

regarding the sentient beings in present worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and their minds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is nothing it does not know, being perfectly clear and luminous.
The Honored One who possesses the Ten Epithets transcends the three realms;
he is the God among gods, the Sage among sages, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, and the Truly Perfectly Enlightened One.

He surpasses all skillful means, accomplishes the Ten Powers, and returns to deliver all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm. Such is the ultimate merit of the Buddha. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition, universally desiring to enable all sentient beings to likewise attain this Way.
This is because his great vow and great power pledge that all living beings shall together realize the wondrous fruit of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, in discerning the three teachings, one must not do so with a private or biased mind.

Regarding the mind of love and hatred, if one discusses it only by leveling the mind and investigating its ultimate efficacy, one will know that when those in the world who study Confucianism reach the point of reaping the fruits of their causes, they achieve nothing more than fame and office;
when those in the world who study the Way (Dao) reach the point of reaping the fruits of their causes, they achieve nothing more than longevity;
and when those in the world who study Buddhism reach the point of reaping the fruits of their causes—
In this place, one can sever birth and death to attain ultimate nirvana and universally deliver all sentient beings so that they may together achieve perfect enlightenment;
is the distinction between [these paths] not clearly visible? Therefore, I shall attempt to illustrate it by analogy: what the Confucian teaching practices is China;
what the Daoist teaching practices is the heavens and the human realm; and as for what the Buddhist teaching practices—
"Exhausting all of space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm" means that while Confucianism governs a single family, its authority and commands extend only within the boundaries of the walls;
beyond those walls, it cannot issue summons.
Daoism is like governing a single district, where its administration and teachings reach only to the four borders; beyond those borders, it cannot exercise control.
This is the decree: the Buddha still possesses the four seas and serves as the sovereign of all under heaven;

throughout the vast heavens and across the lands, there are none who are not his subjects and citizens, and rites, music, military expeditions, and punishments all issue from him. This is the distinction between the breadth and narrowness of the three teachings.
Those who study Confucianism cease their efforts after death; this is a matter of a single hundred-year span. Those who study the Way strive for longevity;
this concerns a period of many thousands of years. Those who study Buddhism eternally sever birth and death, abiding in profound stillness;
this involves passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without end. Confucianism is like a single lamp, its light illuminating but a single night before the bell tolls.
The exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) is like an oil lamp being extinguished when its oil is spent.
The Way is like King Ajātaśatru’s hundred-year lamp that illuminated the Buddha’s *śarīra*; after a hundred years had passed, the lamp was finally extinguished.

The Buddha is like the bright sun that shines throughout the ten thousand ages, ever luminous, setting in the west and rising in the east, circulating without ceasing. This is a brief explanation of the distinction between the long and short durations of these three teachings.
The general meaning of the Three Teachings is detailed and complete in this treatise.
*The Chapter on Turning the Heart and Dispelling Delusions* by Huangmen Shilang [Yin Zhong] of the Northern Qi:

"The matters of the three periods of time are trustworthy and have evidential proof; one should turn the heart toward the family vocation [of the Dharma] and not treat it with negligence or contempt. Within this lie the subtle principles."

Having already mastered the various sutras and treatises, I need not further praise or describe them here; I only fear that you may still lack firm resolve, and thus I urge and exhort you once more briefly.
To trace their origins: the analysis of the four elements and five aggregates deconstructs physical existence; the six boats and three vehicles transport all sentient beings.
The myriad practices return to emptiness, and the thousand gateways enter into goodness. How could eloquence and wisdom be merely the seven classics or the hundred [treatises]?
The Master’s transmission clarifies that this is beyond the reach of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius. The inner and outer teachings are fundamentally one body;
they differ in their gradual progression and extremities, and vary in depth. At the initial gate of the Inner Canon (Buddhism), five prohibitions are established;

the benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and sincerity of the Outer Canon (Confucianism) all correspond to them. Benevolence is the prohibition against killing; righteousness is the prohibition against stealing.
Prohibitions are the means by which ritual prevents deviation; wisdom is the means by which it prevents excess; and sincerity is the means by which it prevents falsehood.

As for hunting, military expeditions, banquets, and punishments, these follow human nature and cannot be suddenly eliminated; one must instead establish regulations for them so that they do not become excessive or chaotic.
To return to the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, yet to turn one's back on the ancestral tradition of Śākyamuni—how deluded this is!
Furthermore, there are generally five types of secular slander: first, regarding worldly affairs and the boundless manifestations of spiritual transformation as being far-fetched and extravagant;
second, regarding the lack of immediate retribution for good fortune, misfortune, calamity, or blessing as being deceptive;
third, regarding the fact that the conduct of monks and nuns is often not pure as being wicked and corrupt; fourth, regarding the wasteful expenditure [of resources].
The depletion of gold and treasures, and the imposition of taxes and corvée labor, are harms to the state—this is the fifth point.

Furthermore, even if there were causes and conditions such as retribution for good and evil, how could one endure the hardships of benefiting "A" in this life for the sake of "B" in a future life? This would be to act like a stranger to oneself.
Now, all of these shall be explained below.

Commentary One states: As for vast and great things, how could they possibly be measured? What humans currently know is nothing like heaven and earth. Heaven is accumulated qi; earth is accumulated clods.
The sun is the essence of yang; the moon is the essence of yin; the stars are the essences of the myriad things—this is what the Confucian school accepts.
Yet when stars fall, they become stones. If their essence were such [as the Confucians claim], how could it turn into stone?
They possess luminous natures and are also substantial and heavy; to what are they attached?

The diameter of a single star is as large as one hundred *li*, and the distance from the head to the tail of a single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) spans tens of thousands of hundreds of *li*. These objects, numbering in the tens of thousands, are linked together; their widths and obliquities remain constant without ever expanding or contracting.
Furthermore, the forms and colors of the stars are identical to those of the sun and moon, differing only in their relative sizes.

However, the sun and moon must also pass through stone; since stone is solid and dense, how could the crow and the hare [within them] find room? Furthermore, if stone exists within the ether, how could it move independently?

If the sun, moon, and stars were all composed of ether, and ether is light and buoyant, they would necessarily merge with the celestial sphere in their coming and going and circular revolutions, unable to deviate from it.
Under such circumstances, the principles governing their speed and slowness ought to be uniform; why then do the sun and moon...?

The five planets and the twenty-eight lunar mansions each have their fixed degrees, yet their movements are uneven; could it be that the vital energies (qi) have fallen and suddenly transformed into stone?
Since the earth is turbid and impure, according to the natural law, it ought to be heavy and sink; yet when one digs into the soil to find a spring, it floats upon the water.
What else lies beneath the accumulated waters? From where do the rivers and hundreds of valleys arise? Why is it that they flow eastward toward the sea?
Where does the water that does not overflow into the Abysmal Void (Guixu) or the Tailgate (Weilu) go? By what force is the Stone of the Consuming Abyss (Wojiao) ignited?
Who regulates the ebb and flow of the tides? Why do the stars of the Milky Way remain suspended without falling, given that the nature of water is to flow downward?

How is it that they surge upward? Since the beginning of heaven and earth, the constellations have existed; though the Nine Provinces were not yet delineated and the feudal states not yet divided, their boundaries were already established.

As for the regional divisions and celestial coordinates established since the system of feudal fiefs, who was it that demarcated these boundaries? While states have increased or decreased in size, the stars neither advance nor recede;

thus, the correspondence between calamities, blessings, misfortunes, and fortunes remains unerring within this framework. Given the vastness of the celestial phenomena and the multitude of the listed stars, why are the *fenye* (stellar domains) restricted solely to the Central Kingdom?
Why is Mao assigned as the domain of the Xiongnu, the "banner-head," while the Western Hu, the Eastern Yue, and those with tattooed foreheads [are not]?

Is it that Jiaozhi alone is abandoned [by Heaven]? To seek [an answer] by this means and yet find nothing to the end—is it because one seeks through the ordinary affairs of human beings, or must it necessarily lie beyond the universe?
Generally, what people believe relies only on the ears and the eyes; regarding all that lies beyond the ears and eyes, they harbor doubts.

The Confucian explanations of Heaven have their own various principles: sometimes it is described as a sphere (*hun*), sometimes as a canopy (*gai*); at times it is proclaimed, at times it is tranquil; the constellations... [are arranged].
To the extent that one surveys the boundaries of the universe and its dependencies, if it were as if one were seeing it directly, one could not claim it is otherwise;

yet if it is merely based on measurement, how can it be sufficient as a foundation? For what reason do you believe the conjectures of ordinary men and remain deluded regarding the subtle purport of the Great Sage, wishing to insist that there are no kalpas numbering as many as the atoms in the sands of the Ganges? Furthermore, even Zou Yan spoke of the Nine Provinces and Mounts.
People of the Central Plains do not believe there are fish as large as trees; people of the coastal regions do not believe there are trees as large as fish.

Emperor Wu of Han did not believe in glue made from bowstrings; Emperor Wen of Wei did not believe in fire-resistant cloth. When foreigners saw brocade, they could not believe it was formed by insects eating trees and spitting out silk.
Formerly, when I was in Jiangnan, I did not believe there were felt tents that could accommodate a thousand people; yet now that I have come to the north of the River, I see them.

It is not that there are no vessels of twenty thousand *hu* [of capacity]; all have been verified by experiment. In this world, there are masters of incantations and various illusionists who can yet walk upon fire, tread upon blades, plant melons, and move wells;

in the space of a mere instant, they undergo ten transformations and five metamorphoses. If what is achieved through human effort can be such as this, how much more so the spiritual powers and responsive miracles, which are inconceivable?
A jeweled banner from a thousand *li* away—[a hundred... (Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary at the end. The translation reflects the available portion.)
"Did a *yojana*-sized seat transform into a pure land and a wondrous stupa emerge from it?
The second explanation states: "The signs of heavenly faith and slander are like echoes and shadows; those who have heard of or witnessed such events are already numerous.

It may be that one's sincerity is not yet deep or that karmic conditions have not yet been met, so that for the time being the response is delayed; yet in the end, one shall surely receive the retribution. Thus it is well said.
That evil deeds bring about misfortune and good deeds bring about fortune is a doctrine shared by all nine schools and a hundred lineages;

how could it be that only the Buddhist scriptures are false? Consider the premature deaths of Xiang Tuo and Yan Hui, the freezing and starving of Yuan Xian and Bo Yi, the longevity and prosperity of Robber Zhi and Zhuang Qiao, and the wealth and power of Jing Gong of Qi and Huan Tai—if one traces these back to past karma, one may hope for better rebirths in the future.

Furthermore, to generalize: if one performs good deeds yet happens to encounter calamity, or commits evil yet perhaps meets with signs of fortune, one might then harbor resentment and claim such things are deceptive.
If this were so, then the accounts of Yao and Shun would be empty, and the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius would be unreal;
furthermore, upon what could one rely for faith in order to establish oneself?
The third explanation states: Since the beginning of creation, unwholesome people have been many while wholesome people have been few;
how could one expect everyone to be entirely pure and refined? If one sees a monk of renown or noble conduct, one neglects to speak of them;

yet if one encounters an ordinary or worldly monk, one immediately gives rise to criticism and disparagement. Furthermore, if students are not diligent, can this be considered the fault of the teacher? As for the study of the scriptures by worldly monks—

How is the Vinaya different from the way scholars study the *Shi* and *Li*? When the teachings of the *Shi* and *Li* are used to regulate those at court, there are hardly any who practice them completely;
yet when the prohibitions of the Sūtras and Vinaya are used to regulate those who have left the household life, why do you alone demand that they remain free of transgressions?
Furthermore, if a minister who fails in his conduct still seeks salary and rank, how can those who violate the precepts feel any shame regarding their offerings? Regarding this—

Regarding the observance of precepts, one may naturally commit transgressions; yet once one has donned the dharma robes and entered the ranks of the Sangha, the merit accumulated over a year through observing the fasts, preaching, lecturing, reciting, and upholding the teachings exceeds that of laypeople by more than the difference between a mountain and the sea.
The fourth explanation states: The internal teachings (Buddhism) have many paths, and the life of renunciation is but one of them.
If one can maintain sincerity and filial piety in the heart and take benevolence and kindness as the foundation, then Sudatta and Jalavāhana need not necessarily shave their hair and beards.

How could it be that the entire system of well-fields must be exhausted to build stupas and temples, or that every common household must become a monk or nun? All of this arises from the inability of governance to exercise moderation.
Consequently, temples that do not conform to the Dharma obstruct the people’s cultivation of crops, and monks who possess no vocation waste the state’s tax revenues;

this is certainly not the fundamental intent of the Great Awakened One. Furthermore, let us consider this: those who seek the Way concern themselves with their own personal destiny, while those who spare expenditure concern themselves with the state’s strategy.

Personal destiny and state strategy cannot both be fulfilled simultaneously. A loyal minister must sacrifice his kin for the sake of the King, and a filial son must prioritize the stability of the household.
Yet, forgetting that each nation has its own way of governance, the Confucian may remain unbowed before kings and lords, exalting his own principles;

the recluse may decline the throne of a king, refuse the office of a prime minister, and withdraw from the world to dwell in mountain forests—how can these be reckoned as crimes based on their tax obligations?
If they could transform the common people together and lead them all into the Way, so that they resemble the world of Maitreya or the kingdom of Śaṅkha, then there would be spontaneity.
Since rice is an inexhaustible treasure, why seek the profits of fields and sericulture?
The fifth explanation states: although the physical form dies, the spirit remains. While a person is alive in this world, they seem unrelated to their future existence;
yet once they have passed away, that future life appears to the previous one as nothing more than the transition from youth to old age, or morning to evening. There is... [in the world...]

The manifestation of spirits in dreams, their descent upon young maidens, or their influence upon wives and children to seek out food and drink and petition for blessings—such instances are indeed not few.
Today, those who are poor, lowly, or afflicted by illness do not fail to resent their lack of merit in previous lives.
Judging from this, how can one not prepare a foundation for them? For those who have descendants...
These are but the common people (*sattva*) within heaven and earth; how could they concern themselves with one's personal affairs?
Yet one still loves and protects them, leaving behind their foundations—how much more so for one’s own spirit (*śrāman*), which one now wishes to abandon!

It is because ordinary people are obscured and do not see the future that they say the life of the next birth and the present life are not of one substance. If one possessed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one would discern that every thought-moment perishes as it arises.

If one’s life is subject to incessant continuity, how can one not feel dread? Furthermore, when a gentleman dwells in the world, he prizes the ability to overcome himself and restore the rites (*li*), thereby aiding the age and benefiting all things.
Those who govern a family desire the prosperity of that family; those who rule a state desire the excellence of that state.

Yet, as for servants, concubines, ministers, and subjects—how are they ultimately related to one’s own person? For what reason, then, do you labor so hard to cultivate virtue? This is surely the way of Yao.

Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius merely failed to find pleasure; yet, when one person cultivates the Way, how many sentient beings are saved and delivered, and how many individuals are freed from the burden of their karmic offenses?

Reflect on this carefully! If you all look toward worldly calculations to establish your families, and cannot abandon your wives and children to leave the household life, you should at least concurrently cultivate the precepts and devote your minds to recitation for the sake of future lives.
The human body is a difficult vessel to obtain; do not let it pass in vain. Among the Confucians, our Master [Confucius] still kept his distance from the kitchen;
seeing life, he could not bear its death, and hearing its cries, he would not eat its flesh. Gao Chai broke his staff [to mourn], yet he was unaware of the Inner Teaching;
nevertheless, all were able to refrain from killing. This is the natural application of the mind of the benevolent person; among all living beings, there are none that do not cherish their own lives.

One must strive to put an end to the practice of killing. For those who delight in slaughter, the retribution will manifest at the moment of death, and the calamities that descend upon their descendants will be so numerous that they cannot all be recorded here;
nevertheless, I shall set forth several instances at the end.

During the Liang dynasty, there was a man who habitually mixed chicken egg whites with his hair wash, claiming it made his hair shiny; every time he washed his hair, he would break twenty or thirty eggs.
When he was on the verge of death, only the chirping of several thousand chicken chicks could be heard within his hair.
The Liu family of Jiangling made their living selling eel soup; later, they gave birth to a son whose head was that of an eel, while from the neck downward he was human.
When Wang Ke was the Governor of Yongjia Commandery, someone sent him a sheep; he intended to entertain his guests with a banquet, but the sheep’s tether snapped and it came forward.
He threw himself before a guest, knelt twice, and then entered into the guest’s clothing. The guest did not say anything at all, and there was certainly no one to offer him succor.
After a short while, fortunately, the sheep was roasted and served; as soon as a single morsel had entered the guest’s mouth, it descended into his skin and spread throughout his entire body.
In agony and screaming, the guest finally spoke of it, whereupon he died, making the bleating of a sheep.

When Emperor Xiaoyuan of the Liang dynasty was in Jiangzhou, there was a man serving as the Magistrate of Wangcai County who, having had his county yamen burned during the rebellion of Liu Jingong, took up residence in a monastery.
The local inhabitants presented him with an ox and wine as a formal offering.

The magistrate tied the ox to a pillar of the *stūpa* (刹柱) and, setting aside the Buddhist images, arranged couches and seats in the hall to receive his guests. Before he had even killed the ox, it broke its tether and bolted straight away.

When he arrived at the steps and prostrated himself, the magistrate laughed loudly and ordered his attendants to slaughter him. Having drunk and eaten until he was intoxicated and satiated, he lay down beneath the eaves.
As he gradually regained consciousness, he felt an itch in his body; as he scratched it, hidden eruptions appeared, which subsequently developed into leprosy.

He died after about ten years. Later, Yang Sidai served as the Governor of Xiyang Commandery. During the chaos of Shi Jing’s rebellion, there was again a drought and famine, and starving people stole from the fields.
Zhong Mai had a subordinate who, upon seeing any thief he captured, would immediately cut off their wrists;
in total, he executed more than ten people. Later, this subordinate fathered a son who was naturally born without hands.
In Qi, there was one who held the rank of Chaoqing; his family was extremely wealthy and extravagant. He would not consider beef delicious unless he had slaughtered it with his own hands.

When he was about thirty years old, his illness became critical, and he had a vivid vision of oxen coming toward him; his entire body felt as if it were being stabbed by knives, and he died while screaming.

Gao Wei of Jiangling followed me into the Qi state for several years; later, while fishing in the marshes of Youzhou, he fell ill and died after being bitten by a school of fish that appeared to him repeatedly.

In the world there are foolish people who do not recognize benevolence and righteousness and do not understand wealth and honor, all because they fail to cultivate their roots and plant their seeds when taking a wife for their son.
One may resent such a person who lacks the basic resources to rely upon as a venerable father-in-law or mother-in-law, whose nature is like that of a serpent or viper,
who poisons others with slander and knows no bounds of propriety, and who insults the parents of his wife while claiming to teach her the ways of a wife;
such a person is unfilial toward his own body, cares for nothing but resentment toward others, and pities only his own children while refusing to accept his own daughter-in-law.
The Yin (dark forces) record one's transgressions, and the ghosts seize one’s allotted lifespan; one must be careful never to have them as neighbors, nor should one ever rely on them for assistance.
One ought to keep them at a distance!
*The Discourse on the True Suchness and Original Nature of the Three Teachings*, Part Two, Section Five.
The true nature of suchness is the one reality, free from delusion, prior to the birth of one's parents;
it is called the "original face. In the Chan school, it is termed the "Treasury of the True Dharma Eye"; in the Lotus school, it is termed the "Original Nature Amitābha";

in Confucianism, it is termed "Heavenly Principle" (*t'ien-li*); in Laozi, it is termed the "Valley Spirit"; and in the Way of the *I Ching*, it is termed the "Supreme Ultimate" (*tai-chi*). Though their names differ, [the essence remains the same].
In truth, it is this very same nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This nature is empty yet spiritual, quiescent yet wondrous.
Before heaven and earth were divided, this principle already existed; it remains undecaying through kalpas of dust and does not shift when the world is destroyed.

The Patriarchs have also said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth, formless and fundamentally silent; it is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not follow the four seasons."

This is precisely what is meant by "decay. Alas! Humans cannot maintain their true state of spontaneous freedom, but are instead fettered by a physical substance composed of the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind.
At the very moment they receive this form, it already clouds their inherently pure essence with the turbid energy of yin-blood.
Furthermore, once born, they are deluded and obscured by the six sense-objects and the five desires, losing sight of their original nature.
Because this true nature exists within us, the Buddha taught that the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates are all means to lead people to turn back from delusion and return to the truth.
The most direct and easy path to practice is the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha;

for those who cultivate it, the mind becomes undistracted and samādhi manifests before them—this is the restoration of one's original nature. Confucius taught people to overcome their private selfishness.

Returning once more to the Heavenly Principle (tianli), when private desires are completely purified and the Heavenly Principle flows forth, this is what Laozi meant by "making people discard their desires and settle their spirits.
This is precisely the "Valley-Spirit that does not die. "Valley" means emptiness; "spirit" means numinous awareness. It refers to being empty yet numinous, unclouded.

This state of being empty yet numinous and unclouded is none other than the nature that cannot be destroyed even if the body is ruined. As the Book of Documents says: "From sincerity comes luminosity."
This is called "nature is itself luminous and sincere. It is said that through instruction, sincerity leads to luminosity, and luminosity leads to sincerity.

Only those who possess the ultimate sincerity in the world are able to fully exhaust their own nature. Being able to fully exhaust one's own nature means being able to fully exhaust the nature of others.

Being able to fully exhaust the nature of others means being able to fully exhaust the nature of all things. Being able to fully exhaust the nature of all things means knowing that the natures of the sage and the ordinary person are identical.
This is the essence. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "This Dharma is equal; it has no high or low.
"This Dharma" refers to one's original nature (*prakṛti*). The original nature is likened to a vajra, signifying its solidity and indestructibility.

"No high or low" means that from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas above down to the most minute insects and sentient beings below, all possess Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); therefore, it is so called.
It is equality. The Heart Sutra says, "neither increasing nor decreasing. This nature does not increase in sages, nor does it decrease in ordinary beings;
therefore, it is called neither increasing nor decreasing. Have you not seen that the Confucians say, "All sentient beings each possess a single Great Ultimate"?
This is precisely the same principle. Alas! Sages and ordinary beings, humans and things, are rooted in this one nature; it is only due to delusion and awakening [that they appear otherwise].
The distinction between the extraordinary and the defiled, the pure and the impure, is such that there are those who become sages and those who become ordinary beings;
there are those who become human and those who become creatures. Given this is so, how could one possibly kill and eat the various classes of living beings?
If you kill others for food now, they will surely kill and eat you in the future. Have you not seen what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says?
When humans die they become sheep, and when sheep die they become humans; as they prey upon one another in this cycle, how can one escape it? Someone might say:
"Heaven produced the myriad things for the nourishment of humanity. If we do not kill and eat them, and thus cause the number of birds and beasts to increase further, how will we manage them?
I answer: Because of this [logic], those who kill and eat are many, and those who fall into the lower realms are likewise many. If one were able to refrain from killing...
If one does not eat, there will be no suffering of mutual retribution. Why is this? If all men and women in the world maintain the precepts of fasting, they will naturally abstain from eating.
If they do not eat, they will not kill; if they do not kill, they will not fall [into the realms of suffering];
and if they do not fall, hell will be transformed into heaven, and ordinary beings will become Buddhas. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "A bhikṣu who maintains the precepts does not kill living beings."
If this is so for mere grass, how much more so for sentient beings? Sentient beings are those who possess life and spiritual essence;
insentient things are grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles. Inferring from this, one must not kill any class of living being, whether large or small.
You all should carefully and thoroughly investigate the mind with diligence, reciting the Buddha’s name to awaken to the true source. If you understand this clearly for yourselves—
To see the Dharma and have it manifest before one is called "seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood," thereby transcending saṃsāra.

If there is even a moment’s delay or hesitation, one will sink forever into the sea of suffering; thus, it can be said that by shedding one's fur, one attains Buddhahood from this very point—this depends on others.
Scholar东坡’s Discourse on Food and Drink Within the space between heaven and earth, and within the realm of yin and yang, all spirits are brought forth and all things are likewise produced.
Among these myriad things, life thrives; among all living beings, humans are foremost. Though they are said to be foremost, they still require food and clothing.
Only when one has fully provided for their basic sustenance can they establish themselves and establish their conduct. What is used to establish oneself?
It is the grains—millet, panicled millet, broomcorn millet, wheat, and beans—as well as fruits, gourds, and edible vegetables. What constitutes establishing one's conduct?

It is practicing benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and sincerity, and engaging in the vocations of scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant. Thus, every person in the world follows their respective [calling].
Having established this intention, consider that even animals are included within the category of the myriad spirits and likewise possess the principles of the Five Constant Virtues.

Their experiences of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure; their movement, stillness, rising, and sinking; their pain, itching, hunger, and satiety; and their procreation and mutual protection are no different from our own.
Alas, it is lamentable that worldly people treat them as food, cruelly subjecting them to roasting and frying—how deeply pitiable! Oh, the physical form!
Although my life is distinct from theirs, my essence is no different;

to nourish my own body by cooking the bodies of others, or to sustain my own life by slaughtering the lives of others, is truly not a heart of benevolence and forbearance, but rather the mind of a fool. All who eat meat violate the Five Constant Virtues;
by slaughtering the bodies of others to fatten and sweeten one's own, one acts with lack of benevolence, severing their kinship and prolonging [one’s own] [life].
To act unrighteously for the sake of one's kin and friends is improper; to offer another’s physical body as a sacrifice to spirits and deities is a lack of ritual propriety;

to claim that one who receives a salary must endure the blade and the chopping block is a lack of wisdom; and to set bait and devise schemes to lure others into traps is a lack of trustworthiness. Alas!
A person living in this dusty world relies entirely upon the Five Constant Virtues (*pañca-śīla*); to knowingly violate them is unworthy of being called human.
Furthermore, it is said that there is a common worldly saying: "If one owes another money or debt, one shall be reborn as an animal to repay it;

when I receive my salary, we shall both be free from fault. I have reflected on this carefully and find it not to be so. For the spirit of sentient beings is none other than human life itself; life is one's own life, and debt is worldly wealth.
While a debt may be repaid by sacrificing one's life, one must not abandon [the principle of] resolving mutual enmity and resentment. Furthermore...
They receive one another’s suffering and will soon be made into food; how can we not feel compassion for them? Alas! Those who eat them are not benevolent men; a benevolent man does not eat them.
Master Mingdao said: "Human beings are my brothers; domestic animals share my same vital breath. Prime Minister Pei said:
"That which belongs to the category of blood and breath must possess consciousness; whatever possesses consciousness must be of the same substance [as oneself]. Mencius said: "When one sees..."
It is unbearable to witness their death, and hearing their cries makes it unbearable to eat their flesh;
therefore, this is what the gentleman must deeply guard against. *The Text on Prohibiting Killing by Master Oudant (Youtan)*, Part Two, Seven.
Whether born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation—be they birds, beasts, insects, fish, or any other creatures—they all belong to the lineage of future Buddhas;

or perhaps they were one's own parents over many past lives. When they look up in dread of death and strive with urgency for life, seeking to avoid suffering and cherish their bodies, this sentiment is uniform;
when they seek security and nourish their lives, this principle is universal. Why, then, do they utter such piteous cries as they are drawn upward?
With eyes fixed upon the blade and the chopping block, they were driven toward the ground of death; nets were spread across the wilds and snares laid out over the mountains.

Flames chased the ridges according to their heights, and smoke followed the terrain with varying density. Hawks as swift as lightning soared up together, and horses as fleet as the wind vied to race forward.
Monkeys’ souls fled at the sight of arrows, and geese’ hearts failed them at the sight of bows—heads severed and brains crushed.

When the pain of sourness is so agonizing that it penetrates the chest and reaches the very marrow of the bones, how can it be restrained? Furthermore, these beings all receive the Five Elements and possess the Four Images;

they equally partake of the Buddha-nature and share in spiritual intelligence. Why, then, do you present these mountains of flesh and set up these instruments of roasting and burning to satisfy your own bellies and gratify your hearts and livers?
You fail to realize that those who take their lives are, in effect, cutting away from the Buddha’s own body.
Those who consume their blood and flesh are surely not sparing the very bodies of their own parents; they commit the profound transgression of killing and sever the seed-nature of compassion.

While alive, their merit and lifespan are consumed in secret; after death, they sink into the abyss, destined for the mountains of knives and trees of swords, where they must successively repay their debts as chickens, pigs, fish, or rabbits.
Consider how the act of slaughtering and roasting is a result that corresponds exactly to its cause.
To contemplate the eating of meat is truly to feel one’s heart turn cold; though it may be sold easily at the butcher’s gate, one cannot escape its grave karmic retribution.
A Bodhisattva would rather break their own bones than ever consume a living being; thus, when the white hare offered its own body as fuel, the immortal did not look upon it with indifference.
If even grass is not to be plucked, how could flesh be permitted to be tasted? One must distance oneself from the kitchen, for those who hear the cries [of the slaughtered] cannot bear it.
To train and raise others for the purpose of selling them is equivalent to killing with one’s own mouth and eating with one’s own mind; this is particularly grave.

It was for this reason that the Great Sage bestowed his compassion and established the precepts to forever sever the taking of life—the virtue of which is immense. Those who cultivate the Pure Land must therefore uphold and observe them.
One may truly be called a dragon in a deep pool only when one no longer craves the taste of fragrant bait.

**Dharma Master Foyin’s Text on Prohibiting the Killing of Animals** The two-legged, the eight-legged, the scaly, the armored, the feathered, and all other species of sentient beings are in their Buddha-nature no different from that of the Buddha.

It is only because they initially applied their minds wrongly that they have resulted in these distinct forms in this present life—wandering in the water or sporting in the forest. How can one bear to take them to provide for daily sustenance?

In a mere instant, they are captured alive and placed upon the cutting block; unable to speak, their eyes stare back in terror. Some are beaten with hammers, others pierced with knives, and they are dragged into the boiling cauldrons—how truly terrifying!
Their feathers are plucked, their scales scraped, their backs split open, and their hearts gouged out, yet they still breathe.
You praise the taste as exquisite, boasting of its fine flavor to your husband and wife, urging them all to eat and relish it, indulging only in the gratification of your own desires.

Ignorance fears not the records of the underworld, where every hair’s breadth of one's life is accounted for; as soon as life ends, karmic retribution arrives. Facing King Yama, how could one dare to conceal anything?
One must report everything from beginning to end without error. Where can one escape the glowing embers and boiling cauldrons?

I exhort the worthy and noble to exercise caution and restraint; do not treat sentient beings as if they were easy to harm. For every morsel you covet from another, a morsel shall be returned to you. Thus spoke the ancient sages.

One who never falsely observes the precept against killing, recites the Buddha’s name while simultaneously practicing the release of captive animals, will certainly reach the Western Pure Land in the highest grade of rebirth.
*The Text on Abstaining from Killing by Chan Master Zhenxie* How lamentable it is that people of the world have made such a great error:
they take what is a source of suffering and treat it as pleasure, arranging the slaughter of living beings to welcome guests and entertain visitors.

As living beings create the agonizing sounds by their ears that have not yet ceased, they are drenched with boiling water; they are not merely being boiled and roasted in cauldrons, but are scorched and seared within fires.

While they gather with kinsmen and friends in the hall above, and the drums and music resound clamorously in the courtyard below, indulging in the splendors of a single lifetime, they fail to perceive that for a thousand lifetimes they shall fall.
When one day their lifespan is exhausted and their retribution ends, their life-force will be claimed.
When an enemy seeks you out to seize you, even if you attempt to evade them by using every excuse, you will nonetheless be bound by spirits and deities.

You may be forced up the mountain of knives or the tree of swords, or enter the flaming furnace and the boiling cauldron to repay your past debts in due order. There, you will be wounded by blades and hacked by axes;
at such a time, your suffering is such that human emotion and reason are utterly useless. Even if you endure this agony until the end, you cannot escape its finality.
If you enter another shell, unless you are to carry iron bits and bear a saddle, you will surely be covered in hair and endowed with horns.
All you virtuous men and women, each turn your head back and examine yourselves: how can you reform and repent your body and mind so as to avoid sinking into the three evil realms?
If you allow yourselves to be led astray from the path, it will be difficult to turn back for ten thousand kalpas. Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and seek rebirth there.
The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
A Text on Refraining from Killing by the Patriarch Puan.
Thirty points worthy of lamentation: people fail to weigh their actions, yet they treat the commission of sins as if they were offering incense at every local shrine, altar, and temple.
This is entirely a place of labor; everyone roasts geese and boils ducks, and at every turn slaughters pigs and sheep.

The clever ones hold knives to draw blood, while the clumsy ones go to heat the water. Stepping forward, they take up their tasks, stripping feathers, breaking open bellies, and searching through entrails.
When the meat is half-cooked, everyone vies with one another to carve and distribute it, looking just like yakṣas and rākṣasas.
It is just as when tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves sacrifice to malevolent spirits and wild ghosts;
how could the orthodox deities ever come to partake? And yet, the ghosts never become satiated; instead, they suffer transgression. As for cats, no one kills them to eat;
they are gathered up and hidden away. As for pigs and sheep, many people kill them, seen in long, continuous rows; birds and livestock are slaughtered at all times.

The executioner has surely departed to take responsibility for this; because of these three calamities and two droughts, how can people not reflect? If one wishes to repay Heaven and Earth, there is no way other than through fasting, abstinence, and virtuous conduct.

O worthy ones, if you take his life, you must first return the thought that would kill him; by turning the light of awareness back upon itself, you may avoid disaster. A verse says: If you wish to repay Heaven and Earth, There is no way other than through fasting and virtue.
O worthy ones, if you take his life, First return the thought that would kill him. By turning the light back within, you may escape calamity.
Beasts were originally humans who came to be so; The cycle of humans and beasts has continued from antiquity to the present.
Do not don fur or wear horns; I urge you to cease the mind of a beast.
Since the body is the root of suffering, awaken and practice cultivation early. (1) Three: One.
The three realms offer no peace, like a house on fire; the conditions of suffering within the three realms are like a prison. Within these three realms dwell the six paths of existence.
What are these six paths? They are: the path of devas and immortals, the path of humans, the path of asuras, the path of hungry ghosts, the path of animals, and the path of hell-dwellers.
According to the principles of the Buddha, there is not one among these six paths that is not suffering.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "With my Buddha-eye, I behold the sentient beings of the six realms who are impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom, entering the perilous path of birth and death where suffering continues without interruption.
Although the heavenly realm is a cause of pleasure, it does not transcend the suffering of saṃsāra.
Within the human realm alone, the suffering is immeasurable; how much more so, then, is the suffering of the four evil destinies?
Now, I shall briefly describe several kinds of suffering seen among human beings to demonstrate them to you. Who would believe that this very physical body is the root of suffering?
One exhausts oneself in craving worldly pleasures, unaware that such pleasure is the cause of suffering. This floating life is easily spent; how could it be a long-term dwelling?
This illusory substance is not solid; it all returns to decay and extinction. Why is this so? Each of you should observe your own body.
From head to foot, there are within it only thirty-six things:

hair, body hair, nails, teeth, eye discharge, tears, mucus, saliva, filth, sweat, the two excretions, skin, blood, flesh, sinews, veins, marrow, fat, grease, brain, membranes, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, red and white phlegm, and the two internal organs—the raw and the cooked. Thus, these nine orifices flow constantly. Therefore...
The Sūtra says: "This body is a collection of manifold sufferings; it is entirely impure. Why is this?
Within the human body dwell eighty thousand families of worms. If one contemplates this in stillness, it is truly something to be loathed and weary of.
Furthermore, even those whose six sense organs are intact may have among them those who are blind, deaf, lame, or withered-handed."
Those with stooping waists and hunched backs; those who are mute and have short tongues; those with rotting noses and crooked mouths;
those with cleft lips and protruding teeth; those with scaly heads and yellow hair; those with tumors growing on their necks and cheeks; those unable to walk who must move about by hand;
those afflicted with sores that flow with pus and blood; those suffering from leprosy, ringworm, and foul odors—these are born as slaves.
Those who are constantly subjected to beating and abuse, born in the borderlands or among the low-born, being no different from beasts—the sufferings within their bodies cannot be fully described.
Furthermore, they are tormented by the eight kinds of suffering, with no moment of respite. What are these eight sufferings?

The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of encountering the hated and the disliked, the suffering of parting from the loved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks...

To undergo the suffering of the five aggregates in their blazing intensity and the suffering of cyclic existence constitutes the eight types of suffering. Within these eight sufferings, the varieties of pain are countless;
the wise should clearly understand this for themselves. Furthermore, there are many kinds of untimely deaths that cannot be avoided:
those who die of hunger, those who die of cold, those who die oppressed by heat, and those who die from overindulgence in food and drink.
Those who die because of alcohol; those who die because of sensual desire; those who die because of wealth;

those who die because of vital energy (*prāṇa*); those who die by fire; those who die by drowning in water; those who die being crushed by mountain precipices or rocky walls; those who die being crushed by the collapse of houses or the falling of walls;
those killed when their homes are plundered by bandits; and those killed when encountering highway robbers on the road.
Those who die crushed by chariots or trampled by horses; those who die in battle while entering the fray; those who die for violating the king’s law;
those who die from contracting a seasonal epidemic; those who die from nightmares; those who die from being deluded by ghosts; those who die from falling into heterodoxy;
those who die from idiocy or paralysis; those who die from being bitten by tigers; those who die from being wounded by snakes; and those who die from a stroke of heavenly lightning.
Those killed by the execution of evil spirits; those killed by poisonous drugs or malevolent *gū* substances; those killed through secret malice;
those killed because their grievances could not be redressed or due to curses; those who died of apoplexy; those who died in childbirth; those who died suddenly from intestinal sand;
those killed by the accidental throwing of tiles or stones; those who died falling from heights; and those who died of terror.
Furthermore, there are those who die of grief because their quest for fame failed; those who die because their schemes for profit were unsuccessful;

those who die by hanging themselves, stabbing themselves, or cutting their own throats; and those who die by throwing themselves into water or fire—there are many such varieties that cannot be fully described.
Alas! There is yet further suffering for those living in the world and managing households; let me show you a few more instances: there are men and women who suffer from poverty...
Suffering exists among both the wealthy and the poor, as well as among men and women. Those who are wealthy fear loss and thus suffer; those who are poor desire gain and thus suffer.
Although the anxieties and sufferings of the rich and the poor differ, their toil and wandering are one and the same. Why is this so?

When human beings dwell in this world, they marry—men taking wives and women taking husbands—and manage their households and gates, engaging in social interactions, welcoming guests, and attending to visitors.
Building houses and purchasing fields and gardens; establishing burial mounds and performing spring and autumn sacrifices; killing living beings and taking life to pray to ghosts and deities;

and the daily livelihoods of the four classes—scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants—including planting rice seedlings, sowing seeds, carrying water, hauling firewood, dyeing and washing, sewing and weaving, spinning cotton and flax, harvesting and drying, pounding and grinding, cooking rice, preparing soups, washing the face, and combing the hair.

Ascending the latrine, bathing to remove dust, sweeping the floor, mending leaks, concealing shame, grasping implements, performing tasks with diligent effort, and managing affairs with restless haste—these are the necessities of daily life.
One ponders them day and night, devising a thousand schemes and ten thousand stratagems;

yet even if one were to speak of these domestic matters, their subtle and manifold details could not be fully exhausted by pen. Alas! While wealth and status may still be managed and secured, poverty is a burden that cannot be lifted.
Regarding the burden of debt: why is this so? Among them, there are those who mortgage or sell their houses and foundations; those who mortgage or sell their mountains, gardens, fields, and lands;
those who mortgage or sell their clothing and household goods; and those who mortgage or sell their wives, concubines, sons, and daughters.
For these reasons, there is nothing that is not suffering. Furthermore, there are many other kinds; to speak of several more types, hunger and thirst are also painful afflictions.
Itching is suffering; extreme heat is suffering; extreme cold is suffering; being bitten by mosquitoes, flies, fleas, and lice is suffering;
being injured by centipedes and vicious dogs is suffering; excessive rain is suffering; excessive drought is suffering;
the invasion of locusts is suffering; the arrival of years of famine is suffering; and the sudden onset of violent winds is suffering.
Furthermore, there is the suffering of being startled by thunder and lightning; the suffering of one's family and kin being in unrest; the suffering of regional rebellion;
and yet further, there is suffering within suffering that is difficult to describe in full. Alas! These aforementioned conditions of suffering are merely minor sufferings among humans.
If one commits evil deeds, the karmic obstacles will cause one to fall forever into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals to undergo their retributions.
If such is the state of great suffering, how much more so must be the minor sufferings of the human realm? Alas! Worldly people do not recognize this as suffering;

instead, they recklessly engage in perverse conduct—being disloyal and unfilial, lacking benevolence and righteousness, using the strong to oppress the weak, the noble to slight the humble, the wealthy to deceive the poor, the crooked to obstruct the straight, the great to crush the small, and the subordinates to be insolent toward their superiors. Such are their unlawful ways.
Thus, one transmigrates through successive rebirths, sinking into the sea of suffering. Alas!

I now speak with repeated and earnest admonition, wishing that all people in the world would fully observe the precepts of fasting and recite the name of Amitābha, so that together we may escape the wheel of suffering and ascend to the Land of Bliss.
O virtuous ones, you must know that when illness comes and death arrives, nothing can take your place; even if you have a father...
Mothers, fathers-in-law, husbands, wives, children, wealth, honor, fame, gold, silver, and precious treasures—all of these are utterly useless.
One must simply exert oneself individually to prepare for the journey ahead;

moreover, as time is limited and does not wait for man, and as life and death are impermanent with every breath uncertain, the masters of old said: "Rest! Rest! Rest! Repair while it is dry, lest you wait for the sun to shine."
"Even if it is dry, one refuses to go; one must wait until the rain drenches one's head. Truly, these words are so!
If a person knows this yet does not believe and practice accordingly, they truly辜负 (betray) my bitter exhortations.

Compiled by the monk Huiri of Wangji Temple in Luoyang during the Tang dynasty; his secular surname was Xin, and he was a native of Donglai.

Having received the tonsure and attained full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) during the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, he later encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing and personally visited him to inquire into the ultimate profundity of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Zhū Qián’s heart had long yearned for the West, and he eventually vowed to travel to the Western Regions. Initially, he embarked on a ship and crossed the sea;
after three years, having traveled extensively through various kingdoms in the South China Sea—such as Kunlun, Foshi, and Siṃhala—he finally reached India.
There, he paid homage at sacred sites, sought out Sanskrit manuscripts, and visited virtuous spiritual friends for thirteen years.
Having received instruction in the Dharma and desiring to benefit others, he struck his mendicant’s staff and returned to his native land, traveling alone and solitary.

For another four years he traversed the snowy ridges and the lands of the Hu; having endured manifold hardships, he grew deeply weary of Jambudvīpa. He sighed to himself, saying: "In what country or direction is there joy without suffering?
What Dharma or what practice can lead one to see the Buddha swiftly? Thus he inquired of the Tripitaka masters throughout India.
It is said that all [the Buddhas] praise the Pure Land, which further accords with their collective voice;

as for its swiftness, it is the path where this single lifetime is exhausted, and upon the end of this retribution-body, one will certainly attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) to personally serve Amitābha Buddha.
Having heard this, they received it upon their heads and gradually traveled to North India. To the northeast of the royal city of Gandhāra, there was a great mountain, and upon that mountain...

When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara appeared in response to his most sincere prayers on many occasions, he would prostrate himself for seven days and abstain from food, vowing to end his life if the deity did not manifest.
On the night of the seventh day, before midnight had passed, Avalokiteśvara appeared in the air with a purple-golden form over ten feet tall, seated upon a precious lotus flower.
He extended his right hand and stroked the crown of Ri’s head, saying: "You wish to transmit the Dharma."

"For self-benefit and the benefit of others, there is only the Land of Amitābha Buddha in the West; I urge you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, recite the sutras, and dedicate your vows toward rebirth there.
Once you have reached that land, you will see the Buddha and I, thereby attaining great benefit—you should know this for yourself.

The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land surpasses all other practices. Having said this, he suddenly vanished. [The monk] had been fasting for days and was exhausted; upon hearing this, he felt renewed vigor.
Ascending the ridges and returning eastward, he traveled through more than seventy countries over a total of eighteen years.

Only in the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era did he reach Chang’an, where he presented the Emperor with true portraits of the Buddha and Sanskrit scriptures, thereby awakening the Emperor’s mind. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Master of the Tripitaka, Born of Compassion" (Cimin Sanzang Sheng Fashi).
Throughout his life, he diligently cultivated the practices for rebirth in the Pure Land and composed the *Wǎngshēng Jìngtǔ Jí* (Collection on Rebirth in the Pure Land) to promote these practices.
In this world, his path and his skillful guidance were such that, though he lived at a different time than the Master Shaokang, his transformative influence was identical to his.
Furthermore, in the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, the Great Master Fazhao resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou, where he practiced diligently without slackening;
making the exhortation of others to practice Buddha-recitation his primary duty, two manifestations appeared within his rice bowl inside the Sangha hall.
Within the magnificent realm of Mount Wutai, there further exists a monastery with a golden plaque inscribed: "The Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Monastery.
Thereupon, Fazhao, harboring a heart of yearning and reverence, desired to pay homage at Mount Wutai;

he thus established a Five-Assembly Buddha-recitation altar at Hude Temple in Hengzhou, vowing to behold the Great Sage. On the thirteenth day of the eighth month in the fourth year, he set out on his journey.
On the fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year, while at Wutai County, he saw from afar several streaks of white light to the south of Foguang Temple.
On the sixth day, upon arriving at Foguang Temple, it was exactly as he had seen in his bowl, with not the slightest discrepancy.
That night, during the fourth watch, he saw a beam of light descend from the northern mountain and shine down; startled, he hurried into the hall and questioned the assembly.

He asked, "What auspicious omen is this? Wherein lies the good or bad fortune? A monk replied, "This is the inconceivable light of the Great Sage, which constantly awakens those with whom it has a karmic connection and illuminates them.
Having heard this, [the king] immediately assumed a dignified demeanor and followed the light for fifty *li* northeast of the monastery.
There was indeed a mountain; at its foot was a stream, and to the north of the stream stood a stone gate. He saw two youths dressed in green, appearing to be about... years of age.
A youth of eight or nine years of age, with a handsome and upright countenance, stood at the entrance of the gate. One was named Sudhana and the other Nanda.
Upon seeing each other, they rejoiced; they exchanged greetings, performed salutations, and were led through the gate.

Having traveled five *li* northward, they saw a golden gate-tower and gradually approached the gateway, which was a great monastery. Before the monastery stood a large golden plaque inscribed with the characters for "Great" (Mahā).

The Holy Bamboo Grove Monastery was exactly as he had seen it in the bowl: it was twenty *li* square in circumference and contained one hundred and twenty courtyards, all adorned with precious stupas.
The ground was made entirely of pure gold, and flowing channels and flowering trees filled the space.
The light shone into the monastery and reached the lecture hall, where he saw Mañjuśrī to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, each occupying their respective positions.

The sound of the Lion’s Throne preaching the Dharma was clearly audible. To the left and right of Mañjuśrī, more than ten thousand bodhisattvas were gathered, and Samantabhadra was likewise surrounded by innumerable bodhisattvas.
Their radiance reached before the two bodhisattvas, who paid their respects and asked:

"In this final age, ordinary beings are far removed from the Sages; those who serve as spiritual friends have become increasingly inferior, and the defilements and obstructions are even deeper. Consequently, there is no way for the Buddha-nature to manifest."
"The Buddha-dharma is vast and profound; I do not yet know which dharma-gate is most essential for practice.
I only pray that the Great Sage will sever the net of my doubts. Mañjuśrī replied, "As you now recollect the Buddha, this is precisely the right time.
Among all gates of practice, none surpasses the recollection of the Buddha. To make offerings to the Triple Gem is to cultivate both merit and wisdom; these two gates are the most direct path."

Why is this so? Because in past kalpas, it was due to my contemplating the Buddha, due to my mindfulness of the Buddha, and due to my making offerings to him that I have now attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Therefore, all dharmas—from the profound meditative concentrations of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the Buddhas themselves—are born from mindfulness of the Buddha. Thus, one should know that mindfulness of the Buddha is [the source of] all...
"O King of Dharma, you should constantly keep the Unsurpassed Dharma King in mind without ceasing, so that he may illuminate [all beings]. Again, [the King] asked, "How should one keep him in mind?
Mañjuśrī replied, "To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha; the power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable.
You should maintain mindfulness of him without interruption, so that after the end of your life, you will certainly be reborn there forever."
When the Bodhisattva Pratyutpanna had finished speaking these words, the two great sages each extended their golden hands and stroked the crown of his head, bestowing upon him this prophecy:

"Because you have already practiced the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), you shall before long realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). If sons or daughters of good family wish to attain Buddhahood swiftly, there is nothing superior to the recollection of the Buddha;
by it, they can quickly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having spoken thus, at that time—
The two great sages recited verses to one another; having heard them, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and their nets of doubt were entirely cleared away.
They prostrated themselves once more in gratitude and withdrew.
