From the *Wanzong Chanshi Zhizhi Pian* (The Section on Direct Pointing by Chan Master Wanzong), Part Three: "Three Times Three.
Now, as for the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, it is called the One-Practice Samādhi (*ekavyūha-samādhi*). This is because the practitioner, having already realized the profound principle...
One who is able to maintain a single mind without engaging in other practices, contemplating only that land and recollecting only that Buddha,
and who realizes that body and land are non-dual such that even recollection is itself one— such a person attains the name "Single Practice" as established above.
Although it is called "Single Practice," for the practitioner, it should nevertheless be understood through all the immeasurable mundane and supramundane Dharma-gates.
When all meritorious practices are taken as aids to the Path, then the practice of rebirth therein proceeds swiftly;
therefore, all practices are cultivated for the sake of the Pure Land, having no separate paths, and are called "the One Practice.

Just as the myriad rivers flow into the sea and all equally receive the name "sea," so too do the ten thousand virtues converge and receive the name "One Practice. By this principle, all applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) [are likewise unified].

The four right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the four great vows, and the six perfections are all practices for the Pure Land; this includes even the slightest virtuous act among humans—
such as a mere touch of the finger— or mindfulness of the Buddha with a distracted mind, or a single recitation of the name, or raising one hand,
or a single prostration, or a single praise, or a single gaze of reverence, or even offering a single incense stick, a single drop of water, a single flower, a single lamp, or a single offering.

Whether one cultivates the requisites for practice for a single thought-moment or up to ten thoughts, or generates a single act of conduct, a single gift, a single precept, a single patience, meditative concentration, or wisdom—
by dedicating all such roots of goodness through the power of the vow to be reborn in Sukhāvatī and by being sustained by that resolve,

one will attain rebirth there regardless of whether it is slow or swift, as stated in the sutras. This is illustrated by the analogy of a person who once deposited a drop of water from a small vessel into a large one.
The ocean’s vow is indestructible, unfailing, unchanging, and inexhaustible; even after passing through many kalpas, it necessarily returns to its original water.
Just as one who has passed through many kalpas may receive a fruit from what was deposited and obtain the original water—indestructible and inexhaustible—it is likewise with this:
dedicating small roots of goodness toward Sukhāvatī is like depositing a drop of water; though one passes through the state of an ordinary being, those roots of goodness are not lost.

Furthermore, one does not destroy or exhaust [the roots of goodness] to be reborn there; of this there is no doubt. How much more so for those with right view or wrong view, the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, the tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), the distracted mind or meditative concentration, and all wholesome matters of conceptualization, contemplation, and wisdom—all these are called "a single practice" and will all result in rebirth there.

It is only those of the lineage of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who are excluded; thus it is said: "If you simply prepare a willing heart, you will certainly not be deceived. Moreover, as the Sūtra says regarding "a single recitation":
Homage to the Buddhas! It is truly worthy of deep faith that all have already attained the path to Buddhahood.

As for those whose causal mind has not yet arisen, whose wholesome practices have not yet been established, and whose body and mind have not yet been subdued—such that they expect a response before their time—it is impossible to speak of them on the same level.
Therefore, among the ultimate discourses of Śākyamuni, the Holy Lord, throughout his entire life, there are immeasurable samādhis, immeasurable liberations, and immeasurable practices.

I vow that this single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha shall perfectly encompass all immeasurable dharma-gates associated with *dhāraṇī*, such that nothing remains outside and all are fully complete.
Just as the great ocean receives all streams without its nature increasing or decreasing,
and just as a wish-fulfilling gem placed atop a high banner can fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings without its essence being diminished, so too is this King of Samādhis.
It can encompass and fulfill [all virtues], and it is likewise so;
for this reason, I, the World-Honored One, have proclaimed this *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* to the entire assembly not less than three times.

Among those present who were listening—great-rooted beings such as Mañjuśrī and others, as well as the sages of the Three Vehicles, and the eight classes of gods, nāgas, and so forth—there was none [who did not hear it].

It was not that they turned their hearts toward faith without hesitation. When the stream of our Dharma reached the eastern lands, there appeared a Great Sage at Mount Lu who propagated the bequeathed teachings.
Those who placed their faith in him were like grass bending before the wind; his reputation reached the ends of the world, and there were none who did not admire his doctrine.
From the Buddha until the present, nearly two thousand one hundred years have passed, during which time many sages and worthies have appeared.

Among these people—high-ranking monks and great scholars, farmers, merchants, officials, and commoners, men and women, slaves, and eunuchs—some practice it themselves and exhort others, while others compose writings and take vows.

Treating the Dharma as precious and their own bodies as mere dust, they face perils without fear and confront death without regard, standing forth to practice and diligently cultivating this path; how many such individuals can be known? Or...
Those who practice sympathetic joy or take refuge through faith, acting with the utmost sincerity according to their virtue, will be increasingly numerous;
indeed, it is truly said that even the stars and the sands of the Ganges cannot serve as a metaphor for their abundance.

If even those who possess half-faith or are indecisive and wavering are still born in that land within the borderlands of the City of Doubt, how much more so those with correct faith and correct resolve!
For one who practices the right vow, what delusions could possibly remain? What is recorded in biographies does not even approach one ten-thousandth of this.
From antiquity to the present, all have received its benefits; how could these be fully recounted by pen or tongue?

Even if one were to separately cultivate the various stages of the path (mārga), there might still be the danger of regression or being possessed by demons; yet for this Dharma-door of Buddha-remembrance, because of... [it is otherwise].
If one practices by relying on the power of the Buddha, success is certain; demonic activities will no longer arise, one will never again fall back, and rebirth [in the Pure Land] is assured.
*A Brief Essential Explanation of the Three Assemblies of Maitreya*. Extracted from the Tripitaka.

In the first year of the Yuan-yuan era, while [the author] was in strict seclusion in silence, several lay devotees knocked on the door and asked: "What is the cause of the Three Assemblies of Maitreya?"
In response to the question, the Master explained, "Why do you ask such a thing?
The layman replied, "Since our youth, we have observed the precepts and recited the Buddha's name, wishing to seek the sublime assembly of the Dragon Flower and realize Bodhi;
for this reason, we ask. Yuanxiao laughed and said, "For you to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, this question is too late. To seek rebirth at the Dragon Flower..."

The Master asked the Layman Tai-zao, "What do you mean by 'early' and 'late'? Tai-zao replied, "Even if one were to attain Buddhahood this very day and depart for the Land of Bliss to act as a guide for others, would that not still be considered late?
How much more so for those who desire it further? One must surely take it that such people will have no end to their cycle of rebirth;
is this not exceedingly late? Maitreya Buddha will only appear after five hundred and sixty million years have passed."
"Is it not far too early for the descent at the Dragon Flower Assembly?

Since you all maintain the fasts and precepts and recite the Buddha's name, you ought to seek the Pure Land and swiftly realize Bodhi in this very life; why wait until the future Dragon Flower Assembly to seek liberation?
The layman replied, "I have often seen people in the world make vows for the Dragon Flower Assembly. We speak according to our own kind, and thus we too have made this aspiration."
Yuan said, "I once vowed not to seek the Pure Land, but to seek the Dragon Flower Assembly;

I do not know how much suffering of transmigration I have endured because of this vow—it is utterly inconsistent with the Way. The Layman said, "We have received your resolution of our doubts; from now on, we shall seek the Pure Land directly.
Yuan said, "If you simply prepare a heart of resolve, you will certainly not be deceived. The Layman said, "I seek rebirth in the Pure Land."
"I have fortunately been able to hear the Dharma of this land; I also wish to hear the account of the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower (*Nāgapuṣpa*). Yuan said:
'To explain it in full would result in excessive verbosity, yet to abbreviate it further would leave the meaning incomplete.

Therefore, I shall now specifically take the sutra translated by Master Kumārajīva and inform the assembly. From the time Śākyamuni Buddha descended into birth, the human lifespan was one hundred years.'"
At the beginning of the first century, the lifespan decreases by one year;
when it has decreased to thirty years, a famine disaster arises; when it decreases to twenty years, an epidemic disaster arises;
and when it decreases to ten years, a war disaster arises—this is what is called the manifestation of the minor three calamities.
Only ten thousand men and women remained, fleeing into the mountains to become the progenitors of the race. At that time, a woman was married at the age of five months;
this constitutes the limit of the *apacayakalpa* (the aeon of decrease). After another hundred years had passed, the human lifespan increased by one year, reaching eighty-four thousand years;
this is called the limit of the *vivardhanakalpa* (the aeon of increase). Then, after another hundred years, the lifespan decreased by one year once more.
When the human lifespan has decreased to eighty thousand years, Maitreya Buddha will descend to be born in the city of Ketumatī, taking conception in the womb of a great Brahmin family;
his father’s name is Śuddhama and his mother’s name is Brahmāvatī.
Although Maitreya dwells within the womb, it is no different from being in a celestial palace; free from defilement and unobstructed, he is spontaneously transformed, and his body is tall.
He is thirty-two *zhang* tall, with a chest ten *zhang* wide and a face five *zhang* long;

he is endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence and radiance, such that sentient beings never tire of beholding him. In his kingdom there is a wheel-turning king named Śaṅkha, who extensively practices the ten virtuous deeds and instructs the people.
The people are so moved by his transformation that they all revere him; their lifespan is eighty thousand years.
The people’s height was sixteen *zhang*; their features were dignified and handsome, free from any ugliness. Women were married only after five hundred years.
At that time, there were no calamities or afflictions, nor were there cold or heat. Doors were not bolted, yet there were no thieves.
Clothing appeared spontaneously without the need for labor; gold, silver, and the seven treasures filled the storehouses, yet no one looked upon them with possessiveness.

The ground there is level and even, without mounds or pits; upon the earth stand trees resembling golden dragons, which bloom with flowers atop them—hence it is called the "Supreme Assembly of Dragon Flowers.
The people enjoy themselves in a realm like that of the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas.
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are only three afflictions that prevent one from experiencing pure happiness: first, food and drink; second, excrement and urine.
Third, when the aged perform the functions of nature, the ground naturally cracks open; once they have finished, it closes again and produces red lotuses that conceal any foul odors.
When their lives are about to end, they go of their own accord to the cemetery and die; their consciousness is reborn in heaven and does not fall into the evil realms.
Why is this? Because the people of that land all cultivate the ten wholesome actions; therefore, many are reborn in heaven.
In the first assembly where Maitreya Buddha preached the Dharma, ninety-six billion people attained the fruit of Arhatship;

three hundred and sixty thousand devas and humans from the eight classes of beings resolved their minds upon unsurpassed Bodhicitta; and many other multitudes attained the four fruits of the Two Vehicles.
In the second great assembly where he preached the Dharma, ninety-four billion people attained the fruit of Arhatship, and six hundred and forty billion devas [attained the same].
Among humans and the eight classes of beings, many more developed the bodhicitta, while others attained the four fruits of the two vehicles.

At the third great assembly for preaching the Dharma, ninety-two billion people attained arhatship, thirty-four billion devas and humans from the eight classes developed the bodhicitta, and many others attained the four fruits of the two vehicles.
Maitreya will remain in the world for sixty thousand years, during which time he will preach.

The duration of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) remaining in the world after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa is likewise; the duration of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) remaining in the world is likewise.
The matters concerning the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower Tree have been briefly explained in this manner;

as for the other subtle meanings, they are fully contained within the scriptural text and cannot be recounted in their entirety. The layman said: "I have certainly already heard of the three minor calamities and the three assemblies. Pray, [explain them] again."
I thank the Venerable Master for his instruction on the characteristics of the small and great kalpas and the three great calamities.
It is thus: I shall speak to you; listen attentively! As for the small kalpa, it has already been mentioned; now I shall explain it in detail.
Human life begins at ten years of age and increases by one year every hundred years until it reaches eighty-four thousand years; this period is called [the increase].
When the period of increase reaches its limit, it again decreases by one year for every hundred years until it reaches ten years; this is called the limit of the kalpa of decrease.
Thus, one cycle of increase and decrease constitutes a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute a medium kalpa (*madhyakalpa*).
The four periods of formation, endurance, destruction, and emptiness each possess twenty such cycles of increase and decrease, which together constitute a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
At the end of one great kalpa, there is a fire disaster that destroys everything down to the First Dhyāna Heaven;

this occurs seven times. Then there is a water disaster that destroys everything down to the Second Dhyāna Heaven. After forty-nine such cycles of seven great fires (seven times seven), there are seven cycles of great waters.

Following another seven cycles of great fires, there occurs a wind disaster that destroys everything down to the Third Dhyāna Heaven. In total, fifty-six cycles of great fires bring about destruction.
The first dhyāna is destroyed by seven cycles of great floods; the second dhyāna is destroyed by one cycle of great winds;

and the third dhyāna involves a total of sixty-four great kalpas as the phenomenal characteristics marking the beginning and end of the three great calamities. As the ancient masters said: "The gods of the six heavens of desire possess the five signs of decay;

yet even in the third dhyāna there is still the calamity of wind. Even if one cultivates until reaching the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), it will not [endure]."
"Returning and going forth, returning and going forth"—this refers to the Western Pure Land.

If people do not cultivate the Pure Land, they will be submerged horizontally and vertically within the four modes of birth and six realms of existence, and amidst the three great calamities, rising and sinking headlong while suffering without end.
The Layman said: "Having heard the Master’s teaching, I shall truly and early on cultivate the Pure Land and depart [from this world]."
"Leaving the wheel of suffering behind, I alone declare: 'I now reveal this to you; you should exhort one another to be reborn together in the Pure Land.
The layman replied, "Yes, we shall respectfully follow the Master’s command to spread this teaching and guide others.
Having paid their respects and expressed their gratitude, they took their leave and departed.
Essential Words from the Mirror of the Source (Zongjing yao yu) Section 35:
Yongming’s *Mirror of the Source* states: "The mind can become a Buddha; the mind becomes a sentient being; the mind becomes heaven; the mind becomes hell.
When the mind differs, a thousand disparities arise in competition; when the mind is level, the Dharma-realm is vast and serene. When the mind is ordinary, it is the three poisons."

When the mind is entangled, the sages possess the six supernormal powers; when the mind is empty, the One Way is pure and serene. When the mind exists, the myriad phenomena manifest in all their complexity;

this is precisely what is meant by "when the mind arises, phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, phenomena cease. It is like an echo responding to a sound—the speech is bold and the resonance is sharp;
it is like a mirror reflecting an image—the form is curved and the shadow is distorted. It is as if a person speaks of sour plums, and the saliva naturally wells up in the mouth.
Yet when water flows from a steep mountain pass, one feels as if their feet ache; when a rope does not move at night, one suspects it is a snake;

and though a dark room is fundamentally empty, one fears it is haunted by ghosts. Thus we know that all phenomena arise from the mind: everything is within oneself. Internally empty, the external can never be real;
externally subtle, the internal can never be coarse. A virtuous cause will inevitably meet with favorable conditions; evil conduct is difficult to escape.

Evil conditions exist only within that very first thought, which leads to this cycle of rising and sinking. O virtuous ones, if you wish for peace and harmony without, simply maintain inner tranquility.
When the mind is empty, objects are still; when thoughts arise, the Dharma becomes turbid; when the water is muddy, the waves are dark; when the pool is clear, the water is bright.
The essential point of cultivation does not go beyond this. It is precisely like wishing to cut off a current—simply block its source—or wishing to avoid its [consequences].

To simply sever its root requires no great effort and is the most concise and essential method; thus, the *Tongxin lun* (Treatise on Penetrating the Mind) states: "Bondage arises from the mind, and liberation arises from the mind;
since liberation and bondage depend upon the mind, they do not concern other places. The art of exiting the mundane is solely to observe the mind;
by contemplating the mind, one attains awakening, and all things are simultaneously understood. Furthermore, this is the transformative ritual that does not depart from the realm of the single truth.
That a hundred arrows could pierce stone was not due to the power of physical strength; that one could announce it to the three armies was not created by fermented yeast or grain.
That bamboo sprouts from a cold valley is not produced by the warmth of spring; that fish leap from icy rivers is not caused by nets or snares.
All are manifestations of the mind’s resonance, revealing such spiritual penetration. One should know that all movements and actions arise from this very source.
If one can believe and accept the power of the mind, possessing this capacity, then the gates of obstruction will be widely opened and the ocean of karma will be completely dried up.

It is further said: "The Dharma is established based on the mind, and names are derived according to that Dharma. When abiding in the state of a sage, it is called 'True' (zhen); when dwelling among ordinary people, it is termed 'Worldly' (su).

It is like gold fashioned into vessels; the vessels receive their names according to their form. Thus, what is on a finger is called a ring, and what adorns the arm is named a bracelet. In this way, the single mind remains unmoving.
If one clings to specific names, the myriad dharmas appear as distinct; yet true gold does not shift. If one recognizes different names, the thousand vessels appear unequal;

yet if one knows that every dharma is made from the whole mind, then when the vessels are exhausted, only gold remains. Thus, names and forms cannot disturb one, and how could right or wrong provoke a response?
It is like round vessels and square vessels, whose names differ; or like raw gold and refined gold, whose terms differ.
To speak of distinctions is to trace back to the origin and investigate the essence; yet all phenomena are empty. Having attained the ultimate meaning, one forgets conditions;

wherever one encounters anything, there is no place for reliance. For names arise because of substance, and substance emerges following names. When substance is empty, names have nothing to apply themselves to; when names are void, substance has nothing to arise from.
Substance and name are mutually quiescent, and the myriad phenomena are unborn. There is only the single true mind, and nothing else exists. This is because of ordinary beings.
The establishment of the Sage is fundamentally nameless; it manifests the Truth through worldly convention, yet Truth itself is originally unestablished.
Both rely upon worldly names and designations arising from mutual opposition. Words are themselves empty, and emptiness likewise has no place of reliance.

If one is a Great Being of superior capacity, why borrow names and forms to manifest the Way? Facing objects, they know the Source in every thought; encountering conditions, their minds accord with the Path in every instant. This is what is meant by...
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is called the fruit of the Supreme Vehicle; those in this world who reach this school are exceedingly rare. As the former masters have said:
"The Perfect Teaching is seldom encountered, like a mustard seed falling upon the point of a needle; the True Dharma is difficult to meet, like a blind turtle encountering a floating log.

Were it not for the seeds of the vehicle having been perfumed in past lives and roots of goodness accumulated over a long time, how could one happen upon such a text and personally receive its transmission?

Because the ancients valued instruction and held wealth lightly, they would bestow gold as if at a marketplace; because they forgot their own persons for the sake of the Dharma, they stood in the depths of the courtyard amidst the snow.

Furthermore, gold is but a fleeting wealth external to the body, how could it ever equal the Supreme Teaching? Life is but a single period of many karmic retributions, how could it be equated with the True Exposition?
Thus we know that words of edification and transformation must not be abandoned for even a moment; they should be engraved [upon our hearts].

The bones are recorded in the sash, the influence permeates the spirit, and the fragrance reaches consciousness. Thus, Chu Zhuangwang lightly regarded a state of a thousand chariots yet treasured the single word of Shen Shu;
Fan Xian despised ten thousand mu of fields yet prized the brief discourse of the boatman. This shows that even in establishing a family or a nation, one prizes words so highly;
how much more so when, within the Mirror of the Essence of the Dharma, one attains non-arising through a single phrase upon hearing it!
Having attained the Great Way, how could one possibly permit negligence or arrogance?

*Text for Making Vows upon Prostrating to the Buddha* (Whether prostrating while standing or kneeling is acceptable; with the body performing full prostration, the mouth reciting the name, and the mind practicing visualization):
I take refuge three times in the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields that fill the entirety of empty space and the Dharma-realm.
Throughout the worlds of the past, present, and future, [I take refuge in] the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

I pay homage to the World-Honored One of Ten Thousand Virtues, the Teacher and Original Master Śākyamuni Buddha, who now sits upon the hundred-petaled lotus pedestal at the site of enlightenment amidst the light of a thousand jewels, preaching the sutras.
I also pay homage to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Benevolent One of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whose great vows...
The Greatly Powerful and Great Sage, the World-Honored One, our Original Teacher Amitābha Buddha;
the Tathāgata Maitreya, who will descend in the future, our Original Teacher Venerable Maitreya Buddha; the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom;
the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, King of Great Vows and Practices; the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Father of Great Compassion; and the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta—these honored ones.
Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, all the Patriarchs and Bodhisattvas of this land and the Western Heavens who protect the Dharma, and the various devas and bodhisattvas seated in assembly:
we humbly entreat you not to violate your original vows and not to forsake your compassion;

we beg that you grant us your celestial eye to behold from afar, your celestial ear to hear from afar, and that you swiftly discern and bear witness to our hearts. From this moment forth, disciples such as I, [Name], and others...
Until the end of the future, throughout all my lives, I vow to rely upon the unspeakably boundless practices and vows of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
as well as these forty-eight kinds of my own unspeakably vast practices and vows;
I shall cultivate and study them in every birth and never deviate from them in any lifetime.
The firmness of resolute faith is ineffable; Certainty free from doubt is ineffable.
The arousal of the bodhicitta is ineffable; The upholding of pure precepts is ineffable.
Seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma is ineffable; Prostrating, honoring, and praising is ineffable.
Serving and making offerings is unspeakable; Repentance and sympathetic joy are unspeakable;
Vigorous diligence is unspeakable; Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are unspeakable;
Practicing boundless conduct is unspeakable; Arousing vast and great vows is unspeakable.
The cultivation and dedication of merit are unspeakable; Wisdom that clearly understands the unspeakable Dharma-body is immeasurable and unspeakable; The adornment of merit is unspeakable;
birth through transformation in the Pure Land is unspeakable; Receiving the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment is unspeakable.
The marks and signs and their radiant light are unspeakable; The perfect voice and skillful means are unspeakable;
Dhāraṇīs and eloquence are unspeakable; Secret samādhis are unspeakable;
Lifespan and names and titles are unspeakable; Subtlety and profundity are unspeakable.
The equality of true thusness is ineffable; The differentiation of wondrous functions is ineffable;
Skillful means, wisdom, and vision are ineffable; Manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment is ineffable;
The great samādhi of the nāga is ineffable; The lion’s roar is ineffable.
The unimpeded supernormal powers are unspeakable; The fearless exercise of spiritual power is unspeakable;
The subduing of all Māras is unspeakable; The crushing defeat of non-Buddhists is unspeakable;
The manifestation of emanated bodies is unspeakable; The appearance of forms according to the capacities of beings is unspeakable.
Turning the Great Wheel of Dharma is unspeakable; Universally delivering all sentient beings is unspeakable;
Accordingly benefiting them is unspeakable; Taking upon oneself the suffering of sentient beings is unspeakable;
Ultimately bringing them to maturity is unspeakable; Causing them all to attain liberation is unspeakable.
Rebirth in the Buddha-lands is unspeakable; Realizing the Buddha-vehicle is unspeakable;
Possessing all Buddha-dharmas is unspeakable; Performing the deeds of Buddhas is unspeakable;
Entering the assemblies of Buddhas is unspeakable; Sharing in the bliss of the Buddhas is unspeakable.
Taking these forty-eight kinds of vast and great vows as the foremost, I vow to fulfill one million asaṃkhyeya great aspirations;
I pray that the Triple Gem, the World-Honored One,
and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, with their compassionate essence, bear witness to and sustain this disciple (Name).
If I should fail to fulfill even one of these vows, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Amitābha Buddha made his vows in this way; the Buddhas of the ten directions made their vows in this way; Samantabhadra Bodhisattva made his vows in this way;
the great Bodhisattvas made their vows in this way; and the Patriarch Zhongfeng made his vows in this way.
Thus, the vows made by the patriarchs of successive generations were like this; the vows made by great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) were like this;
the vows made by disciples were like this; the vows now made for the assembly of fellow students are like this;

the vows made universally for all sentient beings in the *dharmadhātu* are likewise like this. Thus it is, thus it is—there is nothing that is not like this; may all be identical to this, eternally so.
May the assembly of śrāvakas all enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows.
Whatever merit there is from prostrating, praising, and making offerings; from requesting the Buddha to remain in the world and turn the wheel of Dharma;
from rejoicing in others' merits, repenting one's own faults, and all other roots of goodness—may these be dedicated to all sentient beings and to the path of Buddhahood.
All the evil karma I have created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion,
Produced by my body, speech, and mind— I now confess it all. May I,
when the time comes for my life to end, Be completely cleared of all obstacles.
Upon meeting that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, I shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Once I have attained rebirth in that land, I shall manifest and fulfill this great vow in its entirety,
without exception, to bring benefit and joy to all realms of sentient beings.
The assembly of that Buddha was entirely pure; at that time, I was born from a supreme lotus and beheld the Tathāgata Amitābha face-to-face.
Having received the prediction of my future enlightenment from that Tathāgata, he manifested hundreds of billions of countless transformation bodies.
The power of my wisdom is vast, pervading the ten directions,
universally benefiting the realms of all sentient beings until the end of space, until the end of sentient beings, their karma, and their afflictions.
As long as all these things are inexhaustible, may my vows remain eternally and ultimately without end.

I dedicate all these boundless and supreme merits of my sublime conduct as Samantabhadra, universally praying that all sentient beings submerged in suffering may swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha.
May these merits extend to all; may we and all beings together realize the Way of Buddhahood.
Repaying the fourfold supreme kindness above and relieving the sufferings of the three miserable realms below, may all who see or hear this give rise to the bodhicitta;
at the end of this present life, may we together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, Mahāprajñāpāramitā!
Honey.

The Prayer for Making Vows upon Paying Homage to the Buddha concludes. (Those who study the Buddha must make this vow; if one does not rely on this vow, it cannot be called generating the bodhicitta.)
The above text on making vows serves as a model for all people.

Whatever merit you cultivate—whether through reciting the Buddha’s name, performing prostrations and praises, chanting sutras, or even the slightest good deed—dedicate it all toward the Western Land so that there may be a destination for your rebirth;
thus, at the end of life, you will certainly be born in the Pure Land. Friends, if you can truly uphold these precepts, make this vow, and practice accordingly, [you shall attain this goal].
This practice not only leads to rebirth in the Pure Land, but also ensures that one does not fall into the stages of the Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas;
rather, one will personally realize the realm of Samantabhadra until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Attaining Buddhahood in the Pure Land:

The *Sanqi Lianzong Baodian* states that after the Diamond Samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*), the Bodhisattva’s causes are perfected; within the Path of Liberation (*vimuktimārga*), the Tathāgata’s fruition is fulfilled.

He possesses the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*), the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities not shared with the two vehicles (*āveṇikadharma*), and so forth.
With power manifest before him, he fearlessly preaches the Dharma; the dust-like delusions are exhausted, and the merit of the myriad practices is perfected.
The ten titles are fully revealed, and the three bodies are perfectly manifested. He possesses the ninety-seven marks of a great man and emits eighty-four thousand great rays of light.

Compassion and wisdom are fused as one, and merit and wisdom are both complete. Currently dwelling in the tenfold lands of retribution, he is able to manifest transformation bodies throughout the myriad classes of beings.

The great clouds of compassion rain down the great Dharma rain, flowing profusely throughout the Dharma-realm to moisten all living beings, so that they may all awaken to their original mind and together achieve perfect enlightenment.
If one did not possess such an eye for selecting the Buddha, how could the spirit of the school have reached its present state?
The direct phonetic transcriptions for the characters are all located at the end of the lower fascicle.

Attached here are one hundred poems composed by disciples seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land, from the "Section on Universally Exhorting the Cause of Buddha-Recitation" in the first fascicle of the *Zhiguīyuan Zhizhi Ji* (Direct Pointing to the Source Collection).
A Hundred Verses on the West, Announced Universally to the Worthy:
The ancient teachings of the West were proclaimed by the World-Honored One;
In this eastern land, the school was established and named White Lotus, With the Eighteen Great Sages as its foremost leaders; The "Three Laughs at Tiger Creek" remains transmitted to this day.
The Great Way of the West is vast and profound; Its merit is towering and immeasurable.
Not only did Śākyamuni open this path, But all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have praised it.
The Western Teaching was initiated through the inspiration of the Muni; That all Buddhas praise it is known by all.
The *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations* provides direct instruction:
In practicing the supreme mindfulness of Amitābha, the essential first contemplation of the West requires utmost sincerity (*gān-yīn*). Visualize the form of the setting sun as like a suspended drum;
Send your thoughts to the Land of Bliss, returning them to a single point. This is called the unsurpassed, most profound dhyāna.
The two contemplations of the Western Land are most distinct; The water of samādhi is waveless, clear to its very depths.
The moon of mind, solitary and full, manifests its entire form; Sitting in the *paryaṅka* posture (*fu* sound), one contemplates it as ice.
In the third contemplation of the Western Land, the ground is lapis lazuli; The music of Dharma resounds through space, known with perfect clarity.
Adorned with myriad marks, their radiance shines through; With single-minded resolve, they are forever free from doubt.
To the west, rows of four types of wish-fulfilling trees stand in formation; Adorned with a hundred jewels, they all emit brilliant light.
Enjoying the manifestation of eternal bliss, Why do you people not accept this responsibility sooner?
The five contemplations of the Western [Pure Land] are known by all; In the jeweled ponds, four-colored lotuses bloom.
Divine waters and auspicious birds proclaim the Dharma; Wash away afflictions and delusions to realize Bodhi.
The six contemplations of the Western [Pure Land] encompass all; Do not covet the fleeting splendors of this mundane world.
The original nature of Amitābha is fully perfected; there is no need to investigate the "ready-made" kōan.
Only after the seven contemplations of the Western Land do they correspond to reality. Upon the towering jeweled throne, his vow-power has brought him to great sainthood;
Seated upright, he is eternally sovereign— the fruits of the śrāvaka cannot ascend here.
The eight contemplations of the Western Quarter must be clearly distinguished; all Buddhas are born from the mind’s perception.
By relying on the image to concentrate upon the True, one harmonizes principle and phenomena—how could one worry that the Pure Land will not be perfected?
The ninth contemplation of the Western Quarter concerns the body of purple-gold; its marks and signs, its radiance, are beyond compare.
Gathering in sentient beings to lead them to Ultimate Bliss, The Heavenly Father and Son are most intimately related.
With a sincere heart, practice the Ten Contemplations of the West; Constantly recollect the compassionate Avalokiteśvara.
Merely hearing his name brings great merit; How excellent is the Great Being, whose vows are vast and profound!
The eleven contemplations of the Western Quarter are difficult to measure; within the light of Śrī-Ābhāsvara, the Buddhas praise them.
Everywhere he manifests transformation bodies to propagate the teachings, vowing to serve as a bridge across the sea of suffering.
The twelve contemplations of the Western Quarter are harmoniously integrated; with single-minded sincerity, apply yourself diligently in every thought.
One should contemplate oneself being born in Sukhāvatī, sitting majestically upon a precious lotus flower;
the Transformation Buddha of the West emits radiance, with infinite emanations saving sentient beings,
and both the environment and its inhabitants are fully adorned— all of this is perfectly realized within the thirteen contemplations.
The Great Compassionate Teacher of the Western Land, Known as the Guide who receives and leads sentient beings,
Causes all nine grades to ascend to the other shore, Where they shall never again regress and realize Bodhi.
Traveling forward along the single path to the West, They fully give rise to the three minds, and the principle of truth becomes clear.
For those of the highest grade in the highest birth, they reach there in the snap of a finger; First they behold the Buddha and awaken to non-arising.
How truly marvelous is the bliss of the Western Land! Through sincere visualization, the lotus flower easily opens.
Those of the highest grade in the middle birth go according to their vows, Sitting upright and at ease upon the golden pedestal.
In the Western Land, simply resolve with firm resolve for the Bodhi-mind;
May all universally vow to board the ship of Prajñā—rebirth in the Lower Grade of the Upper Tier is surely within reach. Each person holds a single great golden lotus;
the West is clearly manifest, not obscured by mist. Maintain the fasts and precepts steadfastly, realizing the emptiness of suffering.
Through the power of samādhi, one is born in the middle grade, superior; Having attained the fruit of arhatship, one acquires supernatural powers.
In the West, it is fitting to cultivate with the fragrance of precepts; With a single thought, the flower blooms, and one joins the ranks of the sages.
Born in the middle grade, middle level, after half a kalpa, There is no need to seek the wondrous fruit of non-arising.
In the West, filial piety is foremost in aiding the Path; practicing benevolence and compassion in the world is sowing seeds in the Field of Merit.
Those of middle capacity who hear the wondrous Dharma and meet spiritual friends are due to prior conditions.
Rebirth by transformation in the West is a boundless vow; a single thought of taking refuge extinguishes transgressions and offenses.
In the upper grade of the lower birth, one hears the Buddha’s name; Through the teacher’s guidance, one encounters this great causal condition.
The Great Way of the West has been pervasive through antiquity and the present; Yet there is no remedy for the person’s own deep karmic offenses.
In the middle grade of the lower birth, by the power of spiritual friends, Upon hearing a single word of the Dharma, one immediately turns the mind [toward enlightenment].
If one directs a single thought toward the West at the moment of death, When meeting with spiritual friends, the path to life will be opened.
By reciting ten invocations, one is born in the lower grade of the lowest level; Sins are extinguished across kalpas of dust, and blessings are inexhaustible.
Exert yourself toward the West without delay; Once fallen into the City of Doubt, five hundred years pass.
The Great Sage emits light that shines forth and breaks through [delusion]; Returning once more to the Pure Land, he pays homage to the Golden Immortal.
In the West, his resolve for the first stage is firm; Joyfully practicing generosity, he plants fields of merit.
Body, life, and wealth are all cast aside; Ascending high to the superior grade, he sits upon a golden lotus.
For the second stage of the Western Land, one must be devout;

first, clarify contemplation through mindfulness of the Buddha, maintain the precepts with rigorous purity to remain free from defilement and filth, and with the field of the mind thus purified, the Way will be perfected.
For the third stage of the Western Land, the faculty of the mind is clear; through patience and gentleness, transform sentient beings.
All manner of supernormal powers are fully perfected, The luster of purple-golden skin radiates brilliant light.
In the West, the essence of the fourth stage is empty and void; Afflictions and the demons of the mind are completely swept away.
Vigor naturally gives rise to the flame of wisdom, Realizing Suchness as non-dual from beginning to end.
The Western fifth stage is most difficult to ascend; When insight and understanding are clear and penetrating, one surpasses the two vehicles.
Knowing the great principle of the pure Dharma-body, One deeply cultivates dhyāna-concentration to manifest true reality.
In the Western sixth stage, one attains perfect fusion; Meeting the source at every turn, one penetrates all that is encountered.
When Prajñā manifests before one, there is no obstruction; the entire body, hands, and eyes fully open the Great School.
In the West, it first becomes clear at the seventh stage;

the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind resides in the Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi, where every thought-moment penetrates through and knows all distinctions. Without skillful means, it will not be perfectly accomplished.
In the West, at the eighth stage, one awakens to non-arising; The Buddhas and Tathāgatas act as witnesses.
With the immovable Dharma-body, one wanders through the sea of suffering, Extensively propagating great vows to save deluded beings.
In the West, at the ninth stage, the Dharma is boundless; The Great Being’s resolve to propagate it is firm and steadfast.
In both doctrine and exposition, he is universally known as "Excellent Wisdom"; His fourfold unimpeded eloquence is perfectly complete.
In the West, the wisdom of the tenth stage comes first; The rain of Dharma and clouds of compassion pervade the great trichiliocosm.
When he roars the lion’s roar (shī-zǐ-hǒu), all beasts crouch in submission; As one destined for Buddhahood in a single lifetime, he realizes the state of the Golden Immortal.
Sharing the same shoulder with the Buddha of Equal Enlightenment in the West, His conduct and vows are inconceivable; he is named Samantabhadra.
Having personally received the Tathāgata’s entrustment, He benefits beings and connects with all things through unconditioned compassion.
In the West, the fruit of wondrous enlightenment is perfected; Mañjuśrī, who possesses the eye, is complete in merit and wisdom.
The body of Vairocana is replete with merit; Casting off jewels to wear tattered rags is the exercise of skillful means.

The Holy Teacher among the Western Perfectly Awakened Ones, With Samantabhadra possessing great compassion, The ten titles and three bodies are all fully perfected; This is the unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi.
The Western Ancestor first attained knowledge afar;
One hundred and twenty-three people formed a society within the mountains to pay homage during the six periods of the day, vowing to be born together in the Pure Land and realize Bodhi.
The Great Sage of the West, King of the Dharma, Guides the deluded masses by radiating precious light.
Undaunted by weariness, his vast vows are profound; He constantly traverses the sea of suffering, piloting the compassionate vessel (pronounced *hang*).
The Western Land is easy to reach—do not hesitate; It requires only that you cultivate a resolute mind. In a mere snap of the fingers, one transcends the ocean of birth and death;
If one has the karmic affinity to meet it, it is like a mustard seed meeting a needle’s eye.
The West is not far; seek nothing else. Take the single phrase "Amitābha" as your meditation topic.
If you can ensure that throughout your life there is no other thought, You may roam at will through the Land of Lotus-Buddhas.
Exertion toward the West need not be much; The perfection of ten recitations occurs in a single instant.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs have pointed out the path home; In this life, you shall surely escape Saṃsāra.
The Compassionate Father in the West is moved by sorrow; He welcomes the deluded and drifting back—come home!
Hasten to personally entrust yourself to the Lotus Throne; Do not return to the mundane world to enter a womb.
Believe with earnest sincerity in the West and do not give rise to doubt; In the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, one must act while time remains.
This limited span of life should be discerned early; How many know that a skull will soon lie upon the ground?
In the West, the fundamental precepts come first; If the precepts are refined, meditative concentration will likewise be firm.
Through the power of concentration, one is not withered, but gives rise to wondrous wisdom;
With the clarity of wisdom, the mind is realized as the Golden Immortal. In the West, there is no need for manifold studies;
A single phrase of Amitābha, when turned inward, reveals one’s original true face. Only then does one know that birth and death are themselves Nirvāṇa. (End)
Go straight to the West without lingering or loitering; you must take full responsibility for yourself.
Simply maintain single-minded devotion to the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and your name shall be fragrant within the Land of Lotus Flowers.
Within the pond in the western quarter, precious lotuses bloom; Adorned with treasures, they manifest spontaneously.
Amidst the light of a hundred jewels, I behold the Buddha in person, Majestically seated upon a jeweled flower pedestal.
How wondrous is the fruit of the Western Pure Land! Utpala flowers open everywhere throughout the realm.
Various manifestations truly manifest as wealth and honor; upon a single flower pedestal sits a Tathāgata.
In the West, there is a Buddha whose name is identical to mine.
If you can directly accept this without alarm, and awaken at the sound of a single call—what need is there for the journey of one hundred and eight thousand li?
The Transformation Master of the West delivers those mired in delusion; Through the Buddha’s empowerment, the Way is easily accomplished.
Extend your hand and proceed directly—there is no other path; One must be clear about that very first step.
The way to the Western Gate is most distinct; With one invocation of Amitābha, hasten your journey.
Arriving early, sit upon the Vajra Terrace; With the same name and the same title, you shall realize non-arising.
In the West, with a snap of the fingers, you will awaken to non-arising; On the superior golden terrace, you will quickly achieve Buddhahood.
Facing Amitābha, you will receive his personal prophecy; In the future, you shall preach the Dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
In the West, there is the joy of wealth and nobility, peaceful and secure;
Enjoyments appear before one according to one's heart’s desire, beyond comparison between heavens and the human realm.
Seated majestically upon a purple-gold lotus, the Western Buddha-land is superior to rebirth in the heavens; It is also superior to the conditioned immortals of Penglai.
It surpasses kings, nobles, and wealthy households; one should know it also surpasses those sitting in deluded meditation.
The bliss of the West exceeds the celestial palaces, its lifespan immeasurable and its blessings inexhaustible.
Sentient beings lacking faith slander it through their perversions; only those with the karmic affinity, the children of the Buddha, shall meet it.
The Buddha’s disciples in the West possess supernatural powers; In a mere instant, they emit and withdraw them at will.
Manifesting forms according to the species of beings, they bestow wondrous functions; They reveal the provisional to manifest the ultimate, reviving the tradition of the school.
The scenery of the Western Land surpasses that of Penglai; Yet those who swallow qi and consume the rosy clouds merely nourish the seeds of calamity.
Do not practice the methods of "transcending the spirit" or refining the voice; Directly cause the withered tree to blossom forth.
In the Western Pure Land there are lotus wombs; I universally exhort all sentient beings to return—come!
With a single thought the flower blooms and you personally behold the Buddha; Forever free from the eight difficulties and the three calamities.
In the West, the king of wealth, joy, and excellence Is adorned with every kind of perfection.
If you simply prepare a sincere mind to seek that land, The evil paths of saṃsāra will cease all at once.
Cultivate the West early and with diligence; Strike through all idle disputes and criticisms with a single stroke.
Relinquish body and mind and diligently recite the Buddha’s name; There will be neither affliction nor sorrow.
In the West dwells a Buddha named Amitābha, Universally delivering all beings from the river of craving.
The six and eight vows open the way to the nine grades; Every person can reach them—do not let the opportunity slip away.
The Western Land is near; there is no need for many paths. Directly take it up in this very instant;
wherever the eye meets or the conditions encounter, all is Sukhāvatī. The flowing water and moving wind proclaim the Mahāyāna;
This direct path to the West is excellent for practice— Exert yourself with valor and diligence to quickly hasten your progress.
Each of the nine grades of lotus pedestals has its share; Whether the flowers bloom early or late, one awakens to non-arising.
The swift path to the West for seeking birth is easy to attain; It depends solely upon one’s own single thought of sincerity.
If one further cultivates merit and wisdom with diligence, One shall be inscribed as a name among the highest grade on the golden pedestal.
Step by step in the West, one treads upon lotus flowers;

Pointing the way and opening the gates, Śākyamuni thanks us— Repeated three times with earnest instruction, there is no other teaching: With single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, return home early.
The Western Land is truly our own home; The single phrase of Amitābha leads the way without error.
Believe with sincerity and act with substance; Even the iron tree shall bloom through this.
The Western Land is easy to reach, yet few know it; Practice the direct path without doubt.
When the Six-Character Sutra is fully mastered, One shall pay homage to Amitābha upon the Lotus Throne.
The Compassionate Father in the West is named Amitābha; He receives those born into the nine grades of the lotus pond.
This shortcut dharma-gate is easy to reach, Yet alas, many harbor doubts within themselves.
The teaching was inaugurated in the West as the Lotus School; Its flourishing in this Eastern land began with Master Huiyuan.
Reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing Zen are not different paths; The wondrous existence that is original is itself true emptiness.
The Western Land’s vast vows flow forth everywhere; One phrase of Amitābha is the means for applying effort.
With every detail clear and uninterrupted, Every sound awakens the master of the house.
The Western Direction is easy to practice through direct pointing; who among us knows the Original Nature Amitābha?
Transmigrating through the six realms and three miserable paths of birth and death—how can one not feel pain and sorrow when reflecting on this?
Practice the "Western Direction" koan early; remain silent and alert, yet do not harbor intentional doubt.
When doubt reaches the point where emotion is forgotten and the mind is severed, one realizes that one’s own self is Amitābha.
This single phrase regarding the Western Pure Land is the direct transmission; without relying on cultivation, it is already manifest before us.
When those of supreme goodness see their true nature, they stand shoulder to shoulder with Amitābha Buddha.
The Great Path to the West is impartial in both aspects; A single phrase of Amitābha clarifies both principle and phenomenon.
If one realizes the subtle and wondrous meaning herein, One will know that reciting the Buddha’s name is itself Zen meditation.
The various sufferings of the Western realm cannot invade; First, one must cause this person to realize their own mind.
If you can realize that what is before your eyes is the true Land of Ultimate Bliss, then this very red earth you grasp in your hand is pure gold.
The vast lands of the West are all pure gold; jeweled trees reaching to the heavens proclaim the sounds of the Dharma.
Such is called the Land of Peace and Bliss, where the three miserable realms and eight difficulties can never again invade.
A single phrase from the West is the supreme vehicle’s pivot; Do not trust false teachers who speak of right and wrong.
In the past, the World-Honored One personally entrusted this: The direct path for practice is to recite Amitābha’s name.
The merit of the West is truly inconceivable; To slander Amitābha instead is the work of a heretic.
Falling into the hells for immeasurable kalpas, one knows not when the head shall emerge;
In the West there is a path, yet few ascend it. The single phrase of Amitābha is the Supreme Vehicle;
One cannot lead another by the hand. Only when one is willing within oneself does it correspond.
The Western Land is easy to reach and can be practiced; With ten moments of focused recitation, one shall be reborn there.
I exhort all men and women in this world: Everyone, hasten quickly to complete the journey home.
Return early to the ancestral land in the West; Human life is impermanent, lasting but a breath.
One must cherish this limited span of time; once this life is wasted, it is difficult to emerge again.
If the Western Land is not reached, it will indeed be hard; once a human body is lost, even one capable of uprooting mountains cannot regain it.
Entrust this to the heroic and resolute men of the world: you must urgently gather the jewels and return empty-handed no more.
Return to the West without hesitation; Chant the single phrase of Amitābha early on.
Cast your gaze high and act with urgency; Without needing to snap your fingers, you shall realize Bodhi.
Hasten toward the West and practice now; Life and death are impermanent and cannot be predicted.
Sunlight outside the window passes in the blink of an eye; how much time does a person truly have?
Do not delay for even a moment in your single-minded pursuit of the West; rouse your spirit and hasten forward.
Do not wait until you are parched with thirst before digging a well; you should instead seize the opportunity while the drought lasts to board the white lotus boat.
The hundred verses on the Western Land are now complete; Let all people universally board the Dharma-ship.
Do not seek a livelihood for yourself alone; Everyone, return home to face the Golden Immortal.
*Hundred Verses on the Western Land* (End).
