It has been said that there are four perils facing the gates of the teachings: first, when the transmission from master to disciple is not clear, heterodox methods flourish and one loses the truth;
second, when the precepts are not observed, the fundamental social order is thrown into chaos and one violates prohibitions.
First, it is said that because the teachings and principles have not been clearly manifested, erroneous discourse devoid of meaning has deluded the masses.

Fourth, because practices and vows are not cultivated, they wander onto deviant paths and fall into the clutches of Māra. Consequently, names are confused and fabrications are created, leaving later students as deaf and blind;
these harms are not limited to a single aspect—how lamentable this is! Alas, the ancestral Way has not been transmitted for a long time. [I desire that] people...
It is difficult for one who is free from delusion; though I am not quick-witted, I truly feel sorrow for this.

Thus, I have sought out the Great Teachings and consulted the profound texts to establish the orthodox tradition, refute various heterodox views, and clarify the true from the false. Therefore, this single fascicle is titled "Discerning the True and the False:
A Universal Exhortation to Practice."
Distinguishing Heterodoxies: Section 38. Mr.
Wang Yuan of Taiyuan, whose courtesy name was Keping, asked Chan Master Konggu: "The *Analects* states, 'To devote oneself to heterodox teachings—this is harmful.
Master Huian identified Buddhism and Daoism as these heterodoxies. What do you say of this statement? Konggu replied: "..."
Gu said: "Heterodoxy refers to miscellaneous learning. Confucius meant that practicing miscellaneous learning harms the study of the orthodox Way;
he spoke directly and plainly, without any hidden depths. Why would Zhu Xi twist what is straight into something crooked?
During Confucius’s lifetime, Buddhism had not yet reached China; Confucius heard only of the Buddha’s morality and virtue, and thus referred to him as 'the Western One.'"
It was only during the time of Emperor Han Ming that a Great Sage appeared and the Buddha-dharma first reached China;

by then, Confucius had already been dead for six hundred years. Therefore, Confucius did not see the Buddha-dharma. Since he had not seen the Buddha-dharma, on what basis could he have designated the Buddha’s teachings as "heterodox"?
If the Buddha-dharma were indeed heterodox, how could Confucius have designated the Buddha as a sage?
Since Laozi was already considered a heterodox teacher, why did Confucius say, "Lao Dan is broad in his knowledge of antiquity and wise regarding the present;
he is my teacher"? For this reason, after extensively inquiring of Laozi, [Confucius] transmitted and recited his words to instruct his disciples.
Master Huicang not only maliciously excluded Buddhism and Daoism, but also contradicted Confucius’s own veneration of them. Thus it has been in later generations.
Those who label the Buddha and Laozi as heterodox are plotting a "Pengmeng" stratagem to conceal their own virtues;
those among later scholars who lack self-illumination cannot help but follow others' beckoning and calling, mistaking the bell for a jar.
Once one’s learning reaches the level of Li Bing, Lin Xiyi, and masters such as Chen Jingliao and Dai Chang, [the truth will become clear].
You will surely be able to discern this for yourself. Now, as for those who label Buddhism and Daoism as heterodox schools of learning (*daoxue*):
is this wisdom, or is it ignorance? Is it a virtuous heart, or is it an attempt to deceive others?
You, too, are a student of principle, yet you have not yet discerned this. Having now discerned it, can you allow yourself to die at the words of one or two people?
Before Master Han knew the Buddha-dharma, he sought to exclude it; yet after meeting Chan Master Dadian, he came to deeply revere the Buddha-dharma.
Huian’s devoted study of Buddhist learning may indeed be called extensive. His exclusion of Buddhism was a sickness of the heart;
had he not excluded it, later students would have read many Buddhist texts, and in reading those texts, they would have seen his own mind.
It is a sickness! Huì-ān secretly constructed walls and moats to confine his junior disciples, compelling them to return to his own way;
thus, he vigorously rejected Buddhism. To manifest his own achievements while scheming to conceal the virtues of others—what kind of heart is this?
The *Shi* says: "Gathering mugwort, gathering mugwort, on the summit of Mount Shouyang. As for the words of men, do not even believe them. To abandon...
"Zhanshe Zhangu said: 'It is likewise not so with the words of men; how can one gain anything from them? This is precisely what is meant. He continued: "The Master’s words are clear.
Confucius held the various books of Buddhism and Laozi in high esteem, as all the texts record; that Huian [Zhu Xi] rejected them was truly contrary to Confucius.
It is simply that we have not reflected upon this. Although I have never rejected Buddhism myself, I nevertheless do so because of his rejection of it."
I, too, was deluded and was unable to cultivate sincere reverence for the Buddha. Now, reflecting upon this, I realize that my harm to the Supreme Virtue has been profound;
this was a great error. My heart is pained and my head aches as I regret it, yet I cannot turn back the past.
From this day forward, receiving the Buddha’s clear teachings, I shall take refuge and pay homage, hoping to make up even a fraction of my transgressions.
Distinguishing Yang Zhu and Mo Di:
Sanjiu of Taiyuan said, "Some claim that Buddhist learning is counted among the Nine Schools (Jiuliu) and is similar to the school of Yang Zhu and Mo Di.
Is this fact actually so? Konggu replied, "How grave it is that you do not understand! The Nine Schools are recorded in the *Shiji* of the Han dynasty."
This was recorded by Sima Xiangru during the reign of Emperor Wu. At that time, the Buddha-dharma did not yet exist;

how then could one know that the Buddha belonged to the "Nine Schools" (jiu liu)? Now, Yang Zhu and Mo Di were merely men who practiced a single doctrine, whereas the Buddha is a Great Sage who propagates the Way.
How could he be categorized alongside Yang and Mo? Yang and Mo took specific conduct as their teaching and lacked the Dharma of the Great Way.

To say that Mencius refuted [Buddhism] is a public error. The Buddha takes the Great Way as his teaching; he is the ultimate patriarch who unifies the three teachings and encompasses heaven and earth.
It is a pity that Sima Xiangru did not encounter him; had he encountered him, he would have promoted and honored him, and there would surely have been something admirable to behold.
To say that the Buddha’s "universal love" is close to that of Mozi is incorrect; compassion, joy, equanimity, and relinquishment (*maitrī-karuṇā-muditôpekṣā*) are the virtues of the Buddha.
How could this be a love that drowns one’s feelings and muddies one’s will? Compassionate love is virtue; love that drowns one’s feelings is selfishness.
Han Changli said, “Universal love is called benevolence (*ren*); this is a lapse into emotion that leads to confusion.
Confucius said, “To bestow bounty upon the people and be able to save the multitude—one must surely be a sage. Mencius said, “It is the feeling of compassion (*ce*)...”
The heart of concealment is the sprout of benevolence; Confucius and Mencius did not indulge their passions nor allow their wills to be submerged, nor did they confuse the true with the false;

thus, [their teachings] can be seen as complementary to the love of compassion. Alas! The Confucian school prioritizes the social order and constant relationships while encompassing the clarification of the Way;
the Buddhist school prioritizes the clarification of the Way while encompassing the social order and constant relationships. To the common person, it appears as if...
To the realized ones, these appear different while in reality they are the same. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "This Dharma abides in its own place;
the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. It further says that secular scriptures, worldly discourse, and the arts of livelihood all accord with the True Dharma.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "The Buddha-dharma is not different from worldly dharmas; worldly dharmas are not different from the Buddha-dharma."
"If it is so, does this not mean there is no way of the social order (gangchang)? Laozi said:
'To love the people and govern the state, can one do so without non-action? All such things as these exist within both Buddhism and Daoism.

Since the way of the social order exists, how could one fail to be loyal to the sovereign, filial to one's parents, cultivate morality and virtue, or propagate benevolence and righteousness? Viewed from this perspective, the Buddha..."

How could this not violate the fundamental principles of social order? The sages of the Three Teachings stand as pillars throughout the world, presiding over the transformative authority of the Great Way.
To fail to recognize the Way of Buddhism and Daoism is a lack of wisdom; to maliciously exclude Buddhism and Daoism is a lack of benevolence.

The learning of Confucius and Mencius teaches people to study benevolence and righteousness; to read their books yet neglect their benevolence and righteousness, and instead launch immediate attacks [upon them], is surely a failure of virtue.
Regarding the arts, to rely on those arts and indulge one's own whims to the point of maliciously slandering Buddhism and Daoism is an extreme error.
It results in the loss of one's own heart-virtue and misleads future students; everyone should simply engage in self-examination.
Distinguishing between "empty non-existence" (*xūwú*) and "quiescent extinction" (*jímì*).
Taiyuan said: "The teaching of 'empty non-existence' and 'quiescent extinction' belongs to Huian [Zhu Xi]. Xin'an Chen said: "'Empty non-existence' belongs to the school of Laozi;
'quiescent extinction' belongs to the school of the Buddha. Konggu said: "Regarding 'empty non-existence' and 'quiescent extinction,' there are both provisional and ultimate meanings."

Speaking from the perspective of provisional meaning (*upāya*), "emptiness," "non-being," "quiescence," and "extinction" are merely words for the illusory. Ordinary beings cling to existence; those of the Small Vehicle cling to emptiness;
those of the Middle Vehicle cling to neither existence nor emptiness. In the Great Vehicle, the very substance is itself empty, yet it does not fall into the categories of [dualistic] numbers.

It is wondrous existence that is non-existent, true emptiness that is non-empty. Not establishing a single speck of dust, yet not abandoning a single dharma—transverse, vertical, contrary, and conforming.

Because the phenomena that accord with the Dharma are entirely true, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, in order to shatter the "existence" of ordinary beings, says that this body is illusory and causes the mind to attain quiescence;
in order to shatter the "emptiness" of the Lesser Vehicle, he rebukes them for having fallen into the deep pit of liberation and causes them to seek deliverance;
and in order to shatter the "neither existence nor emptiness" of the Middle Vehicle, he rebukes them.
To bind those within the realm of illusory existence and cause them to seek the Mahāyāna—these are all the arts of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
To speak in terms of ultimate reality, however, emptiness and quiescent extinction (*śūnyatā-nirvāṇa*) are the mother of the myriad existents;

they give birth to heaven and earth, to people and things, to the moving and the stationary, the flying and the submerged, and indeed to all phenomena. Thus, Buddhism says: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established."
When there was not even the slightest dharma to be apprehended, Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me the prediction of enlightenment.

Laozi said: "The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao; the name that can be named is not the eternal name. Namelessness is the beginning of heaven and earth; naming is the mother of the myriad things.
Constantly abide in non-desire to contemplate its subtlety; constantly abide in desire to contemplate its manifestations. Confucius said: "The *Yi* is without..."
It is thought, yet it is non-action; it is tranquil and unmoving. This tranquility and immobility are themselves emptiness and extinction.
Within this emptiness and extinction, all myriad phenomena are contained; when there is a response and they are thereby communicated, all myriad phenomena are brought forth.
As for such a most wondrous principle, were it not for the ultimate spirit in the world, who else could participate in it?
In this regard, the *Book of Rites* says: "To act without striving and yet have things accomplished—this is the Way of Heaven. Master Zisi said:

"The workings of the Supreme Heaven are without sound and without smell. The essential teachings of the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings are all the true, eternal, quiescent extinction—the empty yet non-empty—which fundamentally does not differ in the slightest.
When the Buddha spoke of "the extinction of birth and death, wherein extinction is bliss," he intended to cause one to empty [the mind].
This deluded sentiment is precisely what is meant by the saying: "For every fraction of human desire that diminishes, a fraction of the Heavenly Principle (tianli) increases.
How could one ever be taught to utterly extinguish the Heavenly Principle so as to enter a state like withered wood or dead ashes?

One must know that from Heaven and Earth down to all people and the myriad species, everyone possesses the principle of true permanence and quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*), without any gap or distinction. It is simply because the ignorant do not perceive this that they call it [emptiness].
The wandering soul is truly pitiable! When reading Buddhist scriptures, did Master Heican (Zhu Xi) merely perceive them as expedient teachings for ordinary people?
Did he fail to recognize that emptiness and quiescence are the mother of all existence?
Did he fail to recognize that the essential tenets of the sages of the Three Teachings are all the principle of true, eternal quiescence? Was it not that he deceived himself?
Does your mind not err by making such a biased statement that it misleads future students?
To detest the teachings of the Buddha and Laozi as being merely those of emptiness and extinction—to claim they deviate from the Great Principle—is this not a matter of no small consequence?

Since the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, there have been no enlightened rulers or renowned sages who did not esteem the Buddhist Dharma as the study of the Great Way; yet, as for later generations—
Hui-an disparaged it as a teaching of emptiness and extinction; but was Hui-an’s aversion truly justified or not?
Could Hui-an’s insight and vision surpass those of the figures of the Eastern Han, the Three Kingdoms, and the Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties of the Northern and Southern periods?
Could it surpass those of the Sui, Tang, and Five Dynasties?
Are these figures inferior to those of the flourishing Song, Liao, and Jin dynasties? The *Great Declaration* says: "Heaven sees through the eyes of the people;
Heaven hears through the ears of the people. Therefore, Confucius said, "I follow the multitude," for he never heard of following the biased intentions of a single individual.
What kind of vision is this, that Master Huì'ān harbored such bias against Buddhism? As for me now...
I merely offer these broad outlines to awaken the minds of people; I request that you yourself discern what is appropriate for your own realization.
I, Zhongbuo, am not clever, yet upon hearing the Master’s words, it was as if a great clarity opened within my breast.
Discerning the Nature and State of Ghosts and Spirits:

First, Taiyuan [Zhang Zai] said that ghosts and spirits are the "excellent functioning" (*liangneng*) of the two vital energies (*erqi*). Chengzi [Cheng Hao] said that ghosts and spirits are the "traces of transformation" (*zaohua zhi ji*).
Huishan [Zhu Xi] said that ghosts and spirits are the "contraction and expansion of qi. The views of these three men are all based on the single vital energy (*yiqi*).
"Is this statement regarding the creation of all things true or false? Konggu replied, "This single Qi (vital energy) encompasses heaven and earth;
from the beginning, there has been no deficiency. It fills heaven and earth—there is only this one Qi, and there is no second.
What we call 'Yang' and 'Yin' is merely this same single Qi expanding and contracting, thereby receiving those names. Since ghosts and spirits are also nothing other than this single Qi..."
This is because all within heaven and earth is but a single vital energy (*qi*).

If this is so, for what reason do there exist the spirits of Heaven, the deities of Earth, the spirits of the Five Peaks, the spirits of the Four Great Rivers, the spirits of mountains and rivers, the spirits of the Altars of Soil and Grain, and the ghosts and spirits of those who have no sacrifices?
Why are there the rites of *feng* and *shan* performed throughout the ages, and the sacrifices of past and present? Are ghosts and spirits...?
This abundance, when compared with the account of the three men, is not comparable. The *Liji* states: "Taihao was the Lord of Spring, and Goumang was his spirit;
Yan Di was the Lord of Summer, and Zhurong was his spirit; Shaohao was the Lord of Autumn, and Shu Shou was his spirit;
Zhuanxu was the Lord of Winter, and Xuanming was his spirit. If one relies on what these three men [claim], then there are two [additional spirits].
Qi is the trace of the creative transformation; it is the contraction and expansion of qi. Thus, why must there necessarily be Taihao and the others as the Sovereigns of the Four Seasons?
Why must there necessarily be Goumang and the others as the Spirits of the Four Seasons? Guan Yinzi said: "The 'ghost' (gui) is what one calls the transformation when a person dies.

The Master of the Zhongyong said: "How magnificent is the virtue of ghosts and spirits! Yangzi [said]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "Yangzi," indicating the passage likely continued with further philosophical reflections on the nature of spirits and their moral power.]
It is said that Heaven, Earth, and the spiritual intelligences are unfathomable beings; thus, they differ greatly from the account of the Three Persons.
Huì'ān (Zhu Xi) maintained that when one dies, the physical form decays and perishes while the spirit drifts and scatters, vanishing without a trace.

If this were so, then by what means could Tàohào and the others serve as the Lords of the Four Seasons? And by what means could Gōumáng and the others serve as the Spirits of the Four Seasons? This, moreover—

This is the ultimate incongruity. In the *Lixue Leibian* (Classified Compendium of Principles of Learning), there is a question asking whether the soul and spirit (*hunpo*) of a person disperse upon death.
Huian (Lu Jiuyuan) replied, "They disperse. The questioner asked again, "If they disperse, how is it that the descendants' sacrifices still evoke a spiritual resonance?
Huian replied, "The descendants are the vital breath (*qi*) of their ancestors; therefore, a resonance is evoked. According to Huian’s explanation, [the efficacy of] sacrificing to the five...

If those who have no descendants—such as the spirits of the Five Peaks, the Four Rivers, mountains, rivers, the altars of Earth and Grain, and other deities—are not their offspring, do they truly lack the capacity for resonance and response?
Alas! Jǐngyuán conceived Houjì by treading upon human footprints; Jiǎndí gave birth to Yīn Qì by swallowing a bird’s egg;
Yǐyǐn was born from an empty mulberry tree; and Zhìgōng was born from a hawk’s nest. Of whose vital energy were these born?
"Who is it that serves as the ancestor? Huì'ān further said: "When one dies, the vital energy (qi) disperses and vanishes without a trace.
That there is a record of having lived is merely a chance gathering that did not disperse; it then goes to join with that vital energy of life and is thus able to be reborn.

Since it has been stated that 'the form decays and perishes while the spirit drifts and scatters, vanishing without a trace,' what thing could possibly join with the vital energy of life to be reborn?"
Regarding such statements, Huì-ān’s own words are mutually contradictory and cannot be reconciled. The *Book of Rites* states that "the hawk transforms into the dove and the sparrow into the clam";
furthermore, in works such as the *Mèngqíú*, there are accounts by Bão Jìng of the well-sheep and by Shí Huán of the ring, all of which are utterly inconsistent with Huì-ān’s views.
Following Wénzhèng Gōng and the various classics and histories, however, [the matter is clarified].
To oppose Hui-an [Zhu Xi] is to follow Hui-an; to follow Wen-zheng Gong [Cheng Hao] and the various classics and histories causes one to be filled with doubt.
From where can one obtain a definitive principle? Alas! Only when this matter is thoroughly clarified can it be properly addressed;
how can one speak of it with the mundane mind of conjecture and suspicion? How does this compare to what Confucius said: "If one has not yet been able to serve men, how can one serve ghosts?"
"Knowing life, one knows death"—with these words, one pushes the matter aside and remains free from error.

In the *Li-xue-lei-bian* (Classified Compendium of Neo-Confucianism), Zhang Zai, Cheng Hao, Cheng Yi, and others all fuss over the passage "tracing the origin and returning to the end," extending it to argue for ghosts and spirits;
this is merely an excessive preoccupation with the affairs of the living. Generally, regarding worldly matters, it is best not to know them at all; why suffer such toil to peddle them?
To use hollow fame and forceful rhetoric to bind the minds of later students, leaving them deluded and obstructed so that they no longer seek illumination—how tragic!
Heaven’s retribution will be clear; it will strike like thunder. (42)
Tayuan said, "The people of Song say that what is called being struck by lightning is merely the sudden death caused by the accidental friction of yin and yang; it is not unique.
What do you think of this explanation? Konggu replied, "After the Jingshi (Awakening of Insects) solar term, two yin lines are above and four yang lines are below.
After the Mangzhong (Grain in Ear) solar term, five yang lines are above and one yin line is below. When yin and yang interact in this manner, thunder and rain manifest."
If their operations were always to coincide and they were constantly to clash with one another such that thunder and rain never ceased, why would there be alternating periods of clear skies and rain?
One should know that the interaction and movement of the two qi are like the wheel of a well-drawing pulley, rising and falling alternately;

if they were always in mutual conflict, how could they develop and nourish the myriad things? The sun, moon, stars, wind, clouds, thunder, and rain are all the essence and function of Heaven and Earth, each having its own celestial domain.

Because the responses of the divine lords are timely and never err, there is the principle of sacrificing to Heaven and offering to Earth. When wind and rain are harmonized, it is moved by the good karma of the common people;
when they are not harmonized, it is moved by the evil karma of the times. It is not that the High Heaven lacks a compassionate heart.
Regarding those who speak of being struck by lightning: in the twenty-second year of the Yongle era, Shi Hong, the *vīnāyaka* (steward) of Tianfeng Temple in Taizhou, was [struck] by lightning.
Just as he was about to die, he revived and said that while dead he had seen various heavenly deities instructing him, saying:

"In your previous life, you served as a patrol inspector and unjustly punished a single man by impaling him, for which you deserved the ultimate penalty. Because you were able to serve the Buddha, you have not yet repaid that debt of life.
In your next life, you will become a presiding monk (abbot), but you shall secretly bury three caches of the monastery's permanent copper coins; after your death, these shall eventually be lost."

Because he had committed two offenses in his previous life, he was executed in this present life; yet, because he had served the Great Being Avalokiteśvara with utmost sincerity, he was spared for a time.

Later, in the second year of the Xuande era, he died by drowning. In the region south of the Zhejiang River, there was a man who printed paper horses for the Buddhas, devas, and the three realms to sell as a business.
He had constructed a shop, and within it, he laid out flat wooden planks across the beams of the upper story to serve as a bedroom on that loft.
Last night, he overturned the urinal, causing it to leak and soil the horse; he then dried the horse in the sun and sold it.
This year, he was removed from the shop by a thunderbolt and struck dead in front of the gate.
Furthermore, there was a poor couple suffering from the hardship of starvation due to a lack of grain; the husband took a goose to the market to sell it and obtained two measures of rice.
Driven by the extreme suffering of hunger, he purchased two sheng of wine and drank it; on his way back, he fell asleep drunk upon the ground, and someone stole his rice.
When he awoke, he returned home in a state of frantic distress. His wife, learning of this, could not bear the grief and suffering;
her husband then threw himself into the water and died. The wife said, "Since my husband is dead, why should I remain? and she too threw herself into the water and died.
The next day, a man was struck dead by lightning and cast down beside two corpses;
written upon his back was: "This is the man who stole their rice. In Songjiang, someone was struck dead by lightning; written upon his back was:
"Ten years ago, he entered a temple with a woman and committed lewd acts on the second story of the pagoda; therefore, he is punished. In Huzhou, one... [text ends].
While it was raining, the young woman saw several officials arrive at her gate; only two entered her house, appearing like the celestial soldiers depicted in worldly paintings.
They seized her elder brother and struck him dead with thunder before the door. Only then did she realize that the officials were heavenly deities.
There was also another who died from being struck by lightning; his family dressed the corpse in clothes, but the next day, lightning came again and stripped them away.
When they removed the clothing, there was also a corpse placed within the coffin; the next day, thunder struck again, lifting off the coffin lid.
Such manifest proofs have occurred every year from antiquity to the present. I shall not cite more than these few instances.

Those who witnessed them with their own eyes or heard of them personally do not disclose the names of the individuals, fearing it would bring disgrace upon their families. This, indeed, is the punishment of Heaven.
Furthermore, there are centipedes, foxes, snakes, rats, and other malevolent spirits, as well as trees and household objects that harbor demonic influences;

when these provoke thunder, it invariably strikes them down. How could this be merely a matter of negative energies clashing and accidentally causing death? The *I Ching* says: "The hexagram Zhen represents thunder, with its repeated rolling. Its commentary states: "Thunder rolls on and on;
the noble person, observing this, feels awe and fear, and thus cultivates self-examination. This speaks of fearing heavenly retribution and therefore practicing self-cultivation.
To "mitigate" means to compensate for errors. The people of Song taught others not to believe in the execution by thunder;
this is a profound violation of the *I Ching* and shows a lack of awe toward Heaven and Earth. Before they could advance in virtue, they first lost their moral character.

It is a pity that later generations were unwilling to expand their great vision to illuminate the principles of affairs and phenomena, but instead remained bound by the words of the people of Song alone. The people of Song were not only...
To speculate on this: the transgression of those who thunder against Buddhism is an extreme affliction.
While Wenzhongzi composed his writings using the learning of Confucius and Mencius yet revered the Buddha-dharma, the Song people composed their writings using the Buddha-dharma yet reviled it.
They wished to ensure that later students would not read Buddhist texts, so as to remain ignorant of the reason why he used the Buddha-dharma to compose his writings. Regarding the Song people...
Within the Buddha-dharma, that which has been obtained is like taking a single hair’s breadth of water from the ocean; what is obtained is extremely small.

To cause those who are later students to take full satisfaction and use up this extremely small amount of water, preventing them from ever entering the ocean again, thereby corrupting people's minds, contravening the Buddha-dharma, and losing the great goodness—there is no greater fault than this.
The ruler and his ministers, as well as renowned scholars, study Buddhism.
Si San of Taiyuan said, "As for the benefit that the Buddha-dharma brings to the world, people do not know what kind of benefit there is.

Konggu replied, "Those who practice Chan and awaken to the Way gain the benefit of realizing the mind and seeing their nature; those who exhaustively investigate the scriptures and teachings gain the benefit of clear understanding."
Those who practice according to the Dharma gain the benefit of gradually attaining Bodhi; those who uphold the precepts and recite the Buddha’s name gain the benefit of rebirth in the Pure Land;
those who maintain the precepts and practice dhyāna-concentration gain the benefit of rebirth in the heavens;

those who take refuge and receive with faith gain the benefit of roots of goodness, merit, and wisdom; and those who cultivate a virtuous mind and revere the Buddha gain the fruit of merit from the cause of goodness.
As for the benefit of relying on faith to refrain from evil, one obtains the benefit of not being troubled by legal punishments;

as for the Buddha-dharma being practiced in the world, it provides the benefit of assisting the Imperial governance. [The interlocutor] said: "Indeed, although such benefits exist, who among our Confucians studies them? [The respondent] said: "Not only that."
"What the Confucian scholars study, the sagely lords and enlightened rulers also studied. Taoyuan said, "Your request for instruction is clear.
Konggu replied, "If we speak of those who have studied Buddhism throughout antiquity and the present, they are beyond counting; I shall now describe them in brief."
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty was so devoted to the Buddha-dharma that he could not have been surpassed.
On the day Master Xuanzang passed away, Emperor Gaozong looked to his attendants and said, "I have lost a national treasure. He suspended court for three days.
If one were to say that these two emperors were mired in the Buddha-dharma, then what of Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Wei Zheng, Yu Shinan, Chu Suiliang, and Li Jing?

Why did the various lords, such as Dong Chang, not remonstrate more forcefully? It was because when a ruler is sagacious and his ministers are worthy, all know that the Way of the Buddha-dharma is grand and correct;
they recognize its contribution to governance and its benefit to the people, which is why they collectively honor and uphold it.

Regarding the prefaces and records for the construction of temples and the translation of scriptures, if they were not composed by the Emperor himself, they were the works of Fang Xuanling, Du Jing, Wei Zheng, Yu Shinan, or Chu Suiliang.
The gravity and solemnity of his writings and the sincerity of his devotion to the Buddha may be said to have reached the ultimate.

Emperors Xuanzong, Suzong, Daizong, and Xuanzong were particularly devoted to Buddhism; Daizong pointed to National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang, saying, "There are no treasures in the kingdom, but this monk is a national treasure.
The various sagely emperors of the Song dynasty—Taizu, Taizong, Zhenzong, and Renzong—likewise held Buddhism in high esteem.

They were even more exceptional than this: the ancient and successive enlightened rulers revered the Buddha even more profoundly than these examples. Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty prostrated himself before Tanyan;

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty offered his sincere devotion to Baozhi; the ruler of the Yao Qin dynasty bowed his head to Kumārajīva; the sovereign of Qi took Sengchong as his teacher; Fu Jian paid homage to Dao’an;
and the ruler of Jin venerated Huiyuan with the utmost reverence. Alas! Even the sage-rulers of past and present were thus sincere.

"If even those who have taken refuge in the Buddha with faith do so, how much more should we? When the Chancellor Lord Han Qi, the Vice Minister Ou-yang Hsiu, Kuan Yen-ch'ang of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
Chang Piao-min, and the Court Councillor Chen Shun-yü— none of whom had previously read Buddhist scriptures nor knew to revere the Buddha—
encountered the *T'an-chin Chi* (Collected Works of T'an-ch'in) by Master Ming-chiao So, they all without exception bowed their heads in reverence."

They praised one another, saying: "Unexpectedly, there is such a gentleman among the monastics! Not only is he proficient in the Madhyamaka school, but his literary style is also sublime and excellent.
This is the pen of a great historian; it is the way of a great public figure. From then on, after these gentlemen came to revere the Buddha, some became even more devoted to the Dharma.
Confucius said: "Though one has fine delicacies, if they do not eat them, they will not know their flavor; though there is the ultimate Way, if one does not—"
If one studies without knowing that there is goodness in it, then it is only after studying that one realizes one's deficiencies; it is only after teaching that one realizes one's own limitations.
Once one knows one's deficiencies, one is able to reflect upon oneself; once one knows one's limitations, one is able to exert oneself with vigor. Is this not indeed so?
Since the Jin dynasty, as for the breadth of talent and virtue, and the skill of strategic administration, who could surpass Xie Anshi (Xie An)? Wang—
As for Wang Xizhi, whose breadth of knowledge and capacity were lofty and ancient, and whose talent and thought surpassed his peers—who could surpass him?

As for Tao Yuanming, whose nature and temperament were upright and whose resolve regarding leaving or staying was sublime—who could surpass him? As for Xie Lingyun, whose demeanor was elegant and refined, and whose literary compositions were exquisite—who could surpass him?
As for Lord Cui, who governed the empire and was esteemed as a worthy by all under heaven—who could surpass him?—[this is] Heng.
As for Yang Pangyun, whose insight and vision were lofty and whose mastery of the Way was supreme—who could surpass him?

As for Pei Jin Gong, who established great meritorious achievements that were recorded in the flourishing Tang dynasty—who could surpass him? As for Yan Lu Gong, who possessed great integrity and righteousness, as well as excellence in literature and calligraphy—who could surpass him?
As for Prime Minister Pei Gong, whose literary works followed the ancient way and whose mastery of the Dao reached its ultimate height—who could surpass him?
In this regard, as for Su Shi and Huang Tingjian, who reached the pinnacle of Confucian learning and the excellence of Chan Buddhism—who could surpass them?
As for Chen Zhongshu, whose commitment to Daoxue was profound and whose insight and virtue were sublime—who could surpass him?

And as for Scholar Wang Rixiu, whose erudition and intellectual capacity were lofty, brilliant, and upright—who could surpass him? I have not had the leisure to discuss these at length; I have merely stated it briefly.
These renowned worthies were sincere in their resolve and revered the Buddha; who in the world did not know this?
These renowned worthies possessed such brilliant virtue and wisdom—how could they fail to surpass Huì-ān? How could they fail to surpass those of later generations who slandered the Buddha?
It was simply because their intentions were sincere, their minds upright, and they were impartial and selfless, placing the ultimate Way of the Buddha-Sage above all else. Huì...

Because Ānanda annotated the scriptures, later students revered him; moreover, as they did not understand his underlying mental afflictions, they failed to discern his words and followed his teachings in all matters.
(44) The Confucian school investigates the Chan school. 44.
Taoyuan asked, "Among those who study our Confucian Way, how many have attained the Way? Konggu replied, "It is impossible to know how many true Confucians have studied Chan and attained the Way;
one might estimate that there are perhaps a few individuals, such as Xiangzi."
National Teacher Guo transmitted the study of the Way to Chan Master Shouya; Shouya transmitted it to Ma’i; Ma’i transmitted it to Chen Tuan;
Chen Tuan transmitted it to Song Fang; Song Fang transmitted it to Mu Xiu; and Mu Xiu transmitted it to Li Tingzhi. Li transmitted it to Kangjie (Shao Yong).
Furthermore, Mu Xiu bestowed the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (*Tàijí tú*) that he had received upon Zhou Dunyi of Lianxi. Subsequently, Zhou Dunyi...
I inquired of Chan Master Donglin Zong about the profound meaning of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (*Tàijí tú*).
Donglin explained it to me in detail and at length; he stated that Zhouzi had based his *Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* upon the words of Donglin.

Thus, Zhouzi excelled in the practice of Chan cultivation, and for this reason, his path of practice surpassed that of Shaozi; whereas Shaozi excelled in the knowledge of celestial cycles and calendrical calculations.
"Therefore, while the way of mathematics and logic surpasses that of Zhouzi, as far as the Way of Learning is concerned, they are one and the same;

there is never a second path. You say: 'Since the Chan school already possesses the Great Way for transmission, why did our Confucian Master Heishan (Lu Jiuyuan) reject it? I reply: 'Heishan’s rejection of Buddhism was a sickness of his heart.

You say: 'I beg the Master to explain what this sickness of the heart is. I reply: 'You need only go deep..."* *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a philosophical dialogue, likely concerning the relationship between Neo-Confucianism and Chan Buddhism. The final sentence is cut off.)*

"In studying the Buddha, you have broadly perused the works of a hundred schools; you should see for yourself how Luoxi, the two Chengs, and the various masters attained the source and currents of Daoxue (the Learning of the Way).
He said, "I have no leisure to inquire about what the various masters attained, but I beg of you, Master, to speak of what Luoxi and the Master Cheng attained.
The Master replied, "To explain it in full would be tedious; let me provide a brief account."
It is said that Zhou Dunyi, whose courtesy name was Maoshu, was a native of Chongling.

He first sought instruction from Chan Master Huanglong Nan regarding the "special transmission outside the teachings. Master Nan exhorted Zhou, saying in brief: "You need only attend to matters within your own house.
Confucius said, 'If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening. Ultimately, what constitutes this Way?"
"Even if I die this evening, it would be acceptable. Yanzi did not change his joy; what was it that he found joyful?
It is simply that by investigating this matter to its ultimate conclusion over a long period, there will naturally come a point of resonance and accord. (From the *Jia-pu* of the Zhang family.
One day, Zhu Xi questioned Chan Master Foyin Yuan, saying, "Ultimately, what constitutes the Way? Yuan replied, "The green mountains fill the eyes—let them be seen as they are. Zhu Xi was about to—
When Yuan discussed this, he merely laughed heartily; Lián was suddenly enlightened (from the *Postscript to the Zījìàn and the Recorded Sayings of Foyìn*).

Lián heard that Chan Master Dònglín Zǒng had received the mind-to-mind transmission of the two masters Zhúlín Shòuyá and Mányī Dàozhě, through whom they had mastered the study of the *Yī* (*Changes*), exhausting its mysteries and reaching the ultimate nature of things.
Thereupon, he questioned Zǒng, who instructed him briefly as follows: "Our Buddha spoke of the 'actual reality' (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
The ground of principle is precisely the true and non-deceptive; being true and non-deceptive is sincerity. How great is the Qian-primordial! All things take their beginning from it;
taking this real principle as their source, the transformations of the Way of Qian cause each to rectify its own nature and destiny—this is precisely the rectification of this real principle.
The Way of Heaven, Earth, and the Sage consists in nothing other than supreme sincerity. One must apply oneself to a single path of practice upon the ground of reality, proceeding directly until—
"Once there is a sudden, expansive realization, one must not merely understand it through words," and so forth.

One day, Zhu Xi (Lian) went with Zhang Zithou and others to Donglin Temple to discuss the nature (*xing*). He said in summary: "In our teaching, we speak much of the nature; therefore, it is called the 'School of Nature' (*xingzong*).
What is called *tathatā*-nature and *dharmatā*-nature is precisely principle (*li*). There is the realm of principle (*lǐfájì*) and the realm of phenomena (*shìfájì*)."
"Principle and phenomena penetrate one another; there is no phenomenon outside of principle, and every phenomenon must have its underlying principle.

When the various disciples hesitated and could not reach a decision, Lu Jiān (Lǎoziàn) stepped forward resolutely and said, "The substance of human nature is profound and vast, consisting of nothing but principle; what is there to doubt?

Hèngqú remarked, "Regarding the discourse on the nature and principle of Donglin, none but our Mòshū could have achieved it" (*Hongyi Jiwén*). Lǎoziàn asked about the *Taijī*, and [Wáng] answered in general terms that "the *Yì* is present therein."
The pre-heaven state is formless yet possesses principle; indeed, the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) is precisely the *Yi* (the Book of Changes). This formless principle is the "Ultimateless" (*wuji*).
Within heaven and earth, there is but a single vital energy (*qi*) that advances and recedes to form the four seasons;

viewed from the perspective of this single energy, all are the manifestations of the Origin (*yuan*). (These words concerning the *Yi*, written by Donglin in his own hand for Liu Shizhong, are detailed and complete, including notes from Yinshi’s family school and Su Jiming’s records; furthermore, they contain Chengzi’s profound appreciation for the *Yuánbāo*).

Regarding the "Discourse on the Four Virtues," Master Hu Wufeng’s preface to the *Tongshu* states that Lu Jiuyuan obtained the *Taiji tu* from Mu Xiu, Mu Xiu obtained it from Zhong Fang, and Zhong Fang obtained it from Chen Tuan;

this is one of his teachers. [Lu Jiuyuan] clearly stated that the *Taiji tu* was not composed by him, and that Chen Tuan’s learning was obtained from Māyī and from the Chan Master Shouya (as recorded in the *Xing*).

[Preface to] *The Essential Points of Learning and the Rectification of the Mind-Dharma of the *Yijing*:* Lian asked about the origins of the *Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* (*Taiji tu*). He replied in summary:
"The Chan Master Shouyaya of Zhulin received the mind-transmission of Chan Master Guoyi; its lineage is ancient. It does not speak of phenomena or things, but of the ultimate principle.

The intention behind the construction of the diagram at that time was based on our own teaching [of Buddhism], which establishes the world upon emptiness, taking non-being as the source of the myriad existents."

Taking non-being as the cause (non-being is the emptiness that serves as the substratum), taking being as the effect (being is the movement of the interaction of the two qi), taking the Real as the essence (the Real is the ultimate principle of singular truth), and taking the provisional as the function (the provisional is the transformation and birth of the myriad things);
therefore it is said: "The Ultimate Polarity’s Truth mysteriously unites," and so forth.
Furthermore, I, Lián, visited the chamber of the Buddhist Sealer and recounted this; he then realized it through the Seal, saying: "I have long instructed people in the teachings of Confucius..."
"The great principles of Mencius are now carried by you, sir; you ought to exert yourself in putting them into practice without stagnation.

Regarding Donglin, there was also a remark addressed to me, Lü Dian, stating that he advocated for Confucians to pursue the Way of Learning (Daoxue) (from *Songchuang zaji*). I instructed my students, saying:
"This wondrous mind of mine was truly inspired by Master Nan and further elucidated by Master Foyin; the principles of the *I Ching* are thus vast and penetrating."

If these teachings do not receive the illumination, guidance, polishing, and refinement provided by Donglin, they will absolutely be unable to achieve a state where the inner and outer are transparently clear and where all principles are thoroughly integrated and vast.
(From the *Yin Family School* and the *Essentials of the Study of Nature*).

When I went to Lingshan Temple in Chaozhou to visit the remains of Chan Master Dadian, I saw that the many scrolls of the letters sent from Hanzi to Dadian were still preserved there, as well as the "Cloth-Robes Pavilion," which stood solemn and empty.

In memory of this, he composed a poem titled "Tui-zhi (Han Yu) Claims for Himself to Be Like the Master Confucius; 'The Origin of the Way' Thoroughly Refutes Buddhism and Daoism. It Is Not That He Does Not Know Greatian—What Kind of Person Is He?":

"I have written several letters to you, cherishing you deeply; please keep this robe as well. (This appears in the *Xingli Qunshu* [Compendium of Books on Nature and Principle] along with the original calligraphy from the Ling-shan Temple Robe Pavilion.
Lian composed a poem on loving the lotus: "The Buddha loves it, and I love it too; its fragrant scent the butterflies do not steal. In every way, it is marvelous and peerless."
"One should not place [it] upon the head of a woman" (from the *Zheng Gu Ji*). "Lian's nature was simple and frugal; in his daily life he was as tranquil as water.

In his later years, he completely set aside literary compositions, devoting himself solely to the supremacy of stillness, and ultimately attained the transmission of the Daoist learning" (*Biography of Lianxi*). "The teachings of Donglin consist solely in the pursuit of the supremacy of stillness.
Lianxi did not attend to brush or inkstone for a long time, sitting upright before the window all day amidst the colors of the grass."
"The same intention and meaning are indeed attained within stillness" (*Hongik Gigeum*).
"The beginning of the study of Dao and the principles of nature was truly initiated by Master Ya, and reached Master Zong; Zong transmitted it to Zhouzi" (*Hongik Gigeum*). Lord Chen Zhongsu said:
"Regarding the discourse on the principles of nature, Donglin transmitted it to Lianxi, and Lianxi expanded upon it; his words pervade the Buddhist scriptures."

(Yingzhong Lu and the Essential Guide to the Study of Nature): Master Liu Houcun’s poem states, "The learning of Li Ao originated from a high monk," and further says, "Only then did I realize that outside the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, there were others who possessed heroic talent" (from the Houcun Ji).
Chengzi was a native of Luocheng; his courtesy name was Bochun and his style name was Mingdao. His younger brother, whose courtesy name was Zhengshu and style name was Yichuan, was named Yi.
Master Zeng Ye said: "The Cheng brothers, Hao and Yi, together received instruction from Lianxi.
Lianxi first instructed them to seek out what it was that Confucius and Yanzi delighted in. Once their studies were complete, each took it upon himself to carry forward this culture."

(From the *Shilüe* and other sources: Master Cheng bestowed the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (*Tàijí tú*) upon Mr. Hòushān. Hòushān said: "I have observed how Zhou and Cheng extended their own realization to teach others;

yet looking back at the tradition since Confucius and Mencius, I find that there has truly never been such a method of silent meditation, sitting upright, and practicing cultivation to seek the locus of joy as the ultimate inquiry into the Way. Truly, it is Zhou [Dunyi] who [has established this]."
The source through which Cheng [Zhao] embodied the Way certainly branched into distinct streams (from the postscript by Chao Shuo-xin to the *Yuanliu* of Heart-Mind Learning).
Mingdao deeply savored the *Huayan He lun*, claiming that he experienced a profound internal fusion and realization of its meaning;

out of joy, he recorded the circumstances of this in the Yun’gai Temple (the ink rubbing of the inscription at Yun’gai Temple). On the anniversary of the memorial service for his deceased mother, Lady Shou’an, Mingdao went there.
At Changqing Temple in the Western Capital, while personally attending a vegetarian feast to cultivate merit for the deceased, I observed the assembly of monks entering the hall.

Their movements were majestic and dignified; as the drums were struck and the bells rung, both inside and out all was solemn and orderly. Every sitting and every rising conformed precisely to the pure regulations.
I sighed and remarked: "The rites and music of the Three Dynasties are fully present here. (From *Hongyi Jiwen*, recorded by Master Lingyuan Qing). Answering [the inquiry].
In a letter from Yichuan, it says: "I have presumptuously relied upon your gracious attention, being honored by your expectation that I might understand the Way.
Although I have not yet once enjoyed the joy of meeting you face-to-face, I have heard that you have long devoted yourself to this Way.

Having inquired at length with the great masters throughout the world, you still consider me—a person of humble learning—to be insufficient because I have not yet seen [the truth]. Recently, I have heard my late teacher speak of your realization."

Having read the postscript to the *Dharma Essentials* composed by Lord Gong, I deeply contemplate and enter into its truth; it is indeed real and not false. (This is from the *Recorded Sayings of Lingyuan*;

the "former teacher" refers to Chan Master Huìtáng Xīn. Huìtáng once transmitted the Dharma of the mind to Yichān. Subsequently, Yichān frequently entered the chamber of Lingyuan. The *Jiatai Pǔdēng Lù* states:
"Chéng Yichān, Xú Shīchuān, Zhū Shìyīng, and Hóng Jūfù all sought the Way [from him]."
Regarding Master Lingyuan Chan, the late Mr. Yichuan composed a preface for his annotated book, from which he drew extensively upon the words and meanings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
this shows that one can trust that the spiritual lineage has a source from which it proceeds. Mr. Hu Jijun of Shitang said:

"More than fifteen hundred years after Mencius passed away, the transmission of the Way was submerged and its continuity severed. Only with the emergence of Master Zhou did that which was submerged shine forth again and that which was severed be restored."
Continuing the lineage of the two sons of Cheng of Henan, they received the transmission of Zhouzi.
The transmission of Zhouzi originated with Chan Master Shouya of Zhulin Temple on Beigu Mountain, who was its primary proponent. After Chengzi’s fourfold transmission, it reached Zhu Wen Gong.
Wen Gong, in turn, studied this Way under Zhang Jingfu until he attained a state of complete liberation, whereupon he remarked: "In the past..."
Regarding the "Leftover Words from the Bamboo Grove" that I have heard, those points with which I did not yet accord do not deceive me;

it turns out that this matter is ten times more similar to Chan Buddhism than I had realized. That scholars do not know Chan and Chan practitioners do not know scholarship, such that they mutually attack one another without ever striking at the actual point of the illness—this is truly laughable.
(From Hu Shi’s *Discourse on Great Unity*). Ouyang Xuan said: Throughout his life, Master Cheng...
"I am fond of reading Buddhist texts, though I do not match the breadth of learning of Master Zhu" (Recorded by Ouyang Xiu).
Cheng Yi said, "Master Mingdao spent nearly ten years studying both Buddhism and Daoism" (From the *Biography of Master Mingdao* composed by Cheng Yi). Donglin’s discourse on integrity states:

If one does not adopt the great impartiality of these worthies, one must simply submit to the narrow-mindedness of a single person or half a person.
My own view was truly a mistake born of not having reflected upon it.

this is what Shi Zhi meant when he said that those whom they sought to exclude were the very ones they had erected as a defensive wall.

it is the mind-dharma transmitted through a thousand sages, wherein there is a sudden awakening that cannot be reached through seeing, hearing, thinking, or deliberating.
Things and self share the same principle; this is the inherent nature, the essence and function of the mind. When my mind is correct, it is Heaven.
The mind of the earth likewise rectifies the fundamental source of all things; the wondrous function of the one mind is so agile and vibrant that it penetrates from head to tail.
When one practices to this point—biting on the roots of vegetables, the "seamless pagoda," and these three phrases—one strikes the seat of the illness, cutting it in two with a single stroke.

for all other commentaries on the Four Books and his various writings, he extensively employed Buddhist principles.

Huian was like this, yet he also concealed the Buddhist language used by Zhou Dunyi and Cheng Hao while failing to recognize that they were clearly manifesting Buddhist ideas—what kind of mind was Huian’s?

Buchi Qian replied in a letter, saying: "Seize this single thought and call upon the 'dog' koan; do not engage in deliberation.
With courageous directness, cut it through in two with one stroke. Upon reading this, Huian attained realization (from the *Ziji Gongchen Ji* and the *Xingli Qunshu*).
In his small bamboo grove pavilion, Huian recited Buddhist scriptures and composed a poem, which begins: "Sitting alone and doing nothing, I casually open the Śākya teachings..."
This letter briefly brings rest to the burdens of worldly dust; I transcend them all and dwell with the Dao. The gate is closed amidst the seclusion of the bamboo grove;

birds sing after the mountain rains have passed. Having realized this law of non-action (*wuwei*), body and mind are equally at peace. (From the *Complete Collection of Master Zhu* and the *Record of the Path’s Remains*). Master Huì'ān sent a letter to the Chan Master of Guīqīng, saying:

Li Wenjing Gong, Wang Wenzheng Gong, Liu Yuancheng, and Lü Shengong—what kind of men were they?

The *Pò* (the *Awakening of Faith*) explains that the twelve links of dependent origination give rise to the *Avataṃsaka*.

The *Huá-yán Hé-lùn* (Comprehensive Commentary on the Avataṃsaka) states that while the Buddha’s teachings exhaust all worldly affairs, they ultimately reveal the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), where not a single speck of dust is received; yet at the gateway of myriad phenomena, not a single dharma is abandoned.

Bodhidharma completely overturned these conventional molds and advocated the study of Chan, which is even more sublime than the study of doctrine (*yìxué*). This is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The general meaning lies solely in Subhūti’s two questions: "How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind? Therefore, it is said:
"One should not dwell upon dharmas to give rise to the mind; one should not dwell upon form to give rise to the mind," and so forth.

A saying of the Chan school states: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally quiescent and vast. It can act as the lord of all phenomena, yet does not follow the four seasons."
Withered and fallen leaves are not other things; scattered and strewn about, they are no mere dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth fully reveal the body of the Dharma King.
If one recognizes this mind, there is not a single inch of land in the whole world.

Thus, one who can walk may become bewildered and at a loss if they lose their shrimp; or one who relies on a crab for its legs may become bewildered and at a loss if they lose that crab.
Later scholars followed Hui-an in rejecting [the teachings of the Master], much like those two creatures relying on other objects.
One might ask: "Are there not also those who wished to reject them of their own accord, regardless of Hui-an's arguments?"
What do you say to this? It is like a person in the world who only recognizes objects that are easily seen, but does not recognize those that are difficult to see.
Suddenly encountering a bright moon-jewel or a luminous night-gem, its brilliance dazzling and its radiance stealing the sight, they do not recognize it as a treasure but suspect it to be a monster.
They then seize a sharp sword and resist it with fierce force, vying with one another to know what this object is.
To be able to make the poor wealthy and the lowly noble is a merit and virtue of such magnitude.
It is like a blind man who, not seeing the light of the sun and moon, wishes for all people in the world to be blind as well, asserting that the sun and moon have no light.
Alas! Such fools are like earthworms, who know only to feed on the mud within a single foot of ground.

"In the performance of good and the commission of evil, the response follows like a shadow follows a form. Do not say that evil deeds go unpunished; wait until the evil has reached its full measure."
Do not say that the cultivation of goodness has no response; simply wait until the fruits of goodness are fully realized. The *Record of Cause and Effect* states:
"One must know that the causes from previous lives are what one receives in this life; one must know that the effects in future lives are what one creates in this life. It further says:
"Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created does not perish; when the conditions and causes meet, the retribution will be experienced by oneself."

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are three types of retribution for karma: first, retribution in the present life, wherein one performs good or evil deeds and experiences the resulting pleasure or suffering in this very life;

second, retribution in the next life, wherein one either performs deeds in a previous life and receives the retribution in the current life, or performs deeds in the current life and receives the retribution in a future life;
and third, immediate retribution, wherein one performs deeds before one's eyes and receives the retribution immediately thereafter. As the *Book of Changes* says: "Accumulate goodness..."

"The ghosts and spirits harm those who are full and bless those who are humble. The *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "When Heaven and Earth clearly examine one's conduct, the divine intelligence becomes manifest.

Zengzi said: "Be cautious! Be cautious! What goes out from you will return to you. The *Book of Documents* says: "The Way of Heaven blesses the good and brings calamity to the licentious. Laozi [said]: [The Way of Heaven is retributive.]

It is said: "The net of Heaven is vast and wide; though its mesh is coarse, nothing escapes. It is also said: "The net of Yang is coarse and easily escaped, while the net of Yin is dense and difficult to evade.
The Buddha once said to Ānanda: "There are those who perform good deeds in this life yet fall into hell after death, and those who commit evil deeds in this life yet are born in heaven after death.
Ānanda asked why this was so. The Buddha replied: "Those who perform good deeds in this life..."
Those who die and fall into hell are such that the good karma of this life has not yet ripened, while the evil karma of past lives has already ripened.
Those who do evil in this life but are born in heaven after death are such that the evil karma of this life has not yet ripened, while the good karma of past lives has already ripened.

Where the karma has ripened, one first receives its retribution; it is like a debt, where what is most urgent is repaid first. By inferring from this, it is evident that all three teachings are [consistent].
He said, "This principle merely involves a matter of speed; how can one fail to believe in cause and effect simply because the retribution has not yet been seen before one's eyes?
On that basis, one might as well disbelieve in the Pure Land.
I replied, "It appears that your understanding of this principle is truly not clear. Although worldly people..."
It is said: "It is the mandate of Heaven. How could Heaven show partiality toward any person?

It is simply because the deeds performed by people in previous lives were different that the retributions they receive in this life are also different; how could this be something governed by Heaven's own intent?
For this reason, this body is called a 'retribution-body,' for it is born as a result of my own past deeds. What intention could Heaven possibly have in this? It is, for example, like a person..."

When one has merit or transgression regarding external affairs, one ought to receive reward or punishment from the government offices. Do these government offices act out of private favoritism toward individuals?
They simply grant rewards for merit and impose punishments for transgression; how could they apply rewards or punishments to people without cause?
If even the government offices of this world do not apply rewards or punishments without cause, how much less so the Heaven and Earth that bring about all transformations?

How could it be that misfortune and fortune are bestowed upon people without cause? One must know that because of the good and evil deeds performed in previous lives, misfortunes and blessings in this life are given as retribution.
Because one cannot be purely virtuous, one cannot receive pure blessings alone;

thus there are those who are wealthy and noble yet suffer from illness and die young, while there are those who are poor and lowly yet live long and enjoy happiness, and there are those who possess honor.
There are those who are favored yet withered by disgrace; there are those who are lowly and destitute yet live in peace and leisure. There are those who attain high degrees in their youth;
there are those who do not pass the examinations until the end of their lives. There are those whose wealth and grain are abundant yet have no children;
there are those oppressed by hardship who have many troublesome children. There are those whose wives die while the husbands remain; there are those whose husbands die while the wives remain.
There are those whose sons die before their fathers; there are those whose grandsons die before them in the ancestral hall.

There are those who experience pleasure first and suffering later; those who experience suffering first and pleasure later; those who experience pleasure at the beginning and end but suffering in the middle;
those who experience suffering at the beginning and end but pleasure in the middle; those who suffer throughout their entire lives; and those who enjoy pleasure throughout their entire lives.
"I now ask you, my son: for what reason has this come to pass? He replied, "In truth, I do not understand this.
I said, "Since you do not understand, why do you not believe? If a person denies cause and effect, they will surely fall into the Avīci Hell.

When their karmic retribution in hell is exhausted, they will fall further into the realm of hungry ghosts; when their retribution as a hungry ghost is exhausted, they will fall into the realm of animals."
In this life, they repay their past debts by taking one life for every life taken; for every eight *liang* consumed in the past, they must now give back half a *jin*.
Having exhausted their karmic retribution as animals, they obtain a human body only in a degraded form.

Though possessing a human shape, they are impoverished and lowly, blind, deaf, mute, and dumb, with crippled feet or broken hands, and are entangled by malignant diseases and oppressed by hunger and cold. They do not encounter the Buddha and do not hear the True Dharma.
If one encounters neither sages nor worthies, and does not meet with wise teachers, one will transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death, suffering without end. As the ancient masters said:

"If you wish not to incur karma leading to the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. One must know that good and evil are clearly manifest and that cause and effect are never obscured;
these are the sincere words of the Buddha, who would certainly not speak falsely regarding cause and effect, even concerning the Pure Land. Furthermore—
A person must know right from wrong, recognize shame and integrity, believe in cause and effect, fear sin and merit, examine good and evil, and distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox.
Above, they do not resent Heaven; below, they do not blame others. Prosperity and decline cannot move their heart; gain and loss cannot shift their resolve.
They remain without excessive joy when in wealth and honor, and without sorrow when in poverty and low station; they understand how to advance and retreat.
At such a time, one who assesses their strength and undertakes tasks according to their capacity—acting when employed and remaining hidden when dismissed;
whose loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, and compassion remain constant from beginning to end—is not a gentleman, I do not believe it possible; is not a great sage, I do not believe it possible;
and while practicing this mindfulness of the Buddha, does not attain birth in the Pure Land, I do not believe it possible.
I now explain this with earnest diligence to resolve your doubts; you should receive it with reverence and care, and not treat it with negligence.
Regarding the refutation of the belief that hell does not exist:
some say that the doctrine of hell is not to be trusted, while others say that even the doctrine of prisons is not to be trusted.
Xinye said, "The prisons exist in the present; how can one not believe this? [The Master] said, "Though the prisons exist, for me they do not exist.
Someone said, "Even though you, Master, do not suffer the pains of prison, you still cannot claim their non-existence. [The Master] said, "It is so, it is so.
The hells also exist in the present; why do you not believe this? Someone said, "As for what Zhu Xi spoke regarding human death..."

Thereafter, once the physical form has decayed and perished, the spirit likewise drifts away and disperses; even if there were instruments for mincing, burning, pounding, or grinding, they would have no application.
Thus, it is clear that the Ten Kings of the Netherworld are not to be trusted. Yuan-yuan said: "Zhu Xi’s explanation is utterly erroneous.
It not only transgresses the great principles of the Master [Confucius], but also loses itself in his own reckless words. I examined this with scrutiny.
Question: Since Zhu Xi maintains that the spirit (*shen*) also disperses, how can there still be ghosts and spirits? Answer:

Confucius said, "Revere the ghosts and spirits but keep them at a distance," and "Do not sacrifice to those who are not one's ancestors. He also said, "Establish ancestral temples so that the ancestors may partake as spirits," and "Perform seasonal sacrifices so that they may be remembered in due time.
Furthermore, he said, "While they are alive, one brings peace to their parents; when sacrificing, the ancestors partake as spirits."

Furthermore, it is said: "When the ancestral temple is treated with the utmost reverence, the spirits manifest; when filial piety and fraternal respect reach their fulfillment, they penetrate to the divine.
It is also said: "In Yu, I find nothing to criticize; though his food was coarse, he offered the utmost filial devotion to the spirits.

In the *Liji*, Confucius says: "When a person dies, they are called a 'ghost' (gui); this has remained unchanged throughout the five dynasties. Judging from these accounts, it is not only the Master [Confucius] who holds this view.
Regarding the spirits and deities mentioned, all the various schools of thought and philosophers speak of them;

it is not as if the Classics and the Worthy Transmissions do not fully record matters concerning spirits and deities—is there not the word of Zhu Xi? Furthermore, Zhu Xi cited Fan Wenzheng Gong, who said:
"If one enjoys wealth and honor alone while neglecting one's own clan, how will one be able to face one's ancestors on another day?"

With what face could one who is underground enter the family shrine? Since you claim that the physical form decays and perishes while the spirit drifts and scatters, vanishing without a trace, who would remain underground at the family shrine?
Who would go to see their ancestors? Such being the case, Zhu Xi’s deception of his own heart and his groundless talk are clearly evident.
Long ago, Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty heard early on of [the teachings of] Wu...

Later, wishing to destroy his established dharma, [the Emperor] desired to kill him. Yuan Tian'gang said, "If you kill him, he will be reborn in the human realm, and his resentment and anger will become even deeper.
Taizong agreed with this, and thus ordered her to become a nun and reside at Ganye Temple.
(The *Liu Sanwu Xijian* records this in detail; the *Tongjian* merely abbreviates it. Tian'gang meant that he would be reborn in the human realm with deep resentment and anger.

The more deeply one reflects on this, the more one realizes that Zhu Xi’s claim that “the physical form perishes and the spirit disperses” and the assertions of the other [Buddhist] school are worlds apart; which is right and which is wrong?
Furthermore, Sima Guang said to Master Liu Yuancheng: “As for the Buddhist talk of heaven and hell, it is merely...”
"Now, does this [hell] actually exist? Yuancheng said, "The Buddha’s establishment of this has both its principle and its manifestation.
If one examines its principle, it is intended to lead people from evil toward goodness. If one discusses its manifestation, then hell truly exists.

Furthermore, Zou Yan claimed that beyond heaven and earth there are eight or nine realms such as the Divine Continent (Shenzhou) and the Red County (Chixian), while Zhuangzi spoke of the sages regarding what lies beyond the six directions."
To leave this matter as it is without further discussion: how could one know that what is beyond the reach of ordinary people's ears and eyes does not exist?

Lord Ouyang moved with such reverence that he took these words to heart; from then on, he honored the Buddha. He further cited an ancient sage who said: "If heaven did not exist, it would have to; if it exists, the superior man ascends there.
If hell did not exist, it would have to; if it exists, the petty person enters it. Truly, these are profound words! Now, I shall provide a single analogy.
"By means of this, you who have destroyed many delusions, O virtuous ones, do you have dreams? They replied, "We have dreams. He asked, "In your dreams, did you ever experience suffering or pleasure?
They replied, "We have experienced suffering and pleasure. I said, "At the time you experienced suffering and pleasure, did you perceive it as being received by the body or received by the spirit?
Some said, "The body is lying on the bed; how could it be the body [that feels]? I said, "Originally, it was the spirit that received it."
The sufferings of the various hells are all experienced by the soul and spirit; they do not truly pertain to the physical body.

If there is suffering and joy even within the dreams of the living, how much more so after death—how could there be no hells? If one were to follow the words of Zhu Xi, it would instead bring calamity upon later generations by causing them to enter hell.
Why is this? Because it would allow those who do not believe in the retribution of sin and merit to become licentious and unrestrained.
To commit evil and fall into hell is not, in fact, to be harmed by Zhu Xi;
rather, it is because Zhu Xi maliciously rejected the Buddha and falsely uttered these words to delude the masses that he is clearly unworthy of belief. Alas!
Master Hu, fearing neither hell nor karmic retribution, forged the "Discourse on Venerating the Correct" (*Chongzheng bian*) to slander the Great Sage and deceive and mislead the ignorant.
It is truly lamentable that both self and others alike enter hell; alas! Those who construct the prison go to undergo its retribution, and those who enter it likewise go to undergo its retribution.
Since I do not commit the sins of the prison, I shall not receive the punishments of the prison;
since I do not create the karma of hell, I shall not suffer the torments of hell. How can one stubbornly cling to one's own views and sever [the path]?
Regarding this state of non-existence, some may ask: "If it is thus and so, how can one practice and maintain discipline so as not to fall into hell? One person replied:
"If you all firmly uphold the precepts, recite the Buddha's name, and engage in Zen meditation, you will realize Bodhi and transcend to the Ultimate Bliss.
If you act according to this, not only will you not go to hell, but you will not even go to receive rebirth in heaven."
"Descriptions of the Hells and Rebirth Among Various Species," excerpted from the *Rujian* (Classical Confucian Canon).
During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty (49th year), Zhao Wenchang, an assistant director of the Department of State Affairs, died and was restored to life.
He said that someone led him to the abode of King Yama. The King asked what meritorious deeds he had performed throughout his lifetime. Zhao replied, "My family is poor and I have no means."
"You may perform meritorious deeds; simply uphold this King of Prajñāpāramitā, the Vajra-samādhi, and with palms joined, praise it, saying:
'Excellent! This merit is exceedingly great. Immediately release him and let him return to life. Then, a messenger was sent to lead him to the south gate.

Upon arriving at the side chamber of the gate, he saw Emperor Zhou Wu inside, secured by three layers of locks and shackles. The Emperor called out to Chang, saying: "Now that you have returned home, speak on my behalf to the Emperor of Sui."
I have already expiated all my other sins, yet the sin of obstructing the Buddha-dharma remains heavy and cannot yet be fully resolved.
To provide merit for its expiation so that I may escape hell, I emerged from the gate and saw a great pit of excrement with a man’s head protruding from the hair atop it.
When asked who this person was, the guide replied, "This is Bai Qi, the General of Qin; his retribution is still not yet finished."

Chang returned and was restored to life, whereupon he reported the matter to the throne. An imperial decree was issued for the monks and nuns throughout the empire to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra* and to perform great offerings on behalf of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.
Furthermore, this account was included in the "Account of Miraculous Responses" (*Ganying fu*) in the *Sui Shu*, which records that Yu Xin fell into hell and became a nine-headed turtle.
Because Yu Xin lived among men, he employed flowery rhetoric and deceptive speech to disparage and exclude the followers of the Buddha.
To suffer such retribution as this is a belated realization; the *Record of the Words and Deeds of Illustrious Ministers* notes that Wang Jinggong’s son, named Pang, performed many unwholesome acts.
Indeed, most of Jinggong’s deeds that contravened principle and harmed the Way originated with Pang.
After Pang died, Jinggong had a vision of him standing by his gate wearing an iron cangue; it was for this reason that he donated his residence to establish [a monastery].
The temple was established for the sake of Wang Pang’s posthumous merit and to liberate him from suffering and hardship;

if one uses this as evidence, it is clear that the books of the Confucian school already contain doctrines regarding hell. To claim that the Buddhist doctrine of hell is non-existent is the height of thoughtlessness.
The *Nanshi* records that Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty dreamed of a monk with squinting eyes entering the palace holding an incense burner.

Having taken birth in the royal palace, he attained awakening; subsequently, his son was born in the inner quarters. While still young, the child fell ill with an eye disease that medical treatment could not cure, resulting ultimately in the loss of one eye.

This was the Emperor Yuan. The *Record of the Words and Deeds of Famous Ministers* (*Yuan Dian-yu Xingyan Lu*) records that when Fan Zu-yu was about to be born, his mother dreamed of a magnificent man standing by her side who said, "I am the Han General Deng Yu. Upon waking, she gave birth to the child. Thus [it came to pass].

He was named Zu Yu; because of his pure and complete internal conduct, Deng Yu bestowed upon him the style name Chūnfú. Furthermore, one does not see such accounts in works like the *Wénlèi jù* or the *Ménqióu*:

for instance, Yang Hù recognizing the ring, Bào Jìng recording the well, Xiàng Jìng’s daughter being reborn after her death and questioning her parents for the sake of a knife, Wén Dàn’s illusory body returning to life, and the verification through the story of the fragrant pouch.
If one uses this as evidence, then the Confucian classics already contain the doctrine of *saṃsāra*;
how can it be said that the Buddhist doctrine of *saṃsāra* is incorrect? How utterly unexamined this is! The doctrine of hell and *saṃsāra* has already been discussed previously.
As for the transformation into an animal after death, there are accounts recorded by the Confucians themselves that are not [merely Buddhist].
First, Li Shiqian of the Sui Dynasty said: Gǔn transformed into a né (a three-legged turtle); Dùyǔ became a tíjué (cuckoo); Bāojūn became a dragon; Niú'āi became a tiger;
Pénghēng became a pig; Rúyì became a dog; Huángmǔ became a soft-shelled turtle; Yíwǔ became a hard-shelled turtle;
Dèngwén became an ox; Xúbó became a fish; Língxià became a crow; and the scholar became a snake. They cried out.
The accounts recorded in the Confucian classics are as follows; it is not that the Buddhists originated this teaching.
Hong Mai stated that he personally saw those who had slaughtered pigs or sheep lie on the ground at the moment of death, bleating like pigs or sheep.
