The ancients said that the most violent are transformed into tigers, and Chengzi said he personally saw a village dweller transform into a tiger and lead a tiger into his own house to devour him.
In both ancient and modern times, there have been many such cases as this, yet people of the world still do not believe them.
Zhuang Zhou said, "All things emerge from the mechanism and enter back into the mechanism. Jia Yi said, "To be transformed into a different species—what cause for concern is that?

Confucius said, "By tracing the origin and returning to the end, one understands the discourse on life and death. If one believes these words, then one will know that although a person possesses this body, [it is not the self].

Even if one can constantly maintain the practice of turning away from evil and inclining toward good, one cannot avoid becoming a being of a different species. *The Direct Pointing of the August School* says:

"If a person uses the mind of a bird or beast, they will surely become a bird or beast after death; if they use the mind of a human or celestial being, they will surely return to the realm of humans or celestials.
This is an immutable principle. What is meant by "no cycle of rebirth"? Scholar Jingzhai said: "One's intelligence and wisdom cannot [prevent it]."
Even those with wealth and status born of hostile karma cannot escape saṃsāra; reasoning from this, one sees that all three teachings speak of this very matter.
How can one fail to believe it simply because it is not yet visible before one's eyes? Thus, with a mind of vast compassion, the Buddha revealed the teachings of the five vehicles:
the Human Vehicle teaches people to uphold the five precepts so that they may constantly obtain a human body and not fall [into lower realms].
These are of different categories. Those who ride the Celestial Vehicle are taught to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds so as to obtain a celestial body as their retribution;

this goes beyond merely being a human being. As for the latter three vehicles, they teach people to proceed from the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha up to the Buddha-way, eternally severing the cycle of birth and death, returning to the Pure Land to abide forever without extinction, realizing unsurpassed enlightenment, and returning to deliver all beings.
"Birth! Alas! Among the great paths of the world, what principle could surpass this?
To discern and clarify ascent and descent, and the entrusting of the womb—fifty [verses].
Someone may say: 'The words of the Śākya school regarding casting oneself into a womb and entrusting birth, and regarding ascent, descent, and the cycle of transmigration—such words as these...'"
"This is truly detestable; how can it be believed? The foolish men and women of the world are deluded by it, but surely the wise who study the classics are not so deluded?
Wuyuan said, "Are you a man of broad learning and wisdom? The other replied, "Yes.
Wuyuan said, "If you are a wise man, you must certainly be able to exhaustively understand the principles of all things. I beg you to analyze these two matters for me."
To sever [these doubts], some say that the matters of conception and childbirth must arise from the union of husband and wife;
even if there were cases of an external being seeking entry, one must consider from where such a being comes and by what path it enters.

What is called "seeking rebirth" or "entrusting oneself to a womb" is absolutely not to be believed. As for what is called ascending, descending, or transmigrating through the cycles of existence, in reality, it does not exist.
"Supposing such a thing were possible, why would humans not give birth to livestock, and livestock not give birth to humans?
We see only humans giving birth to humans and livestock giving birth to livestock; these two matters must certainly be regarded as untrustworthy.
Yuanxiao laughed and said, "Since you call yourself a wise man, you ought not to be ignorant of your own mind. Although I, this mountain monk, am foolish and lowly, I have not been deceived by you."
Mán said, "Master, if you have attained the principle, why do you not explain it to me in detail? Yìyuán replied, "Indeed, I shall speak to you;
you must listen attentively. Mán said, "You say that entering a womb and taking birth all arise from sexual union.
Yet among those in the world who have no children, many take wives and concubines, yet throughout their lives they ultimately never have a single son or daughter."
Why is this so? It must be understood that entering a womb and taking birth necessarily depends upon both internal and external causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) to achieve completion.
What are these internal and external causes and conditions? One's own past karma is the internal cause; the physical body provided by one's parents is the external condition.

Only through the union of these internal and external causes and conditions does existence come to be. If there were no past karma as its own internal cause, one would never take conception in a womb. Why is this?
The parents are like earth and water, and consciousness is like a seed; without a seed, offspring will certainly not be produced.
One cannot believe in the doctrine of an external soul entering the womb. Even if such a thing were possible, one must see from where it comes and by what way it enters.
Now, I shall again employ an analogy to resolve your doubts for my son. It is like a person inside a deep chamber.
Within a private chamber, when the fragrance of flowers comes from outside and a person smells it, they perceive it as if it were clearly visible before them;
yet the fragrance has no form or substance, nor does it encounter any obstruction—it is simply brought by the wind as a matter of nature.
The transference of consciousness into a womb is exactly like this; moreover, consciousness likewise has no form or substance and encounters no obstruction, being driven by the winds of karma.
The coming [of consciousness] is likewise spontaneous. It is just as when a person’s deluded thoughts encounter no obstruction whatsoever;
it is also like the events in a dream being identical to those in the waking state. Furthermore, dreams have no form or appearance and are not obstructed at all—they are entirely spontaneous.
The spirit-consciousness entering a womb is exactly like this: one must know that the womb and the belly are no different from a house, for the spirit-consciousness is the same in both.
Entering the womb is as natural as a person stepping into a house. Someone asked: "The house may be vast, but the womb is extremely small;
how can it contain the entire body? Wuyuan replied: "The spirit-consciousness is a numinous nature that is without form.
This numinous nature can be large and it can be small. When large, it is boundless; when small, it cannot be seen. Entering the womb, it does not consider [itself limited]."
That a small thing enters a house and does not become large is simply a natural principle; why must you harbor doubts about it?
Furthermore, you say that humans are born as humans and animals are born as animals, as if there were no matter of ascending and descending or revolving through rebirth.
If such a thing did exist, why would humans not be born as animals, and animals not be born as humans? Such ignorant words are the height of folly.
For example, it is as impossible for a man seeking an official post to obtain it by departing from the office of an official as it is for one to obtain it otherwise;

likewise, while the human form is a single entity, if one wishes to engage in the practices of the three teachings or the hundred schools, one must obtain them each through their respective categories—it is impossible to obtain them by departing from their categories.
It is also like the fact that consciousness is a single entity, which arises entirely through karmic conditioning.
Because they differ, their rebirths consequently vary: entering a human womb results in becoming human, while entering an animal womb results in becoming an animal.

How could one say that a human becomes an animal, or an animal becomes a human? It is like the nature of water, which is one and the same, yet receives its name from the various places where it falls.
Likewise, the nature of gold is one and the same, yet it is distinguished by the forms of the various vessels fashioned from it. Thus it is with the spirit.
The spirit’s ascent and descent, and its entrustment to a womb, are likewise so. Someone said: "The Master’s words are clear.

As for the various ways of receiving a womb, I have not been able to describe them all. The meaning of these two matters has been briefly explained as such. What was spoken regarding the formation of a body does not apply solely to those born from a womb;
there are also those born from eggs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation. Your reading of the Confucian [texts]...
If one has not yet fully understood the affairs of even a single realm of human relations, how could one possibly understand the affairs of the ten realms?

Someone asked: "What are the ten realms? The Master replied: "The Buddha-realm, the Bodhisattva-realm, the Pratyekabuddha-realm, the Śrāvaka-realm, the Deva-realm, the Human-realm, the Asura-realm, the Preta-realm, the Animal-realm, and the Hell-realm. These are collectively termed the Four Noble Beings and the Six Paths."

In total, these constitute the ten realms: if the consciousness performs the karma of a Buddha, one is born in the Buddha-realm; if it performs the karma of a Bodhisattva, one is born in the Bodhisattva-realm;
if it performs the karma of a Pratyekabuddha, one is born in the Pratyekabuddha-realm; if it performs the karma of a Śrāvaka, one is born in the Śrāvaka-realm;

if it performs the karma of a deva, one is born in the deva-realm; if it performs the karma of a human, one is born in the human-realm; if it performs the karma of an asura, one is born in the asura-realm; if it performs the karma of a preta...

Through karmic actions of ghosts one is born in the realm of hungry ghosts; through karmic actions of animals one is born in the realm of animals; and through karmic actions of hell-beings one is born in the realm of hell.
This is because the conscious spirit (vijñāna) has no fixed destination and undergoes retribution according to its karma. Does this not accord with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which says:
"If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: everything is created solely by the mind"? Is it not so?
However, if you wish to clarify the Great Principle, you must peruse the Tripitaka and investigate the fundamental nature; only then can you be called a person of broad learning and wisdom.
Be careful not to peer at the sky through a tube-like narrow vision and, in doing so, slander the Great Dharma of our school. Someone might say:
"Although I have read many books, I truly have not yet mastered this principle. Now that the Venerable Teacher has provided this instruction, it is like light entering a dark room."

Obtaining the lamp is like a pauper finding a treasure. One must say: by no means should you cling to petty knowledge or narrow views, for this will mislead you regarding the great matter of birth and death.
You must further cultivate pure karma and vow to escape the wheel of suffering. As the former masters said: "The world has talented men, yet their writings are arrogant and excessive—how pitiable!
Failing to encounter the teaching of the Empty King (the Buddha), how many have in vain betrayed their own intelligence? When the mind finally arrives [at truth], it is already too late.
"Even at the very bottom of birth and death, one cannot strike through it thoroughly"—truly profound are these words! Alas! I shall once again cite cause and effect to urge you to turn back.
In the past, there was a monk named Mingchen who was proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning;

he could paint snakes with the "Constant Mountain Snake" posture and compose a "Treatise on Snakes," such that his living body transformed into a snake. Li Bashi painted horses with the "rolling-and-stumbling horse" posture, making them appear so vividly alive.

The manifestation of the horse’s form and these two events clearly demonstrate that those who practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection) will certainly attain Buddhahood, and those who seek birth in the Pure Land will certainly be born there.
Why, then, do you not take *nienfo* as your core practice and seek birth in the Pure Land? Someone replied: "I shall respectfully obey my teacher's command;
I must now perform the rites of cultivation and prostration with earnest devotion. Having offered his thanks, he withdrew.
Clarifying Emperor Wu of Liang’s Fixed Karma. Commentary by Chancellor Zhang Shangying. 51. Someone asked:
"Emperor Wu of Liang devoted his entire life to Buddhism; why did he ultimately cause the ruin of his nation and the loss of his own life?
Wujin replied: "Those who do not understand fixed karma are truly to be pitied. In the past, Master Guì of Mount Song said that the Buddha has three [kinds of karma]..."

The Buddha can [know] the three capacities but cannot [know] the three incapacities; he can empty all marks and achieve the wisdom of the myriad dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma;
he can know the nature of all beings and exhaust the events of billions of kalpas, yet he cannot transform and guide those for whom there is no karmic affinity;
he can deliver all sentient beings, yet he cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings—this is called the "three capacities and three incapacities."

Now, as for those whose hearts are filled with resentment and whose mouths are stifled with indignation—those who hear of the Buddha as if he were an enemy and see the Sangha as if they were venomous snakes—I am truly helpless against them.
Furthermore, if even the Buddha could not convert or guide those with whom he lacked the karmic affinity, what can I possibly do for such people?
Those who argue that Emperor Wu of Liang perished because he served the Buddha have clearly failed to investigate the principles of Buddhism; their judgment is insufficient.
Regarding these deliberations on the length of dynasties and the order or chaos of successive reigns, I do not know how such things come to be.
Yao and Shun were great sages, yet their states lasted for only a single person; they abdicated their thrones because their sons were unworthy, and it was only after that they passed them on.
Was the unworthiness of those sons perhaps a punishment from Heaven? From the beginning of creation until the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty...
Previously, before the Buddha-dharma had reached this land, why did the state encounter such calamities?

Zhang Yan of the Tang dynasty recorded that the four masters of the Liang dynasty were able to know the transformations of heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits as clearly as looking at the palm of their hand;
furthermore, Prince Zhaoming was himself among the ranks of sages. Moreover, the sage is one who governs the state and the world.

This is merely a fragment; how could he have lacked the clarity of one who has attained prior awakening, such that he would not have carefully selected matters fit for practice to report to Emperor Wu?
It is simply that fixed karma cannot be escaped. Alas! That fixed karma cannot be altered is like water and fire which cannot be entered;
the arrival of its retribution is as unfailing as the succession of the four seasons, as it was in the Western Land.
Even the Venerable Śāriputra and the Second Patriarch of this land could not escape [the consequences of their karma]; how much less could they truly be the Lion or the Second Patriarch?
If even Śākyamuni Tathāgata could not avoid the retribution of the golden needles and the horse-barley, what need is there to mention ordinary beginners?
For that which is called "cultivation" consists of reforming the past and cultivating the future; once past karma has already returned, then as for the future...
How could such goodness abandon me? Now, those who possess female forms are indeed inferior to men; yet can one suddenly desire to serve the Buddha and immediately transform into a male?
Must one exhaust this present retribution-body, leaving the power of aspiration to depend upon a future life?
Emperor Wu of Liang lived to the advanced age of eighty-six, which was no small measure, yet he reached this very point before his death.
It was not that he fell into great evil, but merely that he erred in discarding his body.

Because he had previously perceived omens of calamity and obtained the divination of the *Qian* hexagram with its transformation at the topmost line (*jiu*), he took its meaning—that one is noble yet without rank, high yet without subjects—and used this to humble himself, seeking thereby to avert disaster and summon blessings.
This was merely the personal error of Emperor Wu of Liang; what fault could there be in the Buddha? Emperor Wu possessed the spiritual capacity of a follower of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
To single-mindedly believe in the fruits of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is precisely why one does not encounter the Great Dharma of Bodhidharma.
Is it not also the force of fixed karma that causes those who over-rely on superficial traces and cling to a "middle way" devoid of skillful means?

However, when the Sages first established the Dharma, it was fundamentally for the sake of all people of the world and future generations; how could it have been devised for a single individual? Confucius said, "The benevolent person lives long," yet [he] exerted...
If one praises Yan Hui for his benevolence (*ren*) yet Hui died young, is it that the words of Confucius lack verification?
It is likely that [Confucius] was not speaking of a single individual alone. Emperor Wu of Liang’s devotion to Buddhism was similar to Yan Hui’s practice of benevolence.
When the troops of Hou Jing arrived, he gathered śramaṇas to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; yet they were overly attached to the literal traces [of the text].
They were unable to employ expedient means or adapt to changing circumstances. This was much like the case of Xiang Xu during the Later Han dynasty when Zhang Jue incited a rebellion;

Xu submitted many "memorials on what is expedient" (*bianyi*) that contained frequent satirical criticisms. His subordinates did not wish for the state to mobilize troops, but instead merely followed him as he led his army to the banks of the Yellow River to face north and recite the *Classic of Filial Piety*, believing that the rebels would thus naturally be extinguished.
It is also similar to the account of Gai Xun in the *Book of the Later Han* during the Zhongping era.
In the first year [of the era], the Qiang and Hu tribes of Beidi, along with Bian Zhang and others, incited rebellion and plundered Longyou and Fufeng.

Song Xiao, serving as the local magistrate, was plagued by frequent uprisings and defections. He said to Xun, "Liangzhou lacks a scholarly tradition, which is why rebellions and atrocities have occurred so frequently.

I now wish to transcribe many copies of the *Classic of Filial Piety* so that every household may study it; perhaps this will cause people to understand righteousness. This is also a means of employing it."

Is this not unwholesome? Could it be the fault of the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety)? Furthermore, how could one know that the predestined karma of Emperor Liang would result in calamities no greater than these?
It was precisely because he practiced goodness that he was able to reduce his lifespan to such an extent.
The Emperor once asked Master Zhi about the survival or ruin, and the duration or brevity, of the state; the Master pointed to his own throat to indicate [the answer], thereby manifesting a prophecy.

When the Master was on the verge of death, Emperor Wu again questioned him about past events. Zhigong said, "If my humble monk’s stupa collapses, Your Majesty’s state and altars will follow in collapse.
After the Master passed away, the construction of the stupa was completed by imperial decree.
Suddenly, Emperor Wu thought to himself, "How can a wooden stupa endure for long? He then ordered it demolished and rebuilt as a stone stupa, seeking immortality through its permanence.
In accordance with his prediction, as soon as the opening of the stupa was completed, Hou Jing’s troops had already arrived. How could those who have attained the Way not have foreknowledge?

As for those such as An Shigao and Bo Fazang, they came from afar, traveling thousands of *li*, to cast themselves into places of death in order to settle their karmic retributions from previous lives;
this is because fixed karma cannot be escaped. It was the same with Guo Pu of the Jin dynasty.
If one knows that escape is impossible, how much more so for one who has discerned through wisdom the illusory nature of existence and views death as returning home?
How could there be anyone who, knowing clearly they owe a debt from the past, would wish to cause them to evade or reject it in order to seek a mere temporary escape?
Distinguishing Between the Eastern and Western Regions:
52. A visitor asked Master Miaoming: "Buddhism is the teaching of the barbarians; it is not fitting for our Middle Kingdom to model itself after it.
Confucius said, "The fact that the barbarians have a ruler is not as good as the fact that the various states of China are without one. Mencius said, "I..."
"I have heard of using the Chinese to transform the barbarians, but I have never heard of being transformed by the barbarians.

Furthermore, you previously studied the laws of the Two Emperors and Three Kings and practiced the Six Classics and the various philosophical treatises; to now abandon them and instead study the language of the Western Regions—is this not pitiable?
Miaoming replied, "In the past, before I had seen the subtle and profound principles of the Great Sage, I too..."
I have previously expressed this view, which does not differ greatly from what you have observed; yet now it is otherwise.

It seems you know only the outward splendor of ritual and music while remaining blind to the reality of the Way and its Virtue; you have glimpsed the light of a torch but have not beheld the brilliance of the sun and moon.
What Confucius spoke of was his concern for the age when the superior man neglected the rites, and what Mencius censured was Chen Xiang’s dogmatic adherence to a single teacher.
The intention of the farmer has its own underlying principle, yet it is not absolute:

Shun was born among the Eastern Yi, King Wen was born among the Western Yi, Great Yu was born among the Shidian, Sima Riji emerged from the Fan, Yuan You emerged from the Rong, and Ji Zha emerged from the Man.
Since these three sages and three worthies were all born among the barbarians, how can one claim that those from the barbarian regions cannot serve as models?
Furthermore, Taikang and King You of Zhou were rulers who were dissolute; Shi Le of Zhao and Ying of Qin were rulers who were tyrannical;
Zhao Gao and Li Si were ministers who were sycophantic; and Hou Jing and Yuwen [Taji] were ministers who were rebellious.
These four rulers and four ministers were all born within the Central Xia; how could one take them as models simply because they were from the Central Xia? Formerly, Confucius...

"You wish to dwell among the nine tribes of the Eastern barbarians. Someone said, "They are crude; what will you do? The Master replied, "When a gentleman dwells there, how can it be considered crude?

Now, if this is so, then sages and worthies are not constrained by the distinction between the 'barbarian' and the 'Chinese'; rather, it is people themselves who create the distinction between the barbarian and the Chinese.

Furthermore, consider the North Star: it is in the center of the heavens, yet it lies to the north of Qi. Judging from this, one sees that the lands of Qi, Lu, Han, and Wei [are merely relative positions].
It is not necessarily the center; if this is taken as the center, then that must be taken as the Western Rong, and that must be taken as the Eastern Yi—so who then can claim to be the center?

From the high heavens above to the vast earth below, with its wide mountains and rivers and many realms, it cannot be recorded even by billions; how, then, can one know for certain that this particular place is the center?
Is that [world] a mere borderland? The Buddha regards a world-system of ten billion suns and moons as being like a single mustard seed;
how much more so a small world-system of a single sun and moon! As the saying goes: "Having heard much, choose what is good and follow it.
It is for this reason that I honor its greatness and study it; it is like a single drop of the great ocean, which contains the flavor of all rivers—the Way that transcends the world.
If one understands this, then the Way of the world can be attained without toil.
Having clearly distinguished the classics of the Three Teachings, the five or three guests again asked Miaoming:
"The ultimate treasure is radiant yet not ostentatious; the ultimate expression is sincere yet not ornate; its words are concise."

Those who arrive at the truth have few embellished matters, while those who penetrate it possess clarity; thus, pearls and jade are rare and precious, whereas tiles and pebbles are abundant and cheap.
The sages composed the Six Classics in no more than several tens of thousands of words, and Laozi’s discourse on the *Daodejing* does not exceed five thousand words.
Yet today we see Buddhist scriptures numbering in the tens of thousands of fascicles and billions of words; this could certainly not be the work of a single person.
What one is capable of accomplishing through effort is often merely voluminous yet unnecessary. Miaoming said:
"Mouzi stated that the difference between the rivers and seas and the water in ruts is one of depth and breadth; the distinction between Mount Tai and the low hills is one of height and magnitude.
If its depth were no different from that of the water in ruts, even a young child could bathe in its abyss; if its height did not exceed that of the low hills, even a lame sheep could climb it."
The wings that touch the heavens do not rest upon stalks of reeds; fish that swallow boats do not dwell in mountain brooks and ponds.
To seek the pearl of the bright moon from within the belly of a clam or to seek the eggs of the phoenix from within a thicket of brambles—why would these be difficult to obtain?
It is because the small cannot contain the great, and the great does not reside in the small.
Therefore, a cauldron of ten thousand *hu* cannot be filled with water from a basin; a bell of one *jun* cannot be contained within flowing springs;
how could a tree of a man’s embrace be suitable for a thatched hut? How could a thorn bush of a few feet bear the weight of a vast summit?

Thus, vessels have their breadth and narrowness, capacities have their greatness and smallness, materials have their superiority and inferiority, and things have their lightness and heaviness—such is the nature of virtue.

There are degrees of thickness and thinness in the Way, depths and shallowness in the Dharma, expedient and ultimate truths, and capacities of great and small; yet the distinctions of their respective positions have never been at variance.
Furthermore, as for the Buddha’s scriptures: what was previously taught concerns events of billions of kalpas, while what follows sets forth the essentials for ten thousand generations.
As for the period before the beginning when nothing had yet sprouted, and the moment the two polarities first took form—their distance is such that it cannot be fathomed.
Matters beyond record, the minute that cannot be grasped, and the subtle that cannot be entered—Buddha has fully encompassed them within the vast and wide, and analyzed their profound depths.

From the highest heavens where there is no limit above, to the thickest earth where there is no limit below, there is nothing he does not manifest herein, as clearly as pointing to one's own palm. Since what he illuminates is so extensive, his writings...
Why should one consider ten thousand words in myriad scrolls to be excessive? Even a hundred million would not suffice to be called much; how could there be anything that is not essential?
How could it be that one only considers something attained when it is within the capacity of a single person’s strength?

It is like a thirsty person drinking from the ocean: once satiated, they know nothing of what remains. Nowadays, people engage in superficial learning, biasedly seeking to exclude Buddhism and cease reading its texts.
Having read dozens of scrolls, his mind was filled with indignation, and he suddenly made the refutation of Buddhism his urgent task.

Alas! For people of the world to strive so hard to refute the Buddha’s teachings is like trying to block out the sunlight with a single palm or to dam a vast flood with a single stone—is their effort not truly laborious?
Discerning and Clarifying the Ultimate Way of the Three Teachings: V.

Thus have I heard. It is because all Buddhas enter the mountains to cultivate the Way, realize the fruit, and deliver sentient beings for the sake of this one great cause (ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya) that later students must emulate the deeds of those who first awakened; only then can they clarify this one great cause.
He was also dwelling in deep seclusion in the mountains, contemplating this matter, when a guest arrived and asked, "Master, for what purpose do you reside here?
Wuyuan replied, "I am studying the Way of the Buddha. The guest asked, "May I hear the principles of the Buddhist Way?
He said, "Ask whatever you wish, and I shall answer you immediately. The guest said, "The teachings of the two schools, Śākya and Dao, are fundamentally—"
"How does a heterodox teacher learn this? [The Master] said, "Sir, why do you utter such words?

The guest replied, "Is not the Daoist 'emptiness and non-being' and the Buddhist 'quiescent extinction' heterodox teachings? I smiled and asked him in return, "Have you ever read the books on emptiness and non-being, or quiescent extinction?
The guest said, "The teachings of these heterodox schools are not worth looking at. I said, "As for them..."
If one has not yet been able to read the books, how could they recognize the way of heterodox teachings? It is not that these teachings are heterodox;
rather, it is the benevolent person who clings to them as heterodox. If a benevolent person were to know Confucius, they would understand Buddha and Laozi;
because they do not know Confucius, they instead slander Buddha and Laozi. Have you not heard Zhang Wujin say: "Only after I studied Buddhism was I able to [understand]?"
"Knowing that these words of yours are truly most appropriate," the guest bowed and asked again, "May I hear about the ultimate Way of the Three Teachings?
He replied, "One may hear what is worth hearing, but one must only fear being unable to practice it.
If one can practice and maintain it, one can become Confucius, one can become Laozi, and one can become a Buddha. If one hears but does not believe, or believes but does not..."
"Practice is like painting a cake—it does not satisfy hunger. The guest said, "If you, Master, now explain it to me, I shall practice it.
Wuyuan said, "The ultimate Way of the Three Teachings is simply the One Mind. This mind is the source of humanity. Buddhism says the mind is the king of dharmas;
Daoism says the mind is the lord of the multitudes; Confucianism says the mind is the ruler of man. All things [are governed by it]."
"All dharmas do not transcend the mind. When the king is unmoving, the myriad subjects are naturally at ease; when the mind is not disturbed, all evils do not arise. This is what is meant by:
"When the mind has a master, it can remain unmoving. The Buddhist says: "The Dharma-gate of the mind-ground does not reside in verbal eloquence. The Daoist says:
"Exert effort in the ground of the mind and completely cast aside worldly affairs. The Confucian says: "Speaking is not as good as practicing; practice is better than speaking."

It is better to reach that which is essential, to exhaustively arrive at the ultimate reality, and to finally reach this source. Having realized the definitive meaning, one returns to the fundamental principle and follows the flow to respond to conditions.

Thus, Confucius took "tranquil non-action" as the essence (*tǐ*) and "responding and thereby penetrating all things" as the function (*yòng*); the Buddha took "concentration" (*samādhi*) as the essence and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) as the function;
and Laozi took "emptiness and non-being" as the essence and "wondrous being" as the function—all of which share this same intent.
Alas! It is not only that scholars of the present day fail to perceive the Way of the Master or understand his heart;
even during the Master’s own time, Yan Hui—renowned within the Gate of Sages as one who embodied him in full—exhausted his entire life's strength yet could only say:
"Looking for him, he was ahead; turning away, he was behind; it seemed as if there were something standing tall and distinct before me," yet in the end, he could never grasp it.
The Sage clearly opened up [the truth] with eight characters, saying to his disciples: "Do you, my disciples, think that I have hidden anything from you?
I have not hidden anything from you. Judging by this, the Sage never once avoided his disciples; rather, it was the disciples themselves who missed the mark.
This is also like the Buddha’s preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, which says: "This sūtra reveals the provisional means."
The gateway reveals the true mark; this treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is profound, firm, and remote, such that no one can reach it.
Why is this? Because this Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination;
it is something that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know, and even all great bodhisattvas cannot know. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom it.
Alas! Even the sages and saints of the Three Vehicles cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom; how much less can ordinary beings?
For an ordinary mind to seek to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with the light of a firefly—it has no connection whatsoever and serves only to exhaust one's spirit.
One does not realize that the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space, manifesting forms in response to things just as water reflects them.

When the moon within is expansive, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; when narrow, even a tiny mustard seed finds no place to enter. When employed, ten thousand phenomena manifest in their entirety;

when set aside, not a single speck of dust remains. It is such that empty space is pulverized and the great earth sinks away, leaving demons and heretics with chilled hearts and gods and humans with cowed spirits.
How could such a supreme Way be measured by words or language? Is it not so?
The meaning of seeing the *Avataṃsaka* is that the Dharma-realm is so vast that even the great void cannot serve as a metaphor for its measure;
the wondrousness of the One Truth is such that the thousand sages cannot equal its merit. This very function is detached from this very function:

suddenly manifesting the majesty of a tiger pouncing, whether the head comes from the light or from the dark, it possesses the fierce power of an iron ox. It casts the great trichiliocosm beyond the eight directions.
Neither correct nor biased, it accommodates Mount Sumeru within a single mustard seed without constraint or narrowness; if one calls this emptiness, the absolute truth is fully revealed;

if one calls this existence, not even a trace remains. The Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom its boundaries, and Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) have yet to comprehend its perfect fusion.
Only those of the highest faculties and sharpest capacities can realize it through sudden awakening.

If those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), who possess but small vessels, must further cultivate through many kalpas and many births for even a single moment or a single hour, how could such a matter be fathomed by the shallow views of the ignorant?
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Whoever sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, this person treads upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. It further states: "There is no dharma that can be taught; this is called..."
Regarding the teaching of the Dharma, it is said: "How does one expound it for others? Without grasping at appearances, remaining unmoving in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*).
As for the Way, it is said that it cannot be seen by looking nor heard by listening; being free from all extremes is called the 'Sublime Way.

Furthermore, it is said that the Way is difficult to explain and must be realized through self-awakening; while the Dharma may be transmitted, the Way cannot. Confucianism says: "In seeing, the eyes are not used; in hearing, the ears are not used."

When the ears are detached from the function of the eyes, one naturally attains their true nature. It is further said that the Way is fundamentally without words; when words arise, the principle is lost.

To attempt to transform the people through sounds and forms is merely to dwell on the superficial. A deep investigation of the ultimate Way of the Three Teachings reveals that it does not reside in the transmission of written texts.
Zhuangzi said: "If the Way could be transmitted, there would be no one who would not pass it down to their descendants."
Regarding that which the Way can be presented to others, there is no one who does not present it;

yet as for that which cannot be transmitted or presented, it is for no other reason than that within there is no presiding subject and without there is no evidence of it. It is further said: "The Master had long desired to see Wen Bo Xuezi.
When he finally met him, he remained silent and uttered not a single word. Upon leaving, Zi Lu was astonished and asked, 'The Master had long desired to see Wen Bo.'"
"Xuezi has been here for a long time; why has he not said a single word?
Confucius replied, "This man perceives the Way through direct observation; it cannot be contained within words or sounds.

You must know that the Master’s Way truly transcends language and is unlike the people of the present age, who merely labor over literary texts without cultivating moral virtue, and who seek only human honors rather than [the Way]."
Regarding the cultivation of the rank of Heaven (*tiānjué*), the *Lúnyǔ* states: "What does Heaven say? The four seasons proceed, and the hundred things are produced;

what does Heaven say? It further states: "The patterns and literature (*wénzhāng*) of the Master may be heard, but his discourse on human nature (*xìng*) and the Way of Heaven (*tiāndào*) cannot be heard.
And it also states: "Virtuous conduct (*déxíng*) is the root; literary arts (*wényì*) are the branches."
Zhouzi’s *Tongshu* states: "Those who do not prioritize the Way and Virtue but take proficiency in literary composition as their ability possess merely the arts.
In ancient times, while Duke Huan of Qi was reading books in his hall, a wheelwright informed him, saying, "What Your Lordship reads are but the dregs of the ancients;
they lack the flavor of true essence. This is also like the case of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West.

Establishing the teaching of written words and the separate transmission outside the scriptures, pointing directly at the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha—how can this be constrained by mere letters and language?
The sages of the three ancient teachings were originally without speech and without explanation;
it was only because later generations lost their true wisdom that they were compelled to open a gateway for them. Alas, later people...
"Whose fault is this practice? Master Fuyan Yuan said, "A student must not be mired in words and language.
For words and language lead one to rely on others for understanding; they obstruct the gate of self-awakening and prevent one from transcending the realm of speech and symbols.
In the past, Daguan Ying first encountered Master Shimen Cong in his quarters, where [the master] galloped about with his tongue and mouth."
Bian Cong said: "What you have been discussing is merely talk on paper; it does not yet reach the ultimate profundity. One must employ true investigation and actual realization.
Once realized, one stands transcendentally and preeminently, neither riding upon words nor being obstructed by phrases—like a lion king’s roar that strikes terror into all beasts.
When viewed against this, the study of mere texts is not even comparable to a ratio of ten to a hundred, or a thousand to ten thousand."
Furthermore, O virtuous ones, since the source of the Way is not distant and the ocean of nature is not remote, you should seek it within yourselves and not look for it elsewhere;
if you seek it, you will not find it, and even if found, it is not real. It is the person who can propagate the Way, not the Way that propagates the person. As the *I Ching* says:
"The common people use it daily yet do not know it"—this is truly a matter for deep lamentation. Alas! If one does not realize this in this life, one will enter the cycle of rebirth forever.
If one could hear [the Way] upon returning from court, even to die that evening would be acceptable. Confucius said:

"Those who wish to study the Ultimate Way must sever thoughts before they sprout and govern the mind before it arises. Nothing is more evident than what is hidden; nothing is more manifest than what is subtle.

What is called "sincerizing one's intention" means not to deceive oneself. Laozi said: "Those who wish to attain the Ultimate Way must distance themselves from seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, and forget them all."
When the mind forgets objects, it must directly forget that very forgetting; when there is nothing left to forget, this is true forgetting. The Buddha said:
"To enter the ultimate Way, one must depart from effort, cessation, spontaneity, and extinction. If one speaks of having awareness, one has not yet departed from illusion.

To depart from illusion and further depart from that departure—this is the oneness of three and the threeness of one; all are this Way. The Confucian says: "Do not harbor preconceived intentions; do not be compulsive."
"Do not be stubborn, do not be self-centered. The Way is said to be without marks, without names, without capacity, and without location.
The commentary states: "Without self, without others, without hatred, and without love. Therefore, the sages of the Three Teachings all do not transcend this principle.
Confucius said, "What knowledge do I have? I have no knowledge. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says, "To establish knowing and seeing as a form of knowing is itself ignorance (*avidyā*)."
Fundamental gnosis sees that there is no seeing; this is precisely nirvana. As the Prajñā-gāthā says: "Prajñā has no knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know;
Prajñā has no seeing, yet there is nothing it does not see. Śūnyatā-born spoke by means of non-speaking, and Śakra heard by means of non-hearing;
this is the wondrous path of true prajñā. Lèizi says: "Therefore, the sage’s achievement..."
The Second Part on Ritual Demeanor: Though one’s benevolence may exceed that of the sun and moon, if one lacks benevolence, one remains perpetually obscured;

though one’s illumination may surpass the sun and moon, if one lacks benevolence, one remains perpetually obscured. One who is not benevolent bestows grace without expecting a reward; one who is perpetually obscured illuminates without a deliberate mind. To govern through non-action is likewise so.

Confucius taught people to clarify their own virtue (*ming ming de*), to transform the people (*xin xin min*), and to abide in ultimate goodness (*zhi yu zhi shan*). One can apply this principle in practice.

One who can act in accordance with this may be considered a Confucius. Laozi taught people to enter through sincerity, to maintain themselves through silence, and to employ themselves through flexibility;
one who can extend these principles into practice may be considered a Laozi. The Buddha taught people the way of extensively practicing the path of compassion and the power of vows:
Great Loving-kindness (maitrī) bestows happiness upon all sentient beings, while Great Compassion (karuṇā) uproots their suffering.
The great vow regarding the suffering of all sentient beings is the wish for them to attain perfect enlightenment.
The great power is the ability to deliver sentient beings across the three realms. If one can act by inferring this principle, one may become a Buddha.
Now, the Ultimate Way is like the autumn moon flowing through the sky, or like leisurely clouds emerging from mountain caves—vivid, lively, and perfectly round.
The *tá-tá* light shines brilliantly—mysterious beyond mystery, wondrous beyond wonder! I shall now briefly explain the ultimate Way of the Three Teachings for you to know;
were one to discourse upon these subtle principles, they could not be exhausted even in an entire kalpa. Alas! The Sage has already expended his compassionate wisdom in vain;
his voice does not need to be raised again and again. I exhort you, O benevolent ones, to together give rise to the Buddha-mind.

"May we together cultivate the Buddha-way, be born together in the Buddha-land, and together attain the fruit of Buddhahood. The guest bowed his head and withdrew, expressing his gratitude and saying, "I accept this with faith and shall practice accordingly.
*Discourse on Distinguishing the Superiority and Inferiority of the Three Teachings and Exhorting Cultivation of the Pure Land*, Part Five, Section Five.

Someone asked: "Are there similarities or differences among the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism? Is one superior to another? Wuyuan replied: "They are both the same and not the same;
they are both superior and not superior. The questioner asked: "What do you mean by this, Master? He replied: "For those of great capacity, when they employ them, they are the same and thus superior.
For those of limited faculties, when they cling to them, they are different and thus inferior. In all cases, it is based upon the single nature."
The arising of function is merely a matter of differences in capacity and insight, which may be similar or different, superior or inferior. Someone asked:
"May I hear the principle regarding these similarities, differences, and degrees of superiority? He replied: "When Zhang Wujin asked Chan Master Dahui, 'Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang were all sages;
why did the Buddha not mention them at all? The Master said: 'Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang are comparable to the Brahma King.'"
The Emperor asked, "Is there a difference in rank between Śakra and others? Wujin replied, "How could Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, or even the Brahmā King and Śakra be compared?
They are far, indeed, far apart. The Master said, "The Buddha regards even Brahmā and Śakra as ordinary worldlings; everything else can be understood from this.
The Duke then struck his hand against the armrest in admiration and sighed, saying, "Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang fall far short of Brahmā and Śakra! The Buddha [regards] Brahmā..."

The commentary states that it was only when ordinary people first came to know that the Buddha is the Sage among sages, the God among gods, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, and the Truly Perfectly Awakened One.
Formerly, Sun Quan, the Ruler of Wu, asked Kan Ze, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat:
"Can Confucius and Laozi be compared with the Buddha? Kan Ze replied: "If one were to compare the teachings of Confucius and Laozi with those of the Buddha..."

The distance between the Dharma is vast indeed. Why is this so? Confucius and Laozi established their teachings by taking Heaven as their model and formulated their applications by adhering to its laws, not daring to contravene Heaven.

The Buddha, however, established his teachings such that all the devas receive and uphold them, not daring to contravene the Buddha. Judging from this, it is clearly evident that [the two traditions] are not comparable.
Have you not seen what the Book of Documents says: "The scholar aspires to the worthy; the worthy aspires to the sage; the sage aspires to Heaven"? Within Heaven, there is nothing higher.

"Your Reverence, the Jade Emperor is not inferior [to the Buddha]; yet the Jade Emperor is comparable to an Arhat, while officials are comparable to Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduates)—how much more so the Buddha?
The Buddha is the teacher of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; he is the Holy Teacher. He asked again, "How does the Way of the Immortals compare to the Way of the Buddha?
The answer was, "Even the gods and immortals still remain under the jurisdiction of the Jade Emperor; how could they be compared to the Buddha? How much less so the immortals themselves?"
The Way is difficult to cultivate and there are days when one falls away; the Buddha-way is easy to learn and there is never a time of regression. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"There are ten kinds of immortals in the world, yet none have ever cultivated true awakening; when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back into the various realms of existence.
If one wishes to transcend birth and death and surpass both ordinary beings and sages, only the Buddha-way will suffice. In the past, Śākyamuni praised Puṣya.
The Buddha said: "In the heavens above and the earth below, there is no one like the Buddha; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer.
Of all that exists in the world, I have seen it all, and among them, none is equal to the Buddha.

Furthermore, the *Liezi* records that when Grand Chancellor Shang questioned Confucius, saying, "Master, are you a sage? Confucius replied, "I, Qiu, am merely one who has studied extensively and possesses much knowledge."
"How could I dare to say that? Were the Three Kings sages? He replied, "The Three Kings merely relied upon wisdom and valor;
as for their sagehood, I, Qiu, do not know it. "Were the Five Emperors sages? He replied, "The Five Emperors merely relied upon benevolence and righteousness;
as for their sagehood, I, Qiu, do not know it. "Were the Three Augusts of antiquity sages? He replied, "The Three Augusts of antiquity merely relied upon adapting to the times."
As for such a sage, I, Qiu, do not know him. The Grand Minister asked again, "In that case, who then is the sage?

Confucius moved his countenance and said, "To the west there is a Great Sage who does not govern yet is not in disorder; he does not speak yet is trusted; he does not transform others yet they act spontaneously.
Vast and boundless, the people are unable to give him a name. This is precisely what is called the myriad phenomena of the universe.
The elephant reaches its limit in the void; the myriad streams of the hundred rivers reach their limit in the sea; all worthy sages reach their limit in the Buddha;
and all teachings reach their limit in the mind. This mind is the wondrous root of all dhāraṇīs and the vast source of all phenomena;
it is also called the Great Treasury of Wisdom, Non-abiding Nirvāṇa, and by hundreds of thousands of myriads of names—all are but this mind.
These are merely different names for the same reality. Mencius said, "All people can become Yao or Shun"; Xunzi said, "The common person on the road can become Yu";
and the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging said, "I do not dare to disparage you;
you shall all become Buddhas. Thus, every person can become a sage or a worthy, and every person can become a Buddha. [In the] Western Pure Land...

The earth is the essential gateway; if there are no people at the door, one cannot cultivate [the Way]. It does not matter whether one is a monk or a layperson, provided one simply attends to the mind.
Fundamentally, there is neither male nor female—why then must one cling to appearances? Those who do not understand falsely divide the teachings into three;
those who have attained realization equally awaken to the One Mind. Now, the mind of the Sage is simply correct; the teaching of the Sage is simply good.
It is enough; one need not be a monk, nor need one be a Confucian; one need not rely on that, nor need one rely on this. "That" and "this" are matters of emotion (*qing*);
"monk" and "Confucian" are matters of outward trace (*ji*). The Sage establishes traces so as to preserve the fundamental; the Sage follows emotions so as to accord with nature (*xing*).

One who preserves the fundamental without being hindered by traces can be said to understand skillful means (*quan*); one who accords with nature without being submerged by emotions [can likewise be said to understand the Way].
This is because it accords with the reality of words. Now, the Great Way is what we call the Mind; to expound this Way is what we call Teaching.
Teaching is the manifestation of the traces left by the Sages; the Way is the fundamental source of all living beings.

Therefore, students should only turn their backs on the dust of the world and unite with awakening; they must not mistake the provisional for the real or become deluded regarding the Truth. O virtuous ones, Confucianism is not...
Since Confucianism and Daoism are not fixed paths, one knows that all can achieve Buddhahood;

it is not only the Three Teachings that can achieve it, but all the hundred schools and various masters as well. Why do people fail to practice? Why do they slight the Pure Land and refuse to be reborn there? Someone said:
"If one merely resolves the matter of one's own birth and death, why is it necessary to trouble oneself by exhorting others? I replied: "Not so."
Have you not heard that when the Tathāgata appears in the world, there is not a single dharma that does not benefit sentient beings?

When Bodhisattvas practice, they do not begrudge even a hair’s breadth of their effort for their own sake. If those within this Dharma-gate know this, it is as if they themselves have known it—how joyful!
If people do not know this, it is as if they themselves do not know it—how painful! The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is not at the request of sentient beings [that the Buddha speaks]."

"I have resolved my mind [on enlightenment] for myself and for the sake of all sentient beings, acting as an uninvited friend. As the saying goes: 'What one desires for oneself, one establishes in others;
what one desires to attain, one enables others to attain. To extend oneself to others is the heart of the benevolent person.
If one were to stop at self-cultivation alone, one would be a follower of the Śrāvakas, known as a practitioner of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), like a small vehicle that is capable only of—"
To merely save oneself is what the Buddha calls severing the seeds of Buddhahood. One who can widely exhort others is called a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva;
this is like a great vehicle, meaning that both self and others are saved together.

Because of this, one attains immeasurable rewards of merit, and thus is able to reach the stage of Buddhahood. All the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all join in [this praise].
The praise of Amitābha Buddha’s inconceivable merit means that it cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed in words;
such merit may be called ultimate. Thus, the verse of encouragement by the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrī says:
"If one can encourage two people to practice, it is more meritorious than one's own diligent practice; if one encourages ten or more people, the merit is already vast."
If one encourages even a hundred or a thousand people toward the infinite [Buddha], they are called true Bodhisattvas; furthermore, if one can exceed ten thousand in number, they are indeed Amitābha.
Judging from this, the teaching of the Western Paradise may spread throughout the world, and sentient beings in the ocean of suffering may all be reborn in the Pure Land.
If one sees even a single person falling into indolence, one should join forces to assist and uplift them, so that even one person may abandon the mundane state.
Thus, by taking care of one another, even if one cannot propagate the teachings to benefit all beings, one can still "warm the old and know the new.
Have you not seen that when one gives a person a single coin, people say they have received a benefit; yet when one benefits another with a single word, how could that person fail to recognize it?
Material giving relieves another's poverty; the gift of food relieves another's life; but the gift of the Dharma enables others to transcend the world—this is the supreme merit.

How can virtue be compared to material wealth? Material giving is like a lamp that illuminates only a small room; the gift of Dharma is like the sun that shines universally upon the great trichiliocosm.

To be stingy with the Dharma and fail to encourage others to practice leads to sinking into the black hells for kalpas on end. By taking oneself as the example to guide and transform others, one manifests in this life as Amitābha.
I dare hope that you will exercise compassion to exhort one another, and through these vows of pity, together bring this Pure Land to fruition.

By pulling those submerged in the stagnant current from their drowning and rescuing those with clouded minds from their lost nature, you cause them all to ascend together to the Land of Bliss and fully repay the Buddha’s kindness;
this may truly be called "enabling those who have not yet crossed over to cross over."
A Verse Clarifying the Chronology of the Manifestations of the Sages of the Three Teachings The *Sūtra on the Numerical Sequence of the Dharma of the Five, Six,
and Three Teachings* states:
"In the year Jia-yin of King Zhao of Zhou, the fourth sovereign, Śākyamuni descended and was born in Kapilavastu."
In the fifty-third year of King Mu’s reign, on the day of Renshen, the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty, one thousand eight hundred years ago.
The teaching reached the world of Emperor Ming of the Han during the Yongping era;
four hundred and twenty-two years prior to that, Laozi was born during the reign of King Ding.
The Buddha appeared four hundred and seventy-seven years prior; Confucius was born during the reign of King Ling.
As a retribution for his past existence as a young animal, he knew the nature of such beings. The tripod, though divided into three legs, returns to oneness.

(According to the *Fofa jintang bian*, the above text is corrected as follows: [This refers to] the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao, the son of King Kang, which was a Jia-yin year. While some say it was the ninth year, Jia-yin, others say it was the twenty-fourth year, Jia-yin.)

All of these are incorrect. [Regarding the statement that] King Mu was the son of King Zhao and that his fifty-third year was the *Ren-shen* year—those who claim it was his fifty-second year, the *Ren-shen* year, are likewise incorrect.
Discerning and Clarifying Essence, Vitality, and Spirit:
The *Direct Pointing to the Five and Seven Profound Principles* states: "Precepts nourish essence; meditative concentration nourishes vitality; wisdom nourishes spirit.

That which is called the One Source is Awakening, through which one recognizes the primal essence, primal vitality, and primal spirit. Those who are deluded mistakenly identify the essence, vitality, and spirit within the physical body as these."
What a great delusion! What a great error! Alas, how bitter! Do you not see what Zhang Ziyang said?

That essence, energy, and spirit are the primordial essence, primordial energy, and primordial spirit that existed prior to heaven and earth. The primordial essence is not the essence of lustful indulgence; the primordial energy is not the energy of inhalation and exhalation;
the primordial spirit is not the spirit of discursive thought. Fools who do not understand this meaning call a jar a "jar."

Since Zhongyan neither clarifies the principle nor attains realization, he merely deceives other pure-faith practitioners by constantly fabricating [artificialities] upon this stinking skin-bag, thereby obscuring the one true Buddha-nature.
Thus, they wander through the cycle of birth and death; to falsely claim that this is "cultivation" is truly pitiable.
As I am an unworthy son of the Buddha, how could I harbor such treasures while remaining lost in this land? I must now open [the truth].
"Manifesting the future entry together into the true path of Bodhi: 'Essence' (jing) is the primordial essence, which is the precept (śīla);
it is pure and without admixture, fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and white Brahma-conduct.

This is precisely the Pure Dharma-body (dharmakāya). The Pure Dharma-body is your very nature. 'Vitality' (qi) is the primordial vitality, which is meditative concentration (samādhi); it is tranquil and still."
The Immovable One, endowed with immeasurable and wondrous meanings, is precisely the Perfect Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
This Perfect Reward Body is none other than your own wisdom. The "Spirit" is the primordial spirit, which is wisdom;

it responds to stimuli and penetrates all, fully possessing wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—this is precisely the manifestation of the thousands of billions of Transformation Bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). These are the thousands of billions of Transformation Bodies.
This is precisely your own practice; it is also called the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Liberation;
it is also called Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom; it is also called the Three Jewels as a Single Essence.

Yet those who are deluded and perverse call the essence of lustful indulgence the Buddha Jewel, call the breath of respiration the Dharma Jewel, and call the spirit of discursive thought the Sangha Jewel.
These deluded followers deceive both others and themselves, bringing harm to both self and others; they not only mislead future generations but also slander the ancient sages.

I earnestly warn all people not to misinterpret the ancients; even a single misplaced character can cause one to fall into the state of a wild fox for five hundred kalpas—how could one possibly take the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and turn it into the poisonous medicine of Māra?
Can such sins be forgiven? These heterodox teachers will enter hell as swiftly as an arrow.
I exhort future students to take this to heart, to take it to heart! Cherish it, cherish it!
*A Discourse on Leaving Appearance to Reveal Nature and Attaining Birth in the Pure Land*, Part V, 8.
Someone asked, "Can women attain rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha's name? Yuan said, "What kind of talk is this?
If even parrots and mynas can attain rebirth through reciting the Buddha's name, how much more so for humans? The person asked again, "A woman’s body is subject to the ten evils;
how can she then attain rebirth? Yuan replied: "First, when she is born, her parents do not rejoice. Second, in raising and nursing her, they lack sufficient care and attention."

First, her three minds are constantly fearful of others; second, her parents worry about her marriage; third, she is separated from her parents; fourth, she fears her husband’s moods of joy and anger;

fifth, she suffers great difficulty in childbirth; sixth, in her youth she is constrained by her parents; seventh, in her middle age she is restricted by her husband; eighth, in her old age she is rebuked by her children and grandchildren;
from birth until death, she never attains autonomy. Furthermore, there are five obstacles, the first of which is:
One cannot become a Brahmā King, second, a Śakra Devendra, third, a Māra King, fourth, a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Sage King, or fifth, a Buddha-body.
How then can a female body quickly attain Buddhahood? The answer is: if one discusses it in terms of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the manifestation of results, such a thing exists;
however, if one speaks from the perspective of the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*), there is absolutely no such thing. At that time, the Dragon Girl was only eight years old, yet her wisdom—
If those of sharp faculties attain Buddhahood in a single instant, how could it depend on the characteristics of male or female, old or young?
Under the assembly of the Chan school, many women have realized the mind and seen their nature to become Buddhas and Patriarchs in this very life; how much more so regarding rebirth after death?
That you insistently cling to the female form as real is extreme ignorance of the principles of nature. It is a failure to understand the principles of nature.
Rather, it is women who understand the Essence-Teaching (xìngzōng). The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If there is a man who does not know that his own body possesses the Tathāgata-nature, although the world calls him a man, the Buddha says that such a person is a woman.
If there is a woman who can know that her own body possesses the Tathāgata-nature, although the world calls her..."
The Buddha taught that such women as these are actually men. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states:

"Regarding this body composed of the four elements, one perceives the marks of birth and death, male and female; yet the nature of spiritual awakening truly has no marks of birth, death, male, or female.
If you now awaken to this nature, it is called 'longevity,' it is also called the 'lifespan of the Tathāgata,' and it is also called the 'wondrousness of Nirvāṇa.'"
The *Mind* (Xin) further states: "All who possess mind shall without exception attain Buddhahood.

Since walking now is the walking of a Buddha and sitting now is the sitting of a Buddha, it is said that the environment and inhabitants of Avīci hell are entirely within the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage; the Dharma-body of all Buddhas does not depart from a single thought of an ordinary person at the lowest level.
Pei Xiu, the State Chancellor, said: "Among those belonging to the realm of blood and breath, there must be cognition; whatever possesses cognition [possesses the capacity for enlightenment]."
"Since they must be of the same essence, it is precisely as said: 'All sentient beings, down to the crawling insects, possess Buddha-nature; how much more so for women? Question:
If all crawling insects and sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why do they not become Buddhas, but instead remain in saṃsāra suffering? Answer:

"It is simply because at that time they were attached to appearances, deluded regarding their nature, turned their backs on awakening, and conformed to the dust of the senses, thereby creating all manner of evil karma. Now they have fallen [into this state]."

Setting aside for a moment the discussion of the various classes of beings who suffer and the wriggling creatures that possess spirit, even those who have now obtained this human body are unwilling to observe the precepts, recite the Buddha’s name, and seek rebirth in the Pure Land;
instead, you would teach these other classes of beings how to achieve Buddhahood? Someone might say:
"There are many spiritual friends who, upon seeing women observing the precepts and reciting the Buddha’s name, all wish for those women to transform their female bodies into male ones."
"What do you think of this teaching on cultivating the Way in future lives? One of the group replied:

"These so-called 'good spiritual friends' (kalyāṇamitra) have improperly assumed the title of 'spiritual friend' without having mastered the principle of spiritual friendship; they are truly deluded and ignorant. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
Śāriputra said to a celestial maiden, "Why do you not transform your female body? The goddess replied, "I have been thus for eleven years."
When one comes seeking the characteristics of a woman, they are ultimately unobtainable; how, then, could there be any transformation?
It is like a magician who conjures an illusory woman; if someone were to ask why she does not transform her female body, would that person be asking correctly?
Śāriputra replied, "No, for an illusion has no fixed characteristics; what, then, could there be to transform? The Devaputra said, "All dharmas are likewise thus."
"Since there is no fixed characteristic here, why do you ask how one does not transform out of a female body?
At that moment, the goddess used her supernormal powers to transform Śāriputra so that he appeared like herself, while she transformed herself into the likeness of Śāriputra.
She then asked, "Why do you not transform out of a female body? Śāriputra, appearing in the form of the goddess, replied, "I do not know now."
“How can this female body be transformed? The Deva said: “Śāriputra, if you could transform this female body, then all women would likewise be able to transform theirs.
Just as Śāriputra is not a woman yet manifests in a female body, so it is with all women;
though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women. Therefore, the Buddha has said that all [phenomena]...”
The Dharma is neither male nor female; immediately, the heavenly maiden withdrew her supernatural power, and Śāriputra’s body returned to its former state.
Since this is so, how could there be any signs of male or female within the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*)?

How much more so, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* specifically records that women are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—is this not indeed the case? Furthermore, the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth) contains accounts of women.
Those who have gone to the Western Paradise are beyond counting; why, then, do you not recognize them?
Although their bodies have left the household life, they do not seek the Pure Land.
As the Dharma Master Wutiyan said: "In recent times, there are certain monastics who, though claiming to have departed from the secular world, have not eliminated their worldly habits."
To claim that one has "exhausted all" while the conditions of the mundane world remain unsevered is, according to the scriptures, certainly not knowing;
yet, failing to practice *chan* and being unable to realize the mind, the monkey of the heart runs wild and the horse of the will gallops on, roaming in packs and brawling through the days.

Not only does this waste the offerings of the faithful, but it also buries one's own spiritual brilliance. When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, where will the path lead? This is precisely the case.

Under the blue sky and white sun, you do not recognize your father and mother; claiming what you have not realized as realized, and what you have not attained as attained, you truly enter the Gate of Emptiness in vain, living and dying in delusion.
Alas! I ask you, for what reason did you leave the household life? Was it for the sake of food and clothing? For the sake of wealth and honor?
Or for the sake of seeking peace and happiness? Your parents relinquished you to leave the household life, hoping that you would transcend [suffering] and deliver them, so as to repay their kindness.
The answer is: "Regarding the four debts of gratitude, you yourself currently have no one to rely upon; how then can you rescue others?

A day will come when the Old Man Yama settles your account for the cost of your meals—what will you have to oppose him with? You will surely fall into the hells or become hungry ghosts, wearing horns and shaggy fur.
Such a way of leaving home is pitiable and painful! O virtuous ones, take advantage of this [time] before it is too late."
Before old age and illness strike, you must urgently and early establish a means of salvation:
steadfastly observe the precepts and fasts, recite the Buddha’s name and the sutras, perform prostrations and praises, and make vows to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

Once you have attained the vision of Amitābha, you will be able to deliver your parents, repay the four debts of gratitude, rescue all sentient beings, and enjoy eternal happiness. Such is the way out.

Those on the side of the householders are disciples of the Buddha; alas, there is yet another class of those who have become monks and practitioners of the Way who teach others to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, yet speak only of their own lack of meritorious practice and failure to reach the necessary stage of cultivation.

They claim that one must first seek rebirth in a future life as a man again, leave the household life once more, and engage in successive stages of practice before being able to attain birth [in the Pure Land]. Such people are inferior, base, and foolish.
To be utterly deluded oneself is still tolerable, yet to further deceive others—I ask you now:
why do men who have left the household life not seek the Pure Land? What other birth are they waiting for? A former master said, "If one fails to attain birth in this life, it is a hundred failures;
if this body is not delivered in this present life, toward what other birth shall this body be delivered? How true these words are!
I say this, O virtuous ones: if you discuss the merit, practice, and effort required to attain Buddhahood, then wait for Maitreya’s descent and the appearance of the thousand Buddhas.
But if one speaks of the Dharma-gate of the nine grades and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, with a single thought of faith one can arrive there in the snap of a finger. Why?
Because one relies upon the power of the Buddha. This is not seen in the *Lianzong baojian*, which says that faith in other gates [is sufficient].
Studying the Way is like an ant climbing a high mountain; rebirth in the Pure Land is like a wind-blown sail sailing with the current.
Guided by Amitābha, one proceeds directly toward Bodhi; supported by the various sages, one transcends the Three Realms. Those of the highest grade ascend immediately to the fruit of Buddhahood;

even those of the lowest grade surpass the celestial palaces upon their descent. I pray that you all refrain from doubt and practice together without regression. Furthermore, do not fail to see the certainty [of this path].
The *Yilun* (Treatise on Doubts) asks: "Human birth is difficult to obtain, yet rebirth in the Pure Land is easy. Why is this?
If one does not uphold the five precepts, the path to the realms of humans and devas is cut off; only when the five precepts are pure can one become human.

How much more so, since the five precepts are difficult to maintain and one lacks the power of aspiration to sustain them—this is what is meant by 'human birth is difficult to obtain. Those who cultivate the Pure Land do not necessarily maintain the precepts in their entirety."
It is not necessary to practice all [the various methods]; it suffices merely to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Even if one possesses karmic offenses, they are permitted to be repented.
At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Sea, each with their respective vows, will together come to welcome and receive the practitioner.
This is what is meant by the "Ease of Birth in the Pure Land. The *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations* states: "Recite with a sincere mind..."
One utterance of "Namo Amitābha Buddha" extinguishes the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas;

from the highest level of single-minded non-distraction down to the successful completion of ten recitations, even those who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds can attain rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times at the moment of death—how much more so for those who have left the household life, observe the precepts, and practice mindfulness of the Buddha? Why would they not be reborn there?
Alas! This dharma-gate of such a swift path is simply that no one believes or accepts it;
if one does not believe, accept, and practice it, what benefit is there in leaving the household life?
Thus spoke Minister Pei, whose body and mind were full of hypocrisy. (60)

The Tang Prime Minister Pei Xiu said: "O Great Assembly, that which you have constantly taken for 'your body' since beginningless time is a body composed of the provisional union of earth, water, fire, and wind;
it gathers and disperses in an instant, belonging to the category of impermanent phenomena—it is not your true body.
O Great Assembly, that which you have constantly taken for 'your mind' since beginningless time is a mind of discursive thought, adventitious dust, and false delusion."
Arising and ceasing momentarily, these belong to the phenomena of impermanence; they are not my mind. I possess a true body that is perfect, empty, and quiescent—this is it.
I possess a true mind that is vast, numinous, and cognizant—this is it. This empty quiescence and numinous cognition have sovereign spiritual function;
its nature contains all virtues, while its essence is free from all negations. It is like the pure lunar disc, perfect and without defect, obscured only by clouds of delusion.
Obscured by delusions, one does not realize this for oneself; yet once these false confusions are removed, the true mind is revealed as fundamentally pure.
The minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings are indistinguishable from this mind of mine—this is the very essence of the Bodhicitta.

To abandon this and fail to recognize it, instead identifying with the foul body, is to follow along with delusive thoughts through death and rebirth, suffering alongside the various species of birds and beasts.
How could one who is a man not feel shame?
This is "The Discourse on Lust and Killing by the Layman of Longshu.
In the six desires—food, drink, sex, and human affairs—the great cravings of humanity reside. To restrain them as if they did not exist is to be a sage; to moderate them...
To refrain from indulgence makes one a worthy person; to indulge without restraint is the mark of the lowest ignorance. Indeed, both of these are what destroy one through the creation of karma.
To kill living beings merely to satisfy the palate—what is this but the commission of sin? To lose one’s true nature through lustful desire—how much more so is this the commission of sin?
Furthermore, these two reinforce each other: because of fine food and drink, the blood and vital energy flourish.
When blood and qi are abundant, lustful desire increases; when lustful desire increases, it conversely depletes the blood and qi.

When the blood and qi are depleted, one must again rely on food and drink for nourishment and restoration. These two thus create offenses for one another. If one wishes to reduce the consumption of food and drink, one must first regulate lustful desire.
If one can regulate lustful desire, one can then reduce the consumption of food and drink; this is the way to secure the person and prolong life.

If one can regulate and sever the pursuit of these [delicacies], then even coarse and simple food will naturally seem delicious. If one indulges in them, however, the lifespan allotted to human beings is finite;
