once that limit is exhausted, one meets an early end. As Master Cijue said: "Food and drink are for humans as long as the sun and moon endure;
whether refined or coarse, take what you have according to your lot. Once it has merely passed through the three-inch gullet to fill the wound of hunger, what is it then?"
Use your mind to carefully examine and measure: if you can reflect and contemplate in this way, you will naturally be able to restrain your appetite.

The Rustic Man Who Pursues Reality says: "Skin encases bone and flesh, along with pus and blood; yet one forcibly feigns coquettishness to deceive others. All heroes of the ages have fallen because of this;
for a hundred years we shall all become dust in a single pit. If you can reflect and contemplate in this way, you will naturally be able to restrain yourself.
Regarding lust and desire, if one truly understands these two, how could there be illness or premature death while alive, and how could there be rebirth in the hells or as an animal after death?
Those who cultivate the Pure Land must truly be diligent and cautious in observing the precepts regarding these matters.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching of Principle and Phenomena:

The sixty-two [types of beings] are all true Buddhas; they do not come from outside. All sentient beings each possess [this nature], yet due to wandering through delusion and being shrouded by the two obstacles, they are unable to realize it.
Therefore, Bodhisattvas cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices to realize the Great Perfection.

Awakening through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one illuminates the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) within the Path of the Vajra, thereby severing and exhausting the two obstacles—the afflictive (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
Within the Path of Liberation, the pure *dharmakāya* is manifested, much like using medicinal polish to buff a mirror.
Master Yongming Shou said: "The mind is the sovereign of the *dharmadhātu*; the mind is the foremost of all phenomena."
If one knows the mind, then one is able to know all dharmas. The *Great Abhiṣeka Sūtra* states:
"The bhikṣu who practices dhyāna has no other thoughts; he maintains only a single dharma and subsequently perceives the mind. Master Tóngjiāng Yīng said:
"The mind, the mind—by nature it is originally spontaneous, standing forth in solitary distinction, profoundly still, solitary and firm, the most wondrous within the wondrous, the profound mystery."
Furthermore, within this mystery there is neither coming nor going, neither change nor transition. Because its essence is luminous awareness, it gives rise to all conditions.

Like a mirror containing myriad images, like the ocean receiving a hundred rivers—it withdraws them so that the spirit remains latent within the square inch of the heart; it extends them so that its light fills the great chiliocosm. Its transformations are sovereign and its functions are boundless.
Thus it manifests as sentient beings or Buddhas, as the ultimate reality or as provisional means. To be deluded regarding this...

Vast and surging, it does not turn back; to awaken to this is to understand it clearly as it is transmitted. The commentary states: One Dharma is taken as the宗 (zong/principle), such that all dharmas have no place of reliance;
external conditions are spontaneously severed, and the wondrous nature is manifest. When the will is set upon returning to the One, why would wisdom not be clear?
Having traced the current to find its source, how could doubt remain unresolved? This essential principle is none other than the greatest. As the Book says: "Purity and Oneness."
The second is the cultivation of stillness alone. First one rectifies the body and mind, and subsequently one governs the family and the state.
As the Sūtra says: "Always rectify your mind and do not pursue other studies. Mencius said: "The way of learning and inquiry has no other purpose than to seek the mind that has been lost.
An ancient said: "To realize that the mind has wandered is itself the practice. One need not fear the arising of thoughts; one only fears that realization is slow. Realization must be swift.

One should know that the two sublime qualities of stillness (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are mutually appropriate; by recognizing what is not so and reforming one's errors, the countenance of Qie (Yan Hui) may be taken as a model.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The Buddha’s teaching takes the mind as its core; by subduing the mind, one achieves the Way, and all myriad practices are perfected.

One must never forget this principle that everything is but mind. Only then does one realize that when the ground is attained, all things are born; when the principle is attained, all practices are perfected. Prime Minister Pei said: "The mind is [the source of] the myriad..."
The totality of all phenomena is divided into the precepts, concentration, and wisdom; it unfolds into the six perfections and disperses into the myriad practices.

The myriad practices have never been separate from the one mind, and the one mind has never been at variance with the myriad practices. Therefore, it is said that the myriad practices manifest the True Principle (*zhenzong*).
The *Zongjing* says: "Principle and practice support one another; if either is lacking, it is insufficient. Although conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are artificial, if they are abandoned, then..."
The Buddha-way is difficult to accomplish; although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is true, if one clings to it, the nature of wisdom will not be luminous.

Therefore, Mañjuśrī uses principle to seal practice so that the path of differentiation remains without deficiency, while Samantabhadra uses practice to meet principle so that the gateway of the fundamental is not abandoned.
If one departs from phenomena to pursue principle, one falls into the folly of the Śrāvakas; if one leaves principle to engage in phenomena, one is no different from ordinary people.

One who holds to the principle that both affairs and the Way must be practiced together is a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva. It is further said: "If a person wishes to achieve Great Enlightenment, they must practice the Middle Way.
The Middle Way is neither partial nor biased. It is not partial toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*) nor biased toward existence (*bhava*).
It does not cling to existence, nor is it empty of non-existence (*abhāva*); this is what is called the Middle Way. Thus is the mind.
The prose-poem (*fu*) says: "If one wishes to reach the Pond of Clarity and Coolness (*Qīngliáng chí*), one must further rely upon eyes and feet.
The 'Pond of Clarity and Coolness' is the ocean of nature of the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle (*yīshèng*). Having eyes but no feet, one cannot reach the Pond of Clarity and Coolness.
What are the 'eyes'? They are the thorough investigation of principle (*lǐ*). What is 'principle'? It is the single mind (*yīxīn*). What are the 'feet'? They are the practice of its activities."
What is this "affair"? It is the myriad practices (*samskāra*). This is precisely what is meant by: "In the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is received;

in the gate of Buddha-activity (*buddhakārya*), not a single dharma is abandoned. Why is this so? One must know that the myriad dharmas are rooted in the one mind, and the one mind contains the myriad dharmas.
Dharmas are the dharmas of the complete mind, and the mind is the mind of the complete dharmas. Mind is itself dharma; dharma is itself mind.

This is precisely that the mind is the non-duality of essence and function, where principle and phenomena are manifested together; by practicing the three contemplations in their perfection, one enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
This is spoken for the gentleman. Section Six, Part Three.
Longshu said: "All people can become gentlemen, yet they are unwilling to do so; they need not become petty men, yet they insist on doing so.
If one practices sincerity, trustworthiness, and reverence; if one is gentle, warm, upright, and square; if one recommends the worthy and extols the good;
if one acts appropriately to benefit all things—all such matters as these are the affairs of a gentleman. To practice them is likewise [the way]."
If something is not difficult, why would people be unwilling to do it? Whether it be deception and arrogance, or coarseness and sycophancy;
whether it be slandering others' shortcomings and broadcasting their evils, or indulging one's whims to harm living beings—all such things as these are the deeds of petty men.
What benefit is there in doing them? Why would anyone necessarily do them? If one acts as a gentleman, people will rejoice and the spirits will grant their protection.

Calamities will not arise, blessings and prosperity can be sought, and what is gained will be much. Although there may be times when one loses their life, it is not because of being a gentleman that one loses it;
even if one were not a gentleman, one would still lose it, for destiny has its fixed allotment.
To act as a petty person is to provoke the resentment of men and the anger of the spirits; calamities will then arrive, and fortune and longevity will be shortened—this is what is lost.

It is many; though one may occasionally obtain it, this is due to destiny (*ming*). It is not because of a petty person that one obtains it, yet even if one does not become a petty person, one may still fail to obtain it.
This is because destiny has its fixed allotment. Confucius said, "One who does not know destiny cannot be a gentleman.

Being able to examine this principle is what is meant by being a gentleman. Thus, a gentleman truly earns his status as a gentleman, while a petty person merely wastes his potential as a petty person.
Thus, by cultivating the Pure Land, one will certainly not be reborn in the lower grades. *Qingshuo*:
Sixty-fourth, Longshu said:
"Joy, anger, liking, disliking, craving, and desire are all emotions (*qing*). To nurture these emotions leads to evil; to indulge these emotions constitutes a thief."

To subdue the emotions is to cultivate goodness; to extinguish the emotions is to attain sagehood. To find sweetness in one’s food and drink, beauty in one’s clothing, and spaciousness in one’s dwelling—this sort of thing is called "nourishing the emotions.
To have food and drink like flowing water, clothing that is entirely ornate, and dwellings where there is no satiety—this sort of thing is called "indulging the emotions.
When offended, one does not retaliate; when provoked, one does not become angry; when harmed, one does not harbor resentment.

This is called suppressing the emotions; yet when one encounters or offends them, they provoke injury, and one instead gives rise to a compassionate and deluded mind toward them as if they were empty space.
This is called extinguishing the emotions. To awaken to this principle, the ground of the mind is eternally pure, as if dwelling in a Pure Land.
A Discourse on Minor Causes and Effects. Lu Shu said:
"There are those who repair bridges and those who destroy bridges; these are minor causes for heaven and hell.
There are those who ride in sedan chairs and those who carry them; these are minor effects of heaven and hell. One may extend this principle to other categories accordingly.
All of this can be clearly seen. If one constantly examines the mind in this way to cultivate the Pure Land for birth in the highest grade, what cause for doubt could there be?
Section Two: Words of the Two Deva Kings; Part Six, Chapter Six.
Longshu said: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that when a person is born, there are two celestial beings who follow them:
the first is called "Co-arisen" (*tóng-shēng*), and the second is called "Same-name" (*tóng-míng*). These celestial beings always see the person, while the person does not see the celestial beings.

Are these two celestial beings not perhaps the attendants of the two classes of youths—the virtuous and the evil? Therefore, whenever a person forms an intention, speaks a word, or takes a step, they should constantly keep these two in mind.
If a human being can be free from shame when seen by devas and humans, and practices the Pure Land in this manner, they will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level.
Someone may ask: "There is already one human being; why are there so many devas and humans? The answer is:
"The single moon universally appears in all waters; how could it be that the moon itself is many?"
Exhortation on Cultivating Preparations: Liu Shu said, "Day must be followed by night;
one must prepare for night. Summer must be followed by winter; one must prepare for winter. Existence must be followed by departure;
one must prepare for departure. What is meant by preparing for night? It is lamps, candles, bedding, and mats. What is meant by preparing for winter? It is quilts."
Regarding the furs, charcoal, and firewood: what is meant by "removing impediments" and "purifying the merit, wisdom, and pure land"?
This is an explanation of the merit of depositing goods in the treasury.
Lungshu said: "I have perused the entire Tripitaka and found no such teaching as 'depositing goods in the underworld. I therefore exhort the people of the world [to abandon this practice]."

If one uses the funds spent on "storing merit" (*jiku*) to invite monks for offerings dedicated to the Western Pure Land and focuses the mind single-mindedly upon the West, one will certainly attain rebirth there.

However, if one does not perform meritorious deeds for the sake of the Pure Land but instead performs "storing merit" for the sake of the underworld (*yin fu*), then one’s intent is directed toward the underworld, and upon death, one will surely enter the underworld.
It is like a person who, failing to practice the conduct of a gentleman, seeks to establish a relationship [with others].

To form a bond with a worthy man or gentleman by entrusting money to the jailer at the Judicial Court (Siliyuan), waiting for one’s own imprisonment so that the money may be used to avoid punishment—is this not utterly absurd?
[This concludes] the discourse on the three great kalpas of past, present, and future; [Chapter] Six, Nine.
The Buddhist canon states that the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adornment Eon) is called the past; the *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Eon) is called the present;
and the *Tārakakalpa* (Constellation Eon) is called the future. Within these three eons, each possesses the four sub-eons of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
These four sub-eons together constitute one great eon (*mahākalpa*). Setting aside for now the discussion of the past and future, we shall here speak of the present *Bhadrakalpa*.

The number of kalpas consists of twenty minor kalpas for the kalpa of formation, twenty minor kalpas for the kalpa of abiding, twenty minor kalpas for the kalpa of destruction, and twenty minor kalpas for the kalpa of emptiness.
Regarding the count of these minor kalpas, they proceed through one increase and one decrease;

beginning from the peak of the increasing kalpa at eighty-four thousand years, the lifespan decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches thirty years, at which time the calamity of famine occurs.
When the lifespan decreases from its maximum down to twenty years, the calamity of pestilence arises; when it further decreases to ten years, the kalpa of decrease reaches its limit.
Following this, the calamity of warfare arises. After the calamity of warfare has passed, the lifespan increases by one year every hundred years until it reaches eighty-four thousand years;
this constitutes one minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Within each of the four great kalpas—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—there are twenty such minor kalpas.
Twenty minor kalpas constitute one intermediate kalpa; four such intermediate kalpas together form one great kalpa. To speak further of the present abiding kalpa:
within its twenty minor kalpas, for eight minor kalpas no Buddha appears in the world.
When the ninth minor kalpa arrives at the time of eighty thousand years, and the lifespan decreases to sixty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appears in the world. At sixty thousand years...
When the lifespan decreases to forty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appears in the world; when it decreases from forty thousand to twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appears in the world;
when it decreases from twenty thousand to one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appears in the world.
During the tenth minor kalpa, when the lifespan decreases from eighty-four thousand years to eighty thousand years, Maitreya [appears].
After the appearance of a Buddha, for four intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) following the time of Maitreya Buddha, no Buddha appears in the world.

Then, during fifteen intermediate kalpas, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas appear in succession. After their appearance, there are again four intermediate kalpas during which no Buddha appears in the world.
Finally, from the twentieth intermediate kalpa onward, the human lifespan increases from ten years up to eighty-four thousand years; this is the abiding kalpa (sthāyikalpa).

The fulfillment of the Buddha’s original vows from his appearance in the world until the end of the *vivarta-kalpa* (aeon of formation) and the commencement of the *saṃvarta-kalpa* (aeon of destruction), including the occurrence of the three great calamities and the specific phenomena of the minor and major disasters, are all recorded in detail in the preceding volume, "An Examination of the Three Assemblies at the Dragon Flower. Readers should take full cognizance of this.
The Sūtra on Śakra-vatsa’s Salutation to the Six Directions:
Seventy Buddhas were in Rājagṛha begging for food at dawn when they saw from afar a son of a householder named Śakra-vatsa on Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain,
who had washed his head and face, put on clean garments, and was performing four prostrations toward the east and four prostrations toward the south.

He performed four prostrations facing west, four facing north, four toward the heavens, and four toward the earth. When the Buddha arrived at his home, he asked him, "Śīkhaṇḍin, why are you performing these prostrations?
Śīkhaṇḍin replied, "I am performing these six directions' prostrations. The Buddha asked, "Performing prostrations toward these six directions—what dharma is this?
Śīkhaṇḍin replied, "When my father was alive, he instructed me to rise early and perform these six directions' prostrations."

"How is it that, upon the recent death of your father, you did not dare disobey his command? The Buddha said, "Your father instructed you to perform obeisance toward the six directions, not with your body.
You have misunderstood your father’s intent. Śikhaṇḍī then knelt on both knees and said, "I pray that the Buddha will explain for me the meaning of these obeisances toward the six directions.
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively and take this to heart; I shall explain it in detail for you."
One who possesses the wisdom of an elder and is able to sever these six unwholesome dharmas is, in effect, paying homage to the six directions. What are the six unwholesome dharmas?
First, a fondness for drinking alcohol; second, a fondness for gambling; third, a fondness for sleeping late and rising late; fourth, a fondness for hosting guests;
fifth, a fondness for associating with evil companions; and sixth, a fondness for killing and deceiving.
If you covet the wives of others, yet claim to perform these six acts, it is as if you are merely paying homage to the six directions.

If you do not abandon such conduct, what benefit is there in your prostrations? Furthermore, they will cause an evil reputation to spread, your household affairs to fall into disorder, your wealth to diminish, your own body to become emaciated, and your virtuous deeds to decline day by day, so that you will be disrespected both near and far. O son of a noble family, you ought to choose what is wholesome.

"Follow those who are good and distance yourself from those who are not. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have always associated with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and now I have attained Buddhahood.
The Buddha then addressed Śikhāla-vatsa, saying: "Regarding the practice of bowing toward the east, this refers to a son serving his parents, for which there should be five matters:
first, one must be reverent and filial, attending to them regularly so as to always bring them joy; second..."
First, one should rise early and command the servants and slaves to prepare meals, managing the household with diligence and frugality;
second, one should relieve the toil and labor of one's parents; third, one should constantly keep in mind the kindness and virtue of one's parents;

fourth, when one's parents are ill, one should harbor deep sorrow and seek out physicians to treat them; fifth, [the parents] likewise have five matters regarding their children: first, they should cause them to abandon evil and turn toward the good.
Second, one should teach him to draw near to wise people. Third, one should teach him to study with diligence and care.
Fourth, one should arrange for him to marry at the appropriate time. Fifth, one should give him all the property that exists within the household.
Regarding those who bow toward the south, it is said that a disciple serving a teacher should observe five matters: first, one should maintain reverence and awe; second, one should rely upon...
Regarding the three points of instruction, one should diligently perform all tasks such as washing and maintenance; fourth, one should study with tireless diligence;

and fifth, after [the teacher] has departed, one should look up to them and praise their virtues, never speaking of their faults. There are also five matters regarding how a teacher instructs a disciple:
first, one should teach people without weariness so that they may quickly understand; second, one should ensure they excel others...

Regarding the three things for a disciple: first, one desires that their knowledge and insight be never forgotten; second, when there are points of doubt or difficulty, one should provide explanations;
third, one desires that the disciple’s wisdom surpasses that of the teacher. As for bowing toward the west, this refers to a wife serving her husband, for which there are five matters:
first, when the husband returns from outside, she should rise to welcome him; second, when the husband departs... [text continues].

1. When cooking, steaming, or cleaning, one must treat [the husband] with a respectful heart; these three matters must not involve lustful thoughts toward others, and one must firmly maintain the integrity of the inner quarters.
2. If the husband utters words of abuse, one must not respond with anger or show a wrathful countenance;
all his instructions and admonitions must be respectfully received and followed, and no household goods or utensils may be hidden away for personal use. 3. One must wait upon the husband.
One should first go to bed and then look after the wife before sleeping oneself. There are also five matters regarding how a husband should regard his wife:
first, when going out or coming in, they should treat each other with mutual respect; second, when providing food and drink, it should be done at the proper time so as not to distress the wife;
third, if the wife desires clothing or head ornaments, one should not oppose her wishes—providing everything if wealthy, or according to one's means if poor; fourth, the household... [text fragment].
All that is within [the household] shall be entrusted to them. Fifth, one must not externally commit illicit sexual acts so as to cause one’s wife to harbor suspicions or alien thoughts.
Regarding those who bow toward the north, this refers to the conduct between people, such as relatives and friends; in these relationships, both parties must observe five matters:
first, if either party commits an evil deed, they should mutually exhort, instruct, admonish, and dissuade one another from it. Second, the other...

First, when there is illness or distress, one must provide care, administer remedies, and treat them; second, as both parties have families, one must maintain confidentiality and not speak of internal matters to outsiders;
third, one should mutually respect and praise one another, maintaining constant communication without interruption, and even if occasional friction occurs, one must not harbor resentment;
fourth, as the respective wealth and poverty of both sides may be unequal, one must provide support and relief.

Whatever fine things one possesses should be shared and distributed. Regarding the master’s duty toward those who bow before him—the servants and maidservants—there are five matters he should observe:
first, he must first ascertain their hunger, thirst, cold, and heat before assigning them tasks;
second, if they fall ill, he must summon a physician to treat them; third, he must not whip or strike them wantonly, but must exercise careful deliberation.
1. One should first inquire into the facts before holding someone accountable; those who may be excused should be excused, while those who cannot be excused should be instructed and disciplined.
2. If there is even the slightest private property, it must not be confiscated. 3. When distributing items, one should ensure equality and must not show partiality.
Regarding servants and maidservants serving their masters, there are also five matters: the first is that they should rise early.
1. Do not allow the master to call you for tasks; whatever ought to be done should be undertaken by your own initiative without troubling the master to give orders.

2. You should cherish the master’s property and must not discard it or trample upon it. 3. When the master enters or exits, you should attend to him with a respectful mind, welcoming or seeing him off.
4. You should speak only in praise of the master and must not mention his faults or misdeeds. 5. Bow toward the heavens.
This means that when a person makes offerings to a śramaṇa or a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they should employ five matters:

first, approaching them with a sincere mind; second, serving them with reverence without regarding it as wearisome; third, frequently inquiring about the principles of the Way; fourth, engaging in hearing, contemplating, and cultivating the teachings;
and fifth, requesting resolution regarding the essential meaning of mindfulness of the Buddha and Zen meditation, diligently practicing these day and night. Śramaṇas, you should be diligent in this.
A virtuous friend also instructs that person through five matters: first, they teach them generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
second, they teach them dignified deportment and ritual propriety so as not to allow them to become lax;

third, they teach them to ensure that their words and deeds correspond with one another, preferring that they speak little and act much rather than acting little while speaking much; fourth... [text truncated]
First, teach them to diligently pay homage to the Triple Gem and to have compassion for all sentient beings, both great and small.

Fifth, teach them to dedicate their merit, make vows, and seek rebirth in a Pure Land to attain the path of Bodhi and further deliver all living beings. To practice in this way is called "respectfully obeying one's father's command.
If one does not do so, even if one performs prostrations to the six directions, they will be of no benefit. At that time, Śikhara...
Yue immediately received the five precepts and reverently prostrated before the Buddha. The Buddha then repeated the verse with emphasis: "At cockcrow, one should rise early;

Dress in one's robes and descend slowly from the bed. Wash and rinse oneself until strictly pure; With both hands, offer incense and flowers. Trim the lamp wicks and change the pure water; Make offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Joining palms with reverence and respect, One should make vows to repay the four debts of gratitude And cultivate the dharma-gate of the six perfections."

Within each of these, you should practice and train in the perfection of giving to overcome stinginess, the perfection of ethical discipline to overcome transgressions, the perfection of patience to overcome anger, the perfection of diligence to overcome lethargy, the perfection of meditative concentration to overcome distraction, and the perfection of wisdom to overcome ignorance. Time does not wait for anyone;
practice diligently and do not be negligent. The sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death mean that human life does not remain for long; how much more so when facing the moment of death?
At that time, there is no kinsman to rely upon, no place to hide, and no medicine to provide relief.

Even heavenly blessings have their end; how long can human fortune last? Parents, wives, and children dwell together like guests staying overnight; they rest together in the night, yet at dawn each disperses.
Impermanence is just like this. One must prepare the provisions for the Buddha in advance—how much more so when considering the six realms of existence!

Wandering in the middle realms of saṃsāra, there has been no moment of rest; now, fortunately having attained a human body and further hearing this profound and wondrous Dharma, one should practice for oneself and transform others, so that both self and others may benefit.
With the six perfections as a vessel, one can transcend the ocean of birth and death.
Through the inconceivable power of Amitābha’s vows in Sukhāvatī, one is welcomed up the golden steps and personally receives the prediction of Bodhi. May the fourfold assembly reverently uphold this.
Śikhaṇḍīputra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, was filled with great joy and leaped for gladness;
he paid homage and accepted it with faith.
The World-Alerting Text by Chan Master Yongming Shou (71)
Now, those who do not embody the root of the Way are submerged in birth and death;

among the streams of those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, and among the classes of those that crawl, stand, fly, or sink, they lose their human form as often as there are grains of soil in the great earth. Those who obtain a human body are as rare as the soil upon a fingernail.
Even if one obtains a human body, for the most part one is born among the border tribes or the lowly, or even if dwelling in the Middle Kingdom, one may receive a female form.
Even if one were a man, free from lameness or deformity and possessed of the ten marks of a great person, there would still be many kinds of suffering.

Why is this? Dwelling in a world of fear during the age of the five turbidities, with a body made of flesh and a life sustained by breath, within a single lifetime it is like a spark on a stone, a wind-blown lamp, or the fading light of the setting sun—lasting but for a fleeting instant.
Those who die prematurely in their prime are beyond counting; those who attain a full natural lifespan reaching the age of sixty are rare even in this world.
Even if one escapes death to reach the age of seventy, they remain like ignorant children, lacking the wisdom for introspection and the turning back of the light of awareness;
they know only to love life and loathe death. Alas! Suppose one were wealthy at thirty and prosperous at forty—let us consider the interval between these years.
Within these thirty years, illness, calamities, sorrow, and affliction occupy more than half of one’s time.
Thus, there was a saying of old: "In a single month of this floating life, one can only smile with open mouth for perhaps four or five days.

Therefore, we know that anxiety is long and joy is brief; pleasure is scarce while suffering is abundant—like standing upon a perilous peak ten thousand fathoms high, or dwelling amidst a thousand... [thousand dangers].

If one searches through the vast ocean, even if a small measure of pleasure is found, one must ultimately consider the risk of drifting and sinking. Furthermore, birth exhausts me; dwelling in the womb is its toil.
Old age robs me of my youthful complexion; illness impairs my physical form; death pursues my spirit.
Prosperity indulges my arrogance and extravagance; disgrace shatters my spirit and resolve; nobility makes me haughty and overbearing; meanness crushes me.
When there is abundance, it indulges my greed; when there is poverty, it becomes the basis for my dependence.
When there is pleasure, it stirs my emotions; when there is pain, it afflicts my spirit. When there is praise, it gives rise to arrogance;
when there is disparagement, it destroys my reputation. Even when cold, it oppresses my body; when hot, it vexes my breast; when thirsty, it dries my throat; and when hungry, it leaves me emaciated.
When my belly is startled, my *pò* (vital breath) is cowed; when I am fearful, my *hún* (soul) is lost; when I am anxious, my spirit is disturbed; when I am vexed, my will is ruined.
When things are favorable, my affection grows; when they are adverse, my hatred arises. When there is intimacy, I am drawn toward joy; when there is distance, resentment is born.
When harmed, my body perishes; when grieved, my intestines knot together. Thus, encountering objects gives rise to the mind, which follows along with the sensory dust.
Whether a thought is beautiful or evil, if it does not accord with the heart, it all perpetuates the wheel of karma and utterly destroys the foundation of the Way.

Should one further act deceptively toward the ruler, rebel against one’s father, be arrogant toward things, rush after the times, have the heart of a beast, harbor the intent of a fox, seek profit by any means, pursue fame at all costs,
deceive others, flatter in conduct, and cling to power to exploit the orphaned— such a person will sink into a bottomless abyss of calamity.

They exalt their own practices, fan the fires of passion, blow upon the winds of delusion, and stir up the dust of affliction. Their awakening was long past, their karmic seeds have diverged from the straight path;
they look only to their former errors and contemplate only what lies ahead. They scheme only for departure and never think of returning; they seek only life and know nothing of extinction.

Thus, every thought-moment is a burning cauldron, and every step is a trench of suffering. If you should now obtain even a single kṣaṇa of existence in this world, you must cultivate benevolence within your aggregates.

By accumulating the merit of loving-kindness, perfecting one's virtue through fasting and purification, and reciting the Buddha's name with the vow to go to the Western Land, one may practice accordingly and thus escape suffering;
this can be called transcending the three realms so that all sufferings no longer touch one.
*On Cultivating the Pure Land Perfectly and Resolving Doubts*, from the *Tripitaka*.

Someone may say: "The Amitābha of intrinsic nature is originally complete; the pure land of the mind-only is already manifest. Why then must one recite the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in another land?
If one recites the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth, is it not to abandon what is near—one's own mind—and seek something ten thousand *li* away? If this is so...

Is it not erroneous to speak of distances spanning billions of lands? Yuan said: "Though those who speak of 'Mind-Only' may indeed utter these words, they have not truly mastered the principle of Mind-Only.
They are utterly deluded. One must know that there is no phenomenon outside the mind, and no mind outside phenomena.
The Buddha-lands of the ten directions, empty space, and the myriad phenomena of the universe all exist within my own nature."

How could there be any phenomena outside the mind within this? Have you not seen the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* state: "Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean"?
And it further states: "The empty space of the ten directions arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky.
If this is so, how can one consider ten trillion [yojanas] to be distant? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says that a single phrase—
Within the ten realms, one places the dust-motes of infinite lands within a single hair-tip without it being cramped; as Master Li said:
"The oceans of boundless lands do not separate self and other at the tip of a hair; the ten periods of past and present never depart from the present thought-moment.
How could one consider ten million billion *yojanas* to be distant? Formerly, when the youth Sudhana [was with] Samantabhadra...

If a Bodhisattva were to travel through the lands within a single pore, taking a single step that transcends worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—passing through that many worlds with every step and continuing for that many eons—they would still be unable to know the limits of the ocean of lands within a single pore.
How could one speak of even a hundred thousand billion lands? One must realize that all else is merely "other."
"Is this mind of yours the same as or different from the 'mind-only' [of the Buddha]? Someone said: 'The Way has neither past nor present;
how could there be two? I replied: 'If that is so, why do you needlessly confine it within the square inch of the heart?
Is this mind-only not all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm? Your words merely follow along with my speech; they are truly not your own wisdom.'"

I shall divide this for you so that you may recognize the wondrous, luminous mind-ground: it does not fall into partiality or deficiency, nor does it cling to Chan meditation as being the only truth, nor does it slander the recitation of the Buddha's name as being unnecessary.
You must know that Chan meditation is also "mind-only" and the recitation of the Buddha's name is also "mind-only";

that Chan meditation is for the sake of transcending birth and death, and the recitation of the Buddha's name is likewise for the sake of transcending birth and death. Thus, Chan meditation and the recitation of the Buddha's name are one.

The principle is the same: if one says that mindfulness of the Buddha is neither mindfulness of dhyāna nor dhyāna itself, then since the principle of the Buddha is not realized, the principle of the Mind-Only is likewise obstructed;
how can one falsely claim to have attained awakening to the Mind-Only?

That which is the Pure Land of the Mind-Only is the Constant Abode of Quiescent Light (*sada-prabhāsvara*). One who truly realizes this Abode of Quiescent Light does not cling to it, nor do they become attached to it.
Wherever he may be, every location in the West becomes a Pure Land; he can transform the great earth into gold and churn the long rivers into butter and milk.
A single utterance is always the perfect sound (*sambhinnapratibhāna*), and every action performed is nothing other than a Buddha-work.
If one reaches such a state, none but a Buddha can know it; there is no one else who knows it—this is not seen in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is said that even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, though they contemplate and seek with a single mind, cannot know it;
only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it—how much less can we inferior ordinary beings?
If one reaches the realm of the Tranquil Light, not a single dharma can be apprehended; what pure land could there be to be born in? Not only is there no pure land...
Yet one's own mind is likewise unattainable, and this very unattainability is itself unattainable;
how much less can one cling to the notion of an inherent Amida or a Pure Land of Mind-Only?

Although the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the inherent Amida are indeed primordially possessed by all people, those who have not yet reached this stage are not permitted to speak such words. I shall therefore question you in return: you—
Do you see this Sahā world as being composed of golden and seven-jeweled lotuses, or as being filled with pits, ravines, rubble, and thorns?

Do you see all those in the six realms and four modes of birth, or those in the three miserable paths and eight difficulties, as Buddhas experiencing bliss, or as sentient beings undergoing suffering?
Consider the inconceivable radiance and the inconceivable lifespan of that land of Amitābha Buddha.
Inconceivable compassion, inconceivable power of vows, inconceivable supernormal powers, inconceivable wisdom, inconceivable samādhi,
inconceivable eloquence, inconceivable emanations, inconceivable preaching of the Dharma, and inconceivable deliverance of sentient beings—
with all manner of inconceivable perfections of both the primary and secondary marks of adornment, you now possess them all.
Is it sufficient? Is it not yet sufficient? If it is not, one must quickly cultivate with utmost sincerity, worshipping the Buddha, reciting His name, and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
Why is this so? Those who practice while clinging to partiality and remaining deluded are like a person with crippled legs traveling on land, covering no more than a few li in a single day.
In contrast, worshiping, reciting, and seeking rebirth is like boarding a boat to travel by water; when aided by wind and sails, one can reach the destination in an instant.
This journey of a thousand *li* is also like a weak man following a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) who, in a single day and night, traverses the four continents;

this is not by his own power, but by the power of the Wheel-Turning King. Or it is like a person caught in the perils of official service who, lacking the strength to escape on his own, must rely on a powerful person for rescue.
It is like a person pulling a heavy object who is unable to do so by his own strength.
One must rely on the power of others to move [an object]; likewise, it is the same for practicing recitation and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Master Yongming Shou said:
"Furthermore, the single dharma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the root of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

it is the cause for transforming the mundane and treading the path of the sage. Because one gathers the mind for even a short time, it is called 'supreme goodness. However, one must clearly understand how to eliminate dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*)."
The *Xi zhishi jing* (Sūtra on Knowing the Time for Cessation) states: "If one becomes drowsy while sitting in meditation, one must arise and practice the Way by recollecting the Buddha;
or, with utmost sincerity, perform ablutions and repentance to remove heavy obstructions and rouse the body and mind.

One must not dogmatically cling to a single gate as the ultimate, for there are those who attain liberation through recollecting the Buddha and reciting sūtras, those who attain liberation through observing the precepts and preaching the Dharma, and those who attain it through ascetic practices."
There are those who attain deliverance through diligent labor; those who attain deliverance by prostrating before the Buddha and repenting their transgressions;
those who attain deliverance by beholding the radiance of the Buddha; those who attain deliverance by making offerings to the Triple Gem;

those who attain deliverance by molding and sculpting golden images; those who attain deliverance by painting Buddhist icons in color; and those who attain deliverance through the practice of charity and the performance of good deeds.
There are those who attain liberation by being encouraged to recite the Buddha’s name; there are those who attain liberation by observing the precept against killing and releasing captive creatures;

and there are those who attain liberation by listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion. One should know that although the nets of teaching are boundless, upon realizing them, one returns directly to the truth;

though the gates of deliverance are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, entering through any of them leads to liberation. It is like traveling a long distance: one takes reaching the destination as the goal, rather than fixating on the arbitrary divisions along the way.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Even those who recite the Buddha's name with a distracted mind, offer praise with a faint voice, draw images with their fingernails, or heap up sand to form stupas—all gradually accumulate merit and shall attain the Way of Buddhahood.
How much more so for one who clearly realizes the single mind while concurrently cultivating the myriad practices—how could such a person fail to become a Buddha?
O virtuous ones, if you wish to understand the principle of the Perfect and Sudden practice, you must examine [this].

Since those who do not understand the perfect cultivation (*yuanxiu*) of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras merely call themselves "sons of the Buddha," the Tripiṭaka Master out of compassion stated:

"That which is called 'true meditative concentration' (*dhyāna*) in the holy teachings consists of restraining the mind to a single point with continuous mindfulness, remaining free from dullness and distraction, and maintaining the mind in equanimity.
If one is obscured by sleep, one must immediately exert oneself in recollecting the Buddha, chanting the sūtras, prostrating, and performing circumambulations."
Expounding the Way, preaching the sutras, and teaching and transforming sentient beings so that the myriad practices are never neglected;

dedicating the merits of one's cultivated deeds toward rebirth in the Western Pure Land—if one can thus cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the Buddha’s meditative concentration, which accords with the holy teachings.
It is the eye for all sentient beings and is certified by all Buddhas; all Buddha-dharmas are equal and without distinction.
Riding upon the single suchness to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, it is taught that mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*) is the direct cause for Bodhi;
how can one thus give rise to false views? Nowadays, there is a certain class of coarse and superficial people who are neither clear about the scriptures nor have they penetrated the profound pivot;
they do not understand cause and effect, nor do they fear the retribution of sin and merit, yet they still wish to put on the airs of being great men.
A certain "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra), whose principles of cultivation were not yet thorough, merely advocated keeping one's mouth shut and remaining silent.

He caused all his junior disciples to fall into a dark mountain and a ghost cave; seeing people prostrate before the Buddha, recite the Buddha’s name, chant sutras, preach the teachings, and extensively perform various good deeds, he would instead say that practicing with attachment to forms only leads further and further away from the goal, and that it is better to simply hold onto a single thought and suppress the breath.
To say that effort itself is the actualization of one's own Amitābha and that there is no need to seek rebirth in a pure land elsewhere—such people are pitiable, lamentable, and worthy of compassion;
they are laughable. While their approach is indeed beautiful, it is not yet complete.
I know that when dull-witted ordinary beings practice *chan*, they are either in a state of drowsiness or distraction; I do not know how many times this occurs in a single day.
How many deluded thoughts leave one dazed and exhausted! Even when encountering a time of strength, the consciousness still arises;

once the period of retreat has ended, one again clings to objects and, as before, becomes defiled by worldly toil—speaking of right and wrong with the mouth while harboring hatred and love in the heart.
To practice Chan in this manner, do not speak of Maitreya’s descent; you would fail to understand even a single Buddha among the thousand who have appeared.
The world has already come to an end, yet the day of its final conclusion remains unknown;

how can one simply say that the Amitābha of one's own self is already manifest and need not seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land? Such blind people are like commoners who style themselves kings—they bring about their own destruction.
Furthermore, there is another class of deluded individuals who, though they enter the Zen hall to study the path, do not recognize the three poisons.
Upon seeing others excel and advance, one gives rise to jealousy; one cannot practice oneself, nor can one rejoice in the merit of others.

One fails to recognize the King of Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices, fails to recognize the *Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Goodnesses*, and fails to recognize the Eight Overflowing Gates of Noble Liberation.

Instead, one obstructs others from prostrating to and recollecting the Buddha, obstructs them from chanting sutras and expounding the teachings, and obstructs them from making offerings to the Buddhas and providing for the Sangha.
These people who construct artificial temples and erect statues obstruct others from making offerings to form karmic connections; they hinder others from extensively cultivating myriad virtues.
Such thieves wear the robes of the Buddha as a disguise to steal the Buddha’s food; they are truly heretics, Māras, and seeds of hell.
Furthermore, Master Yun Guang was able both to preach the Dharma and to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); he remained in samādhi for years and months without reckoning the passage of time.
They consider this to be rare, yet because they fail to sever greed and anger, they fall directly into the *Benniu* (Running Bull) hell.

As for people like us, who practice meditation while mired in dullness and distraction, we instead disparage bowing to the Buddha and reciting his name. Udraka Rāmaputra possessed sharp faculties and great intelligence, capable of subduing afflictions;

he was regarded by the world as a rarity, reaching the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), yet because he failed to sever his obstacles, he later fell back down.
If even a flying weasel can obstruct the sensory realm in such a manner, how much more so can it obstruct a person from bowing to the Buddha or reciting his name?
The Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was able to expound upon the twelve divisions of the scriptures and had attained the fruit of the fourth dhyāna;

yet, because he associated with evil friends and became single-mindedly attached to emptiness, he falsely claimed that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no nirvāṇa. Consequently, he fell alive into hell and entered forever into the Avīci. I...

How can one not feel a chill in the heart? One must quickly and urgently repent! Yongjia said: "To recklessly dismiss emptiness and cast aside cause and effect is to wander aimlessly and invite calamity.
To abandon attachment while clinging to emptiness is likewise a sickness; it is like avoiding drowning only to leap into a fire. This is precisely what that refers to. The Sūtra says:
"The Buddhas preach the Dharma of emptiness for the purpose of delivering those who cling to existence. If one, in turn, becomes attached to..."

"Emptiness is that which none of the Buddhas can transform. It is further said: "It would be better to speak of an existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to slander non-existence by even a speck as small as a mustard seed.
Why is this? In the past, there was a bhikṣu of pure livelihood who, abiding in right view, offered flowers to the Buddhas and received a prediction of enlightenment.
On the other hand, there was another bhikṣu of Dharma practice who, though having attained the four dhyānas, remained in wrong views.

Attached to a biased emptiness, he slandered the Venerable Dharmabhāṇaka, saying: "The flowers received by the Venerable Dharmabhāṇaka were not used for offering, but were instead consumed by him himself.
Because of these words, he remained without a tongue for sixty thousand lifetimes. The Buddha said:

"One who looks upon a person who has generated the bodhicitta with an evil eye shall receive the retribution of being blind; one who slanders a person who has generated the bodhicitta with evil speech [shall likewise suffer such retribution]."

If a person receives the retribution of being tongueless, or if one clings to a biased emptiness as being correct while slandering the cultivation of the myriad practices as incorrect, such a person shall fall into hell for many hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Why is this? Because they sever the seed of the Buddha. Does the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* not say:
"If a person, with a distracted mind, offers even a single flower as an offering to a painted image, they will gradually see [the Buddha]?"
How could the words of countless Buddhas be false? The *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma* states:

The Buddha said, "If there is another person who, upon seeing others cultivate merit or give alms to the poor, speaks words of derision and slander, saying: 'This person of wrong livelihood seeks only fame and profit;
what use is giving for one who has left the household life? One should only cultivate the practices of meditative concentration and wisdom; why engage in such worldly agitation?'"
One who forms such thoughts regarding useless matters belongs to the retinue of Māra. When that person’s life ends, they will fall into the great hells and undergo suffering there.
Emerging from the hells, they will fall among the hungry ghosts; for five hundred lifetimes they will fall among dogs.
Having emerged from being a dog, they will be constantly born into poverty and low status for five hundred successive lives, undergoing all manner of sufferings. Why is this? Because...
Because in a previous life they did not rejoice when seeing others give, how could they not have seen what is taught in the *Āyuṣman-mukha-rakṣā-sūtra*?
There is a hungry ghost of hideous form, at the sight of whom one’s hair stands on end and all are struck with fear.

From his body issues a fierce flame like a mass of fire, and from his mouth emerge maggots without end. Pus, blood, and various decaying things emit a foul stench that penetrates far, as he raises his voice.
Wailing and crying out, they ran hither and thither. At that time, a perfected Arhat asked the hungry ghosts, "What sins did you commit in your past lives that you now endure this suffering?
The hungry ghosts replied, "In the past, we were once śramaṇas who uttered evil words to obstruct others from practicing virtue;
thus we have encountered this suffering, and there is no way to escape it. We would rather cut out our own tongues with a sharp blade."

I truly dare not obstruct his roots of goodness. Venerable One, upon returning to Jambudvīpa, please admonish the bhikṣus and instruct your disciples that when they see others performing even the slightest virtuous deed, they should only rejoice and assist them;
do not cause them to be thwarted or fail. Since I fell into this class of hungry ghosts, I have suffered for many tens of millions of kalpas, even if I were to somehow escape from it.
The ghost-form returned once more to hell. At that time, having spoken these words, the hungry ghost wailed and threw himself to the ground like a great mountain collapsing;

hearing this account, one’s heart is truly chilled with dread. If even a single evil word uttered by this ghost led him to suffer for many kalpas, how could we—fearing neither sin nor merit—dare to act recklessly or behave with such wild abandon?
Not even a hair’s breadth of wholesome deed can be tolerated [if such transgressions are made].

If even those who commit the heinous crime of parricide cannot obstruct others from bowing to the Buddha or reciting his name, how much less could they do so? The Buddha said that the sin of obstructing others from practicing goodness is inescapable.
Even an *Abhisambodhi* Bodhisattva is like the moon on the fourteenth night;

because one portion of ignorance remains unexhausted, they are like a faint wisp of smoke, yet they still prostrate to the Buddha and repent to purify themselves for the sake of attaining perfect, unsurpassed *bodhi*. How much more so for us, ordinary beings bound by karma!

If even a Buddha does not discard the merit of threading a needle when one simply bows lightly and recites His name, how much more so for an ordinary person to bow lightly and recite the Buddha’s name!
In the past, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni praised Puṣya Buddha with his mouth and prostrated before Puṣya Buddha with his body;
in this manner, for seven days and seven nights, he was able to instantly transcend nine kalpas. How could it be that such a thing is achieved through seeking while attached to marks?

Is it not far-fetched to say that by bowing to the Buddhas one does not attain Buddhahood? When the three thousand Buddhas were still in the state of ordinary beings, they formed a fellowship of dharma-practitioners;
each, with one voice and in unison, invoked and paid homage to the fifty-three Buddhas, and all attained the Way simultaneously.
If the three thousand Buddhas were thus, so too are the Buddhas of the ten directions. Why, then, do people today not [do the same]?
To emulate their practice, one should instead honor the Buddha with prostrations and recite his name.

King Ajātaśatru committed the five heinous crimes, yet later, by knowing to bow to the Buddha and repent, he was able to extinguish those offenses and realize the fruit of enlightenment. In the past, Gavāmpati had been a cow;
while seeking water and grass, he circumambulated a vihāra clockwise and beheld the Buddha’s golden marks and signs of excellence, whereby he gave rise to a single thought of joyful faith.
If even those who were subsequently reborn as animals could attain the Way, how much more so for a human being who bows to the Buddha and recites his name—would such a person not become a Buddha?
Formerly, there were two Heavenly Kings whose lifespans had ended; one was about to enter the womb of a donkey, while the other was about to fall into the belly of a pig.

Each was filled with grief, fear, and unease, so they went to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek salvation. The Buddha instructed them to take refuge in the Triple Gem, whereupon they were able to escape that suffering and calamity. Hereafter...
To serve the Triple Gem with diligence and further realize the fruits of the Path, one does not even see [the need for] the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states:

"If there are those who hear the two characters 'Eternal Abiding' (nitya), they shall not fall into hell for seven kalpas; how much more so for the merit of prostrating and reciting! This is precisely what is meant by:

"Hearing the name and beholding the form extinguishes sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; prostrating, reciting, and taking refuge increases blessings immeasurably. How could one fail to follow the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
How could one dare to act with such recklessness and disorder? The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states:

"In a single prostration to the Buddha, from the knees down to the vajra-ground, for every particle of dust there is the attainment of the rank of a Cakravartin King, and furthermore, ten kinds of merit are obtained:
first, obtaining a wondrous physical form; second, words spoken being believed by others; third, being fearless when among the masses; fourth, being protected by the Buddhas."

1. One is mindful of the five great dignified postures; 2. The six classes of beings will draw near and attach themselves; 3. All devas will love and revere one; 4. One possesses great merit and virtue; 5.
At the end of life, one is reborn in a pure land; 6. One swiftly realizes *nirvāṇa*. If even a single prostration yields such merit, how much more so for many prostrations?
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "There may be someone who performs prostrations, or perhaps merely joins their palms..."

If one raises a single hand or slightly bows the head to make this offering to the image, one will gradually come to see immeasurable Buddhas and personally attain the Unsurpassed Way to widely deliver countless multitudes—is this not a statement free from falsehood? The *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* says:
"A single sincere recitation of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha' extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas."

If even those who have committed the ten heinous evils can attain rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times at the moment of death, how much more so for those who observe the precepts for a long time and practice mindfulness of the Buddha?
In the past, Zhang Shanhe spent his entire life slaughtering oxen;

yet at the moment of death, when he personally beheld the manifestations of hell, he encountered a monk who instructed him to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Before he had finished ten recitations, he saw the Buddha coming to receive him.
Is it not inconceivable that the Buddha’s power leads one to rebirth in the Pure Land? The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states:

"If, at the time of a person's death, they hear the name of even a single Buddha or a single Bodhisattva, or a single phrase or verse from the sūtras, they shall immediately transcend to a good realm and directly escape the wheel of suffering.
O virtuous ones, if merely hearing [the teachings] brings such great benefit, how much more so [is the case for those who practice them]?

Regarding the merit of upholding and reciting [the Buddha’s name]: The *Mahāratnakośa Sūtra* states that if a person were to offer the four most excellent requisites to as many Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas as would fill a great trichiliocosm, the merit obtained would not equal that of a person who joins their palms and recites the Buddha’s name but once;
the former is not even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the latter, nor can it be compared by calculation or metaphor.

If the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name even once is already so great, how much more so when it is done without ceasing, thought after thought! Does one not see that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"Those who have recited 'Namo Buddha' even once have all already attained the path of Buddhahood"? How could this be empty talk?

The *Karmavipāka-vibhaṅga Sūtra* states that there are ten kinds of merit for those who recite the Buddha’s name and the sūtras with a loud voice: first, it can dispel the obstacle of sleep; second, ... [and so forth].

1. The celestial Māras are struck with terror; 2. Three sounds pervade the ten directions; 3. Suffering in the three evil realms is stilled; 4. External sounds do not enter; 5. The mind is not distracted; 6.
One practices with courageous diligence; 7. All Buddhas rejoice; 8. Samādhi manifests before one; 9. One is reborn in the Pure Land at the end of life.
Having attained Buddhahood through reciting the Buddha’s name and chanting the sutras, how could it be said that this involves attachment to signs or the frantic pursuit of external goals?

Is it a matter of trivialities? In ancient times, there were many enlightened and eminent monks who specialized in upholding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, those who specialized in upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and those who specialized in the practice of Amitābha Buddha;

they all attained rebirth in the Pure Land and proceeded directly to Buddhahood. How could reciting the sūtras and chanting the Buddha’s name be considered a minor matter, or an attachment to appearances? Formerly, there was...
A certain woman constantly contemplated the fragrance of blue lotuses, white lotuses, flowering trees, and fruiting trees;
by the merit of these four lines alone, she attained rebirth in the Pure Land—how much more so for one who recites the entire sutra?
Master Tanyi’s previous life was that of a pheasant; upon hearing a monk reciting the Lotus Sutra, he immediately attained rebirth as a human being.
If even a monk can attain the Way, how much more so a person who recites the sutras and preaches the Dharma—how could such a person fail to become a Buddha?

Formerly, there was a parrot and two *ju-ru* birds that, by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, attained rebirth in the Pure Land; how much more so for a human being who recites the Buddha’s name—how could they not be reborn there?
Someone asked: "What evidence is there for this? Wuyuan replied: "You do not know the verse of the vows made by Amitābha Buddha."
"I declare that when I attain Buddhahood, my fame shall transcend the ten directions;

humans and devas will joyfully hear of it and all come to be born in my land, and even those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals shall likewise be born within my land—how could this be a false or deceptive claim? The *Vajra Ritual Manual* states:
"Even wild foxes listen to Baizhang’s Dharma conch; even snails protect the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; and ten thousand wandering fish hear the Buddha."
The transformed Heavenly Son heard the sound of the Dharma with five hundred bats; they all became sages and worthies. A python was reborn in heaven upon hearing the repentance ritual;
a dragon attained enlightenment while listening to the Dharma. If even such creatures as these were able to comprehend and awaken, how can humans fail to turn their minds?
Some bury their heads in eating and pass their entire lives in vain; others practice on mistaken paths and remain unaware of it.
If this is so, how could expounding the sutras and preaching the Dharma be considered a minor matter or something of no merit?

Have you not seen what the *Lotus Sutra* says: "Even those who hear but a single verse will undoubtedly all attain Buddhahood"? "If there are those who hear this Dharma, they have all already attained the Way of the Buddha.
"If there are those who hear the Dharma, there is not one who does not become a Buddha. How could these words be false? Alas!

If even animals of different species can attain realization upon hearing the Dharma, how much more so for humans who prostrate to the Buddha, recite his name, chant the sutras, preach the teachings, and extensively cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds—will they not surely become Buddhas?
I have briefly cited several instances here to dispel your doubts: Puan saw the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and awakened to the Way;
Yongjia read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and clarified his mind; Guifeng studied the *Awakening of Faith* and suddenly realized the ground of consciousness.
When those of wisdom open [this teaching], they recite the Lotus Sutra and see Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as if it had not yet dispersed.
How could one possibly slight such benefits, or fail to respect its teachings? The *Lotus Sutra* states:

"By making offerings to sentient beings in four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, they cause them all to attain the path of Arhatship, exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*), and to abide in profound meditative concentration."
To attain mastery and possess the eight liberations is not equal to the merit of the fiftieth person who hears even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices;

a hundred thousand million billion parts of that merit do not equal one part of the merit from hearing and rejoicing in a single verse—this merit is inconceivable, let alone reciting and upholding the entire scripture.
The *Huayan Yinggan Fu* states: "There was a person who heard [it] and attained..."

Regarding the seven characters of the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, one does not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras—how much more so for the merit of upholding and reciting it?
Formerly, there was a monk who specialized in upholding the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*. A celestial palace descended specifically to invite him for a meal.
Once the Dharma Master had arrived and taken his seat, five hundred arhats suddenly gathered, soaring through the air. Just as the Master was about to descend from his seat, [the deities departed].
As they went out to welcome him, the Heavenly Emperor said, "Today my intention for this vegetarian feast rests solely upon you, Master.

Although five hundred arhats were invited for the occasion, you are a master who upholds the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which is the realm of the Buddha; how could you sit at the same level as lesser sages during the meal?

After the meal was concluded, he immediately attained the power of flight, transcending ordinary beings and surpassing the sages all at once. Furthermore, there was another monk who upheld the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to whom the Heavenly Emperor granted [this same result].
When the asuras were engaged in battle, they specifically requested this monk to ascend the seat and recite sutras while traveling through the air;

consequently, the Heavenly Emperor attained victory and the asuras fled in terror. Within the pores of a lotus fiber, the Heavenly Emperor was filled with joy and wished to offer him the medicine of longevity, but the Master rebuked him, saying:
"If one does not cultivate the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha, how can one avoid death? How could such a person [attain it] by means of this?"
Is reciting the sutras a minor matter? The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that there was once an Indian monk who was spinning the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in his hands;
when he washed his hands, a drop of water fell onto the body of an ant, and the ant immediately attained rebirth in heaven.

During the time of the Buddha, a young frog in Kālaka Pond heard the Buddha preach the Dharma and likewise attained rebirth in heaven. How could one consider reading the scriptures and expounding the teachings to be insignificant?
Is it not beneficial for the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) that one is not born in the Pure Land? Furthermore, several passages are cited to resolve doubts and provide verification:

the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each from their own land, extend their broad and long tongues to completely cover the trichiliocosm, speaking words of truth and collectively praising the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha. And...
The adornments of that land are so sublime that even the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions still contemplate the name of Amitābha Buddha and vow to be born in Amitābha’s land;
how much more so for those of us who are ignorant and turbid ordinary beings? During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;

after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna; and during the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there were the Venerable Deven and others. How could we compare ourselves to them?
In this solemn assembly are the Bodhisattva Śrī-Ābhāsvara, Master Yuǎn of this land, Master Yuán, Great Master Zhìzhě,
National Teacher Qīngliáng, Patriarch Fǎzhì, Dharma Master Cí'ēn, Venerable Shàoniàn, Dharma Master Shàokāng,
Repentance Master Cíyún, Grand Master Zhōngguó, Dharma Master Huáigǎn, Chan Master Huáiyù, and Dharma Master Dà'ān.
Master Daochuo, Master Xingchang, Master Fazhao, Master Caotang, Master Gushan, Master Dazhi,
Master Zongtan, Master Yuanchen, Master Wanyan Yi, Master Changlu Ze,
Master Tianyi Huai, Master Yuanzhao Ben, and Master Yongming Shou.
The Chan Master Yuanbian, Dharma Master Facheng, National Preceptor Puying of Zhongfeng, Venerable Tianru Weize, the Eighteen Sages of Mount Lu,
the Universal Deliverer Youtan Zongzhu, and all such Buddhas, patriarchs, and spiritual friends as these cultivated this path and further transformed others through it;
why should we not emulate them in our practice and aspire to be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss?
Are these Buddhas, Patriarchs, and spiritual friends those who have not yet passed through the Zen barrier, or are they dull-witted ordinary beings? Are they those who chase after appearances?
Consider how many venerable masters of antiquity and famous worthies of successive generations all recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land;
how much more so for us, lowly, inferior, and ignorant commoners! Alas, in this remaining age of the five turbidities and evil world...
The study of other paths is difficult to accomplish; only the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land is truly a direct and swift path.
That people do not know this is truly pitiable; that they know it yet do not practice it is even more pitiable. Alas!

My current earnest and bitter exhortation is for no other reason than to urge everyone to deeply contemplate birth and death, to quickly and urgently practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and to take the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land as their primary goal, while concurrently [practicing other virtues].
If one who practices Chan of the fundamental nature attains awakening, it is like adding embroidery to brocade—it is not an extra burden.
Even those who cannot yet fully comprehend reality may attain rebirth by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows. Once rebirth is attained, what need is there to worry about not awakening?

Only after seeing Amitābha will one know that the minds of Chan and the Buddhas are non-different in the three aspects, and that the three contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle are fused as one.

Having attained penetration into the principle of perfect interfusion, one realizes that as soon as thought is recognized, non-thought arises; as birth occurs, there is no birth; as there is cultivation, there is no cultivation;

as there is realization, there is no realization; and as there is speaking, there is no speaking. Yet, from non-speaking, one speaks: phenomena are themselves principle, and principle is itself phenomena;
appearance is itself non-appearance, and non-appearance is itself appearance; the infinite is the one, and the one is the infinite; other Buddhas are oneself.

"My Buddha, my Buddha is precisely the Buddha of other Buddhas; the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is precisely my preaching of the Dharma; my preaching of the Dharma is precisely the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma.
This is what is meant by sharing a single nostril, joyfully able to extend or contract at will.
When one reaches this stage, one finally believes that what I have said today is not false."

**An Essay on Heaven, Earth, the Divine Spirits, and the Prohibition Against Killing** Question 73: Someone asked, "I have heard that the Master’s compassion is exceptional; I have come specifically to resolve my doubts. The Master said, "I am but an ordinary fool; I shall simply answer you directly. The questioner said, "The Master speaks of encouraging goodness, reciting the Buddha's name, abstaining from killing, and practicing kindness. Yet, when the world sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, they kill [animals]. [The Master continued: "This is because they do not understand the principle of the Way. They do not know that Heaven and Earth are the parents of all things, nor do they realize that the myriad creatures are their descendants. To kill them for sacrifice is to commit a great offense against the Way. It is like a child striking its own father or a younger sibling slapping their elder brother. How could such an act be considered filial piety? Furthermore, the spirits of Heaven and Earth are omnipresent and all-pervading. They dwell within every blade of grass and every grain of sand.

If one kills living beings to offer as a sacrifice, it is as if one were to take a handful of earth and throw it at the face of one’s own father. Would this be called filial piety? Moreover, the spirits of Heaven and Earth are impartial and do not harbor favoritism. If one kills to offer a sacrifice, the spirits will surely punish that person with calamity. This is why the sages established the prohibitions against killing. They taught people to cultivate their hearts through kindness, to refrain from slaughter, and to practice compassion. This is the true way to serve Heaven and Earth."

Regarding the offering of oxen, horses, and sacrificial animals to the spirits and deities, and the slaughter of pigs, sheep, and the six domestic animals—how should one proceed? The answer is: Heaven and Earth are benevolent and cherish life;
they regard great spiritual clarity as their essence, and being loyal, upright, and loathing killing as their priority.

Why would one go against the natural order of Heaven and act in such a perverse manner? To act perversely in this way is to invite calamity; it is precisely what is meant by "incurring the offense of Heaven."
"It is said that there is no need for prayer; that 'not killing' is already the highest [principle]. What, then, would be required for sacrificial rites? "It is replied:

Sacrificial rites consist solely in sincerity and reverence, not in the life of creatures. Have you not heard Confucius say: 'Even when eating coarse grain with leaf-soups and offering melons, one must always maintain a state of solemn concentration'?

As for Yu, I have no fault to find with him; though his food was simple, he offered the utmost filial devotion to the spirits. "Extensive... (The text continues with "yang," indicating the passage is incomplete.)
"How vast it is! It seems as if it were above us, as if it were at our left and right—is this not so? The *Tripitaka* states that the Buddha told the various kings:

"If you wish for rain and sunshine to be timely and for crops and fruits to flourish in abundance, you must cultivate morality and virtue, show compassion to the myriad people, implement benevolent governance, and refrain from taking life;
only then can the great peace of the world be preserved. Have you not seen the *Huá*?

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Within Jambudvīpa, sentient beings of the five turbidities do not cultivate the ten wholesome paths but exclusively commit evil deeds—killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, greed, anger, and wrong views; they are unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward śramaṇas;
they contend with one another in fury and mutually insult each other; they give rein to their own whims to form biased views and seek their goals through unrighteous means."
Because of these causes and conditions, wind and rain do not come at their proper times, the crops fail to ripen, the people suffer from scarcity, and many pestilential diseases prevail;

they flee in all directions, having no one to rely upon. Alas! If the people of this world can rely on the Buddha’s teachings to reform their errors and renew themselves, they will surely obtain auspiciousness in all affairs and experience every kind of favorable fortune.
Furthermore, have you not seen the incense-offering text by Shao Yaofu, which says: [Insert the relevant passage from Shao Yaofu's text here.]
Each day at dawn and dusk, offer one incense stick in gratitude.
Thank Heaven, thank Earth, and thank the Three Luminaries. May all prayers be fulfilled:

may the crops ripen in every field, may the lifespan of every person be long, may the state have loyal ministers to support the altars of the land, may no family have a rebellious child to distress their parents, and may the four quarters be pacified so that weapons of war are laid to rest.
