"Resting my breath as I did when I was poor—this is truly a magnificent statement! If every person possessed such a mind and made such a vow, it would naturally move the Supreme Deity to bestow compassion, and the devas and nāgas would provide protection.
Then the winds and rain would be harmonious, the state would be peaceful, and the people would be at ease. This is precisely what is meant by:"
"Calamity results from the accumulation of evil, while fortune arises from the celebration of goodness; this is the inevitable principle.

O virtuous ones, even the Lord of Mount Tai, being a supreme deity whose Way penetrates both heaven and earth, still received the precepts from Master Wen Chan and abandoned offerings of blood for vegetarian feasts.
How much more so for you ordinary, deluded mortals, who indulge in slaughtering living beings to serve at licentious shrines—seeking blessings, yet only obtaining calamity! Have you not heard?"
The Emperor of the Mountains said: "Heaven and earth are impartial; the divine spirits observe all in secret.

They do not bestow blessings because of sacrificial offerings, nor do they inflict calamities because of a lapse in ritual propriety. How profound these words are! I urge those who worship the deities:
if you can prepare simple vegetarian offerings and recite sutras for their dedication, then both the spirits and I shall obtain wholesome merit. Why must one kill living beings for sacrifice?"
However, let me further cite a verse from an ancient master, which says:
"If all sentient beings commit no acts of killing, Where in the ten directions could weapons be raised?
If every household constantly cultivates goodness, Why worry that the world will not be at peace?"
On Great Filial Piety in Serving One’s Parents: A Text on Prohibiting Killing Question 74:
It is said that when one’s parents are advanced in years, they must eat meat; if one does not kill living beings, how can one provide for their support? Answer:
Such is the vulgar view of the common world, but the Great Sages do not hold it so. Practicing filial piety does not consist in killing living beings; it lies only in...
It lies in encouraging virtue. If one's parents have faults, one should remonstrate with them; if they do not comply after three remonstrances, one should wail and weep.

If one does not act in this manner, even if one provides the nourishment of the "three sacrificial animals" daily, it is still considered unfilial. This is also as stated in the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety):
"In nourishing their parents, a child may provide the hundred flavors of ambrosia to satisfy their palate, and the manifold sounds of celestial music to delight their ears."

To delight their ears with famous names and to dazzle their bodies with superior garments, while carrying burdens upon both shoulders as one wanders throughout the four seas—none of these can surpass filial piety in its greatness.
Yet the Buddha’s words do not yet constitute true filial piety.

If one's parents are obstinate and ignorant, failing to honor the Triple Gem, being cruel, tyrannical, and committing various evil deeds, the child ought to admonish them, causing them to give rise to faith and take refuge in the Right Path.

The Way constantly practices the six perfections—generosity, discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom—as well as kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. When in the presence of a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), one should always respectfully listen to and follow their teachings, practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and cultivate these virtues.
One should vow to escape the wheel of suffering and vow to be reborn in a land of bliss. Only by practicing filial piety according to this path can it be called true requital of gratitude;
otherwise, it is merely being a human child in name. Have you not seen the Zen Master Ze of Changlu, who composed the "Treatise on Exhorting Filial Piety"?
Of the one hundred and twenty chapters, the first hundred speak of filial piety through providing delicious food as worldly filiality;
the final twenty chapters exhort parents to cultivate the Pure Land as supramundane filiality.

Worldly filiality ends with a single lifetime, whereas supramundane filiality is inexhaustible throughout time. To enable one's parents to be reborn in the Pure Land is the greatest form of filial piety.
Furthermore, while one's parents are still alive, one should not merely grieve for them in the future nor offer elaborate funeral rites;
rather, one should practice filial support as taught in both the preceding and following sections of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. This is precisely that meaning. It is further said:

"When parents believe in and know of *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation), it is the time to plant seeds beneath the lotus pond. By single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name, the lotus flower will emerge from the water."
The time has come for the merits of mindfulness of the Buddha to bear fruit, and the flowers have blossomed; this is the moment to behold the Buddha.

A filial child, perceiving that the hour of their parents' rebirth in the Pure Land has arrived, should compile a record of all the various good deeds performed by their parents throughout their lives into a single document.

They should read this document to their parents from time to time, ensuring that the parents’ hearts are filled with joy. Furthermore, they should request their parents to sit or lie facing west, never forgetting the Western Pure Land.

If one sets up an image of Amitābha, burns incense, strikes the chime, and the assembly chants the Buddha’s name without ceasing, then at the moment the breath is severed, one must apply oneself with even greater focus;
do not lose right mindfulness through weeping and wailing. That one’s parents may thereby attain rebirth in the Pure Land—how wonderful this would be!
The filial care practiced throughout one’s life reaches its true fulfillment precisely at this time. I address you, filial sons and obedient grandsons: do not forget this matter. If you wish to...
One should exhaust the worldly rites of mourning and wait until the breath has ceased for a considerable time before weeping; it is strictly forbidden at the very moment of death.
Furthermore, since ancient times, there have been many who attained rebirth in the Western Paradise through *nien-fo*;
I shall briefly cite several instances to serve as a mirror for those who practice *nien-fo*. Thus, when the King of Udyāna beheld the various sages coming to welcome him, he [attained rebirth].
Empress Wen ascended on a rare fragrance and departed toward the west; the nun Yao Xing invited the Buddha to wait for her;

and the Prince of Song attended his mother as they returned home together—this may be called "leaping directly into the stage of the Tathāgata. Someone said: "If one relies on this practice, it is indeed true filial piety;
yet if there is no fish or meat, how can one nourish one's parents? He replied: "Your ignorance is truly profound."
"Compassion for the world requires fragrant, pure, and simple flavors; why must there be such pungent, rancid, and foul-smelling fish and meat? The Master replied, "The words are clear.
[The interlocutor] said, "It lies in diligent practice.
*A Text on Breaking the Excuse of Entertaining Guests to Cease Killing*, No. 75.
Someone said: "If guests, relatives, or friends arrive and one does not kill living beings to entertain them, it would be a great affront to human sentiment;
everyone will mock me as being pedantic, stingy, and miserly. I replied: "The foolish person lacks understanding and thus harbors fear and hesitation.

However, for one who understands the principles of the Buddha, they would instead encourage their relatives and friends to observe the precepts, recite the Buddha's name, and go together toward the Western Land. Why should such a person fear their mockery?"
To laugh at this is merely the host’s own greed for food and drink, which leads him to speak such words.

If one understands the laws of cause and effect regarding sin and merit, one would certainly never do this. Why? Because you must know that the meat you eat has all been your own relatives from past lives and your own kin from previous incarnations;
it is only because their heads have been changed and faces altered that they no longer recognize one another. Alas! To cause...
One who eats meat and possesses the knowledge of past lives will experience such mental anguish that even food cannot pass down their throat. Someone might say:

"When people hear these words, they mostly feel doubt and alarm, and do not believe them; moreover, since sentient beings are infinite, how is it certain that what one eats was precisely a relative from a former life?
The answer is: "The Buddha’s wisdom perceives events across immeasurable kalpas, and sentient beings have been bound together through successive kalpas."

Throughout all places of saṃsāra, one has been born and has always been a relative to others; it is only because of ordinary vision that this is not seen. How could one know this when eating? Regarding their biographies:
King Zhou of Shang imprisoned the Marquis of Xi (King Wen) and secretly cooked his son to feed him. The Marquis ate it without knowing it was his own son.
Zhou said with delight, "Who would have thought the Marquis of Xi was a sage? He ate the flesh of his own son and did not realize it! Alas, such was the case with the Marquis of Xi!
If even a sage cannot distinguish the flesh of his own son, how could ordinary eyes recognize those who were one's own kin in past kalpas?
Have you not seen the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* state that when the Buddha observes sentient beings cycling through the six realms, they all dwell together in birth and death, devouring one another;
there are none who have not been one's own kin? It further states: "For the sake of profit, one kills sentient beings; with wealth as a net, one ensnares various meats."
Since both parties commit evil karma and fall into the Raurava Hell upon death, one knows that those who kill and those who eat are truly criminals within the hells.
Alas! To act with ease for a single moment is to undergo hardship for ten thousand kalpas;
when the retribution arrives, there is nowhere to escape. O virtuous ones, if you follow the deluded sentiments of sentient beings, you will instead [be led astray].
The great wisdom of the Buddhas is endowed with the compassionate wisdom of Great Enlightenment, enabling both host and guest to attain liberation;
whereas if one exhausts the worldly sentiments of an ordinary person, both self and other will sink into ruin. Alas! How can one compare their relative weight, gain, and loss?
Let the wise discern and choose between them.

On Dividing Property, Resolving Enmity, and Refraining from Killing Question: Regarding those in the world who divide property, is it difficult for them to avoid killing, or is it easy? If it is easy, there is no need to speak of it; but as for those for whom it is difficult, how should they protect and save [life] through killing? Answer: To try to extinguish fire with oil—how could that put out the flames? It would only cause them to flare up even more. Therefore, one must first abandon the causes of killing before one can hope to save life. If one does not abandon the causes, how can one achieve the effect? This is why the sages established the precept against killing. If one wishes to practice the Way, one must first sever the roots of the three poisons. If one does not sever the roots of the three poisons, how can one attain the Way? Furthermore, if one wishes to resolve enmities, one must first eliminate the causes of resentment. If one does not eliminate the causes of resentment, how can one resolve the enmity? Thus, one should diligently cultivate the precept against killing to save all living beings. If one does not save them, how can one be called compassionate? One should also practice the virtue of giving to provide for their sustenance. If one does not provide for their sustenance, how can one be called generous? By practicing these three virtues—refraining from killing, resolving enmity, and giving—one will naturally be free from suffering and attain peace and happiness in this life and the next. This is the essential principle for transforming the world. Those who wish to benefit others should first benefit themselves by cultivating these practices. The more one burns [incense] for those who find it difficult to be born into this world, the more one realizes that all such births arise from karmic acts of killing.
If prior grievances have not yet been fully resolved, how can subsequent grievances be allowed to form again? Have you not seen it stated in the sutras and repentance rituals:

"For those with no karmic debts from past lives, birth may occur in an instant, so that the mother gives birth without even being aware of it; however, if they are karmic creditors, they will not separate from the mother for three or two days."
It causes the mother’s womb to feel as if it were being cut with a blade; the suffering is so unbearable that the entire family is struck with alarm, anxiety, and fear.
Furthermore, there are many difficult births that increase the agony:

some are born by twisting through the grass, some are born by treading upon lotuses, some are born with their entrails protruding, and some are first born with the left hand and left foot, or the right hand and right foot.
Birth may be difficult in various ways: one may be born sideways or inverted, or one may be born after the infant has been cut into pieces;

such diverse forms of difficult birth are truly the result of karmic retribution for killing. Among those with particularly heavy grievances, either the child is born only after the mother’s life is extinguished during childbirth, or the mother survives while the child perishes immediately.
Furthermore, there are those with even heavier karmic debts where both mother and child perish together and descend into hell.
Those in such prisons all suffer because of killing living beings and committing various evils. Someone said, "Your reasoning is most clear;
I beg you to transmit the method for preserving life and resolving grievances, as it would be a great boon to the world. [The Master] replied, "So it is, so it is.
If one wishes to ensure that both mother and child emerge safely, they must follow my teachings. This applies to all pregnant women."
One must not eat dog meat, eels, birds, sparrows, snails, or similar creatures;

rather, one should strictly observe the precepts and fast in advance, prostrating three to five times before the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra* or five to seven fascicles of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, repenting for sins, resolving grievances, and praying for blessings and the preservation of life.
Furthermore, by performing various virtuous deeds such as purchasing living beings to set them free, one will surely ensure that both mother and child survive.

This completely eliminates calamities and prolongs life; if one does not do so, it will be difficult to remedy later regrets. He asked again: "What of those in the world who drown their children? He replied:
"Fools lack clarity in their rational nature and thus commit this karmic act of killing.

Furthermore, regarding the birth of human beings, whether they are wealthy or poor, long-lived or short-lived, is all predetermined by past karma. Why inflict such suffering upon your children by drowning them in a basin of blood?"
How tragic! Alas, how could it be that one dies prematurely without any grievance or fault?

If one intentionally causes another to drown, they will certainly suffer retribution. O virtuous ones, if you do not reform and renew yourselves, yet instead propagate the theory of murder, do not speak of the Buddha-dharma;
for even within the secular laws of crime, such an act is not tolerated.
A Text on Celebrating Birth by Repaying One's Origins and Refraining from Killing Question:
When people encounter their birthday, they speak only of "celebrating birth" while slaughtering a vast number of living beings.

They solemnly arrange music, song, wine, and ritual offerings, inviting neighbors and friends to drink to their hearts' content and revel in joy for several days. How can this be justified? Answer: These are but ignorant folk.
Such is their view; however, the wise are not thus. If one wishes to celebrate life and prolong it, one must cherish life and practice the release of living beings.
There is no way to celebrate life through killing. One should realize that one’s own birthday is the mother’s day of hardship;
rather than contemplating how to repay the kindness of one’s parents, one instead commits sins and seeks pleasure. One ought to reflect upon how one’s compassionate mother carried one for ten months.
Carrying [the child] for three years while nursing, she endured countless hardships and bore much anxiety and toil;
yet when the time came for birth, her life was as fragile as a candle in the wind, and she fainted on the ground, only reviving after a long time.
At that moment, the mother disregarded her own person and asked only whether the newborn child was a boy or a girl, whether it was complete, and whether its physical marks were fully endowed.
Only when she has attained full maturity does her mind find peace. If there is someone in the household who can manage the work, they seek out a wet nurse to raise her;
if the family lacks the means, the mother herself calls for her to nurse her. She feeds her sweet milk and embraces her with affection as if she were a precious pearl.

Even when the child’s body is soiled by impurities, she feels no aversion. When cold or heat oppresses her, she washes and cleanses her herself. Pushing the child toward dryness and warmth, she swallows bitterness while spitting out sweetness, nurturing her until she reaches adulthood.

When one reaches adulthood, it is truly as the saying goes: "Alas, alas, my parents! Their toil in giving birth to me was great; I wish to repay their profound kindness, yet the vast heavens are boundless.
Therefore, the *Tàigù jīng* (*Sūtra on the Bones of the Womb*) states: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, within this Great Trichiliocosm, what thing is the greatest?
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this through skillful means. The Buddha said, "Among the myriad dharmas of the world, nothing surpasses..."
The toil and labor of parents is of great kindness, O virtuous ones. Viewed from this perspective, even grinding one's bones and crushing one's body would not suffice as a repayment.
Have you not heard the Verses on Encouraging Filial Piety by Maitreya? They say: "In the hall above dwell two Buddhas; alas, the people of the world do not recognize them.
It is not with gold and colors that they are adorned, nor are they carved from sandalwood. One need only look at one's present father and mother."
If Śākyamuni and Maitreya can attain [liberation] through making offerings, what need is there for others to perform separate meritorious deeds? Alas! Even the Great Sages speak these words;
how much more so for ordinary people? As a person, if one does not repay the kindness of one’s parents, one is no better than birds and beasts.

We have never heard it said that sheep cannot kneel to suckle their mothers, nor that crows cannot return to feed them—how could such things be false? Someone said: "The Master’s words are indeed urgent."

"If one dares not obey, how can one practice so as to be called 'repaying their kindness'? He replied, "When a person's birthday arrives, they must first observe fasting and purification, solemnly preparing the ritual site;
they may either make offerings to the Buddha and feed the Sangha, recite sutras and chant the Buddha’s name, perform sincere repentance rituals, or purchase lives and release animals.
If one can truly act in this way, it is called repaying the kindness of one's parents."

The living shall enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years, and the deceased shall transcend to the Buddha-land; this not only benefits one's parents but also increases one's own field of merit.
If one does not act thus, it constitutes a great transgression.

A Text for Granting Vows and Securing Protection by Refraining from Killing Some say that among the people of the world, those who make vows involving the killing of living beings are not limited to one kind; I shall briefly cite several types to present them here:

some do so because of official litigation, some because of the suffering of illness, some to avert the calamities of water or fire, some to seek fame and profit, and some for the purpose of pacification.
"Some protect households, some protect roads, some bring peace to local districts, and some pray for the five grains.
Some perform the sacrifice first and then seek security; others perform the sacrifice later and offer their vows of gratitude. What do you think of this?
He replied, "Your first statement makes me choke with emotion, unable to speak. [The other] said, "Even so, I humbly beg for your enlightenment. [He] said, "Did I not say before?"

That people encounter calamities and suffer through years of famine is entirely the result of the karmic retribution for the act of killing. Why is this so? Among the ten non-virtuous actions, the karma of killing is the most grave.
As the *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "Building a monastery is not as meritorious as saving a single life. Thus, there is a popular proverb that says:
"Saving one person's life is superior to building a seven-story pagoda"—this is precisely that meaning. It is essential to understand this.
One knows that while the forms of humans and animals differ, their destiny regarding life is the same. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"All who cherish their bodies and lives fear nothing more than blades and staves; one may take oneself as a metaphor for this. Do not kill, do not wield the staff.

Although there is a distinction between birds and beasts, they all preserve their lives and fear death. If humans cannot endure even the slightest pain or itch, how much less could they bear such [violence]?"
To think that one can cause others to suffer while remaining safe and secure oneself—such a thing is impossible.

As the masters of old said: "If one harms or kills by mistake, one still receives the karmic retribution; how much more so for intentional acts? How could one possibly escape the traces of such karma? Alas!

If you wish to ensure your own security and fulfill your vows, you must practice all manner of good deeds: whether it be making offerings to the Buddha and providing meals for the Sangha, printing sutras, or creating images. Or...

Whether it be ransoming life by releasing captured animals, aiding the poor and relieving suffering, reciting sutras and performing repentance rituals, confessing transgressions and resolving grievances, repairing bridges and paving roads, or universally distributing tea and food—if one can truly practice in such ways, one will surely obtain the fulfillment of one's wishes according to one's heart. Alas!
Those who today desire to achieve their own aspirations—why do they not observe the deeds of the ancients? As for matters such as these...
Lord Gong’s administration of justice flourished so greatly that his family came to possess the "Gate of Four Horses"; the Dou clan saved lives and subsequently broke five stumps of cassia;

the ants were rewarded with the status of a provincial examination winner; the geese were protected and the cause of a Bodhisattva was attained; Yang Sheng rescued sparrows and was repaid with a jade ring;
Kongzi released a tortoise and was compensated with a golden seal—this is precisely what is meant by practicing compassion without seeking karmic retribution.
The retribution for this is that one will never forget [the debt], attaining enduring wealth and nobility with flourishing descendants;
furthermore, Master Sun redeemed a snake by disrobing and obtained from the Water Bureau the method for reviving the living, thereby ascending to the ranks of the immortals;

and Chan Master Shou saved lives by stealing from the treasury, becoming a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the Zen school who realized the Bodhi of the Buddhas. Alas! The people of the world do not know to refrain from killing.
To practice the release of living beings while instead creating perverse and artificial acts is truly lamentable.
A Text on Saving from Calamity through Sacrificial Flattery and Abstinence from Killing.
Someone said: "In this world, those afflicted by illness see that taking medicine is ineffective; they then proceed to kill pigs, sheep, and other domestic animals to perform sacrificial flattery."

When spirits and ghosts sought peace, how did he respond? He said: "It is like adding frost to snow, or adding bitterness to suffering. One does not understand the law of cause and effect. The *Sūtra on Cause and Effect* says:
'Those who suffer short lifespans and many illnesses in this life all come from the karma of killing.

Why do you not repent your past transgressions? Instead, you increase your future offenses. To kill another to save your own life—wherein lies the peace of the human heart? It only brings further suffering to others."
"To preserve my life is a matter of Heaven’s principle that cannot be questioned; yet there are also those who cure their illnesses by killing living beings to offer in sacrifice.
Why is this? The answer is: "When one's life is destined not to end and the illness is cured, it is not because of the killing of living beings that the illness is cured.
Why? If killing a life could save a life, then the kings, lords, generals, ministers, and the wealthy and noble people of the world should all attain eternal life."

Furthermore, why is it that some have many illnesses and meet with premature death? It is simply because one who knows their destiny and finds joy in Heaven naturally remains free from calamity and suffers little illness.
Even if misfortune should befall them, it is entirely the result of karma from past lives. As the *Analects* says: "Life and death are determined by destiny;
wealth and honor depend on Heaven. And again: "To sacrifice to spirits that are not one's own is flattery. When the Master was ill, Zilu...
I pray that you, my son, have long been in this state of prayer. Alas! If one can act in accordance with the deeds of Confucius, what need is there to flatter and sacrifice to false deities?
If one does not do so, it will instead diminish one's lifespan. Have you not seen what the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* says?

"The people of the world do not know how to practice goodness or accumulate merit; instead, they place their faith in teachers of demons, external paths, and malevolent spirits, who falsely proclaim calamity and fortune. Thus it is said.

Giving rise to fearful and agitated thoughts, they fail to rectify themselves; seeking out calamity through ten questions, they kill various sentient beings, offer sacrifices to the spirits, summon all manner of *piśācas*, and pray for blessings and protection, hoping to extend their years, yet in the end they cannot achieve it.

Foolish and deluded, they believe in heterodox and inverted views, which ultimately causes them to die an untimely death and enter hell from which there is no time of escape—this is precisely what is meant by "seeking [misfortune]."
To attain honor only to return to disgrace is not the conduct of a gentleman. Someone asked: "If one does not provide protection and salvation within the mind, how can there be peace?
I replied: "The requirement for protection and salvation does not lie in the mere sparing of life;

it necessitates the entire family observing the *zhāijì* (fasting and abstinence), purifying the kitchen and the altar, or reporting to the Dipper (*dǒu*) and appeasing the stars, or reciting sutras and performing repentance rituals, or purchasing lives and releasing captive creatures, or painting images of the Buddha."
The Buddhas and Patriarchs permit such conduct as this. Why is this? Because by performing good deeds, one will transcend birth into the wholesome realms at the end of life.
Not only does the deceased attain rebirth in higher states, but those who remain alive also obtain merit.
If you do not believe this, I can do nothing for you. It is all over.
A Text on Benefiting the Deceased by Prohibiting Killing Question:

"I often observe that when people die, they do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. Instead, they perform funeral rites by slaughtering living beings to prepare wine and entertain guests during the departure of the corpse.
What do you think of this? Answer: "The words of the benevolent one are most excellent. I, too, am unable to save them."

[The questioner] asked: "What does this mean? [The teacher] replied: "Those who are greedy for food, wine, and meat are many; even the Buddhas cannot save others, much less me alone. [The questioner] said: "That is so.
Even if it is thus, there are still those who believe and practice it. [The teacher] said: "Excellent, excellent! Have you not seen what the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* says?
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, I observe the multitudes of Jambudvīpa...'"
In this life, every lifting of a foot or stirring of a thought is nothing but sin; even if one cultivates wholesome deeds, there is much regression from the initial resolve.

If one encounters adverse conditions, these [defilements] increase with every thought-moment; failing to meet a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who exhorts and transforms one to practice cultivation, one undergoes suffering in succession without end.
Furthermore, when the parents or kinsmen of others have passed away, one should establish merit for them to support their journey on the next path, perhaps by hoisting banners.
Whether by lighting oil lamps, reciting the honored scriptures, making offerings to Buddha images, or even chanting the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, these acts reach the ears of the deceased;
thus, even if they have committed sinful karma, it may be eliminated.

Furthermore, by practicing the fast and chanting the Buddha's name within the seven seven-day periods following the death, one can cause the deceased to transcend to a higher realm and enable those still living to obtain [merit].

For this reason, I now address the Buddha, the World-Honored One, along with the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, humans, and others, and exhort the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa:
on the day of their final passing, they must carefully refrain from killing or performing sacrifices to ghosts and spirits. Why is this?

Such acts possess not even a hair’s breadth of power to benefit the deceased; instead, they merely create conditions for transgression, causing their karmic burden to increase and deepen further. Even if the deceased were present...
Those who have cultivated wholesome deeds and ought to attain transcendence may, upon encountering evil conditions from their former associates, instead fall into the evil realms;

how much more so for those who have not practiced virtue, who can possibly escape suffering? It is like a person coming from a distant land who has gone three days without food, yet the burden they carry exceeds a hundred pounds;
suddenly meeting a neighbor who adds a small amount of goods, they become even more exhausted and weighed down. Thus it is said.
When these words were spoken, there was an elder in the assembly named Mahāpratibhāna who, with palms joined in reverence, addressed Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, saying:

"Great Being, when the lives of beings in Jambudvīpa have ended, do their small and large retinues—by performing meritorious deeds and even by establishing vegetarian feasts—enable that deceased person to attain liberation? Kṣitigarbha replied: "Elder..."
I now, for the sake of all sentient beings of the future and the present, relying on the Buddha’s majestic power, have briefly explained this matter.

If you ask again now, the benefit will be even greater: when a person’s life comes to an end, if they hear the name of a single Buddha, the name of a single Bodhisattva, or even a single verse or a single phrase from a sutra—regardless of whether they have committed offenses or not—they shall all attain liberation.
Although one may attain liberation, it constitutes but one-seventh of the whole; the remaining six-sevenths of merit are received by those born [into this world].
I exhort all you virtuous men and women: having heard this, cultivate yourselves diligently.

If you have already attained these portions for yourself, then when performing rites for the deceased, you should use pure offerings of incense and food, and pay reverent homage with earnest sincerity. If you do not act in this way, there will be little benefit for either the living or the dead.

At that time, the elder rejoiced, joined his palms, and withdrew. Alas! The compassionate skillful means of the former sages were intended solely so that future generations would believe and practice them;
if future generations do not believe or practice, they will bring shame upon the bequeathed instructions of the former sages. Oh, for the people of the world!
To be reverent in the face of death and to honor the distant ancestors lies precisely at this moment; one must not fail to be cautious.
Text for Preparing Merit in Advance for the Salvation of the Deceased and the Prohibition of Killing (81) Someone said:
"Those who prepare merit in advance in this world are quite numerous, and those who resolve to observe the fasts are not uniform.
Some observe them for three years; some for one year; some for the first, fifth, and ninth months; some for the first, seventh, and tenth months; or some observe [them for shorter periods]."
Regarding those who observe the ten fast days on the Buddha’s birthday, or the six fast days, or the first and fifteenth days and the eighth, thirteenth, and eighteenth days:
before these periods of fasting, many people kill living beings and purchase meat to maintain their vegetarian vows;

yet when the specific month, year, day, and hour have not yet passed, they immediately kill or purchase meat, thereby breaking their fasts. How is this to be judged? The answer is: while the initial resolve is indeed firm...

It may seem beautiful on the surface, but it is because the rational nature is not clarified that one fails to understand that those who observe the fast do so precisely for the purpose of refraining from killing.
Why is this? Before blessings have been cultivated, sins are already committed; before goodness has been perfected, evil is already imposed.

To act with such disorder and recklessness—how can this be called a fast? Do not speak of there being no merit; rather, one fears there will be sin. If one is willing to maintain a single-minded resolve for long...
If you maintain the fast and recite the Buddha’s name with determination, you will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land; if you do not do so, you will continue to revolve in saṃsāra as before.

Consequently, in future lives, there will be both sin and merit, and both suffering and joy. Why is this? The times when one undergoes suffering and affliction are the retribution for killing and committing transgressions;
the times when one receives blessings and joy are the retribution for maintaining the fast and accumulating goodness. My son, if you do not...
"Believe my words; there are four types of people currently existing that can be verified in this life:
those with both merit and longevity, those with merit but no longevity, those with no merit but longevity, and those with neither merit nor longevity.

Someone asked, "I beg the Master to clarify these four aforementioned doubts. He replied, "Those who have merit and longevity in this life did so because they practiced giving and observed the fasts in their previous lives."
Regarding the precepts: there are those who possess merit but lack longevity, such as those who practice giving yet do not refrain from killing;

those who possess longevity but lack merit, such as those who strictly observe the fasts yet do not renounce wealth; and those who possess neither merit nor longevity, being both stingy and greedy while also taking life.

Someone may say: "Although these doubts have been resolved, let me ask about one further point: among those in the world who cultivate meritorious deeds for the prolongation of life, or who perform rites for the salvation [of others]..."
Regarding those who perform Buddhist rites for the deceased, there are many who, before the merit-making has even begun, insist on having others provide assistance;

they first slaughter living beings to prepare wine to await the assembly, and later, when the merit-making is not yet finished, they falsely claim to be "closing the hall" to enshrine the spirit, using the slaughtered meat and wine to open the banquet.
How can this be justified? He replied: "These foolish people are pitiable and tragic. For example:"
If someone whose body is stained with blood were to wash it with more blood, could they ever become pure? Such people do not understand the law of cause and effect;

instead, they increase their karmic suffering through the transgressions of life and death. Thus, Hanshan and Shide said: "Yesterday you prepared a vegetarian feast, yet this morning you slaughter livestock.
One time you build a heaven, a hundred times you build a hell. Alas! The merit of observing the fast has not yet been fulfilled."
If one partakes [of meat], the sin of killing is already complete in its hundredfold measure. How could such a person obtain benefit?

Their existence will not transcend the realm of the dead, nor will their life be at peace in the world of the living. If one cultivates meritorious fruits, even wine should not be drunk; how much less so the breaking of precepts by killing living beings and eating their flesh?
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states regarding cause and effect: During the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, there was a commoner in Huaiyin who suffered a bereavement.
The woman, grieving over the Cold Food Festival, lamented that she had nothing with which to make offerings for her mother.
She cut off her hair and sold it for six hundred coins, intending to invite a monk to perform Buddhist rites. Suddenly, five monks passed by her door;

she welcomed them in, but they deferred to one another for some time until one finally consented. He then went to neighboring houses and obtained a copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, which he read aloud.

Having finished his recitation, he turned over the merit for the deceased and departed for his meal. On the street, he happened to encounter four monks who invited him to a wine shop where they took their seats.
Suddenly, he heard a voice from outside the window calling out, "Monk who recites the sutras, do not drink wine! When the monk asked who it was, there came a sobbing reply:
"I am the daughter of the family who commissioned this scripture; I have been lingering in the dark realms for a long time, but now I have received the benefit of your master’s recitation."
"Only through the merit of the Sūtra can one be liberated from sin and transcend rebirth. If you drink wine and break your fast, it will cause me to sink back into the depths as before.

Having spoken these words, he vanished; the monk withdrew in shame. Subsequently, those five monks fully observed the precepts and fasts, recited the Buddha’s name, and practiced Chan meditation, all attaining the realization of Bodhi and becoming eyes for the world and its devas. Alas! One ghost saved five monks—truly extraordinary!
This is what is meant. Since cause and effect are thus clearly manifest, how can one drink alcohol or eat meat?
If one does not maintain the purity and rigor of fasting and precepts, even spiritual merit and fruitfulness will be of no benefit.
*The Text on Releasing Living Creatures with a Compassionate Heart*, 82.
Someone asked, "Is observing the fast and abstaining from meat superior to releasing living beings? How is this?
He replied, "One who merely abstains from meat can only sever the conditions for killing and avoid personal transgression, yet lacks the merit of benefiting other beings.
The reason the Buddha taught people to observe the fast was precisely to increase their heart of compassion. Those who observe the fast today, though they themselves do not..."

To eat meat and yet refuse to release living beings is to be called a person devoid of compassion. The Buddhas of the ten directions regard all sentient beings with pity as if they were their own children;

seeing someone killing these "children" of the Buddha, though one has the power to save them, to sit by and watch without offering rescue—even if one does not eat the flesh—is to be called a great violation of the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts.
The *Śīla-sūtra* contains three kinds of pure precepts that encompass the Vinaya.

The precept of ritual and morality (*śīla-śīla*) entails that no evil remains unsevered, which is "to refrain from all evil deeds. The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) entails that no good is not accumulated, which is "to practice all wholesome deeds.
The precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) entails that no living being is not delivered, which is "to universally save all sentient beings.
If one cannot release life and rescue sentient beings from suffering, it is called a great violation of the precepts. Alas!

Throughout one's entire life, abstaining from meat may lack the merit of saving beings or relieving suffering; yet, in a single instance of relinquishing wealth, one possesses the virtue of redeeming lives and releasing creatures.

If even our Buddha once cut flesh from his own body to save a dove, how can those who claim to be his disciples bear the face to see him if they cannot relinquish illusory wealth to redeem lives? [Question: Is it not certainly true that releasing life...
Question: Why does compassion not release chickens, geese, pigs, ducks, oxen, sheep, and so forth, while instead releasing creatures such as eels, fish, and snails?
Answer: There are two kinds of animals in the world. The first are those who have received the karmic fruit of certain death, such as chickens, geese, oxen, and sheep;
this is because in their previous lives they certainly did not believe in cause and effect and took pleasure in [killing].
Because they committed killing with a resolute mind and lacked any intention of repentance, they now undergo the fixed fruit of being killed as animals;
having no way to escape, they await the cauldron. Even if they encounter someone who releases living beings, that person cannot save them.

Second, there are those who undergo the unfixed fruit of being killed, such as birds and fish; this is because although they committed evil karma in their previous lives, it may have been intermittent.
If one has no choice but to kill and subsequently feels remorse, one will receive the indeterminate fruit of being killed as an animal in this present life:
if one encounters a cruel killer, one will surely be slaughtered for cooking; yet if one encounters a compassionate person, one may even be spared at the moment of death.
Now there is a class of people with false views who, unable to release living beings themselves, instead obstruct others from releasing them.

Those who cannot sever their own killing yet instead exhort others to kill—such as these individuals will first enter hell to undergo immeasurable suffering, and later fall among the animals to undergo certain slaughter;
even if they encounter one of compassion, they cannot be saved. Question:
If one wishes to practice the release of living beings (*fangsheng*), it requires wealth and power. If one lacks such resources, what should be done? Answer: Wealth and nobility.

The hearts and customs of the people are most susceptible to transformation through spiritual cultivation; if one can widely promote Buddhism and vigorously revitalize the wind of compassion, one can truly change social mores and transform customs.

We hear that Yan Lu-gong established *fangsheng chi* (pools for releasing living beings) in every prefecture he governed, and that Zhang Wu-jin, while serving as a high-ranking official, demolished licentious shrines, prohibited the slaughter of life, and bestowed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. These were all acts of Bodhi...
In the practice of a bodhisattva, if one lacks wealth and power, one should extensively expound the Buddha’s words to exhort and transform others;
upon seeing those who release living beings, one should rejoice and praise them, constantly making great vows: "May my wealth and power be sufficient so that I may widely employ skillful means;
may I be like Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in rescuing sentient beings from suffering; may I be like Samantabhadra Bodhisattva in accord with all."
The Vow of Infinite Life for Sentient Beings and the Sentient Realm: A Text for Universally Exhorting Against Killing and Resolving Doubts.
Part Eighty-Three. A Flesh-Body Bodhisattva of the Present Age who is able to practice and maintain this accordingly.
Someone said, "I have heard the Master’s words that for all matters such as capping ceremonies, weddings, funerals, and ancestral sacrifices, one must not kill living beings.

He replied, "That is so. But what shall we do when the people of the world do not believe this? The Master answered, "It all depends on one's own fundamental mind. Since others act for themselves, they must experience the consequences themselves.
Furthermore, a Buddha can only deliver those with whom he has a karmic affinity, not those without such affinity; a Buddha can deliver those who have faith, but not those who lack it."

To be able to deliver those who lack faith: why is this so? One cannot lead another by taking their hand and pulling them along; it only corresponds to the truth when one causes the person to consent of their own accord.
As the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Buddha’s Final Teachings) says: "The Buddha is like a skilled physician who diagnoses the illness and prescribes the medicine;

whether the patient takes it or not is not the fault of the physician. Again, he is like a guide who leads people onto the good path; that they hear it and yet do not act upon it is not the fault of the guide."
"If even the Buddha was thus, how much more so am I? As the former masters said: "The gates of heaven and hell stand opposite one another;

it is up to you which path to take. Truly, these words are true. Someone might say: "According to your teacher’s teaching, the six realms and the three miserable paths of rebirth truly exist, where beings transmigrate and suffer. [The Master] replied:
"If the six realms of transmigration and the three miserable paths and eight difficulties did not exist, then I, this old monk, would also [not exist]."

Because you were unwilling to observe the fasts and precepts, abstain from wine and meat, practice meditation with arduous diligence, and earnestly recite the Buddha’s name, you have consequently endured the sufferings of saṃsāra.

Now that you are finally willing to recite the Buddha’s name and practice cultivation, you vow to abandon this Sahā world and aspire to be born in the Pure Land. I tell you this directly, O worthy one:
look at those in this world—who does not love sensual desire? Who does not enjoy wine and meat? Who does not crave fame and profit?

The Three Doubts at the Hour of Death:

The Ninth and Fourth [Chapter], "Instructions on the Ten Gates of Pure Land," by the Patriarch Cizhao, states: For a practitioner of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), three doubts must not arise at the time of death if one is to be reborn in the Pure Land.
The first is the doubt: "I have committed extremely heavy karma since birth, while my practice has been shallow for only a few days; I fear I shall not attain rebirth."

Second, one may harbor doubts such as: "I owe debts to others," or "I have unfulfilled aspirations," or "My greed, anger, and ignorance have not yet ceased, and I fear I shall not attain birth [in the Pure Land].
Third, one may doubt: "Although I am mindful of Amitābha, I fear that when my life ends, the Buddha will not come to welcome me.
Because these three doubts create obstacles, one loses right mindfulness and fails to attain rebirth; therefore, one must practice mindfulness.
Buddhas are the most essential and vital truth; one must faithfully believe in the clear intent of the Buddhist sutras and not give rise to doubt. The *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* states:

Wind and moon fill my breast with boundless joy; I sing a song in harmony with the "Spring Radiance.

Without needing extra oil, its light is brilliant and radiant; The worlds of the ten directions are all made bright.
Living in the mountains, every day is a fine morning; Coarse grain fills the belly with a single ladle of water.

Living in the mountains is indeed a life of bitter austerity; I overturn the meditation seat, too lazy to exert effort.
The sage’s realization and the commoner’s delusions are both unestablished; A single bright moon shines upon the void.
Dwelling in the mountains, the gate closed, the bamboo grove is secluded; Clouds drift on their own and the waters flow by themselves.
Guarding my integrity, living in poverty, passing my days as circumstances allow; When someone questions me, I simply lower my head.

Gathering body and mind to return to one’s native village, One avoids being splashed by water or dragged through mud.

Dwelling in the mountains, there is but the singular fragrance of radish roots;

If you ask me what is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West— Three times three before, and three times three after.
Dwelling in the mountains, I always keep the main gate open; The Great Way stands ready as guests arrive.
If one can pass the personal examination of this old monk, Every person may become a pillar and beam of the world.
To dwell in the mountains and seek true nature, First read the "Opening the Ignorant" and the "Great Person."
When reading to the point where the essential barrier is known, the entire body manifests throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Dwelling deep in the mountains, hidden within the embrace of white clouds (Wei-yin), the wind enters the pine forest and shakes forth the Dharma-thunder, startling the drowsy sleepers of the world.
Quickly open your two eyes; do not hesitate!
The mountain dwelling is high and receives the light before others; looking straight down, one’s eye opens at once.
Having realized the perfect and sudden meaning of the One Vehicle, what need is there to labor further visiting Mount Tiantai?
Smoke and mists rise on all four sides of the hermitage; atop the stone cauldron [stone peak], incense burns as the *Lotus Sūtra* is recited.
The three realms offer no peace, like a burning house; This old monk forever drives the white ox-cart.
Amidst mountain dwellings, at midnight, the cuckoo cries; Before the cliffs, the cascades pour down like a torrent.
Those who have not yet arrived are all startled by the mountain’s steepness; Only those who have come before know the heights and depths of the path.
Dwelling in the mountains, cease deceiving your own mind; Only then will you realize that the field of vision atop a high peak is vast.
Let it go, and the great trichiliocosm cannot contain it; Draw it back, and it resides within a single hair-tip.
A man of knowledge dwelling in the mountains is beyond ordinary peers; Like a bright mirror set upon its stand, he discerns and examines all people.
The mirror of original nature reveals both the beautiful and the ugly, leaving nothing hidden; it is utterly beyond intimacy or estrangement.
Dwelling amidst steep cliffs, it is starkly cold; who would dare look upon this precious sword as it stands before the hall?
Heretics and malevolent spirits have their brains split asunder, while the old monk remains in samādhi, perfectly at ease.
Living in the mountains is a distinct style; its flavor differs from that of the human world.
The wooden horse gallops and neighs (pronounced *xī*) beyond the heavens; Vast and silent, there is no news and no trace of its path.
The mountain roads are perilous and communication is difficult; How could a blind fellow ever penetrate this principle?
Only allow the master to employ his skillful means; when meeting, all is found in silence.
When a mountain-dweller arrives to inquire about the Zen school, one only then realizes that all previous efforts were misapplied.
Once the mouth opens, the origins are already known; alas, they do not recognize the realization of true emptiness.
Dwelling in the mountains, I have realized the one true emptiness; What need is there to ask about the Southern or Northern Schools?
Holding the wish-fulfilling jewel in my hand, Where would its radiance not be perfectly pervasive?
For one dwelling in the mountains, studying the Way is not difficult (rhyming with *jiān*); Only settling the mind and guarding the Way is truly hard.
Take another step forward from the top of the hundred-foot pole; With a single blow, shatter the ancestral barriers and mountains.
Turning one's head back from mountain dwelling, sigh for the return home; Having realized that all is originally but emptiness.
Do not go wandering from door to door begging for food; The bright pearl is already within your own clothes.
Dwelling in the mountains, pure and austere, without luxury; When guests arrive, mugwort broth serves as a sufficient tea set.
The tongue and palate know its fine flavor; With one’s whole being free and easy, one returns home early.
Dwelling in the mountains, always hidden amidst the white clouds; The Way is within, and the mind is naturally at ease.
The public case is manifest before people, yet they do not recognize it; They vainly chase after branches and leaves outside.
In the mountain dwelling, yellow leaves flutter with the wind; Holding an empty fist in one’s hand, there is still nothing lacking.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs transmit only the affairs of the family; When meeting people, they are too weary to trouble their mouths with idle chatter.
When leaves fall in the mountain retreat, they all return to their roots; The true and eternal alone is revealed, manifesting the Dharmakāya.
If this matter is not understood, much effort is wasted; A hundred cities of misty waters stretch out boundlessly (rhyme with *yin*).
What ability does a practitioner dwelling in the mountains possess? Every dharma fully manifests the Most Supreme Vehicle.
A flash of an eye and a lift of the brows are all the Patriarch’s intent; Raising the mallet and holding up the whisk are likewise his true feelings.
Dwelling in the mountains, one covers the roof with nothing but thatched reeds; In this cool, sparse, and empty state, one severs worldly ties.
A single sheet of white clouds spans the valley mouth; How many returning birds lose their way to their nests?
Dwelling in the mountains, I never grow weary of the mountain life; I have cleared the brush from beneath a tree to bind together a half-room hut.
Even for a single old monk it is still cramped; How could it allow worldly guests to reach the Zen gate?
Dwelling in the mountains, having seen the Way, I have forgotten the mountains; The myriad dharmas have been fundamentally at ease from the start.
North, south, east, and west are entirely indistinguishable; This body dwells eternally in silent, vast emptiness.
Dwelling in the mountains, my eyes meet nothing but green peaks; Steep, layered, and rugged, the path is difficult to traverse.
When one reaches the point where the water ends and the mountains cease, One naturally arrives at that which is not empty and returns.
Dwelling in the mountains is also a hardship in this Sahā world; A hundred years of time pass in a single kṣaṇa.
Exhausting this retributive body, may I be born in Sukhāvatī; The perilous paths ahead will then be few.
Dwelling alone in the mountains, I delight in the natural truth; With bright moon and clear breeze, I turn the Dharma wheel.
The entire great treasury of the scriptures has been fully expounded; Who among us knows who truly dwells within this realm?

*Hundred Odes on Dwelling in the Mountains* (Concluded) In the stillness of mountain dwelling, I have realized true emptiness; I universally exhort all people to cultivate the merits of the Pure Land.
Having personally received the topknot jewel, the hermit of Yunlin follows from afar.
